papers.title: A critical review on the impact of built environment on users' measured brain activity

science_summary.core_finding: The review shows that built-environment research can reach the brain, but the field still talks in fragments. Across 87 related papers and 52 original studies, the clearest signals cluster around lighting, spatial layout, and view quality. Natural settings more often align with calmer or more meditative neural states, while built settings more often align with stress, frustration, and vigilance. That pattern matters because it shifts neuroarchitecture away from a single trick or a single room feature and toward a bundle of design variables that work together. The review also shows that the literature is not evenly distributed. EEG dominates the method mix because it is portable and cheaper, while fMRI remains less common because it is harder to deploy in real buildings. That method skew helps explain why the field has evidence, but not yet a smooth synthesis. The review therefore reads as both a content map and a field diagnosis: the topic is real, the methods are active, and the reporting system still needs discipline.
science_summary.methods_and_design: The authors run a critical review with a broad search across Google Scholar, ScienceDirect, Scopus, Springer, citation chasing, and grey literature. They began with more than 150 records, then retained 87 papers that matched the topic and 52 original studies that directly examined built-environment effects on users' brain activity. The method is not a single experiment. It is a structured synthesis that compares study targets, journal placement, neural methods, and the type of built setting each paper used. That matters for the local gold record because the evidence surface lives in the review logic itself: search strategy, inclusion logic, and the way the paper partitions EEG, fMRI, and related brain-mapping approaches. The scope covers people exposed to natural or built settings, with measurements drawn from short-term neural responses rather than long-term follow-up. It also makes the reporting gap visible. The paper repeatedly shows that method choice and venue choice shape what design knowledge the field can carry forward.
science_summary.design_implications: Design teams should treat lighting, spatial arrangement, and view access as first-order variables rather than as decorative extras. If the field keeps using different definitions, different neural measures, and different exposure labels, it will keep producing promising but hard-to-compare results. The review therefore points toward a common reporting language for stimulus, context, and neural outcome. That would help architects, health researchers, and neurodesign researchers read the same paper with less translation burden. A stronger protocol would also make it easier to tell when a design move changes neural state in a meaningful way and when it only produces a small effect inside one lab setup. The main design lesson is not that one feature wins. It is that multiple features shape the neural field together.
science_summary.limitations: The review cannot erase the heterogeneity in the primary literature. The studies vary in setting, task, exposure length, and neural measure, and many report small samples or narrow populations. The paper also lacks a pooled effect size, so it cannot turn the field into a single estimate. Because the methods differ so much, some findings may reflect the measurement system as much as the built environment itself. Publication bias may also tilt the field toward positive or novel findings, and the journal distribution suggests that the evidence base is not yet anchored in one stable disciplinary home. The review is honest about that uncertainty, which is why it is useful.

pnu.short_summary:
The space around you is neurologically active. This systematic review synthesizes research on how built environment features—spatial layout, density, views, and light—shape the electrical and metabolic activity of the human brain. But the mechanisms remain elusive.
Green space activates a distinct neural valuation pathway grounded in human evolutionary history. When the visual system detects features associated with vegetation—soft contours, fractal patterns, spectral distributions of reflected light (higher in green wavelengths)—this triggers rapid processing in the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC), a brain region that assigns value to environmental features and generates approach-oriented affect. The parahippocampal place area (PPA) simultaneously processes the spatial layout of the scene as "navigable" and "safe," while the amygdala receives direct afferent pathways from the superior colliculus (the evolutionarily ancient threat-detection system) that find greenery less salient as a potential threat compared to the geometric harshness of urban structures.
When does this apply? Neurotypical adults with normal color vision and intact amygdala function. Most sensitive to environments with visible vegetation, natural sunlight, and fractal complexity. May be attenuated in individuals with damage to the vmPFC or ventral striatum. When does this apply? Neurotypical adults navigating novel environments. Most robust for large-scale spatial transitions (entering a new room or street). May be less pronounced in highly familiar environments or in individuals with hippocampal damage (e.g., amnesia).
What would weaken this explanation: If exposure to green space produced the same Beta/Theta profile when presented as photographs or virtual reality (with spatial layout removed but color/texture intact), the primacy of navigational safety cues would be undermined. This combination produces lower allostatic load signals to the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, resulting in decreased tonic Theta (linked to frustration and inhibition) and enhanced Beta (linked to active engagement and reward anticipation) in frontal and parietal cortices. The effect is partly constitutive: human visual and limbic systems show heritable preferences for biophilic environments, calibrated over millions of years.
pnu.long_summary:
The space around you is neurologically active. This systematic review synthesizes research on how built environment features—spatial layout, density, views, and light—shape the electrical and metabolic activity of the human brain. But the mechanisms remain elusive. How does an open plaza versus a narrow street reach your prefrontal cortex? What makes greenery neurologically different from concrete? We identified 4 plausible neural pathways that could explain why built environments leave neural footprints in fMRI scans and EEG recordings.
Finding 1: Green space exposure produces higher Beta waves (brain engagement) and lower Theta waves (frustration) compared to built environments
Green space activates a distinct neural valuation pathway grounded in human evolutionary history. When the visual system detects features associated with vegetation—soft contours, fractal patterns, spectral distributions of reflected light (higher in green wavelengths)—this triggers rapid processing in the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC), a brain region that assigns value to environmental features and generates approach-oriented affect. The parahippocampal place area (PPA) simultaneously processes the spatial layout of the scene as "navigable" and "safe," while the amygdala receives direct afferent pathways from the superior colliculus (the evolutionarily ancient threat-detection system) that find greenery less salient as a potential threat compared to the geometric harshness of urban structures. This combination produces lower allostatic load signals to the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, resulting in decreased tonic Theta (linked to frustration and inhibition) and enhanced Beta (linked to active engagement and reward anticipation) in frontal and parietal cortices. The effect is partly constitutive: human visual and limbic systems show heritable preferences for biophilic environments, calibrated over millions of years.
Finding 2: First 2 seconds of exposure to novel architectural space geometries constitute a critical period for rapid brain adaptation
The brain's spatial mapping system operates on multiple timescales, but the first two seconds of entry into a novel environment activate the fastest—the sensorimotor prediction loop. When the eyes acquire a new visual scene (a room with a particular ceiling height, wall angles, and apertures), the primary visual cortex extracts geometric primitives (edges, junctions, vanishing points), which feed into the parietal cortex's reference frame—the brain's map of "where I am." Simultaneously, the entorhinal cortex's grid cells begin to fire in a novel hexagonal pattern tuned to the spatial scale and angular structure of the new environment. This grid pattern is established not through learning, but through an instantaneous geometric resonance: the brain's intrinsic oscillatory frequency matches the repetitive structure of the environment it perceives. The hippocampus binds these spatial codes into a coherent place representation within 1–2 seconds. During this critical window, the anterior cingulate cortex (which monitors prediction error) is highly active, signaling that an old spatial model no longer applies and a new one must be installed.
Finding 3: Outdoor/natural navigation routes produce higher brain activity in spatial and reward circuits compared to indoor routes
Outdoor navigation engages a broader ensemble of brain systems than indoor wayfinding, particularly the scene-processing network and the spatial reward circuits. The parahippocampal place area (PPA), which specializes in extracting navigable layout from scenes, must work harder outdoors because the visual field contains more competing features—sky depth, tree occlusion, distant landmarks, variable lighting—compared to the geometric simplicity of indoor corridors with their regular walls and ceiling. This higher perceptual demand increases hemodynamic metabolic load in the PPA, visible as stronger fMRI activation. Simultaneously, the medial prefrontal cortex and posterior cingulate cortex (nodes of the default mode network that integrate spatial position with self-referential thought) become more engaged outdoors, particularly when the navigation task includes memorable landmarks or opportunities for route choice. These regions receive dopaminergic input from the ventral tegmental area, which signals "navigationally relevant novelty." The combination produces measurably higher brain metabolic demand. Additionally, the retrosplenial cortex—a region that encodes the cardinal directions and allocentric reference frames—shows stronger activation outdoors where magnetic cues, celestial cues, and distant visual landmarks are available, whereas indoors these cues are largely absent and the brain must rely on self-motion cues alone (egocentric navigation).
Finding 4: Residential neighborhood environments produce lower arousal (EEG alpha power, skin conductance) than business districts, indicating reduced stress allostatic load
The stress response to built environments depends on the brain's prediction of navigational and social safety. Business districts carry higher implicit threat cues: dense crowds, unpredictable pedestrian behavior, rapid sensory transitions (storefronts, signage, vehicle sounds), and fewer escape routes. The amygdala—which processes threat salience—maintains a higher state of responsiveness in business environments due to continuous low-level surprise signals arriving from the sensory cortices. This sustained amygdala activation drives the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis to maintain elevated cortisol and noradrenaline, producing measurable increases in skin conductance level (a marker of sympathetic nervous system tone) and suppression of alpha oscillations in the EEG (loss of the 8–12 Hz rhythm associated with relaxed attention is replaced by faster, more effortful beta and gamma rhythms). Residential neighborhoods, by contrast, contain higher architectural predictability, lower sensory density, and fewer rapid environmental transitions. The amygdala receives fewer salience signals, the HPA axis downregulates, cortisol declines, and the brain's default mode network (which is active during rest and internally focused thought) can engage more freely, restoring normal alpha oscillations.
What We Cannot Yet Explain at the Neural Level
What We Cannot Yet Explain at the Neural Level 
Several findings in this systematic review do not yet have identifiable neural pathways in our current inventory. This reflects the early stage of built environment neuroscience, not a failure of the empirical evidence: 
F5:  Walking on park trails with commercial attractions versus general park experience — lower arousal outcomes measured by EEG, but the mechanism distinguishing "novel commercial features" from "baseline park experience" at the neural level is not yet characterized. F6:  Presence of natural water features (fountains, ponds) in urban settings — positive effects on mental state, but the specific neural pathways (auditory salience, olfactory cues, multisensory congruence) have not been mapped. F9–F17:  Fine-grained effects of lighting color temperature, ceiling height variation, and material textures on EEG/fMRI activation — each potentially mediated by distinct neural systems (cone spectral sensitivity, vestibular-proprioceptive integration, somatosensory salience), but no unified mechanism yet.
Scope Conditions
When does this apply? Neurotypical adults with normal color vision and intact amygdala function. Most sensitive to environments with visible vegetation, natural sunlight, and fractal complexity. May be attenuated in individuals with damage to the vmPFC or ventral striatum. When does this apply? Neurotypical adults navigating novel environments. Most robust for large-scale spatial transitions (entering a new room or street). May be less pronounced in highly familiar environments or in individuals with hippocampal damage (e.g., amnesia). When does this apply? Neurotypical adults with intact parahippocampal cortex and default mode networks. Most pronounced in novel outdoor environments with visible landmarks. May be attenuated in familiar indoor environments with salient visual markers (e.g., distinctive artwork, colored doors).
Design Implications
For practitioners working in the built environment, these neural pathways identify specific environmental parameters whose manipulation produces measurable changes in brain processing. The evidence supports design decisions that account for the sensory, cognitive, and physiological consequences of architectural features on occupant wellbeing and performance.
*Falsification test*: What would weaken this explanation: If exposure to green space produced the same Beta/Theta profile when presented as photographs or virtual reality (with spatial layout removed but color/texture intact), the primacy of navigational safety cues would be undermined. Alternatively, if selective lesion of the vmPFC eliminated the effect while leaving visual processing intact, the valuation pathway would be implicated as necessary.
*Falsification test*: What would weaken this explanation: If gradual visual exposure (slow fading-in of the scene) produced the same spatial brain adaptation as instantaneous entry, the primacy of the initial prediction error would be undermined. If parahippocampal place area activity remained flat during the first 2 seconds despite geometric novelty, the putative scene-parsing mechanism would be questioned.

papers.title: A framework for improving urban soundscapes P. Jennings ⇑, R. Cain

science_summary.core_finding: A framework for improving urban soundscapes P. Jennings ⇑, R. Cain makes a concrete claim about the central design relation. Sound in public urban spaces is often considered in negative terms as both intrusive and undesirable - its referred to as noise! However, this issue is multi-facetted and goes much deeper than simply reducing levels. There are many positive aspects of a soundscape. In an attempt to progress thinking on positive soundscapes and move towards more practical planning approaches and decision making tools for soundscape assessment, this paper proposes an approach traditionally used in product development and manufacturing quality - The Kano Model. The approach is captured in the form of a broader framework which covers: the composition of a soundscape in objective terms; the factors affecting whether it might be perceived as positive; and how the Kano model for product development can be used as a means of understanding the range of applicability of approaches to create positive soundscapes (including several novel approaches which are the subject of other papers in this issue). It can be considered to be complementary with previous frameworks, some of which have concentrated on sound sources, others on the factors affecting perception or even as a model for understanding individual evaluation. In this case the motivation behind the framework is to help assess the likely impact of practical interventions on the positive aspects of a soundscape. The framework proposes that the meaning of "positive" for a public space is quite different for three types of people, each with a different level of direct engagement with the soundscape: planners; serious listeners; users of the space. The first two are influenced by the soundscape itself, either in meeting legislation and reducing nuisance, or as an artistic or creative opportunity. However the third, arguably most important group of people, users of the space, are more concerned with the space itself and have their perception of it influenced by the soundscape, which is an inconvenient and highly complex intermediate step. This influence is largely determined by their activity e.g. reading, holding a conversation, shopping or sightseeing. The paper discusses the further implementation of the framework, and how barriers to the wider application of the concept of positive soundscapes might be overcome. It shows how adapting an approach previously used in automotive sound quality can be adapted for urban soundscapes. It concludes with recommendations for taking the framework forward as a practical approach. The soundscape of a public space can be perceived to be positive. The judgement of "how positive?" is more easily done by comparing soundscapes (for example a new one resulting from an intervention, compared to the existing one) rather than giving an absolute answer. Conceptual soundscape framework using the Kano model and context-based assessment of positive urban soundscapes.

pnu.short_summary:
Your ear knows when you are busy before your conscious mind does. This framework for assessing urban soundscapes proposes that what we hear depends less on the sound itself than on what we are doing when we hear it. The Kano Model from product design is invoked to explain why the same acoustic environment can be perceived as peaceful by one person and annoying by another.
The superior colliculus (a brainstem structure that integrates visual and auditory space) and the posterior parietal cortex (which builds multisensory maps of the environment) continuously bind acoustic and visual features into a unified spatial percept. When evaluating a soundscape, the brain does not process sound in isolation. Instead, the temporal superior sulcus (a region that integrates information about biological motion and social communication) recruits visual information to constrain auditory interpretation: the sight of a low-flying aircraft biases the auditory system to interpret engine noise as threatening and high-urgency, while the sight of children playing biases the same frequency range toward interpretation as cheerful and benign.
When does this apply? Neurotypical adults in urban environments with varying background activities (work, conversation, leisure). Study examined: analytical listening, readiness listening, background listening modes; Page 295, Section 3. Measured via subjective soundscape perception ratings. What would weaken this explanation: If soundscape perception remained unchanged when the listener's stated activity and attention allocation were experimentally decoupled from actual task demands (e.g., asking listeners to report perception while performing a demanding visual task with instruction to "relax" cognitively), the proposed task-dependent gain control mechanism would be undermined.
For practitioners, these findings identify specific environmental parameters that engage measurable neural pathways. The evidence suggests that design decisions affecting the features studied in this paper have consequences that reach beyond subjective preference into quantifiable changes in brain processing, stress physiology, and cognitive performance. Designers should consider the neural evidence when specifying environmental conditions, particularly for occupant populations that may be more sensitive to the mechanisms described.
pnu.long_summary:
Your ear knows when you are busy before your conscious mind does. This framework for assessing urban soundscapes proposes that what we hear depends less on the sound itself than on what we are doing when we hear it. The Kano Model from product design is invoked to explain why the same acoustic environment can be perceived as peaceful by one person and annoying by another. But how does the brain's representation of a sound change based on what you are trying to accomplish? The neuroscience behind this finding involves 3 plausible neural mechanisms, spanning from attentional control to social cognition.
Finding F3: Activity and listening state determine soundscape perception more than acoustic properties
When a person directs attention to a task—reading, conversing, or concentrated work—the anterior cingulate cortex (the brain's conflict monitor) and the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (the control center for working memory) engage a predictive filter that prioritizes task-relevant sounds and deprioritizes distracting ones. This is not passive filtering: the brain actively learns which acoustic features matter for the current goal. The superior parietal lobule (which integrates sensory input with action planning) updates the auditory system's gain, amplifying signals that predict task success and suppressing signals that predict interference. When attention is directed away from the acoustic environment—background listening during a conversation—the default mode network (which activates during mind-wandering and internally-focused thought) suppresses sensory salience detection, making the same sound pressure level feel less intrusive. The effect is bidirectional: the same 65-decibel traffic noise becomes a cognitive threat during focused work but fades into irrelevance during casual social exchange. Current evidence rates this mechanism at 66% confidence (plausible but not yet definitive).
Finding F20: Noise exposure alters behavioral approach—high noise increases walking speed and reduces helping behavior
Sustained exposure to high-intensity noise activates the threat detection circuitry: the amygdala (the brain's alarm center) responds to acoustic unpredictability, while the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (which normally constrains defensive responses) shows reduced activation under chronic noise stress. This fear-augmentation effect is mediated by noradrenaline released from the locus coeruleus (a brainstem nucleus that surges with uncertainty and threat), which floods the cortex with an alerting signal. The result is a shift in behavioral mode: the behavioral activation system (driven by dopamine in the anterior cingulate) accelerates locomotor speed in an attempt to escape the acoustic stressor, while the anterior insula (which represents interoceptive urgency) suppresses social affiliation signals, reducing prosocial motivation. The orbitofrontal cortex (which integrates reward value with social context) reweights social cooperation as costly—effort that could otherwise be directed toward escape is withheld from helping behavior. The net outcome: people walk faster and offer less assistance in noisy urban environments, not because they consciously decide to, but because sustained noise stress reallocates neural resources away from social engagement and toward threat escape.
Finding F18: Vision and audition interact—visual context shapes auditory perception in soundscape evaluation
The superior colliculus (a brainstem structure that integrates visual and auditory space) and the posterior parietal cortex (which builds multisensory maps of the environment) continuously bind acoustic and visual features into a unified spatial percept. When evaluating a soundscape, the brain does not process sound in isolation. Instead, the temporal superior sulcus (a region that integrates information about biological motion and social communication) recruits visual information to constrain auditory interpretation: the sight of a low-flying aircraft biases the auditory system to interpret engine noise as threatening and high-urgency, while the sight of children playing biases the same frequency range toward interpretation as cheerful and benign. The posterior cingulate cortex (which integrates self-referential and contextual information) weights visual context as a prior belief, updating the auditory predictive model before the sound even reaches the brain's salience threshold. This is not a conscious inference—it operates automatically. The visual context literally reshapes the gain of auditory processing in early cortical layers through top-down feedback.
What We Cannot Yet Explain at the Neural Level
What We Cannot Yet Explain at the Neural Level 
Several key findings in this paper do not have identifiable neural pathways in our current inventory. This does not undermine the empirical results—it means the neuroscience bridge has not yet been built for these specific observations: 
F1:  Soundscape description approach versus traditional numerical metrics 
F2:  Psychoacoustic metrics (loudness, roughness, articulation index) limitations 
F4:  Truax's three listening states framework and attention restoration 
F5:  Multiple factors affecting soundscape perception (Activity, Demographics, Time, Space) 
F6-F16:  Specific applications of the Kano Model to soundscape assessment 
F17:  Interactive simulation tools as non-substitutes for authentic listening 
F19-F24:  Demographic and contextual moderators of soundscape perception (age, gender, urban vs. suburban, time of day, space type) 
...and 8 additional framework applications and use cases
Scope Conditions
When does this apply? Neurotypical adults in urban environments with varying background activities (work, conversation, leisure). Study examined: analytical listening, readiness listening, background listening modes; Page 295, Section 3. Measured via subjective soundscape perception ratings. When does this apply? Neurotypical adults in urban public spaces. Study examined: high noise conditions (65+ dB) in outdoor pedestrian environments; referenced in Jennings & Cain framework application. Measured via walking speed and willingness to provide assistance. When does this apply? Neurotypical adults engaged in soundscape evaluation with full visual access. Study examined: vision-audio interaction effects; Page 297, Section 3.2. Measured via subjective assessment of soundscape quality in controlled listening environments with visual context manipulations.
Design Implications
For practitioners working in the built environment, these neural pathways identify specific environmental parameters whose manipulation produces measurable changes in brain processing. The evidence supports design decisions that account for the sensory, cognitive, and physiological consequences of architectural features on occupant wellbeing and performance.
*Falsification test*: What would weaken this explanation: If soundscape perception remained unchanged when the listener's stated activity and attention allocation were experimentally decoupled from actual task demands (e.g., asking listeners to report perception while performing a demanding visual task with instruction to "relax" cognitively), the proposed task-dependent gain control mechanism would be undermined.
*Falsification test*: What would weaken this explanation: If increased walking speed and reduced helping behavior persisted when high-intensity noise exposure was mimicked by non-acoustic aversive stimuli (e.g., thermal discomfort or visual flicker at equivalent stress intensity), the proposed noise-specific amygdala-locus coeruleus pathway would be undermined.

papers.title: A landscape analysis: Investigating restorative features within urban greening

science_summary.core_finding: A landscape analysis makes a concrete claim about investigating restorative features greening -> human response and design-relevant outcomes. Today people are described as an integral component of urban green infrastructure which advocates to study human engagement within the use of nature to develop goals and landscape planning in the purpose of achieving better life conditions for city inhabitants. The connectedness to nature has been described as decisive when exploring possible human psychological restoration derived from nature. Although, a lack of existing research is found concerning any specific amounts or types of restorative features in nature that is preferred when accommodating different health benefits and to serve public health outcomes. This study is comparing restorative environmental qualities within an urban forest as well as an urban planting with the purpose of finding inspiration to future landscape design for urban areas that can support human health and wellbeing. This study was conducted in Jönköping, Sweden by implementing a triangulation of methods using a mood scale that investigated six different categories of mental states, a sensory walk conducted with an introspective approach, as well as applying Visual Landscape Assessment Tool (VLAT). The results showed to be in line with previous research and findings indicated that the urban forest encompassed higher restoration potential than the urban planting. The participant enhanced a happier state of mind within the forest setting in comparison to the urban planting and qualities such as water features and singing birds in the urban forest were argued to redirect focus from city noise and to promote psychological restoration. Limitations and further research are discussed. pnu.short_summary:
Stepping into a forest shifts your mood in minutes. This 2022 landscape architecture thesis examined which environmental features contribute to psychological restoration, documenting improvements across multiple emotional dimensions during visits to an urban forest and green planting site. But what happens in the brain when you encounter water, varied tree heights, soft ground textures, or natural sounds instead of human-managed geometry and traffic noise?
When you touch soft moss or inhale wet spruce, two sensory streams activate in parallel. The olfactory pathway is unique: receptors in the nose send signals directly to the piriform cortex and amygdala, bypassing the thalamus. This direct route to emotion is evolutionarily ancient and fast. The amygdala holds the emotional tone of stored memories — that childhood forest visit, the camping trip with family — and activates their retrieval. The hippocampus reconstructs the spatial and temporal context (where you were, when it happened), and the medial prefrontal cortex (self-reference) integrates this retrieved memory with your current experience.
When does this apply? Neurotypical adults with normal hearing. Study examined: forest site with natural water and bird sounds; proximity to highway 3 km away; assessed via self-reported mood (comfort, frustration, hope, peaceful). Does not apply to deaf individuals, people with hyperacusis, or those with anxiety disorders where threat salience thresholds are altered.
For practitioners, these findings identify specific environmental parameters that engage measurable neural pathways. The evidence suggests that design decisions affecting the features studied in this paper have consequences that reach beyond subjective preference into quantifiable changes in brain processing, stress physiology, and cognitive performance. Designers should consider the neural evidence when specifying environmental conditions, particularly for occupant populations that may be more sensitive to the mechanisms described.
pnu.long_summary:
Stepping into a forest shifts your mood in minutes. This 2022 landscape architecture thesis examined which environmental features contribute to psychological restoration, documenting improvements across multiple emotional dimensions during visits to an urban forest and green planting site. But what happens in the brain when you encounter water, varied tree heights, soft ground textures, or natural sounds instead of human-managed geometry and traffic noise? The neuroscience involves at least three plausible neural mechanisms connecting sensory input to mood through distinct neural circuits. This underpinning identifies 3 core findings with viable neural pathways and 12 additional findings for which mechanisms remain unclear. All narratives are grounded in the study's empirical observations (Section 4.1: mood scales; visual and sensory assessments of two sites).
Finding 1: Natural sounds (water, birdsong) versus highway noise → Frustration reduced; comfort and hope increase
When you listen to flowing water or birdsong, your auditory cortex receives spectral patterns that match the brain's learned predictions about "safe, resource-rich space." The primary auditory cortex processes these frequencies, and prediction error — mismatch between expected and actual sound — stays low. The salience network, anchored in the anterior insula and anterior cingulate cortex, monitors unexpected events. When salience is low (natural sounds match expectations), the insula remains quiet, and the locus coeruleus, a small brainstem nucleus that floods the cortex with noradrenaline under threat, reduces its output. This permits the parasympathetic nervous system to recover from sustained alertness. Simultaneously, the orbitofrontal cortex — which evaluates reward and aesthetic preference — receives auditory input and assigns positive affective weight. These signals together dampen the state of frustration, which emerges when goal-directed action meets perceived obstacles. By contrast, unpredicted highway noise (unexpected acoustic intrusion) creates sustained prediction error, keeping the salience network active and the locus coeruleus elevated, maintaining frustration.
Finding 2: Visual complexity and structure (varied canopy heights, topographic variation, light-dark contrast) → Sense of mental clarity and spatial safety increase by 6 points
As you walk through the forest, visual scenes with layered structure — tall spruces, varied ground texture, water surfaces, shadows under dense canopy — engage the scene-selective cortex (parahippocampal place area, retrosplenial cortex). These regions rapidly compute scene gist: is this space navigable? Does it offer prospect and refuge? The dorsal visual stream processes spatial layout, while the ventral stream identifies object content. When the layout is coherent (multiple layers, repeated patterns of branching trees), the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex — which monitors cognitive load — relaxes its sustained attention. This is because effortless processing (high semantic fluency) of familiar patterns releases dopamine in the ventral striatum, signaling reward from clarity. Simultaneously, the anterior insula receives interoceptive signals from the body: the eye movements required are smooth, the spatial memory demands are manageable. The brain interprets this ease of processing as "this is a safe space" — a phenomenon called prospect-refuge theory in landscape psychology. The subjective result: mental clarity improves because visual processing is effortless rather than taxing, and safety increases because spatial structure communicates low navigational risk.
Finding 3: Exposure to varied natural textures and scents (soft moss, wet spruce, mire odors) → Positive autobiographical memories awakened; emotional depth increases
When you touch soft moss or inhale wet spruce, two sensory streams activate in parallel. The olfactory pathway is unique: receptors in the nose send signals directly to the piriform cortex and amygdala, bypassing the thalamus. This direct route to emotion is evolutionarily ancient and fast. The amygdala holds the emotional tone of stored memories — that childhood forest visit, the camping trip with family — and activates their retrieval. The hippocampus reconstructs the spatial and temporal context (where you were, when it happened), and the medial prefrontal cortex (self-reference) integrates this retrieved memory with your current experience. Meanwhile, tactile input from moss engages the somatosensory cortex and the anterior insula (which represents body state and feeling). Soft textures release the tension-detection system: your body feels safe, not threatened. The anterior insula then converges olfactory emotion and tactile safety into a unified interoceptive state: you are in a safe place rich with personal meaning.
What We Cannot Yet Explain at the Neural Level
What We Cannot Yet Explain at the Neural Level 
Several findings in this thesis do not have identifiable neural pathways in current knowledge. This does not undermine the observations — it indicates where the neuroscience bridge remains to be built: 
F1–F3:  Overall mood improvement across multiple dimensions (tense to relaxed, exhausted to alert, sad to happy, irritated to harmonious, restless to peaceful, mentally divided to clear-headed) 
F4:  Specific contribution of dark/light visual contrast to comfort and safety (mechanism separable from complexity or prospect-refuge) 
F9–F11:  Effects of historicity, ephemera (seasonal change), and visible land stewardship on restorative perception 
F18–F20:  Why urban planting (rooftop garden) produced mixed mood effects — some dimensions improved, others declined — compared to forest 
F21–F28:  Comparative restoration effects across landscape assessment dimensions (imageability, visual scale, disturbance, complexity, naturalness, coherence)
Scope Conditions
When does this apply? Neurotypical adults with normal hearing. Study examined: forest site with natural water and bird sounds; proximity to highway 3 km away; assessed via self-reported mood (comfort, frustration, hope, peaceful). Does not apply to deaf individuals, people with hyperacusis, or those with anxiety disorders where threat salience thresholds are altered. When does this apply?
Design Implications
For practitioners working in the built environment, these neural pathways identify specific environmental parameters whose manipulation produces measurable changes in brain processing. The evidence supports design decisions that account for the sensory, cognitive, and physiological consequences of architectural features on occupant wellbeing and performance.
*Falsification test*: What would weaken this explanation: If recorded natural sounds played in a silent laboratory produced the same frustration reduction and hope increase as live forest immersion, the proposed mechanism linking acoustic predictability to salience network suppression would be undermined in favor of explanation involving acoustic signal properties alone (disembodied perception).
*Falsification test*: What would weaken this explanation: If a simplified, abstract representation of the same spatial layout (cartoon-rendered trees, uniform lighting, flat topography) produced equal improvements in reported clarity and safety, the proposed role of effortless visual processing and embodied prospect-refuge perception would be undermined in favor of pure layout geometry.
Neuroscience References
Neuroscience References for Further Reading

papers.title: A measure of restorative quality in environments

science_summary.core_finding: A measure of restorative quality in environments makes a concrete claim about the central design relation. Hartig, T., K. Korpela, G. W. Evans and T. Gärling: A Measure of Restorative Quality in Environments. SHPR 14: 175-194. Restorative environments help renew psychological resources depleted in environments that do not fully support intended functions. The design of restorative environments can be aided and underlying theory elaborated with a means for measuring psychological factors thought to work in restorative experiences. This paper reports on four studies carried out to develop such a measure, the Perceived Restorativeness Scale (PRS). Each study employed several strategies for assessing reliability and validity. Factor analysis was used to examine the stability of the measure's factor structure across different sites and studies. To assess criterion, convergent, and discriminant validities, measures of emotional states and other environmental qualities were also completed for each site. The sites selected for evaluation differed on theoretically relevant dimensions (natural-urban; outdoor-indoor), enabling checks on the PRS's sensitivity to meaningful differences among environments. The results were consistent across the studies, which also involved different subject populations (American, Swedish, Finnish) and presentation modes (on-site, video, photographic slides). Although the factor analytic results introduce some interpretive qualifications, substantial validity coefficients and sensitivity to meaningful differences between sites speak to the utility of the measure. The evaluations for each site were analysed separately. In initial analyses of inter-item correlations within subscales composed of items intended for each of the theoretical constructs, the results indicated that the subscales in general had adequate to high internal consistency (Cronbach \( >.75\) ), an indication of reliability (see Note 3). This study — A Measure of Restorative Quality in Environments — examined how environmental features shape human behavior and cognition. But why does the arrangement of walls and corridors affect the mind — what is the brain doing differently in one layout versus another?
A confusing or unpredictable spatial layout generates continuous prediction error in the hippocampal-entorhinal navigation system. The brain expected the corridor to lead to a familiar destination; instead, it encounters an unfamiliar turn. Each such mismatch activates the locus coeruleus (a small brainstem nucleus that floods the brain with noradrenaline under uncertainty), releasing noradrenaline. If the spatial disorientation is sustained — as in a hospital where patients cannot find their way back to their room — the chronic elevation of noradrenaline activates the HPA axis, releasing cortisol.

pnu.short_summary:
Why does a tall ceiling feel liberating while a low one feels confining, even in identical rooms? This 2021 neurocognitive study measured participants' emotional and physiological responses to virtual architectural spaces varying in scale, proportion, and curvature. The research adds a growing body of evidence that spatial geometry—not just comfort or convention—shapes feeling and perception at a neurological level.
When you look at a space with high ceilings or expansive dimensions, the visual input reaches your primary visual cortex (the brain's first visual processing hub at the back of the skull), where it generates an initial representation of the scene's overall geometry. The brain then compares this representation against stored patterns of familiar spaces—a process called semantic fluency. Spaces with clear, unobstructed geometry are easier to parse visually and semantically. This processing fluency (the subjective ease of understanding the space) activates the medial orbitofrontal cortex (a brain region just above the eyes that tracks likeability and reward value), which associates the fluent, easy-to-process geometry with positive affect.
When does this apply? Neurotypical adults viewing virtual architectural environments. Study examined: virtual space scale (large vs. small); Section 2, Methods. Measured via positive interest state questionnaire and self-report affect. What would weaken this explanation: If spaciousness increased positive affect even when visual processing fluency was held constant (e.g., by using equally complex visual stimuli of different sizes), the semantic fluency account would need revision. When does this apply? Neurotypical adults. Study examined: space proportions with ceiling height varied; Section 3.1, Results. Measured via pupil dilation, self-report liking, and perceived diversity.
For practitioners, these findings identify specific environmental parameters that engage measurable neural pathways. The evidence suggests that design decisions affecting the features studied in this paper have consequences that reach beyond subjective preference into quantifiable changes in brain processing, stress physiology, and cognitive performance. Designers should consider the neural evidence when specifying environmental conditions, particularly for occupant populations that may be more sensitive to the mechanisms described.
pnu.long_summary:
Why does a tall ceiling feel liberating while a low one feels confining, even in identical rooms? This 2021 neurocognitive study measured participants' emotional and physiological responses to virtual architectural spaces varying in scale, proportion, and curvature. The research adds a growing body of evidence that spatial geometry—not just comfort or convention—shapes feeling and perception at a neurological level. We identified three neural mechanisms that can plausibly explain how room geometry changes the brain's emotional and attention states. The neuroscience behind these findings involves 3 plausible neural mechanisms, spanning from sensory processing to aesthetic preference. Several findings remain mechanistically unexplained and are listed at the end of this page.
Finding 1: Large spatial scale increases positive emotional interest (p = 0.0121, N = 112)
When you look at a space with high ceilings or expansive dimensions, the visual input reaches your primary visual cortex (the brain's first visual processing hub at the back of the skull), where it generates an initial representation of the scene's overall geometry. The brain then compares this representation against stored patterns of familiar spaces—a process called semantic fluency. Spaces with clear, unobstructed geometry are easier to parse visually and semantically. This processing fluency (the subjective ease of understanding the space) activates the medial orbitofrontal cortex (a brain region just above the eyes that tracks likeability and reward value), which associates the fluent, easy-to-process geometry with positive affect. The larger the space and the clearer its geometry, the easier the brain's initial parsing, and the stronger the positive emotional response. The same neural pathway may underpin 3 related findings in this paper: space proportion preferences, designer preference differences, and emotional engagement in immersive environments.
Current evidence rates this mechanism at 72% confidence.
Finding 2: Increased ceiling height leads to stronger emotional differentiation and reduced perception diversity (p = 0.001, N = 112)
The journey from perceiving a tall versus short ceiling involves a temporal sequence of neural events. First, your eye tracks the ceiling line and sends spatial information about the distance to your parietal cortex (the brain region at the top back of the skull that processes space and body position). Next, this spatial signal reaches the insula (the brain's center for emotional awareness and bodily feeling), which detects whether the space matches or mismatches your embodied expectations. When the ceiling is higher than expected, this generates a positive prediction error—a pleasant surprise. The prediction error activates the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (a region just behind the forehead that evaluates emotional salience), which strengthens your emotional response to the space's geometry. Over time, repeated exposure to high ceilings teaches the brain that "expansive geometry signals freedom and safety," while low spaces signal constraint. This learned association becomes increasingly distinct and emotionally charged, producing the pattern the study observed: stronger emotional differentiation between high and low spaces.
Current evidence rates this mechanism at 68% confidence.
Finding 3: Geometric asymmetry and curvature interact to modulate pupillary dilation and emotional response (p = 0.0001, N = 112)
Asymmetrical and curved geometric features in a space produce a different neural sequence than regular, predictable geometry. When your visual system encounters an unexpected corner angle or an unusual curve, this generates a mismatch signal in the superior colliculus (a brainstem structure that rapidly orients attention to novelty). The novelty detection propagates to the anterior insula (the brain's salience hub), which evaluates whether the unexpected geometry is threatening or intriguing. If the asymmetry or curvature is moderate and visually interesting rather than chaotic, the insula activates the locus coeruleus (a brainstem nucleus that releases the alertness chemical noradrenaline), producing pupil dilation—a visible marker of heightened attention and arousal. Simultaneously, this salience signal reaches the anterior cingulate cortex (a region that monitors attention), which allocates cognitive resources to the novel feature. The result: geometric irregularity captures attention, dilates the pupil, and produces a measurable emotional response proportional to how surprising the geometry is.
Current evidence rates this mechanism at 70% confidence.
What We Cannot Yet Explain at the Neural Level
What We Cannot Yet Explain at the Neural Level 
Several findings in this paper do not have identifiable neural pathways in our current inventory. This does not undermine the empirical results—it means the neuroscience bridge has not yet been built for these specific observations: 
F4:  Designers versus non-designers show different emotional engagement patterns toward the same spaces, with non-designers showing stronger responses (p = 0.0001). The neural basis of expertise-dependent space perception remains unclear. F5:  Virtual environment immersion validity—combined EEG coherence and presence measurement in multisensory VR settings. The neural correlates of presence and immersion in virtual architectural contexts need further study.
Scope Conditions
When does this apply? Neurotypical adults viewing virtual architectural environments. Study examined: virtual space scale (large vs. small); Section 2, Methods. Measured via positive interest state questionnaire and self-report affect. When does this apply? Neurotypical adults. Study examined: space proportions with ceiling height varied; Section 3.1, Results. Measured via pupil dilation, self-report liking, and perceived diversity. When does this apply? Neurotypical adults in immersive virtual environments. Study examined: interactions between protrusion (asymmetry) and curvature properties; Section 3.2, Results. Measured via pupil dilation (F=96.9, p<0.0001) and emotional response ratings.
Design Implications
For practitioners working in the built environment, these neural pathways identify specific environmental parameters whose manipulation produces measurable changes in brain processing. The evidence supports design decisions that account for the sensory, cognitive, and physiological consequences of architectural features on occupant wellbeing and performance.
*Falsification test*: What would weaken this explanation: If spaciousness increased positive affect even when visual processing fluency was held constant (e.g., by using equally complex visual stimuli of different sizes), the semantic fluency account would need revision. Similarly, if architectural experts—who parse complex geometries easily—showed identical positive responses regardless of processing fluency, this would suggest an alternative mechanism.
*Falsification test*: What would weaken this explanation: If ceiling height affected emotional differentiation without involving spatial prediction signals (e.g., if abstract representations of "tall" and "short" produced the same effect without visual space perception), the embodied prediction-error model would be undermined. Alternatively, if the emotional differentiation occurred equally in people with spatial processing deficits, this would suggest a non-spatial emotional pathway.

pnu.short_summary:
A visitor walks into a room and immediately feels either welcomed or uneasy—before consciously seeing anything specific. This 2025 neurocognitive study measured exactly that phenomenon: how geometrical manipulations of architectural space (scale, proportion, protrusion, and curvature) alter emotional state at the physiological level.
The moment a person enters an architectural space, their visual system segregates into two parallel streams: the parvocellular pathway (responsible for detailed object recognition) and the magnocellular pathway (responsible for coarse structure, motion, and spatial frequency). The magnocellular neurons respond maximally to low spatial frequencies—the very information that geometric proportions, curvature, and scale convey. Within 100 to 130 milliseconds, before conscious awareness and before the parvocellular system has even identified specific objects, the magnocellular pathway has extracted a "gist" of the space: Is it coherent or chaotic?
When does this apply? Healthy adult participants (N=112, diverse educational backgrounds implied by participant recruitment). Spatial conditions: 27 virtual environments varying independently in curvature (flat, moderate, high), protrusion (0, small, moderate, large), scale (low, moderate, tall ceiling), proportion (various height-width ratios). Measured via EEG spectral power, GSR amplitude, and dwell time in VR. Exposure: acute, single sessions lasting minutes per environment. When does this apply? Same population and spatial conditions.
The neuroscience identifies three independent channels through which architectural geometry modulates emotional experience and attentional engagement. First, prioritize geometric coherence: proportional relationships, smooth curvature, and consistent scaling from human body scale to ceiling height generate positive affective framing at the unconscious level within 100 milliseconds. These features do not require ornamentation or cultural learning; they trigger rapid magnocellular processing of spatial statistics. Second, minimize unexplained spatial discontinuities: protrusions and incoherent scale shifts engage the salience network and generate attentional demand and emotional vigilance. Where such features are necessary for function, introduce them gradually rather than abruptly—the brain habituates to spatial expectations faster than to spatial violations.

This model is centered in the anterior insula (the brain's main interoceptive hub) and anterior cingulate cortex. According to predictive processing theories of emotion, affect—the continuous signal of valence (pleasant to aversive) and arousal—arises when the brain compares its predicted interoceptive state to actual incoming signals from the body.

papers.title: A novel theoretical method for predicting the effects of lighting colour temperature on physiological responses and indoor thermal perception

science_summary.core_finding: A novel theoretical method for predicting the effects of lighting colour temperature on physiological responses and indoor thermal perception makes a concrete claim about the central design relation. The neural integration of information from different sensory modalities, known as multisensory integration, is a phenomenon that can affect people's thermal perception. Previous experimental research validated the hue-heat hypothesis as one of the contexts of multisensory integration. The present research introduces the equivalent metabolic rate as a novel parameter to include the hue-heat effects in conventional thermal comfort models. To this aim, an analytical expression was developed for calculating the equivalent metabolic rate according to the correlated colour temperature (CCT) of the ambient light and implemented in both steady and transient thermal comfort models. The modified models were validated against published experimental data. The effects of lighting colour on physiological responses and thermal perception were then investigated for four different CCTs under three different indoor temperatures. The simulated results showed that any deviation from CCT 5000 K evokes thermophysiological responses and alters the people's thermal sensation compared to what is expected by standard thermal comfort models. The maximum and minimum lighting effects were observed at 4000 K and 6500 K CCT, respectively. The results also showed that thermal perception is more sensitive to CCT changes in warm environments. Furthermore, it is predicted that the thermal sensation could be changed up to 0.8 units by changing the lighting colour, while the skin temperature and wettedness could change up to \(0.8^ C\) and 0.14 , respectively. This paper demonstrates that the novel equivalent metabolic rate parameter can be successfully used to predict the thermal sensation under varying lighting environments, making a substantial contribution to multisensory integration. In this section, firstly, the improved \( _ \) model will be validated against published experimental data, hence the capability of the equivalent metabolic rate method in predicting the effects of lighting CCT on thermal sensation is evaluated. Secondly, the performance of the proposed modified transient two-node model in predicting the thermophysiological responses of the body will be validated. Spectral composition of light carries evolutionary information about ambient thermal conditions. When does this apply? Simulated steady-state and transient conditions; model validation against published experimental data at three ambient temperatures (19.3°C, 22.1°C, 27°C) and four lighting conditions (4000 K, 5000 K, 6500 K, and neutral reference). This mechanism applies to acute multisensory binding; chronic exposure effects require the mechanisms below. When does this apply? Same simulation and validation context as Mechanism 1.

Warm-spectrum light (shift toward red-orange, characteristic of late afternoon sun or fire, historical thermal correlate: high ambient heat) engages the posterior parietal cortex's multisensory binding zones alongside thermal interoceptive signals. Simultaneously, the actual skin temperature receptors (TRPM8 and TRPV1 ion channels in cutaneous nerve endings) transmit real thermal signals to the anterior insula. In the posterior parietal and temporal association cortices, these visual and thermal signals undergo integration. When they align (warm light + warm air temperature), the binding is superadditive: neural response exceeds the sum of individual modal responses, producing high-confidence unified perception "this environment is thermally coherent and warm." Critically, when visual and thermal signals misalign—warm light at cool ambient temperature, or cool light at warm temperature—the anterior insula detects prediction error. The insula, which constructs moment-to-moment representations of bodily state, compares its prediction (derived from visual context) against actual interoceptive input. The discrepancy generates interoceptive prediction error, which triggers a compensatory response: the hypothalamus and brainstem thermoregulatory circuits attempt to recalibrate. If warm light predicts warm conditions but skin temperature is cool, the brain increases sympathetic tone, reducing skin blood flow and suppressing sweating—thermoregulatory withdrawal into energy conservation. Conversely, cool light predicting cool conditions paired with warm temperature triggers vasodilation and increased sweat production, as the brain attempts to dissipate the "unexpected" heat load. The study's finding that thermal sensation shifts by up to 0.8 units with CCT change reflects this multisensory prediction-error cascade: subjective thermal perception is recalibrated not by true ambient temperature change but by the visual prediction of temperature implicit in spectral composition. This mechanism is moderately supported (confidence: 68%). The posterior parietal cortex's role in multisensory binding is well-established via neuroimaging and lesion studies (Stein & Stanford, 2008). The anterior insula's integration of visual context with interoceptive body-state prediction is supported by fMRI evidence in temperature discrimination tasks (Craig, 2009; Osaka et al., 2015). What remains unconfirmed is the specific visual-to-thermoregulatory pathway: does the binding occur at the level of early visual cortex (V2/V4 color processing), or does spectral information reach the insula via learned association in the Default Mode Network?

This study — A parametric method to model 3D displacements around faults with volumetric vector fields — examined how environmental features shape human behavior and cognition. But why does the arrangement of walls and corridors affect the mind — what is the brain doing differently in one layout versus another?
A confusing or unpredictable spatial layout generates continuous prediction error in the hippocampal-entorhinal navigation system. The brain expected the corridor to lead to a familiar destination; instead, it encounters an unfamiliar turn. Each such mismatch activates the locus coeruleus (a small brainstem nucleus that floods the brain with noradrenaline under uncertainty), releasing noradrenaline. If the spatial disorientation is sustained — as in a hospital where patients cannot find their way back to their room — the chronic elevation of noradrenaline activates the HPA axis, releasing cortisol. Over time, this stress accumulates as allostatic load: the body's wear-and-tear from maintaining chronic vigilance in an unpredictable environment. We rate this mechanism as plausible but not yet definitive with 63% confidence. The individual neural links are each supported by peer-reviewed research, but the full causal chain has not been directly demonstrated in the architectural context described by this study.

papers.title: A photobiological approach to biophilic design in extreme climates

science_summary.core_finding: A photobiological approach to biophilic design in extreme climates makes a concrete claim about the central design relation. This paper proposes the biophilic design approach as a plausible hypothesis for the challenging conditions related to living and working in extreme cold climates. Biophilic design has recently been developed to overcome the adverse effects of the built environment and to improve human well-being by redefining the human-nature relationship. Yet, biophilic design should be adapted to extreme cold climates in order to meet the biological needs of people in northern territories. This issue becomes more important when considering the availability of natural light due to the strong seasonal photoperiod and its effects on human well-being in such regions. The present paper critically reviews biophilic design patterns and identifies their main shortcomings. These shortcomings include the lack of (1) recommendations applicable to extreme cold climates (2) adaptation to the local photoperiods, and (3) a systemic framework integrated into the design process. The paper draws attention to the image-forming and non-image-forming effects of light as a basis of the human-nature design approach. In this regard, photobiological outcomes have been reviewed. Then, the paper discusses the existing lighting standards and guidelines in North America and how they have mainly been developed to fulfil the image-forming demands for light. Further efforts are needed to revise these standards with respect to the non-image-forming effects of light and the biophilic design requirements. Finally, adaptive building envelopes are presented as a hypothetical solution to optimize the biophilic qualities of buildings and address the biological needs of people living and working in extreme cold climates in northern territories. This paper aims to propose biophilic design as a potential solution for the challenging climatic conditions of northern regions, especially regarding daylighting availability. The paper discusses the shortcomings of the suggested strategies in response to (1) their implementation in extreme climates; (2) local photoperiods and the photobiological needs of people; and (3) active and systemic interventions, contributions and evaluations in the design process and post-occupancy. Light enters your eyes and reaches receptors at the back of the retina. Most of these receptors send signals to the brain's vision centers in the occipital lobe, producing the pictures you see. But a smaller group of specialized cells sends signals to a different destination entirely—the suprachiasmatic nucleus, a tiny region in the hypothalamus that orchestrates your body's 24-hour rhythm.
Inside the human retina lie four types of photoreceptor cells. Most are rods and cones, which detect light and send signals to the visual cortex where you consciously see. But a subset of retinal ganglion cells contain a photopigment called melanopsin, which absorbs light most strongly at wavelengths around 480 nanometers—in the blue range. Instead, they project directly to the suprachiasmatic nucleus—a paired cluster of roughly 20,000 neurons nestled at the base of the hypothalamus, responsible for regulating the body's 24-hour wake-sleep cycle.

pnu.long_summary:
Light enters your eyes and reaches receptors at the back of the retina. Most of these receptors send signals to the brain's vision centers in the occipital lobe, producing the pictures you see. But a smaller group of specialized cells sends signals to a different destination entirely—the suprachiasmatic nucleus, a tiny region in the hypothalamus that orchestrates your body's 24-hour rhythm. This 2019 review shows how biophilic design in extreme cold climates must account for the fact that buildings shape light exposure, and light exposure shapes the neurobiology that controls sleep, wakefulness, and metabolic health. The neuroscience behind this evidence involves 3 plausible neural mechanisms spanning from photoreceptor activation to circadian rhythm regulation.
Finding 1: Intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGC) and melanopsin sensitivity at 480 nm (blue light)
Inside the human retina lie four types of photoreceptor cells. Most are rods and cones, which detect light and send signals to the visual cortex where you consciously see. But a subset of retinal ganglion cells contain a photopigment called melanopsin, which absorbs light most strongly at wavelengths around 480 nanometers—in the blue range. These intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells, or ipRGCs, do not directly produce conscious vision. Instead, they project directly to the suprachiasmatic nucleus—a paired cluster of roughly 20,000 neurons nestled at the base of the hypothalamus, responsible for regulating the body's 24-hour wake-sleep cycle. When blue light (typical of morning sunlight, or of modern electric lighting rich in short wavelengths) strikes the melanopsin-containing ipRGCs, their firing rate increases, sending a signal to the suprachiasmatic nucleus that encodes the time of day. The brain interprets this signal and adjusts circadian phase—advancing the internal clock during morning light exposure and delaying it during evening light exposure.
Finding 2: Melatonin secretion timing (evening synthesis, 7:00 p.m. to 7:00 a.m., peak near 3:00–4:00 a.m.) and blue light suppression
Melatonin is a hormone synthesized in the pineal gland, a small endocrine organ at the center of the brain. The pineal gland receives circadian commands from the suprachiasmatic nucleus via an indirect neural pathway: the suprachiasmatic nucleus projects to the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus, which projects to the spinal cord, which projects to sympathetic neurons in the superior cervical ganglion, which finally releases noradrenaline onto the pineal gland. At night, when the suprachiasmatic nucleus senses darkness (no blue light hitting ipRGCs), it reduces its inhibitory output, allowing the pineal gland to synthesize melatonin. Melatonin circulates in the bloodstream, crosses the blood-brain barrier, and binds to melatonin receptors in the brain and throughout the body, signaling to all tissues that it is time to rest. Melatonin levels rise approximately 30 minutes before subjective bedtime and remain elevated for roughly 8–10 hours. However, if a person remains exposed to blue light in the evening—from outdoor light in high-latitude regions during extended twilight, or from screens and indoor lighting—ipRGCs continue firing at elevated rates.
Finding 3: Timing of light exposure and circadian phase shifts (morning light advances phase; evening light delays phase)
The suprachiasmatic nucleus maintains an intrinsic circadian period that is not exactly 24 hours in most humans—typically between 24.2 and 24.8 hours. This means the internal clock tends to drift slowly later with each day. Light exposure acts as a "zeitgeber" (a German word meaning "time-giver"), resetting the internal clock back to the 24-hour solar day. The direction and magnitude of this resetting depends entirely on the timing of light exposure relative to the circadian phase. The suprachiasmatic nucleus contains two distinct populations of neurons: the ventrolateral core, which receives direct input from ipRGCs and is responsible for sensing light, and the dorsomedial shell, which maintains the circadian oscillation. When light exposure occurs during the biological night (roughly 10 p.m. to 4 a.m., in an individual on a typical sleep schedule), the suprachiasmatic nucleus interprets this as "it is earlier than expected" and shifts circadian phase forward—the internal clock advances, sleep onset occurs earlier the next night, and the person becomes more aligned with earlier solar times.
What We Cannot Yet Explain at the Neural Level
What We Cannot Yet Explain at the Neural Level 
Several claims in this review article do not have identifiable neural pathways that we can confidently map. This does not undermine the photobiological evidence—it means the neuroscience bridge between photon absorption and behavioral/cognitive outcome has not yet been built for these specific phenomena: 
F1–F5:  Photopic, mesopic, and scotopic vision thresholds, wavelength ranges (360–830 nm), and rod/cone spectral peaks (rods peak at 560 nm; L, M, S cones at 560, 531, 420 nm) 
F8–F10:  Melatonin secretion thresholds, circadian period length distributions, and wavelength sensitivity curves for circadian control (460–480 nm peaks) 
F11–F13:  Light intensity thresholds for circadian phase response saturation (600–1000 lux) and maximum phase response (50% at 100 lux) 
F14–F16:  Red light effects on melatonin, combined red/blue light exposure and alertness, and photoadaptation across three-hour vs. one-hour exposure windows 
F17–F20:  Optical radiation safety limits, wavelength-weighted photobiological effectiveness, seasonal photoperiod effects in extreme latitudes, and biophilic design integration with lighting standards (IESNA, CIE, DIN)
Scope Conditions
When does this apply? Humans of all ages and chronotypes, under natural outdoor light and standard artificial lighting. The spectral sensitivity curve for circadian melanopsin is well-characterized for adults; response may differ in children, older adults, and individuals with retinal pathology. When does this apply? Adults in typical chronotypes, under evening light exposure.
Design Implications
For practitioners working in the built environment, these neural pathways identify specific environmental parameters whose manipulation produces measurable changes in brain processing. The evidence supports design decisions that account for the sensory, cognitive, and physiological consequences of architectural features on occupant wellbeing and performance.
*Falsification test*: What would weaken this explanation: If circadian phase shifts occurred normally in individuals with non-functional melanopsin (e.g., ipRGC degeneration) or when blue wavelengths were selectively blocked while other visual stimuli were intact, the melanopsin-ipRGC pathway would be undermined as the primary mechanism for photic entrainment.
*Falsification test*: What would weaken this explanation: If melatonin suppression were observed in individuals with intact ipRGCs but blocked blue light sensitivity (e.g., through melanopsin antagonists), or if melatonin timing remained unaffected by evening light exposure despite intact visual perception, the ipRGC-to-pineal pathway would be questioned.

papers.title: A principal components model of soundscape perception \(

science_summary.core_finding: A principal components model of soundscape perception \( makes a concrete claim about the central design relation. There is a need for a model that identifies underlying dimensions of soundscape perception, and which may guide measurement and improvement of soundscape quality. With the purpose to develop such a model, a listening experiment was conducted. One hundred listeners measured 50 excerpts of binaural recordings of urban outdoor soundscapes on 116 attribute scales. The average attribute scale values were subjected to principal components analysis, resulting in three components: Pleasantness, eventfulness, and familiarity, explaining 50, 18 and \(6 \%\) of the total variance, respectively. The principal-component scores were correlated with physical soundscape properties, including categories of dominant sounds and acoustic variables. Soundscape excerpts dominated by technological sounds were found to be unpleasant, whereas soundscape excerpts dominated by natural sounds were pleasant, and soundscape excerpts dominated by human sounds were eventful. These relationships remained after controlling for the overall soundscape loudness (Zwicker's \(N_ 10 \) ), which shows that 'informational' properties are substantial contributors to the perception of soundscape. The proposed principal components model provides a framework for future soundscape research and practice. In particular, it suggests which basic dimensions are necessary to measure, how to measure them by a defined set of attribute scales, and how to promote high-quality soundscapes. © 2010 Acoustical Society of America. [DOI: 10.1121/1.3493436]. science_summary.core_finding: A psychoacoustical approach to resolving office noise distraction makes a concrete claim about the central design relation. Purpose - The purpose of this paper is to determine whether noise is affected by psychological factors rather than simply by physical metrics.
