pnu.short_summary:
An architect designing an office building faces an inescapable tension. The latest energy codes demand deep floor plates and tinted glass that minimizes solar heat gain and glare. Yet the evidence from occupants and from organizational productivity is unambiguous: workers with windows perform better, feel better, and maintain better circadian health than those in windowless interiors.
The eye contains two classes of light-sensitive cells. Rods and cones generate the visual image you see — the colors, the details, the view itself. But embedded within the retina are intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs), neurons that contain melanopsin, a photopigment tuned to blue light at approximately 480 nanometers. These ipRGCs do not contribute to conscious vision. Instead, they project directly to the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), a small region in the hypothalamus that acts as the body's master clock.
When does this apply? Office workers and knowledge workers in buildings with windows. The mechanism operates on a timescale of 30 minutes to hours for immediate melatonin suppression, and days to weeks for circadian phase adjustment. Most relevant for chronic occupancy (8+ hours per day, 5+ days per week). Effectiveness depends on window distance (within 10 meters shows robust effect), glass transmission at 450–500 nm (must preserve blue-enriched spectrum), and timing (morning light is most critical for phase-advance).
The neuroscience identifies three independent but synergistic pathways through which daylight and views influence human cognition and health. These suggest concrete design strategies. First, preserve morning daylight access: prioritize southern or eastern window orientations for workstations, minimize external shading, and specify glass that preserves blue-enriched wavelengths (≥480 nm transmission ≥70% relative to clear glass) to sustain ipRGC stimulation and circadian entrainment. Second, maximize view quality through integrated design: use dynamic shading systems (electrochromic or redirecting blinds) that manage solar gain and glare without blocking views, and site workstations to provide stable views to vegetation or sky when possible.

Mechanism 1: Daylight triggers ipRGC-mediated circadian entrainment, maintaining daytime alertness and nocturnal melatonin suppression (CB-CIRCADIAN-ENTRAINMENT-001) The eye contains two classes of light-sensitive cells. Rods and cones generate the visual image you see — the colors, the details, the view itself. But embedded within the retina are intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs), neurons that contain melanopsin, a photopigment tuned to blue light at approximately 480 nanometers. These ipRGCs do not contribute to conscious vision. Instead, they project directly to the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), a small region in the hypothalamus that acts as the body's master clock. The ipRGCs evolved to measure the spectral composition of daylight — the ratio of blue to longer-wavelength light — as a proxy for solar position and time of day. When an office worker sits at a desk more than 10 meters from a window, the ipRGC input to the SCN drops sharply. The brain's master clock does not receive adequate melanopic lux — the biological measure of blue-enriched light impact, distinct from visual lux (which weights the photopic response). Without sufficient morning ipRGC stimulation, the SCN cannot maintain its normal phase-advance, resulting in delayed melatonin offset and diminished daytime alertness. The worker may feel fatigued by mid-morning despite sleeping adequately, a symptom of mild circadian misalignment. Over days and weeks of chronic insufficient daylight exposure, the SCN's free-running period begins to drift relative to solar time, progressively worsening sleep quality and daytime cognitive performance. The paper identifies this as one of the primary mechanisms through which building depth and window location systematically degrade occupant health. The circadian entrainment mechanism is among the most robustly validated in behavioral neuroscience (confidence: 88%). Melanopsin and the ipRGC-SCN pathway have been characterized at molecular and cellular levels (Berson et al., 2002).

pnu.short_summary:
A building's beauty reaches you before you think about it. Your eye catches the line of a façade, the play of light on a material, the proportion of a doorway — and you feel something: pleasure, interest, comfort, or their opposites. This 2023 narrative review applies the Mehrabian-Russell Pleasure-Arousal-Dominance (PAD) model to architecture, proposing that the emotional texture of buildings can be systematized along three independent neural dimensions.
Visually beautiful architectural forms — coherent proportions, aesthetic façades, harmonious materials — enter the visual system and produce rapid prediction signals in the ventral visual stream (the pathway that processes object identity and scene meaning). Within the first 300 milliseconds of viewing, the inferior temporal cortex and perirhinal cortex classify the architectural stimulus as familiar, coherent, and aesthetically congruent with learned preferences. This rapid gist representation propagates to the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), which compares the actual visual input against stored affective expectations and generates a reward prediction signal.
When does this apply? Neurotypical adults viewing architectural spaces with high coherence, visual balance, and aesthetic refinement. Stronger for spaces with biophilic elements, natural materials, and proportions matching human-scale expectations. May be attenuated in individuals with autism spectrum conditions or visual-spatial processing differences. What would weaken this explanation: If architectural beauty produced pleasure responses in behavioral tasks but failed to activate the orbitofrontal cortex and ventral striatum in neuroimaging, or if blocking dopamine transmission pharmacologically eliminated the pleasure without changing the visual assessment of beauty, the reward-based mechanism would be undermined.
For practitioners, these findings identify specific environmental parameters that engage measurable neural pathways. The evidence suggests that design decisions affecting the features studied in this paper have consequences that reach beyond subjective preference into quantifiable changes in brain processing, stress physiology, and cognitive performance. Designers should consider the neural evidence when specifying environmental conditions, particularly for occupant populations that may be more sensitive to the mechanisms described.
pnu.long_summary:
A building's beauty reaches you before you think about it. Your eye catches the line of a façade, the play of light on a material, the proportion of a doorway — and you feel something: pleasure, interest, comfort, or their opposites. This 2023 narrative review applies the Mehrabian-Russell Pleasure-Arousal-Dominance (PAD) model to architecture, proposing that the emotional texture of buildings can be systematized along three independent neural dimensions. But how does visual form translate into the affective states the PAD framework describes? The neuroscience behind these architectural-emotional responses involves 4 plausible neural mechanisms spanning reward processing, attentional dynamics, spatial cognition, and affective valence.
Mechanism 1: Beautiful architecture activates the dopaminergic reward system (Pleasure dimension)
Visually beautiful architectural forms — coherent proportions, aesthetic façades, harmonious materials — enter the visual system and produce rapid prediction signals in the ventral visual stream (the pathway that processes object identity and scene meaning). Within the first 300 milliseconds of viewing, the inferior temporal cortex and perirhinal cortex classify the architectural stimulus as familiar, coherent, and aesthetically congruent with learned preferences. This rapid gist representation propagates to the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), which compares the actual visual input against stored affective expectations and generates a reward prediction signal. When the building matches or slightly exceeds expectations, the OFC signals reward salience to the ventral tegmental area (VTA) and striatum, releasing dopamine throughout the nucleus accumbens and medial prefrontal cortex. This dopaminergic response drives the experience of pleasure and aesthetic satisfaction — the warm, positive feeling elicited by a well-proportioned space. The pathway operates through two parallel channels. The first (liking) involves direct OFC-to-VTA projections that encode the hedonic value of the stimulus itself.
Current evidence rates this mechanism at 79% confidence.
Mechanism 2: Visual complexity follows an inverted-U curve driven by predictive precision weighting (Pleasure via Goldilocks complexity)
Architectural complexity exists on a continuum. Stark, minimalist spaces provide little visual novelty; excessively ornate spaces overwhelm with detail. The paper's core finding is that moderately complex spaces produce the strongest positive emotional responses — the Goldilocks principle applied to architecture. The neural mechanism underlying this inverted-U preference involves predictive precision weighting in hierarchical visual cortex. When viewing an architectural scene, the visual cortex constructs a generative model of what it expects to see. Simple spaces (low complexity) make strong predictions with high certainty — the model "knows" what comes next, and there is little prediction error. The brain finds this boring; it generates a low-confidence prediction error signal that fails to engage attention and dopamine. Excessively complex spaces generate overwhelming prediction errors — the model cannot predict the incoming visual information, and high-level cortical regions receive chaotic, conflicting error signals. The insula (the brain's alarm center for prediction failures) flags this as aversive, and the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex must work hard to construct post-hoc explanations, leading to cognitive fatigue and negative affect.
Current evidence rates this mechanism at 73% confidence.
Mechanism 3: Spatial openness and visual prospect activate the salience network and produce the Dominance dimension
The PAD model's third dimension — Dominance — captures the degree to which a person feels in control of and empowered within a space versus subordinate to it. Open, prospect-rich spaces (with clear sightlines and visual control of the environment) produce high Dominance; enclosed, constrained spaces produce low Dominance and can feel oppressive. The neural mechanism involves the salience network and threat-detection circuits in the amygdala and anterior insula, working in concert with parietal-frontal networks that encode peripersonal space and agency. When a person enters a space with restricted sightlines — narrow corridors, high ceilings without clear endpoints, visual occlusion of exits — the amygdala (which rapidly detects potential threats) receives reduced visual information about the environment's structure and potential escape routes. The brain interprets this sensory restriction as a loss of control. The anterior cingulate cortex signals this loss-of-control state as aversive, and the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex must work harder to maintain cognitive maps and plan navigation.
Current evidence rates this mechanism at 71% confidence.
Mechanism 4: Aesthetic coherence and visual flow activate the default mode network and produce sustained positive Arousal regulation
Architectural spaces with high visual harmony, logical material choices, and coherent organizational logic activate a different neural system: the default mode network (DMN). The DMN is the set of regions (medial prefrontal cortex, posterior cingulate cortex, precuneus, and angular gyrus) that engage when the brain shifts from externally focused task execution to self-referential thought, aesthetic appreciation, and mental simulation. When a person enters a well-designed space with obvious internal logic — materials that match their function, proportions that make spatial sense, visual flow that guides the eye without constraint — the DMN engages in what neuroscientists call "fluent processing." The visual information aligns with implicit expectations, so the brain does not need to allocate sustained attention resources to threat detection or route planning. Instead, it enters a state of aesthetic contemplation and self-directed thought about one's place within the environment. This DMN engagement produces a lowered baseline in the salience network (reduced amygdala and anterior insula tone), which manifests behaviorally as reduced Arousal — the space feels calm, contemplative, and regulated rather than stimulating or overwhelming.
Current evidence rates this mechanism at 75% confidence.
What We Cannot Yet Explain at the Neural Level
Scope Limitation: The PAD Model's Orthogonality 
The paper asserts that Pleasure, Arousal, and Dominance are three independent orthogonal dimensions. Neuroscience does not yet have a comprehensive mechanism explaining why these three specific dimensions emerge as fundamental emotional axes in architectural response, or how they map onto the broader dimensional structure of affect in the brain (the two-dimensional Valence-Arousal space, the three-dimensional Valence-Arousal-Dominance space, or higher-dimensional models). The claim that architectural features can be systematically mapped onto all three dimensions simultaneously remains theoretical — it has not been validated against neuroimaging data from subjects viewing diverse architectural spaces while rating themselves on calibrated PAD scales.
Scope Conditions
When does this apply? Neurotypical adults viewing architectural spaces with high coherence, visual balance, and aesthetic refinement. Stronger for spaces with biophilic elements, natural materials, and proportions matching human-scale expectations. May be attenuated in individuals with autism spectrum conditions or visual-spatial processing differences. When does this apply?
Design Implications
For practitioners working in the built environment, these neural pathways identify specific environmental parameters whose manipulation produces measurable changes in brain processing. The evidence supports design decisions that account for the sensory, cognitive, and physiological consequences of architectural features on occupant wellbeing and performance.
*Falsification test*: What would weaken this explanation: If architectural beauty produced pleasure responses in behavioral tasks but failed to activate the orbitofrontal cortex and ventral striatum in neuroimaging, or if blocking dopamine transmission pharmacologically eliminated the pleasure without changing the visual assessment of beauty, the reward-based mechanism would be undermined.
*Falsification test*: What would weaken this explanation: If spaces with intermediate complexity produced negative affective responses despite generating moderate prediction errors in visual cortex, or if removing architectural elements that generate prediction errors (simplifying moderately complex spaces) failed to shift hedonic ratings, the predictive precision mechanism would need revision.

papers.title: Aesthetic experience of texture in architectural surfaces

science_summary.core_finding: When architects select materials for a building interior, they typically focus on structural performance, cost, and maintenance rather than the perceptual experience those materials create. Zuo and Jones argue that this neglects a systematic dimension of design. They propose that material texture aesthetics can be organized along four perceptual dimensions: roughness–smoothness, warmth–coolness, hardness–softness, and naturalness–artificiality. Each dimension maps to specific lexical descriptors that occupants use when evaluating surfaces, creating a Dimension–Lexicon system that bridges physical material properties with psychological aesthetic responses.
science_summary.methods_and_design: This is a theoretical framework paper, not an experiment. The authors synthesize research from psychophysics of texture perception, material science, and architectural aesthetics to build the four-dimension model. The Dimension–Lexicon system draws on haptic and visual texture processing literature to link measurable physical properties (surface roughness in micrometers, thermal conductivity in W/m·K, Shore hardness) to the adjective descriptors that people naturally use when describing how materials feel and look. Methods identified via Mathpix: virtual reality.
science_summary.design_implications: For architects and interior designers, the framework offers a structured vocabulary for specifying material textures beyond generic labels like “warm” or “natural.” Each dimension can be independently specified: a surface can be smooth yet warm (polished wood), or rough yet cool (exposed concrete). This decomposition allows design teams to target specific perceptual outcomes rather than relying on intuition about material selection.
science_summary.limitations: The framework is proposed rather than empirically validated in this paper. Whether the four dimensions are truly orthogonal (independent of each other) in occupant perception has not been tested with factor analysis or multidimensional scaling. Cultural variation in texture preferences and lexical descriptors is acknowledged but not measured.

There are no new inferential statistics here. The contribution is conceptual: organizing existing perceptual research into a usable architectural framework.
The paper’s central contribution is the Dimension–Lexicon mapping table, which pairs each of the four perceptual dimensions with its associated descriptor terms and physical correlates. For architects and interior designers, the framework offers a structured vocabulary for specifying material textures beyond generic labels like “warm” or “natural.” Each dimension can be independently specified: a surface can be smooth yet warm (polished wood), or rough yet cool (exposed concrete). This decomposition allows design teams to target specific perceptual outcomes rather than relying on intuition about material selection.
The framework is proposed rather than empirically validated in this paper. Whether the four dimensions are truly orthogonal (independent of each other) in occupant perception has not been tested with factor analysis or multidimensional scaling. Cultural variation in texture preferences and lexical descriptors is acknowledged but not measured.
Would a multidimensional scaling study of occupant texture ratings confirm four independent dimensions, or would fewer or more dimensions emerge? A direct test would present participants with 30–40 architectural material samples varying systematically on all four proposed dimensions and ask for paired-comparison similarity judgments. If MDS recovers four dimensions with stress < 0.10, the framework gains empirical support. If only two or three dimensions emerge, the model would need to be simplified, which would increase its practical utility by reducing the number of design parameters architects must consider.
The four-dimension taxonomy (roughness-smoothness, warmth-coolness, hardness-softness, naturalness-artificiality) draws on decades of psychophysical research showing that these perceptual dimensions are the primary axes along which people differentiate material surfaces. Roughness is linked to the spatial frequency of surface irregularities and correlates with tactile receptor density at the fingertip. Warmth is driven by thermal conductivity: materials with lower conductivity (wood at 0.12-0.18 W/m K) feel warmer to the touch than high-conductivity materials (steel at 50 W/m K, concrete at 1.7 W/m K). Hardness maps to Shore durometer values and affects both tactile feedback and acoustic behavior of surfaces. Naturalness is the dimension most relevant to biophilic design, as it captures the distinction between materials perceived as authentic versus synthetic. The Dimension-Lexicon system bridges these physical measurements with the vocabulary architects and clients actually use. Rather than specifying surface roughness in micrometers, a designer can describe the target as having the smooth-warm character of oiled walnut or the rough-cool character of bush-hammered granite. This mapping gives design teams a shared language that connects measurable physical properties with experiential outcomes. The framework also suggests that material combinations in a room should be evaluated along all four dimensions simultaneously rather than selecting materials one at a time, because the perceptual experience of a space is shaped by the contrast and harmony across multiple surfaces.
The framework's practical significance extends beyond individual material selection. When specifying a palette for a healthcare waiting room, for example, the architect must consider how the texture dimensions of multiple surfaces interact. A floor perceived as hard-cool (terrazzo) paired with walls perceived as soft-warm (fabric acoustic panels) creates a cross-dimensional contrast that may be experienced differently from a uniform palette where all surfaces share similar texture characteristics.

This study of 29 young Chinese adults reveals that architectural features—ceiling height, spatial openness, and the curvature of walls and forms—shape aesthetic ratings through multiple neural pathways, some universal to human perception and others sensitive to cultural context.
When you look up at a high ceiling, your brain's spatial navigation circuits—centered in the posterior parietal cortex (a region that encodes your location in space) and medial temporal lobes (memory centers that bind location to context)—recalibrate how you sense the surrounding space. These circuits compute peripersonal space (the reachable zone immediately surrounding your body) by comparing your body size to environmental scale. A high ceiling signals to premotor and parietal regions that space extends well beyond your reach.

What would weaken this explanation: If high ceiling effects on beauty ratings persisted when spatial-scale cues were removed (e.g., by blurring ceiling boundary information while keeping all other visual features), the peripersonal space mechanism would be undermined. Your arousal drops, and you feel positive aesthetic affect because the space signals: "This environment is open, navigable, and does not constrain movement" (Blanke, 2012). pnu.long_summary:
When you step into a building with a high ceiling and open floor plan, your brain immediately makes a judgment about whether this space is pleasant or confining. This study of 29 young Chinese adults reveals that architectural features—ceiling height, spatial openness, and the curvature of walls and forms—shape aesthetic ratings through multiple neural pathways, some universal to human perception and others sensitive to cultural context. The neuroscience behind these findings involves 4 plausible neural mechanisms that explain how ceiling height, openness, and contour translate into beauty and pleasantness ratings. These mechanisms span from moment-to-moment aesthetic valence to spatial navigation circuits that have evolved to calibrate our sense of being in space.
Mechanism 1: High Ceilings Trigger Peripersonal Space Plasticity
When you look up at a high ceiling, your brain's spatial navigation circuits—centered in the posterior parietal cortex (a region that encodes your location in space) and medial temporal lobes (memory centers that bind location to context)—recalibrate how you sense the surrounding space. These circuits compute peripersonal space (the reachable zone immediately surrounding your body) by comparing your body size to environmental scale. A high ceiling signals to premotor and parietal regions that space extends well beyond your reach. Your arousal drops, and you feel positive aesthetic affect because the space signals: "This environment is open, navigable, and does not constrain movement" (Blanke, 2012). The mechanism operates at the network-state timescale—your sense of space recalibrates over 5–15 minutes of occupancy. Chinese observers, like those in Western studies (Vartanian et al., 2013), rate high ceilings as more beautiful (p<0.001, η²=0.728), suggesting this pathway is universal across cultures. As your peripersonal space expands, your brain makes a positive interoceptive prediction: the environment demands low metabolic effort in an open, navigable space.
Mechanism 2: Open Spatial Layout Reduces Prediction Error in the Salience Network
Open architectural space (versus closed, compartmented space) generates lower prediction error in the anterior insula (your brain's alarm center for unexpected events) and anterior cingulate cortex (a region that monitors conflict and allocates attention)—the brain's prediction-comparison center for spatial surprise. When you view an open layout, your visual system rapidly generates a spatial model of flow and navigation. A closed, maze-like layout generates competing spatial predictions and ambiguity: "Can I easily reach the other side?" This prediction uncertainty—an unpredicted surprise about spatial layout—activates the salience network to re-evaluate the space. Open layouts satisfy spatial predictions, generating zero salience demand and neutral or positive affect. The mechanism operates at fast neural timescale (400–800ms during initial visual evaluation). Chinese observers rate open spaces as significantly more beautiful (p<0.001, η²=0.771), a pattern consistent with predictive processing. Openness is universal because the prediction-error signals that drive this mechanism reflect fundamental spatial navigation constraints built into human neurobiology across cultures.
Mechanism 3: Curvilinear Contours Modulate Complexity Preference in Context
The paper's most striking finding is context-dependent: Chinese observers prefer curvilinear (curved) contours only when ceilings are low and space is closed. In high-ceiling, open configurations, curvilinear preference disappears or reverses. This interaction points to predictive-processing mechanisms governing complexity preference. Curved, flowing forms are visually intermediate in complexity—more detailed than a bare rectilinear box, but less chaotic than a maximally ornate baroque interior. This intermediate complexity sits in the "Goldilocks zone" where prediction errors are resolvable and generate sustained engagement (Berlyne, 1960). However, when ceiling height is high and space is open—which already generate low arousal via peripersonal space expansion—adding curvilinear complexity may push the environment beyond the participant's optimal arousal level. A high, open space is already sufficiently interesting; adding curves can feel unnecessary or ornamental. Conversely, in a low-ceiling, closed space (already higher arousal, more constrained), curves introduce visual fluency and complexity that resolve prediction error. This explains why curvature preference is not universal but contingent on whether the broader spatial context is under-stimulating or over-stimulating.
Mechanism 4: Beauty Activates the Reward Prediction-Error Signal in the Ventral Tegmental Area
Beneath all aesthetic judgment sits a deeper neural signal: the dopamine neurons of the ventral tegmental area (VTA), which evolved to flag outcomes better than expected. When architecture reveals coherent, proportionate, and navigable structure—cues that signal "this environment is comprehensible and safe"—the VTA generates a dopamine burst that reinforces the aesthetic preference and embeds the space in memory. This is not a conscious judgment but a learning signal. High ceilings and open spaces signal low cognitive demand (prediction of ease); the brain treats finding such spaces as a mild reward, generating positive affect and approach. The mechanism operates at the fast neural timescale (200–300ms for initial dopamine burst). The reward-prediction account explains why beauty itself—the positive valence attached to architectural features—is partly universal (dopamine responds to structure and predictability across populations) and partly cultural (what structures seem "coherent" depends on childhood exposure to architectural styles). Chinese and Western observers both prefer high ceilings and openness, suggesting these are universally comprehensible.
What We Cannot Yet Explain at the Neural Level
Limitations and Open Questions 
Several features constrain the generalizability of these neural accounts. The sample had only 29 young, college-educated participants from one Chinese university, so the mechanisms may not generalize to older adults, people from different cultural-architectural backgrounds, or those with neurodevelopmental conditions (autism, ADHD). The stimuli were static 3-second images, not real buildings or extended immersive spaces, so researchers have not yet tested mechanisms involving sustained spatial navigation or long-duration peripersonal space changes. The three-way interaction between ceiling, openness, and contour also suggests missing variables—individual differences in spatial reasoning, autism traits, or cultural exposure to architectural styles may modulate the effects. The PNU cannot explain why curvilinear contour preference depends so strongly on ceiling and openness context, indicating a gap in neuroscience understanding.
Scope Conditions
When does this apply? Young, neurotypical adults; study examined ceiling height (high vs. low) in architectural images; measured via 3-second viewing and beauty ratings (1–5 scale). When does this apply? Neurotypical adults viewing static architectural images; study examined openness (open vs. closed floor plan) with 3-second exposure; measured via beauty and pleasantness ratings. When does this apply? Young adults; study examined contour curvature (curvilinear vs. rectilinear) in combination with ceiling height and spatial openness; effects depend on the interaction of all three factors.
Design Implications
For practitioners working in the built environment, these neural pathways identify specific environmental parameters whose manipulation produces measurable changes in brain processing. The evidence supports design decisions that account for the sensory, cognitive, and physiological consequences of architectural features on occupant wellbeing and performance.
*Falsification test*: What would weaken this explanation: If high ceiling effects on beauty ratings persisted when spatial-scale cues were removed (e.g., by blurring ceiling boundary information while keeping all other visual features), the peripersonal space mechanism would be undermined.
*Falsification test*: What would weaken this explanation: If the openness effect persisted when spatial cues were systematically removed (e.g., by eliminating visual pathways or sightlines while keeping the floor plan geometry identical), the prediction-error account would be questioned.

science_summary.core_finding: Kaplan argues that two crossing dimensions govern what people prefer in a scene. The first dimension asks how immediately the scene can be understood (present information, here right now) versus how much it promises to teach if explored further (inferred information, what lies past the visible edge). The second dimension is content: 2D surface patterns versus 3D spatial depth. Crossing those two dimensions yields four predictors: Coherence (how well the scene 'hangs together'. 2D, immediate); Complexity (how much is going on. 2D, exploratory); Legibility (how easy the scene would be to navigate and remember. 3D, immediate); and Mystery (how much the scene promises new content if you walked deeper into it. 3D, exploratory). Across dozens of studies, Mystery and Coherence are the strongest and most consistent predictors of preference. Complexity shows an inverted-U pattern -- people like moderate amounts. But content type swamps the Complexity effect when natural scenes go up against urban ones.
science_summary.methods_and_design: This is a theoretical paper, not an empirical study. Kaplan synthesises evidence from roughly 15 years of preference research, his own and others'. The papers he leans on most include Wohlwill (1968) on Complexity in urban vs. natural scenes; Kaplan et al. (1972) on content vs. Complexity as predictors of scenic preference; the Kaplans' (1982) *Humanscape* and *Cognition and Environment* on the information-processing model; Wohlwill (1976) on the Complexity-preference downturn for urban scenes; and R. Kaplan (1975, 1977) on nature preference across diverse populations. The paper reports no new data. The 2 × 2 matrix is reached by argument rather than by analysis -- the four predictors are derived logically from the two crossing dimensions and then matched against the prior literature for fit.
science_summary.design_implications: Kaplan's framework is among the most operationalised theories in architectural and landscape design. Mystery -- how much the scene promises if you walked further into it -- can be built in through winding paths, partial views, screening planting, and openings that reveal successive spatial layers. Consistent material palettes, clear spatial hierarchy, and repeating rhythms reinforce Coherence -- how easily the scene makes sense at a glance. Landmarks, differentiated zones, and vista points support Legibility -- how navigable and memorable a space looks. Complexity should be kept moderate, avoiding both bare minimalist corridors and cluttered retail interiors. The evolutionary frame gives designers a principled rationale: design for information gain, not just for beauty.
science_summary.limitations: The framework is post-hoc. Kaplan derived the 2 × 2 matrix to fit existing data patterns rather than testing it prospectively. The evolutionary claim -- that what we prefer reflects ancestral survival value -- is unfalsifiable as a just-so story without phylogenetic or cross-cultural experiments that pull apart cultural learning. Later work shows that Kaplan's predictors interact with expertise, familiarity, and cultural background in ways the 1987 frame does not address; farmers rate agricultural landscapes differently from city dwellers, for example. The visual-information frame also leaves out other sensory channels -- soundscapes, thermal comfort, smell -- that demonstrably shape what people prefer in a place. The model has been more successful as a design heuristic than as a testable scientific theory, which raises the open question of whether its predictive success reflects real cognitive machinery or post-hoc design intuition.

pnu.short_summary:
Why do some environments draw us in while others repel us? Stephen Kaplan's theoretical framework argues that environmental preference cannot be explained by a simple curve relating preference to complexity alone. Instead, he proposes that three mechanisms—cognition, affect, and evolutionary relevance—operate together when people encounter a landscape or built space.
Berlyne's classical finding—that preference for visual stimuli follows an inverted-U relationship with complexity—has a precise neural explanation rooted in how the brain learns. When a viewer encounters an environment, the visual cortex generates a prediction: "This space contains X amount of detail, symmetry, and visual hierarchy." If the environment is extremely simple (a blank white room), the prediction error is minimal—the brain rapidly learns the pattern, and within seconds, attention collapses into boredom. Predictive coding systems have nothing to learn from zero surprise.
When does this apply? Neurotypical adult observers of landscapes, buildings, and visual scenes. The mechanism operates at sub-second timescales during visual inspection and over 5–15 minute exposure windows before habituation. Preference is measured via explicit rating or implicit approach/avoidance behavior. Scope includes indoor and outdoor environments with controllable visual complexity. When does this apply? Same population. The affect-valence pathway operates on a timescale of hundreds of milliseconds (initial gist-based response) to sustained exposure (5+ minutes for affective state modulation).
What would weaken this explanation: If extremely simple and extremely complex environments were paired with high-valence content (animals, faces, threat signals), and preference increased toward the extremes rather than remaining intermediate, the Goldilocks mechanism would be undermined—complexity would be secondary to evolutionary salience. Conversely, if the environment is extremely complex (a maximally ornate baroque interior with competing focal points, broken symmetries, and unpredictable detail), the prediction errors are so large that the brain's generative model cannot absorb them efficiently. The system shifts to alarm mode, with scattered attention and negative affect.
pnu.long_summary: Kaplan proposes that environmental preference is governed by two orthogonal dimensions: (1) the degree to which a scene is immediately accessible to understanding (present information) versus the degree to which it promises further exploration (inferred/predicted information); and (2) the content dimension, subdivided into two-dimensional surface patterns versus three-dimensional spatial depth. Crossing these two dimensions produces four predictor variables: Coherence (how well the scene "hangs together" — 2D, immediate understanding), Complexity (how much is going on — 2D, exploratory engagement), Legibility (how easy the scene would be to navigate and remember — 3D, understanding), and Mystery (the degree to which the scene promises new information if one moves deeper into it — 3D, exploration). Empirically, Mystery and Coherence are the strongest and most consistent predictors of preference across dozens of studies; Complexity shows an inverted-U relationship (preferred at moderate levels) but is dominated by content when nature vs. urban scenes are compared. This is a theoretical paper, not an empirical study. Kaplan synthesizes evidence from approximately 15 years of environmental preference research (his own and others'), including: (a) Wohlwill (1968): Complexity and preference in urban vs. natural scenes; (b) Kaplan et al. (1972): content vs. Complexity as predictors of scenic preference; (c) Kaplan and Kaplan (1982): the information-processing model of preference from "Humanscape and Cognition and Environment"; (d) Wohlwill (1976): Complexity-preference downturn for urban scenes; (e) R. Kaplan (1975, 1977): nature preference across diverse populations. No new data are presented. The paper develops the theoretical model through argumentative synthesis, arriving at the 2 × 2 matrix by logical derivation from evolutionary-informational principles. No original statistics are reported in this theoretical paper. Kaplan references effect patterns from prior work: natural scenes are "so uniformly preferred over scenes of the built environment that only a single built environment scene (an urban park) was as preferred as the lowest rated natural scene" (Kaplan et al., 1972; referenced on page 5). Complexity showed "no predictive role" across all 56 scenes when content type was included. Within content domains, Complexity showed a "linear relationship" (natural scenes) or a "downturn" (urban scenes, Wohlwill 1976). Mystery was identified as the "single best predictor of preference" in multiple data sets. No figures, tables, or diagrams are included in the paper. The two-by-two preference schema (Coherence, Complexity, Legibility, Mystery) is presented as a textual description integrated into the argument, not as a formal table or diagram. This is characteristic of the essay-style theoretical writing in Environment and Behavior in the 1980s. Kaplan's framework has become one of the most operationalized theories in architectural and landscape design. Mystery — the degree to which a scene promises new information upon movement — can be engineered through winding pathways, partial views, screening vegetation, and strategically placed openings that reveal successive spatial layers. Coherence — the degree to which a scene makes sense at a glance — can be enhanced through consistent material palettes, clear spatial hierarchies, and repeating rhythms. Legibility — how navigable and memorable a space appears — can be supported through landmarks, differentiated zones, and vista points. Complexity — the richness and variety of elements — should be maintained at moderate levels, avoiding both sensory deprivation (minimalist corridors) and sensory overload (cluttered retail). The evolutionary framing gives designers a principled rationale: design for information gain, not just beauty. The framework is entirely post-hoc: the 2 × 2 matrix was derived to fit existing data patterns, not tested prospectively. The evolutionary claims (preference reflects ancestral survival value) are unfalsifiable just-so stories in the absence of phylogenetic or cross-cultural experiments that control for cultural learning. Subsequent research has shown that Kaplan's variables interact with expertise, familiarity, and cultural background in ways the 1987 framework does not address (e.g., farmers rate agricultural landscapes differently from urban dwellers). The visual-informational framing neglects other sensory channels — soundscapes, thermal comfort, olfactory experience — that substantially contribute to environmental preference. The model has been more influential as a design heuristic than as a testable scientific theory, raising the question of whether its predictive success reflects genuine cognitive mechanisms or post-hoc design intuition. The critical next test would be a neuroscience experiment using fMRI or EEG to determine whether scenes varying in Mystery, Coherence, Legibility, and Complexity differentially activate neural circuits associated with exploration motivation (nucleus accumbens, dopaminergic reward pathways) versus understanding/categorization (prefrontal cortex, hippocampal cognitive mapping). If Mystery preferentially activates reward-prediction circuitry and Legibility preferentially activates spatial-navigation circuitry, the 2 × 2 matrix would gain mechanistic grounding beyond behavioral preference ratings. Mechanism 1: Intermediate visual complexity triggers optimal prediction-error learning, explaining the inverted-U between complexity and preference (PP-GOLDILOCKS-003) Berlyne's classical finding—that preference for visual stimuli follows an inverted-U relationship with complexity—has a precise neural explanation rooted in how the brain learns. When a viewer encounters an environment, the visual cortex generates a prediction: "This space contains X amount of detail, symmetry, and visual hierarchy." If the environment is extremely simple (a blank white room), the prediction error is minimal—the brain rapidly learns the pattern, and within seconds, attention collapses into boredom. Predictive coding systems have nothing to learn from zero surprise. Conversely, if the environment is extremely complex (a maximally ornate baroque interior with competing focal points, broken symmetries, and unpredictable detail), the prediction errors are so large that the brain's generative model cannot absorb them efficiently. The system shifts to alarm mode, with scattered attention and negative affect. Optimal preference emerges in the intermediate zone: environments with sufficient visual structure and coherence to sustain prediction-error learning—new details emerge, but they follow comprehensible patterns—without overwhelming the system. In the predictive processing framework, this zone optimizes what neuroscientists call the "learning rate." Too much prediction error and learning stalls (the signal-to-noise ratio collapses); too little, and there is nothing to learn. The Goldilocks intermediate complexity region balances these demands. Salimpoor et al. (2011) demonstrated this in music: passages with intermediate rhythmic complexity (syncopation near the listener's statistical model) elicit robust dopamine release in nucleus accumbens and medial prefrontal cortex, whereas highly predictable or completely random passages do not. The same principle applies to visual environments. Güçlütürk et al. (2016) quantified image complexity using deep neural networks and found an inverted-U relationship between compression entropy and human aesthetic preference—intermediate entropy was most preferred. For architecture, this means spaces with visual rhythm, coherent material transitions, proportional relationships, and texture variation at multiple scales sustain engagement and positive affect, while either extreme (monotonous modernism or incoherent eclecticism) produces learned helplessness or anxiety. This mechanism is well-established (confidence: 73%). Berlyne's inverted-U has been replicated across stimuli domains (music, visual art, poetry). The predictive-processing account of why this occurs is strongly supported by neuroimaging and computational modeling. What remains incompletely mapped is the specific role of meaningful content in shifting the complexity-preference curve: does a simple room become more engaging if it contains evolutionarily relevant objects (animals, plants, social cues) versus inert geometric forms? Kaplan's framework predicts yes, but the neural mechanism (enhanced prediction-error sensitivity for evolutionary-relevant content) has not been directly tested in the context of environmental complexity. When does this apply? Neurotypical adult observers of landscapes, buildings, and visual scenes. The mechanism operates at sub-second timescales during visual inspection and over 5–15 minute exposure windows before habituation. Preference is measured via explicit rating or implicit approach/avoidance behavior. Scope includes indoor and outdoor environments with controllable visual complexity. Mechanism 2: Architectural coherence generates positive affect by signaling low metabolic demand to the brain's body-budget prediction system (IC-AFFECT-VALENCE-002) Affect—the continuous experience of valence (pleasant to aversive) and arousal (calm to agitated)—is not a response to beauty; it is a prediction. According to predictive processing theories of emotion (Barrett, 2017; Damasio, 1999), the anterior insula and anterior cingulate cortex constitute the brain's body-budget prediction system. These regions maintain an internal model of what the body will need in the near future: energy, hydration, sleep, social contact, safety. When an environment enters perception, the brain's visual and spatial systems immediately query this body-budget model: "How much metabolic work will this environment demand?" A proportionally coherent classical façade with regular fenestration, readable structural logic, and harmonic color generates a prediction of low cognitive demand and navigable structure. This prediction of low cost generates positive affect and approach behavior. A chaotic or threat-signaling architecture—broken symmetries, unpredictable material transitions, harsh contrast, visible decay—predicts high cognitive and metabolic demand. This generates negative affect and avoidance. The mechanism is not perceptual acuity; it is prediction error within the body-budget system. Bies et al. (2016) found that environments with fractal-like self-similarity (natural landscapes, classical architecture) produce lower reported cognitive load and more positive affect than non-fractal designs. The reason is that fractals—structures that repeat the same pattern at multiple scales—allow efficient visual sampling. The brain can predict what comes next because the pattern holds across scales. This efficient prediction is experienced as aesthetic pleasure.

pnu.short_summary:
Why are some people devastated by open-office noise while others work productively in the middle of conversational chaos? The answer lies in how your brain processes patterns. This study identified that individuals with strong global sequence-processing ability suffer greater performance impairment from irrelevant speech and office noise — not because their hearing is better, but because their cognitive system is tuned to automatically extract temporal structure from sound.
Individuals high in local processing focus on specific acoustic features — phoneme boundaries, individual words, discrete acoustic segments — rather than broad temporal relationships. This detail-focused cognitive style engages different neural pathways. The primary auditory cortex (Heschl's gyrus) continues to receive the acoustic input, but the connections to the superior temporal sulcus (which specializes in temporal pattern extraction) operate with lower gain in local processors.
When does this apply? Neurotypical adults in laboratory conditions with controlled irrelevant speech and office noise. The study examined serial recall and working memory performance under acoustic distraction. Global sequence processing is a stable cognitive trait measurable across populations, though expression varies by individual differences in attention control and task engagement. What would weaken this explanation: If global processors showed equivalent distraction by noise even when the auditory input was spectrally scrambled (removing temporal structure while preserving loudness and overall acoustic properties), the proposed temporal-pattern-detection pathway would be undermined.
For practitioners, these findings identify specific environmental parameters that engage measurable neural pathways. The evidence suggests that design decisions affecting the features studied in this paper have consequences that reach beyond subjective preference into quantifiable changes in brain processing, stress physiology, and cognitive performance. Designers should consider the neural evidence when specifying environmental conditions, particularly for occupant populations that may be more sensitive to the mechanisms described.

Several important questions remain unresolved in this research domain. How much would change in our understanding if future research addressed these gaps with controlled longitudinal designs, larger and more diverse samples, and validated outcome measures across multiple environmental contexts?
Finding 1: Global sequence processing ability predicts disruptibility from irrelevant speech and office noise (p = 0.05) When a globally oriented individual enters an open office, their brain's auditory cortex processes the ambient speech as a rich source of temporal patterns — rhythm, prosody, intonation contours, and sequential structure. The superior temporal sulcus (the brain region specialized for extracting temporal and sequential information from sound) automatically detects these patterns without conscious effort. This automatic pattern detection activates the anterior insula (the brain's salience hub that marks unexpected or task-relevant information), which compares the acoustic input against current behavioral goals. When the brain detects task-irrelevant patterns in speech, the anterior cingulate cortex (a region that monitors conflicts between task demands and intrusive information) signals this mismatch. The noradrenaline system in the locus coeruleus responds to this conflict signal by releasing noradrenaline throughout the prefrontal cortex, which attempts to suppress the intrusive representation. However, the stronger the global sequence-processing trait, the more readily the superior temporal sulcus continues to extract new patterns from the speech stream, creating an ongoing cycle of pattern detection, conflict detection, and suppression attempts. This continuous reallocation of cognitive control resources depletes working memory capacity available for the primary task. Current evidence rates this mechanism at 72% confidence (plausible but not yet fully empirically integrated). The component processes are individually well-established in neuroscience, but the specific cascade from global processing trait through pattern detection to working memory depletion has not been mapped in a single integrated study. When does this apply? Neurotypical adults in laboratory conditions with controlled irrelevant speech and office noise. The study examined serial recall and working memory performance under acoustic distraction. Global sequence processing is a stable cognitive trait measurable across populations, though expression varies by individual differences in attention control and task engagement.
Finding 2: Local sequence processing ability does not predict disruptibility from irrelevant sound (p nonsignificant) Individuals high in local processing focus on specific acoustic features — phoneme boundaries, individual words, discrete acoustic segments — rather than broad temporal relationships. This detail-focused cognitive style engages different neural pathways. The primary auditory cortex (Heschl's gyrus) continues to receive the acoustic input, but the connections to the superior temporal sulcus (which specializes in temporal pattern extraction) operate with lower gain in local processors. This reduced temporal-pattern extraction means the amygdala (the brain's rapid threat detector) receives less continuously updated pattern information, and consequently produces fewer salience signals to the anterior insula about "unexpected patterns emerging." The dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (the brain's executive control center) maintains focus on the serial recall task because the intrusive auditory information never coalesces into distracting patterns that trigger the conflict monitoring system. Local processors do experience the acoustic environment as present and potentially irritating, but the cognitive pathways required for working memory distraction are not activated to the same degree. Their working memory remains protected because the auditory information does not recruit the temporal-pattern-detection machinery that would compete for limited cognitive resources. Current evidence rates this mechanism at 65% confidence (plausible but less directly tested than the global processing pathway). The baseline architecture — that local processors activate different cortical regions — is well-established, but the specific prediction that reduced temporal-pattern-gain explains immunity to distraction requires direct empirical validation. When does this apply? Neurotypical adults; specifically those scoring high on local/detail-focused processing styles on standardized cognitive assessments. The protective effect emerges in laboratory settings with irrelevant speech and office noise; application to real open-office environments depends on whether the acoustic complexity remains moderate enough that local processors can maintain focus without exceeding cognitive load from the task itself.
