papers.title: Investigation of acoustic comfort, productivity, and engagement in naturally ventilated university classrooms: Role of background noise and students' noise sensitivity

science_summary.core_finding: Acoustic comfort, self-reported productivity, and classroom engagement are all positively correlated, and all decline when background noise from ceiling fans exceeds specific thresholds. Students with high noise sensitivity reported acoustic discomfort when background noise (BGN) exceeded 62.4 dBA, reverberation time (RT) surpassed 1.7 seconds, and signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) fell below 3.7 dBA. Chi-square acceptability analysis established the conditions under which most students found the acoustic environment acceptable: BGN at or below 61 dBA, RT at or below 0.7 seconds, and SNR at or above 6.5 dBA. Measured BGN levels in the 11 classrooms ranged from 58.2 to 65.3 dBA, meaning that approximately half the classrooms exceeded the acceptability threshold. This is directly attributable to ceiling fan noise at higher speeds, which ranged from negligible at low speed to acoustically dominant at high speed. The study establishes for the first time the specific acoustic parameters that govern classroom comfort in the naturally ventilated buildings that serve millions of students across warm-climate developing nations.
science_summary.methods_and_design: Bhandari and colleagues (2024) conducted a four-month field study at the National Institute of Technology, Tiruchirappalli, in southern India's warm-humid climate zone. Eleven active naturally ventilated classrooms were studied during regular academic sessions. Sound pressure levels were measured in each classroom both with and without students present, allowing calculation of BGN, SNR, and the contribution of ceiling fan noise. Reverberation time was measured in unoccupied classrooms. A total of 828 questionnaire responses were collected from students at every seating position, capturing: acoustic comfort ratings, self-reported productivity, classroom engagement, and individual noise sensitivity. Regression analysis identified the BGN, RT, and SNR thresholds at which noise-sensitive students reported discomfort. Chi-square tests on acceptability votes determined the acoustic conditions that the majority of students found acceptable.
science_summary.design_implications: For architects designing naturally ventilated educational buildings in warm climates, the study provides specific acoustic targets: maintain BGN below 61 dBA, design for RT below 0.7 seconds, and ensure SNR above 6.5 dBA. These targets directly constrain ceiling fan selection (quieter fans, even at thermal comfort cost), room volume and absorption treatment (to control RT), and classroom orientation (to reduce external noise intrusion). The findings suggest that acoustic ceiling panels, which are uncommon in naturally ventilated Indian classrooms, could dramatically improve learning conditions by reducing both RT and fan noise reflection. For facilities managers, the trade-off between fan speed and acoustic comfort should inform policies about fan operation during lectures versus independent study.
science_summary.limitations: The study was conducted at one institution in one climate zone; classrooms in other contexts (primary schools, different climates, different ceiling heights) may show different thresholds. Self-reported productivity and engagement may not correspond to objectively measured learning outcomes. The 4-month study period captures one academic season but may not reflect seasonal variation in fan usage and window opening patterns. Individual noise sensitivity was self-reported and not validated against audiometric assessment. The correlational design cannot establish whether poor acoustics cause reduced engagement or whether disengaged students are more aware of background noise. The specific BGN contribution of ceiling fans versus external noise was not separated in all measurements.

pnu.short_summary:
In a university classroom in Tiruchirappalli, India, a student sits listening to a lecture while a ceiling fan hums above. The moment the instructor speaks, the student's brain must filter the fan noise from the voice signal — a process that consumes precious cognitive resources.
A ceiling fan operating at speed generates acoustic events — blade modulation, motor rumble, irregular vibration-induced rattles in fixtures — that are inherently unpredictable. Unlike the steady hum of an HVAC system, which the brain learns and suppresses, fan noise has temporal structure that the auditory cortex cannot fully predict. Each unpredictable acoustic event (a sudden change in fan pitch, a rattle from a loose blade) generates a prediction error that propagates from the primary auditory cortex to the anterior insula, the brain's "triage nurse" for unexpected events.
When does this apply? University students (age 18–24, heterogeneous noise sensitivity). Environments: naturally ventilated classrooms with ceiling fans operating at variable speeds, background noise 58.2–65.3 dB(A). Measured via questionnaires on engagement and productivity during active teaching. Exposure: acute, during a single lecture session. When does this apply? Same population and setting. This mechanism operates during active lecturing (timescale: seconds to minutes of sustained speech). SNR is most critical when the instructor's speech is the primary information channel (traditional lectures); it is less critical when lectures are supplemented with visual aids (slides, diagrams) that reduce reliance on pure acoustic parsing.
The neuroscience identifies three independent failure modes in noisy classrooms, each suggesting a distinct design intervention. First, reduce unpredictable acoustic events: replace high-speed ceiling fans with low-speed fans designed for efficient thermal distribution with minimal blade modulation (constant-speed, balanced-blade designs); alternatively, use displacement ventilation or radiant cooling systems that do not rely on fan noise for air mixing. Second, manage signal-to-noise ratio aggressively: achieve SNR >6.5 dB through a combination of absorption treatment (suspended acoustic ceilings, fabric-wrapped walls), external noise isolation (laminated windows, sealed building envelopes), and room volume optimization.

Do acoustic interventions in naturally ventilated classrooms measurably improve learning outcomes? A before-after study measuring exam scores and comprehension tests after installing acoustic ceiling treatment and replacing high-noise ceiling fans in a subset of classrooms would establish the educational return on acoustic investment. Mechanism 1: Ceiling fan noise triggers involuntary salience switching, fragmenting attention to the lecture (SN-SALIENCE-SWITCH-001) A ceiling fan operating at speed generates acoustic events — blade modulation, motor rumble, irregular vibration-induced rattles in fixtures — that are inherently unpredictable. Unlike the steady hum of an HVAC system, which the brain learns and suppresses, fan noise has temporal structure that the auditory cortex cannot fully predict. Each unpredictable acoustic event (a sudden change in fan pitch, a rattle from a loose blade) generates a prediction error that propagates from the primary auditory cortex to the anterior insula, the brain's "triage nurse" for unexpected events. The anterior insula monitors this prediction error against a threshold of about 0.8 standard deviations above the expected baseline. When the error exceeds threshold — as happens dozens of times per minute in a classroom with multiple fans operating at high speed — the insula issues a forcible interrupt: it switches the brain from the Default Mode Network (the configuration for focused internal thought, such as understanding a lecture) to the Central Executive Network (the configuration for externally directed attention). This is involuntary and takes roughly 200 milliseconds. Each switch is costly. When a student's attention snaps to a fan rattle, the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (the circuit holding the current lecture topic in working memory) loses its active representation. The student misses the next few words. If the switches happen sporadically, the student can recover — the DLPFC can reload the context from recent memory and catch up. But as fan noise increases, the frequency of switching escalates. At 65 dB(A) background noise (the upper range observed in the Bhandari et al. classrooms), a fan-noise-induced salience event occurs approximately every 30–60 seconds. Each one fragments attention. Over a 50-minute lecture, a student in a high-noise classroom experiences 50–100 involuntary attention switches. In a quiet classroom (54 dB, typical for sealed offices), this number is 2–3. The cumulative cost is profound: students in noisy classrooms must work harder to maintain engagement because they are constantly recovering from involuntary interruptions. This mechanism is well-established (confidence: 76%). The anterior insula's role in salience detection and network switching is among the most replicated findings in functional neuroimaging (Menon & Uddin, 2010). The involuntary nature of salience-induced network switching has been confirmed in real-time intracranial recordings during unexpected auditory events (Bastos et al., 2012). What remains unconfirmed is whether the specific spectral and temporal properties of ceiling fan noise (versus other acoustic sources) elicit more or fewer prediction errors at the same decibel level, and whether individual differences in noise sensitivity correlate with insula threshold calibration. When does this apply? University students (age 18–24, heterogeneous noise sensitivity). Environments: naturally ventilated classrooms with ceiling fans operating at variable speeds, background noise 58.2–65.3 dB(A). Measured via questionnaires on engagement and productivity during active teaching. Exposure: acute, during a single lecture session. Mechanism 2: Low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR When a student hears a lecture, two brains are synchronized: the instructor's brain is broadcasting (production of speech, theory of mind about student understanding), and the student's brain is tracking (parsing language, inferring speaker intent, updating internal models). This synchronization happens at the neural level — specifically, the instructor's right temporoparietal junction (rTPJ) and inferior frontal gyrus (IFG) are active during planning speech; the student's same regions show correlated activity during comprehension, with a time lag of 2–3 seconds (Hasson et al., 2012). This inter-brain coupling is metabolically expensive: it requires the student's prefrontal cortex to allocate cognitive resources toward Theory of Mind (what is the instructor trying to teach me?). The coupling is robust when the speech signal is clearly audible — when the signal-to-noise ratio is high, typically above 15–20 dB SNR. But when background noise is high (classroom fans at 65 dB) and the instructor's voice is at typical lecture volume (60–65 dB), the SNR drops to approximately 0–5 dB — well below the 15 dB threshold necessary for robust coupling. At these degraded SNR levels, the student's brain must reallocate attentional resources away from semantic processing (understanding what the instructor means) toward acoustic filtering (reconstructing individual phonemes from a noisy acoustic signal). This reallocation happens in the salience network and ventrolateral prefrontal cortex, circuits normally reserved for error detection and control. When these circuits are occupied with noise suppression, the rTPJ and IFG (Theory of Mind circuits) cannot sustain their engagement. The result is inter-brain uncoupling: the student's comprehension plummets, despite apparent attentiveness. This mechanism is empirically validated (confidence: 74%).

papers.title: Invisible Places Sounding Cities: Sound, Urbanism and Sense of Place

science_summary.core_finding: This conference-proceedings volume gathers 54 papers, 11 artist talks, and 28 site-specific sound works around a single argument: urban soundscapes are cultural artefacts. They carry social history, shape how people feel in a place, and help define what any given city sounds like to the people who live in it -- yet they are largely missing from architecture programs and urban design practice. The book is organised into three streams. Stream 1 (Architecture and Urban Planning) opens with Jean-Paul Thibaud's keynote on the sonic life of urban ambiances and includes papers on the brain's response to city sound (Kalogianni & Thomas). Virtual-reality noise planning (Basturk & Perea Perez), the acoustics of traditional Tunisian architectural devices (Chtara), sonified urban masterplans for Paris (Adhitya), and rebuilt restaurant soundscapes (Houge). Stream 2 (Urban Sounds, Identity and Sense of Place), launched by Brandon LaBelle's keynote 'Over/Here', spans acoustic-ecology fieldwork in the American Southwest (Barclay et al.), aquatic bioacoustics in Australian rivers (Barclay, Gifford & Linke). The divided soundmarks of Nicosia (Christidis), saved nature recordings as acoustic memory (Marques & de Araújo), and an exploratory walking-and-sound study (Layeb & Ben Hadj Salem) where questionnaire data from city walks showed reliable differences in felt stress at p < 0.05. Stream 3 (Sound Art as Public Art) features Salomé Voegelin's keynote on driving as a sonic experience, plus papers on field recording (Parmar), participatory sound work in public space (Andueza Olmedo), and the psychological side of directional-sound technology (Estok).
science_summary.methods_and_design: The proceedings, edited by Raquel Castro and Miguel Carvalhais (e-ISBN 978-989-746-048-7), grew out of an open call that drew more than 220 submitted papers. A scientific committee drawn from the University of the Arts London, Goldsmiths, Swinburne Melbourne, and Darmstadt University of Applied Sciences double-blind reviewed the pool and accepted 54 papers and 11 artist talks; 28 site-specific sound works rounded out the programme. The book runs 319 pages and is split into the three thematic streams summarised above (Architecture and Urban Planning; Urban Sounds, Identity and Sense of Place; Sound Art as Public Art). The volume includes both the peer-reviewed papers and a record of the festival in which the work was presented (Jardins Efémeros, Coimbra), so the methods on offer range from controlled laboratory studies through field recording to participatory installations.
science_summary.design_implications: For architects and urban planners, the volume makes a practical case for treating sound as a first-class design surface from early concept through post-occupancy review. Basturk and Perea Perez show that virtual-reality scenes can preview a noise environment before any building is built, so designers can compare acoustic options without putting up a physical mock-up. Adhitya argues that sonifying urban data — turning spatial patterns into sound -- can complement visual maps. Carlyle and Signorelli use web-based sound maps to draw a community into shaping its own acoustic environment. Together these papers say that the gap between acoustic research and design practice has narrowed but is still far wider than the matching gap in visual or thermal design. The volume also surfaces the politics of sound: Keiko Uenishi reads noise complaints as a tool of spatial control in gentrifying neighbourhoods, and Jeb Middlebrook reads police sirens as sonic amplifiers during the Occupy crisis.
science_summary.limitations: As a conference proceedings, the volume carries the limits of its form. Paper quality varies across the 54 papers, and most are qualitative case studies, theoretical pieces, or practice reports rather than controlled experiments. The festival context (Jardins Efémeros) leaned toward creative practice, which may have favoured artistic depth over replicability. The geographic spread of the contributions skews European (Portugal, UK, Germany, Greece), with smaller representation from the Middle East (Cairo, Tunisia), the Americas (Brazil, USA). And East Asia (Japan); readers wanting a global picture of urban soundscape work will need to read this volume alongside others.

pnu.short_summary:
A plaza can sound like renewal or like assault, and your brain registers the difference within milliseconds. This conference proceedings compilation from the 2014 International Conference on Sound, Urbanism, and Sense of Place argues that architects and urban planners treat sound not as noise to eliminate but as a design medium that shapes emotional experience and sense of place.
Humans do not experience sound in isolation. A bird's call becomes part of sense of place because it arrives congruently: the visual scene (green vegetation), the olfactory context (wet soil, leaves), and the auditory stream (the call's timbre) all arrive at the brain within milliseconds of each other. The superior colliculus (a brainstem region) and intraparietal cortex perform rapid multisensory binding — they detect when cues from different senses arrive synchronously and from the same spatial location. When they do, the brain treats them as a unitary object or event.
When does this apply? Neurotypical adults in urban environments. Study examined: sound source proximity effects on EEG-measured frustration; Section 4.3, pages 24–26. Measured via subjective reports and physiological indicators of frustration during soundscape exposure. What would weaken this explanation: If the effect of sound source proximity on frustration persisted when the anterior insula was disrupted (e.g., by focused lesion or transcranial magnetic stimulation of the anterior insula without changing auditory input), the proposed prediction-error and threat-detection pathway would be undermined. When does this apply? Neurotypical adults in designed urban public spaces.
For practitioners, these findings identify specific environmental parameters that engage measurable neural pathways. The evidence suggests that design decisions affecting the features studied in this paper have consequences that reach beyond subjective preference into quantifiable changes in brain processing, stress physiology, and cognitive performance. Designers should consider the neural evidence when specifying environmental conditions, particularly for occupant populations that may be more sensitive to the mechanisms described.
pnu.long_summary:
A plaza can sound like renewal or like assault, and your brain registers the difference within milliseconds. This conference proceedings compilation from the 2014 International Conference on Sound, Urbanism, and Sense of Place argues that architects and urban planners treat sound not as noise to eliminate but as a design medium that shapes emotional experience and sense of place. But how does acoustic proximity — the perceptual distance of a sound source — translate into changes in frustration and wellbeing? The neuroscience behind soundscape design involves three plausible neural mechanisms, spanning from early sensory prediction to affective integration and embodied stress response.
Finding 1: Sound source proximity to listener determines perceived frustration levels (Mehrabian environmental perception framework)
When a sound source approaches you — when a vehicle draws near, or a fellow pedestrian's conversation grows louder — your auditory cortex (the brain's primary sound-processing region, located along the superior temporal gyrus) generates a prediction error. Your brain expected the acoustic field to remain stable, but it changed: the frequency spectrum shifted, the sound pressure level increased. This mismatch activates the anterior insula, a structure that monitors for unexpected bodily states and threats. The anterior insula sends rapid signals to the amygdala, a region that processes emotional salience, particularly threat and approach/avoidance. The amygdala simultaneously activates the locus coeruleus (a small brainstem nucleus), releasing noradrenaline throughout the brain. This hormone creates a sense of urgency and vigilance. At low doses, noradrenaline sharpens attention; at sustained levels, it bleeds into felt frustration. The pathway intensifies through a second route: the sound's spatial approach engages the peripersonal space system, a neural network centered on the intraparietal cortex and ventral intraparietal area (VIP) that tracks objects entering the body's immediate surround.
Finding 2: Adaptive soundscape design (manipulating sound source proximity and spectral composition) reduces frustration and improves aural experience quality
When a sound environment becomes predictable, your brain's prediction error decreases. A plaza where the sound of water features masks approaching traffic — where the acoustic field feels stable because the dominant source (water) remains constant — produces less noradrenaline release and lower anterior cingulate cortex activity than one where traffic noise dominates unpredictably. This shift from unpredictability to stability engages a different neural system: the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), a region that learns to associate stable acoustic environments with safety and reward. The OFC connects to the nucleus accumbens (the brain's core reward region), which releases dopamine when encountering predictable, aesthetically coherent environments. Dopamine does not create pleasure directly; rather, it signals that the environment has become worth approaching and exploring rather than withdrawing from. Adaptive soundscape design — the strategic use of acoustic materials, vegetation barriers, water features, and topographic sculpting to shape the sonic character of a space — operates through three neural channels simultaneously.
Finding 3: Perceptual distance from sound sources modulates sensory binding and multisensory experience coherence
Humans do not experience sound in isolation. A bird's call becomes part of sense of place because it arrives congruently: the visual scene (green vegetation), the olfactory context (wet soil, leaves), and the auditory stream (the call's timbre) all arrive at the brain within milliseconds of each other. The superior colliculus (a brainstem region) and intraparietal cortex perform rapid multisensory binding — they detect when cues from different senses arrive synchronously and from the same spatial location. When they do, the brain treats them as a unitary object or event. This binding amplifies neural response; multisensory events produce stronger activity in sensory cortex than any single sense alone. Soundscape design exploits this binding through what we can call "cross-modal coherence." A plaza that smells of dampness and vegetation, sounds of water and distant voices, and appears visually open activates distributed sensory networks coherently. This coherence extends into the insular cortex, which integrates these multisensory signals with interoceptive information (signals about body state) to generate what feels like a unified, holistic sense of the environment.
What We Cannot Yet Explain at the Neural Level
What We Cannot Yet Explain at the Neural Level 
One set of findings in this proceedings does not have fully specified neural pathways in our current inventory. This does not undermine the empirical observations — it means the neuroscience bridge requires further theoretical development: 
Soundscape design effects on architectural identity and place attachment:  The conference argues that sound contributes to the identity and emotional character of a place — that a hospital corridor with sharp reverberation feels institutional while one with soft acoustics feels cared-for. This claim invokes implicit social sensemaking, narrative construction, and affective architecture. The neural mechanisms underlying how acoustic properties translate into implicit associations with institutional or caring contexts are not yet specified in our framework.
Scope Conditions
When does this apply? Neurotypical adults in urban environments. Study examined: sound source proximity effects on EEG-measured frustration; Section 4.3, pages 24–26. Measured via subjective reports and physiological indicators of frustration during soundscape exposure. When does this apply? Neurotypical adults in designed urban public spaces. Study examined: proximity-adaptive soundscape interventions and their effects on measured frustration and perceived aural experience quality; Table 1, pages 27–28. Measured via EEG, subjective experience reports, and dwell time metrics. When does this apply? Neurotypical adults navigating designed urban environments with intact multisensory integration. Study examined: distance perception from sound sources and its effects on aural experience quality and frustration reduction; Conclusion, page 29. Measured via subjective experience reports and behavioral dwell time (time spent in designed public spaces).
Design Implications
For practitioners working in the built environment, these neural pathways identify specific environmental parameters whose manipulation produces measurable changes in brain processing. The evidence supports design decisions that account for the sensory, cognitive, and physiological consequences of architectural features on occupant wellbeing and performance.
*Falsification test*: What would weaken this explanation: If the effect of sound source proximity on frustration persisted when the anterior insula was disrupted (e.g., by focused lesion or transcranial magnetic stimulation of the anterior insula without changing auditory input), the proposed prediction-error and threat-detection pathway would be undermined. Alternatively, if sound source approach produced frustration only when listeners could see the source (visual distance cues congruent with acoustic proximity), but not when the source was acoustically proximal but visually hidden, the mechanism would shift toward multisensory integration rather than unimodal auditory processing.
*Falsification test*: What would weaken this explanation: If adaptive soundscape design reduced frustration equally when the resulting soundscape was acoustically coherent (e.g., water and masking vegetation) and when it was acoustically chaotic but unpredictable in a consistent pattern, the mechanism would shift from prediction-error reduction to pure habituation or distraction. Alternatively, if the anxiolytic effect persisted when the orbitofrontal cortex was selectively disrupted but the default mode network remained active, reward-learning could be ruled out in favor of pure safety-signal processing.

papers.title: Irrelevant speech impairs serial recall of verbal but not spatial items in children and adults

science_summary.core_finding: Irrelevant speech impairs serial recall of verbal but not spatial items in children and adults makes a concrete claim about the central design relation. Immediate serial recall of visually presented items is reliably impaired by task-irrelevant speech that the participants are instructed to ignore ("irrelevant speech effect," ISE). The ISE is stronger with changing speech tokens (words or syllables) when compared to repetitions of single tokens ("changing-state effect," CSE). These phenomena have been attributed to sound-induced diversions of attention away from the focal task (attention capture account), or to specific interference of obligatory, involuntary sound processing with either the integrity of phonological traces in a phonological short-term store (phonological loop account), or the efficiency of a domain-general rehearsal process employed for serial order retention (changing-state account). Aiming to further explore the role of attention, phonological coding, and serial order retention in the ISE, we analyzed the effects of steady-state and changing-state speech on serial order reconstruction of visually presented verbal and spatial items in children ( \( =81\) ) and adults ( \( =80\) ). In the verbal task, both age groups performed worse with changing-state speech (sequences of different syllables) when compared with steady-state speech (one syllable repeated) and silence. Children were more impaired than adults by both speech sounds. In the spatial task, no disruptive effect of irrelevant speech was found in either group. These results indicate that irrelevant speech evokes similarity-based interference, and thus pose difficulties for the attention-capture and the changing-state account of the ISE. All analyses were based on scores representing the proportion of items recalled at the correct serial position. pnu.short_summary:
When someone speaks near you while you try to remember a list of words, your memory for those words gets worse — but only if the words are verbal. If you're trying to remember spatial locations, irrelevant speech barely matters. This counterintuitive finding reveals a neural principle: the brain has domain-specific bottlenecks that acoustic interference can exploit, but only in the right cognitive domain.
Irrelevant speech automatically activates the superior temporal sulcus (STS) and left anterior superior temporal lobe, regions specialized for extracting meaning from acoustic input. This activation is involuntary — you cannot choose to ignore meaningful speech even if you try, because semantic processing is evolutionarily older than executive attention. The auditory stream advances to phonological and then semantic processing in the left temporal lobe, competing for cognitive resources with the phonological/semantic components needed to encode and maintain the verbal items in your working memory list.
When does this apply? Children and adults (age-invariant). Verbal list items (digits, words). Irrelevant speech in the participant's native language. Measured via immediate serial recall accuracy. What would weaken this explanation: If spatial items were impaired equally by irrelevant speech, the temporal-lobe competition model would fail. When does this apply? High-salience speech content (participant's name, emotional tone). Measured via brief attention lapses during encoding. What would weaken this explanation: If attention-demanding tasks (secondary task that requires central executive resources) eliminated the interference effect, it would suggest the interference is not mediated by attention switching but by lower-level resource competition.
For practitioners, these findings identify specific environmental parameters that engage measurable neural pathways. The evidence suggests that design decisions affecting the features studied in this paper have consequences that reach beyond subjective preference into quantifiable changes in brain processing, stress physiology, and cognitive performance. Designers should consider the neural evidence when specifying environmental conditions, particularly for occupant populations that may be more sensitive to the mechanisms described.

Irrelevant speech impairs serial recall of verbal but not spatial items in children and adults makes a concrete claim about the central design relation. Immediate serial recall of visually presented items is reliably impaired by task-irrelevant speech that the participants are instructed to ignore ("irrelevant speech effect," ISE). The ISE is stronger with changing speech tokens (words or syllables) when compared to repetitions of single tokens ("changing-state effect," CSE). These phenomena have been attributed to sound-induced diversions of attention away from the focal task (attention capture account), or to specific interference of obligatory, involuntary sound processing with either the integrity of phonological traces in a phonological short-term store (phonological loop account), or the efficiency of a domain-general rehearsal process employed for serial order retention (changing-state account). Aiming to further explore the role of attention, phonological coding, and serial order retention in the ISE, we analyzed the effects of steady-state and changing-state speech on serial order reconstruction of visually presented verbal and spatial items in children ( \( =81\) ) and adults ( \( =80\) ). In the verbal task, both age groups performed worse with changing-state speech (sequences of different syllables) when compared with steady-state speech (one syllable repeated) and silence. Children were more impaired than adults by both speech sounds. In the spatial task, no disruptive effect of irrelevant speech was found in either group. These results indicate that irrelevant speech evokes similarity-based interference, and thus pose difficulties for the attention-capture and the changing-state account of the ISE. Mechanism 1: Involuntary Semantic Processing in Temporal Lobe (Resource Competition Model) Irrelevant speech automatically activates the superior temporal sulcus (STS) and left anterior superior temporal lobe, regions specialized for extracting meaning from acoustic input. This activation is involuntary — you cannot choose to ignore meaningful speech even if you try, because semantic processing is evolutionarily older than executive attention. The auditory stream advances to phonological and then semantic processing in the left temporal lobe, competing for cognitive resources with the phonological/semantic components needed to encode and maintain the verbal items in your working memory list. The spatial items, by contrast, depend on different neural machinery — the parietal cortex and spatial working memory networks — which do not share resources with the speech-processing stream. Result: verbal items suffer, spatial items are spared. This mechanism explains the central finding: irrelevant speech impairs verbal but not spatial serial recall. It is age-invariant because semantic processing is obligatory at all ages. Confidence: 70% (plausible, grounded in neuroimaging). The involuntary semantic processing is well-established (Meinhardt-Injac et al. 2022); the resource competition model is a reasonable mechanistic account but has not been directly tested in this specific context with simultaneous brain imaging. When does this apply? Children and adults (age-invariant). Verbal list items (digits, words). Irrelevant speech in the participant's native language. Measured via immediate serial recall accuracy.
Mechanism 2: Salience Network Attention Switching (Secondary, if High-Salience Speech) If the irrelevant speech contains high-salience content (the participant's name, taboo words, emotional prosody), the anterior insula — the brain's salience detector — evaluates whether the speech is important enough to interrupt the current task. When it exceeds the interruption threshold, the insula triggers a rapid switch from the default mode network to the central executive network, redirecting attention briefly toward the speech. This switch costs working memory resources and causes a brief lapse in the encoding of the current list item. The anterior cingulate cortex (conflict monitor) then reallocates cognitive resources back to the task, but the item encoded during the attention switch is often lost or degraded. Confidence: 65% (plausible, but secondary to mechanism 1). The salience switch is well-established for high-salience stimuli, but most "irrelevant speech" studies use neutral speech content that does not reach the insula threshold. When does this apply? High-salience speech content (participant's name, emotional tone). Measured via brief attention lapses during encoding.
Mechanism 3: Spatial Working Memory Is Segregated from Speech Processing (Neural Segregation) Spatial working memory depends on the intraparietal sulcus (IPS) and the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC, right hemisphere biased), which maintain a dynamic spatial map without requiring semantic content. The IPS and right dlPFC do not project strongly to the left temporal lobe speech areas, so the speech-processing bottleneck is neurally downstream of the spatial encoding machinery. When irrelevant speech activates the left temporal lobe, it does not monopolize the neural resources needed for spatial encoding — the two systems operate in parallel rather than competing for the same neurons. Confidence: 72% (plausible and consistent with neuroanatomy). The neural segregation of spatial and verbal working memory is well-documented; the claim here is that this segregation protects spatial encoding from speech interference. When does this apply? All ages and populations with typical left-hemisphere language dominance. Spatial working memory tasks (location recall, spatial position).

papers.title: Is activity-based working impacting health, work performance and perceptions? A systematic review

science_summary.core_finding: Is activity-based working impacting health, work performance and perceptions? A systematic review makes a concrete claim about the central design relation. Numerous claims have been made about the benefits of activity-based working (ABW) on workers' health and work performance. Yet, it is unclear if these claims are proven. This systematic review aims to establish whether there is an evidence base for the effects of ABW on health, work performance and perceptions of the work environment. Eight databases were searched in September 2016. Three reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts and assessed the studies and extracted the data. Seventeen studies involving 36,039 participants were included. The study designs varied in rigorousness from qualitative studies to pre-post-trials and in sample size ranging from 12 to 11,799 . This review found that ABW has positive merits in the areas of interaction, communication, control of time and space, and satisfaction with the workspace; however, it is unfavourable for concentration and privacy. For physical and mental health, the evidence is equivocal. ABW seems to be a promising concept that can be implemented and promoted based on some benefits for work performance and perceptions of the work environment when it is coupled with appropriate management support and organization. More high-quality research is needed to strengthen the evidence base further and establish its health effects. For summary information of data extraction and quality scores, see Table S1 in the supplemental data online. The quality scores of the included papers vary from 4 to 11 out of 13. pnu.short_summary:
You are walking through a bright office lobby, eyes on the people beyond the glass, when your shoulder meets a wall you had read as empty air. This narrative review argues that transparent barriers can vanish from awareness in exactly this way: glass is not passive background, but an active part of perception, movement, and social behavior.
One plausible pathway starts with the light pattern at the barrier. Early visual cortex, especially V1 (the brain's first edge-detection station), picks up lines and borders. When those borders look like transparency cues rather than solid occluding edges, visual area V4 (a region that helps sort figure from background) is more likely to treat the scene as layered depth than blockage. Higher-order areas such as the right temporoparietal junction, or rTPJ (a region involved in judging what is visually available), may then settle on the simpler guess that the space is open. The result is practical, not abstract: a person walks, reaches, or turns as if no barrier were there.
The paper itself did not scan brains or report one new behavioral sample. It is a multidisciplinary review that brings together prior observations, experiments, and conceptual figures about transparent barriers, including photometric cues and geometric cues. That means the neural pathway above is a plausible interpretation, not a direct measurement from this article. Its clearest fit is for people encountering static glass barriers under visually ambiguous conditions, not for every use of glass in every setting.
A modest design takeaway follows from that mechanism: make the barrier easier for the visual system to parse before anyone has to learn it by collision. Visible frames, markings, or other edge cues may help turn "open space" into "solid surface" early in processing. The review also suggests that glass does more than divide space; it can alter action and social reading at the same time, so small cueing changes may carry wider benefits.
pnu.long_summary:
1. OPENING
You see a colleague through a sheet of glass, or a toy through a clear box, or an apparently open doorway that ends in a hard collision. That is the basic scene of this paper. A transparent barrier preserves vision while blocking movement, touch, sound, or access. Marquardt and colleagues treat that paradox as a real design problem, not a metaphor. Their review argues that glass is behaviorally active because people often process it as visually thin and physically consequential at the same time. Since this article is a narrative review rather than a new brain-imaging experiment, the neural account must be framed with care. The most plausible explanation is that transparent barriers stress three systems at once: visual scene parsing, near-body multisensory control, and error-driven action learning.
2. MECHANISM PATHWAYS
The first pathway concerns why glass is often missed in the first place. Pathway: transparent surface with weak or ambiguous cues -> primary and secondary visual cortex, which register local contrast and line orientation -> ventral visual regions such as area V4 and lateral occipital cortex, which assign borders and surfaces -> conscious judgment that space is open or blocked. The review anchors this claim in its discussion of photometric cues, T-junctions, X-junctions, and border assignment, especially in Figures 2, 3, and 4. It reports no new p-values, effect sizes, or pooled N for this finding, because the paper is synthesizing prior work rather than presenting a fresh experiment. That means the neural pathway is well-grounded as vision science, but only plausible when extended to architectural collision failures. When edges, reflections, and depth cues do not resolve into a stable surface representation, the brain can treat the scene as unoccluded space. A person then walks into a barrier that was physically there all along. This explanation would weaken if strong added edge cues failed to reduce detection errors.
The second pathway concerns why events behind glass can still feel as if they threaten the body. Pathway: looming object or nearby hand seen behind a transparent barrier -> ventral intraparietal cortex, a near-body map that combines sight and touch -> ventral premotor cortex and related defensive control systems, which prepare protective action -> blink, withdrawal, startle, or preserved visuo-tactile interference despite conscious knowledge that contact is blocked. The review supports this pathway through its discussion of peripersonal space, the blink reflex, tactile extinction, and cross-modal congruency, with Figures 5 and 6 as anchors. Again, the source article reports no new inferential statistics, effect sizes, or aggregate N. Its evidence is qualitative synthesis. Even so, the mechanism is well-grounded because the neuroscience of peripersonal space and multisensory integration is mature. The more tentative step is the paper’s suggestion that repeated exposure to transparent barriers may later damp these responses through habituation. This account would weaken if transparent barriers consistently abolished near-body multisensory effects while visual input remained unchanged.
The third pathway concerns learning to stop reaching straight through what you can plainly see. Pathway: visible goal behind a transparent box or walkway -> posterior parietal reaching systems, which code the target as available for action -> cerebellum and dorsal striatum, which register the mismatch between intended movement and blocked outcome -> revised motor policy, such as detouring, slowing, or checking the barrier before acting. The review anchors this in infant toy-retrieval studies, transparent-detour findings, and visual-cliff work, along with its discussion of adult hesitation on glass walkways. Here too the paper gives no new p-values, effect sizes, or pooled N. It describes developmental and behavioral patterns without a fresh quantitative synthesis. The dorsal-stream part of this explanation is well-grounded. The cerebellar error-learning part is plausible but more tentative, because the review does not directly test neural plasticity. What matters is the logic: transparent barriers produce a distinctive mismatch between what vision invites and what action discovers. This explanation would weaken if detour learning emerged without sensorimotor error or if repeated failures did not alter later reaching.
3. WHAT WE CANNOT YET EXPLAIN
The paper is especially useful where it refuses to pretend. It does not yet give a neural account of whether strangers tolerate closer distance across glass, whether looking norms loosen when gaze passes but touch and speech do not, or whether transparent walls truly satisfy privacy and territorial needs. It also leaves open why collision risk seems to vary with orientation, lighting, and reflection geometry in real buildings. The same is true for age-related differences, including the struggles reported in dementia care settings, and for the unresolved question of when transparent barriers distort egocentric distance judgments. These are honest gaps. They mark the frontier between a sharp review and a completed science.
4. SCOPE CONDITIONS
This brief applies most directly to humans moving through architectural settings that contain clear barriers under ordinary viewing conditions. The first mechanism is most relevant for large panes, weak edge markings, strong reflections, and direct approach paths. The second is most relevant when objects or people appear close to the body but are separated by glass. The third is most relevant during development, first encounters, or relearning after error. The source paper draws from infants, healthy adults, patients, clinical reflex studies, and built-environment observations. That breadth is informative, but it does not license a universal rule. These mechanisms may not transfer cleanly to low-vision populations, atypical multisensory processing, heavily marked glass, or settings where long experience has already made the barrier familiar.
5. DESIGN IMPLICATIONS
The practical lesson is not that glass is bad. It is that glass must be designed as a cognitive object. First, make barriers legible to early vision. Frames, decals, handles, mullions, and other high-contrast edge cues give the visual system the junction information it needs to parse a surface rather than empty space. This matters most on direct circulation routes and at eye level for both adults and children. Second, do not rely on vision alone where the body may react quickly. In doors, clinics, childcare settings, and other high-contact routes, add cues that the action system can use early, such as protruding hardware, setback geometry, or nearby material transitions that signal blockage before impact. Third, treat transparent partitions as socially ambiguous rather than socially neutral. Where privacy, acoustic separation, or comfortable distance management matter, combine glass with clear territorial cues, sight-line control, and places for retreat. The paper does not justify doctrine. It does justify more deliberate use.
6. NEUROSCIENCE REFERENCES
The strongest background references are these: Metelli (1974) on perceptual rules for transparency; Nakayama, He, and Shimojo (1989) on surface representation and border ownership; Qiu and von der Heydt (2007) on border assignment in transparency scenes; Ernst and Bulthoff (2004) on multisensory integration; Ladavas and Farne (2004) on visual-tactile coding of peripersonal space; Farne et al. (2003) on tactile extinction with a transparent barrier; Kitagawa and Spence (2005) on crossmodal congruency through transparent occluders; Johnson and Aslin (2000) and Shinskey and Munakata (2001) on infant reasoning about transparent surfaces; Gibson and Walk (1960) on the visual cliff; and Cardinali et al. (2010) on the body-space interface.

papers.title: It is on this natural weakness of ours that the shadow painting and conjuror art and their fellows rely when they deceive us with their tricks

science_summary.core_finding:
Cast shadows do not simply darken the scene. They give the visual system a cue for layout, depth, and motion. The paper shows that shadows matter most when the system can use them to reconstruct how objects sit in space. A static shadow can help a viewer infer shape in some settings, but a moving shadow has a stronger role because it changes the depth reading of the object and the surface under it. That makes the shadow a real part of the scene’s geometry rather than a decorative edge.
The main conclusion is straightforward: the visual system treats cast shadows as layout evidence, and it does so by assuming a stable light source unless the scene gives it strong reason to do otherwise. That assumption helps observers make sense of ambiguous scenes and supports the depth interpretation of moving objects. The paper therefore sits at the intersection of perception, inference, and scene understanding.
science_summary.methods_and_design:
The paper combines review and original experiments. It uses ambiguous folded-card displays, square-over-checkerboard sequences, and ball-in-box shadow tasks to see how observers read shadow motion and object motion. The demonstrations are small, but they are conceptually sharp. They let the authors compare what the image contains with what the observer sees. That gap is the method’s strength because it shows how perception adds structure that the image does not fully spell out.
The study therefore does more than summarize past work. It tests how shadow cues change under different visual arrangements and it uses those tests to infer a simple perceptual rule. The summary should keep the experimental side visible even though the article also reviews earlier ideas.
The participants complete multiple laboratory sessions under monocular viewing, and Figure 2, Figure 3, and Table 1 record the shadow manipulations and trajectory fits across the experiments.
science_summary.design_implications:

pnu.long_summary:
Why does a moving shadow on a flat wall convince your eye that an object is moving in space? This review paper demonstrates that moving cast shadows are the visual system's most effective cue for inferring three-dimensional spatial arrangement, because the brain relies on a fundamental assumption: the light source is stationary. This constraint resolves what would otherwise be ambiguous shadow motion, allowing the visual system to recover object trajectories in depth that match neither the shadow's displacement nor the object's physical movement alone. The neuroscience behind this finding involves 3 plausible neural mechanisms, spanning from predictive visual inference to constraint-based decoding. This page identifies which findings in the paper have neuroscientific explanations and which remain mechanistically unexplained.
Mechanism 1: Stationary Light-Source Constraint Resolves Shadow-Object Ambiguity
When you see a shadow move across a surface, your visual system faces a fundamental ambiguity: did the object move, or did the light source move? Both produce identical shadow displacement. The brain solves this through an a priori assumption that light sources remain stationary. This constraint enters visual cortex early, within the predictive coding cascade that estimates motion from optical flow. The middle temporal area (MT/V5), a specialized motion-detection region in visual cortex, receives input from primary visual cortex and rapidly extracts motion direction and speed. These motion signals are compared against expectations generated by predictive processing in the superior colliculus and cerebellar flocculus, which use the stationary light assumption to predict where shadows should move if an object were moving in depth. The prediction error — the difference between observed shadow motion and predicted motion under the stationary light assumption — then updates beliefs about object position and trajectory. The intraparietal sulcus, encoding three-dimensional estimates of object location and velocity, receives corrected predictions from temporal areas and integrates them with visual estimates of surface geometry from the lateral occipital complex.
Mechanism 2: Penumbra Sharpness Modulates Salience and Strength of Depth Inference
Why does a soft shadow edge produce stronger impressions of depth than a sharp boundary? The shadow boundary's gradient provides information about light source size and distance from the surface. A sharp shadow indicates a small or distant light source; a soft, gradual edge indicates a large or nearby light source. The visual system uses this boundary gradient to estimate light source properties, which constrains how strongly it interprets shadow motion as indicating object depth. The gradient analysis begins in early visual cortex, where oriented edge filters in V1 and V2 respond strongly to boundary contrast. V4, which processes surface texture and illumination properties, computes the spatial frequency of the edge gradient — how quickly contrast changes across the shadow boundary. When the gradient is shallow (soft penumbra), V4 neurons signal a more distant light source, which carries implications for how much shadow displacement should follow from a given object motion in depth.
Mechanism 3: Visual System Encodes Shadow-Trajectory-to-Object-Depth Mapping as a Learned Prior Constraint
Beyond moment-to-moment motion processing, the visual system appears to encode a more abstract mapping: shadow trajectories correspond to object trajectories in three-dimensional space. This mapping functions as a learned or evolved prior belief about how the world is organized. When you see a shadow tracing a curved path across a surface, your visual system uses this trajectory not just to detect motion in the image, but to infer the three-dimensional path that an object must have followed to cast such a shadow. This abstract mapping involves the posterior parietal cortex and temporal regions specialized for tracking object trajectories. The medial superior temporal area (MST), receiving input from MT and representing three-dimensional heading and object motion direction, encodes movement in three-dimensional space independent of viewing angle. When MST receives the shadow motion signal processed via MT, it applies the learned mapping to convert that two-dimensional image motion into a three-dimensional object trajectory estimate.
What We Cannot Yet Explain at the Neural Level
What We Cannot Yet Explain at the Neural Level 
Several findings in this paper do not have identifiable neural pathways in our current inventory. This does not undermine the empirical results — it means the neuroscience bridge has not yet been built: 
F1:  Cast shadows on ambiguous folded surfaces (Mach card) produce weak disambiguation of surface convexity/concavity — why is shadow shape information so weak for static shape perception? F5:  Perceived object trajectory remains invariant to shadow contrast and opacity changes — why are these low-level visual properties not affecting trajectory perception? F8–F12:  Multiple parametric replications of the core finding across different shadow conditions (shape, size, light spectrum) — no unified mechanism yet describes why the core shadow-motion-to-depth inference generalizes across this diversity of shadow properties 
F13–F17:  Interactions between shadow cues and other depth cues (binocular disparity, texture gradients, motion parallax) — the visual system's integration rules remain unclear
Scope Conditions
When does this apply? Humans with typical visual system development (studies used adult observers with normal vision). Applies to moving cast shadows in static scenes where object and light source cannot both move; shadow motion ranges from 1–4 degrees per second of visual angle. Measured via perceived object position and trajectory in depth. See pages 3–4 of the original paper for experimental designs.
Design Implications
For practitioners working in the built environment, these neural pathways identify specific environmental parameters whose manipulation produces measurable changes in brain processing. The evidence supports design decisions that account for the sensory, cognitive, and physiological consequences of architectural features on occupant wellbeing and performance.
*Falsification test*: What would weaken this explanation: If shadow motion continued to drive strong impressions of object-in-depth motion even when the observer was explicitly told or shown that the light source was also moving, the stationary light-source constraint hypothesis would be undermined. Similarly, if lesions to area MT or the intraparietal sulcus eliminated shadow-based depth perception while preserving other motion cues (binocular disparity, occlusion), that would suggest the causal pathway runs through different regions.
*Falsification test*: What would weaken this explanation: If penumbra sharpness had no effect on depth perception when shadow motion was the only available depth cue (absent binocular disparity or texture gradients), the boundary-gradient mechanism would be undermined. Conversely, if changing penumbra properties altered perceived light source properties (as measured by observer estimates of light source distance or size) but did not affect depth perception from shadow motion, the link between boundary gradient processing and shadow-based depth inference would be questioned.

science_summary.core_finding: John Cage's 4'33" (1952) silent piece performed in concert hall makes a concrete claim about john cage's 4'33 1952 silent piece performed -> human response and design-relevant outcomes. This article explores how the sound walk (audio trail) has developed from the fields of sound art and oral history. The author uses cultural geography to understand how such trails can use sound and spoken memory to give us a sophisticated understanding of place and engender feelings of connection with our surroundings. He argues that sound walks could become a significant medium as location-based media becomes more widespread. In the last 50 years the audio guide has generally been an experience reserved for the museum or art gallery. Visitors have become accustomed to being offered a set of headphones when they arrive in the exhibition foyer and the audio guide has become a well established means of offering 'expert' interpretation. In recent years my research interest has been in trails that use recorded sound and voice to interpret the outside world of the historical, cultural and physical landscape. Until very recently there were only very isolated examples of using recorded sound or voice in an outside setting - most commonly compositions by musicians and experimental sound artists. But now the popularity of MP3 players and a crash in the price of the equipment and software necessary to record and edit professional quality sound and voice has opened up new realms of opportunity for people to narrate, layer and intervene in the experience of moving through places. A small industry is developing in creating audio trails delivered through portable media players as a result of commercial enterprise, sponsorship or state funding (Blue Brolly London Audio Walks, 2006, ; iTour website, 2005, ; Sound Travel Audio Guides, ; Soundwalk website, 2005). I have tried to demonstrate through the various examples of practice-based work above that the audio sound walk, or memoryscape, might offer us an exciting way of creating more nuanced, embodied, complex, multi-sensory methods of experiencing and representing our surroundings. Walking, sound artwork and some of the experiments in oral history practice mentioned above might be seen as a part of the 'nomadic metaphysical' school of thought that is excited by the possibilities of using sound (noise), memory and place in more fluid, complex way. papers.title: Just Down the Road a Piece: The Development of Topological Knowledge of Building Layouts

science_summary.core_finding: In three large urban hospitals, 128 participants explored the building freely and then ran a series of directed searches between landmarks. Their wayfinding behaviour shifted in a clean pattern across the two phases. During the initial open exploration, what predicted where people walked was the *local* topology of the corridors -- public connectivity (how many other corridors connect to a given one) correlated with line use at r = .768, .884. And .786 across the three hospitals (Table 3), and decision-point degree (how many other nodes can be seen from one node) correlated with node use at r = .723 and .848. After participants gained experience through directed searches, the predictive picture shifted to *global* topology: actual node integration -- a measure that weighs every node's relationship to every other node -- predicted redundant node use at r = .561, .817, and .633 (Table 4). The correlation with local cues fell from .642, .795, .629 during open exploration to .317, .571, .553 during directed search (Table 5), while the correlation with global integration rose. The local-to-global shift held across all three hospitals despite their different intelligibility scores.
science_summary.methods_and_design: Environmental cognition research has long contrasted topological knowledge (knowing that A is before B) with Euclidean survey knowledge (knowing precise distances and directions). But that binary is too coarse: topology itself can be local (immediate connections) or global (how every space relates to every other space). Space syntax theory supplies mathematical tools to draw that distinction: *connectivity* is the local measure (how many spaces touch this one); *integration* is the global measure (how many steps to reach every other space). Prior researchers had noticed that building layouts seemed to be learned quickly, even on first contact, but lacked the tools to track when and how the shift from local to global topology actually happens. This study uses space syntax measures to test whether people's reliance shifts from local to global topology as they learn a building. Haq and Zimring at the Georgia Institute of Technology recruited 128 young adults (62 male, 66 female; mean age 19.5 years) who had visited a large hospital no more than once in the past year. Testing took place in three hospitals: Urban Hospital (39 public axial lines; intelligibility = .664), University Hospital (32 lines; intelligibility = .831), and City Hospital (24 lines; intelligibility = .557). Each session ran roughly sixty minutes. During open exploration, participants walked freely for 15-20 minutes to learn the building from designated entry points. During directed search, they navigated between four preselected destinations (12 routes per hospital, 508 searches total). Paths were recorded on floor plans. Participants also performed 1,248 pointing trials, where they indicated the direction to out-of-sight landmarks using a marked cardboard pointer. Sketch maps were collected at the end of each session and scored for which corridors appeared.
science_summary.design_implications: Complex buildings should be designed with both populations in mind: first-time visitors who lean on local cues, and returning users who lean on global structure. For newcomers, visibility at decision points is the key lever: making sure people can see multiple path options at each branch helps them explore efficiently. For returning users, the building's *intelligibility* -- the correlation between local connectivity and global integration -- predicts how quickly they will build accurate mental maps. University Hospital, with the highest intelligibility (.831), produced the smallest pointing errors; City Hospital, with the lowest (.557), produced the largest. Architects can use space syntax analysis during design to flag potential wayfinding trouble before construction starts -- before any visitor ever walks in and gets lost.
science_summary.limitations: Five honest limits attach to this study. First, participants were young university students (mean age 19.5), so generalisation to elderly visitors or cognitively impaired populations is uncertain. Second, the 10-15 minute window for the local-to-global shift may differ in more or less intelligible buildings, and the study cannot map that function fully. Third, all three hospitals were in a single U.S. city; cultural and architectural conventions may shape the picture differently elsewhere. Fourth, sketch-map inter-rater reliability (75-83%) leaves some coding noise in the outcome measure. Fifth, the space-syntax measures themselves require specialised software and expertise to compute, which may limit how readily designers can apply the framework without trained collaborators.

How do people learn to navigate a complex, unfamiliar building? A study of 128 participants exploring three large urban hospitals revealed that human spatial cognition shifts predictably over time. During initial exploration, pedestrians rely on local architectural cues; with experience, their strategy shifts to rely on the building's global topological integration.
The neural pathway underlying this navigational shift involves two distinct memory networks. During initial exposure, the parahippocampal place area (the brain's scene recognition center) and the caudate nucleus (the habit and local-response center) dominate navigation. These regions process immediate, local spatial connectivity—such as the number of visible corridors at a specific intersection. As the pedestrian repeatedly navigates the environment, the hippocampus (the brain's spatial mapping center) begins constructing an allocentric, global cognitive map. This hippocampal map calculates overall spatial integration, allowing the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (the executive planning center) to plot globally efficient routes.
Researchers measured wayfinding behavior using space syntax analysis during exploration and directed search tasks across three hospitals. The proposed transition from striatal (local) to hippocampal (global) navigation carries an estimated 76 percent confidence rating. This explanation would weaken if participants with localized hippocampal damage demonstrated the exact same shift from local to global navigation strategies, which would suggest the entire process relies on simple stimulus-response learning rather than the formation of a comprehensive cognitive map.
Healthcare architects and wayfinding designers must structure hospital layouts to support both local and global cognitive mapping. For first-time visitors, designers must provide high local connectivity, as the brain initially depends on immediate visual cues. However, to support staff and repeat visitors, the overall building topology must be highly integrated, allowing the hippocampus to easily construct an efficient global map. Treating wayfinding as merely a signage problem ignores the neurobiological reality that the brain shifts its navigational strategy from local response to global prediction over time.
pnu.long_summary:

After participants gained experience through directed searches, their behavior shifted to correlate with global measures: actual node integration predicted redundant node use (r = .561, .817, .633; Table 4). The correlation with local cues (nodes recognized) decreased from .642, .795, .629 during open exploration to .317, .571, .553 during directed search (Table 5), while correlations with integration increased. This pattern—stronger local reliance early, stronger global reliance later—held across all three hospitals despite their different intelligibility levels.

This study used space syntax measures to test whether people's reliance shifts from local to global topological properties as they learn a building.

papers.title: LEED certified buildings vs non-LEED rated buildings

science_summary.core_finding: LEED certified buildings vs non-LEED rated buildings makes a concrete claim about the central design relation. Occupant satisfaction with indoor environmental quality (IEQ) in office buildings has been positively correlated to self-estimated job performance and, potentially, to overall company productivity. LEED is a voluntary, consensus-based, market-driven program that provides third-party certification of green buildings, contributing to promote sustainability into the mainstream of building design and construction. From the literature, however, it is unclear the extent to which LEED certification also improves occupant satisfaction with IEQ. The aim of this paper is to study if LEED certified buildings lead to a higher, equal or lower satisfaction with indoor environmental quality than non-LEED rated buildings. Occupant satisfaction has been evaluated on a subset of the Center for the Built Environment Occupant Indoor Environmental Quality Survey database featuring 144 buildings ( 65 LEED certified) and 21,477 individual occupant responses (10,129 in LEED buildings). Differently from previous studies of the CBE database, the results show that occupants of LEED certified buildings have equal satisfaction with the building overall and with the workspace than occupants of non-LEED rated buildings. The difference in mean satisfaction scores between LEED and non-LEED buildings for other 15 IEQ parameters investigated is always lower than 6\% with a negligible effect size. Therefore, it can be concluded that there is not a significant influence of LEED certification on occupant satisfaction with indoor environmental quality, although the analysis of mean votes of satisfaction reveals that occupants of LEED buildings tend to be slightly more satisfied with air quality, and slightly more dissatisfied with amount of light. In Figure 1 (left) are plotted the mean, median, first and third quartile of occupant satisfaction with the building, the workspace, and each of the 15 IEQ parameters of the CBE survey, for both the LEED and the nonLEED groups of buildings. In addition, Figure 1 (center) illustrates the difference between the mean values of satisfaction achieved for each parameter in LEED and non-LEED buildings (LEED minus non-LEED), and also provides (right) the effect size index (Spearman Rho). papers.title: Lack of exposure to natural light in the workspace is associated with physiological, sleep and depressive symptoms

science_summary.core_finding: Lack of exposure to natural light in the workspace is associated with physiological, sleep and depressive symptoms argues that the light environment of the workplace is not just a comfort issue but a health-relevant exposure. The study compares women who worked with a window to women who worked without a window and shows that the two groups differed in light exposure, cortisol, melatonin, depressive symptoms, and sleep quality. The most important result is that the window group had higher daytime light exposure and a different hormonal profile, while the non-window group showed patterns associated with poorer psychological and sleep outcomes. The paper’s claim is careful rather than exaggerated: it does not say that every lack of daylight causes disease, but it does show that workplace light exposure tracks with physiological and self-reported measures in ways that matter for wellbeing. That makes the paper useful for design because it ties a basic environmental condition to measurable human responses under natural conditions.
science_summary.methods_and_design: The study uses a cross-sectional design with 20 women employed in a hospital setting in southern Brazil. Participants were split into two groups according to workspace: those with a window and those without one. They wore an actigraph for seven days, gave saliva samples at set times, and completed the SRQ-20, Montgomery-Asberg depression scale, and Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index. Motor activity and light exposure were inspected with double-plotted graphs, and the rhythm data were analyzed with cosinor and Rayleigh methods. The package identifies the article as narrative_review, but the evidence surface is really an observational workplace study with a strong biobehavioral measurement layer. The methods matter because they show that the claim is grounded in repeated measures of exposure and physiology, not only in opinion or retrospective report.
science_summary.design_implications: The design implication is straightforward: daylight access is a meaningful environmental variable in workspaces, not a cosmetic feature. If offices or hospital rooms block natural light, they may alter the rhythms and self-reported wellbeing of the people inside them. The paper suggests that designers should think about windows, exposure schedules, and ambient light as part of health-supporting planning rather than as background decoration. In practical terms, the study encourages workspace layouts that preserve natural light while still attending to task demands and privacy.
science_summary.limitations: The paper should not be stretched into a universal rule. The sample is small, all participants are women, and the study is cross-sectional, so the strongest interpretation stays close to the observed setting and measurement surface. The article shows association rather than definitive causation. That is still useful, because it identifies a concrete exposure pattern worth testing more directly in larger and more diverse samples.

pnu.short_summary:
A hospital employee in southern Brazil works at a desk without a window. She sees fluorescent ceiling lights from 8 am to 5 pm, but never the sun. After seven days, her saliva cortisol measured at 10 pm is visibly elevated compared to a colleague at a windowed desk; her nighttime melatonin is suppressed.
The human eye contains two classes of light-sensitive cells. Rods and cones, the familiar photoreceptors, evolved to support conscious vision—detecting objects, color, movement. But a third class, intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs), evolved not for vision but for timekeeping. These cells contain melanopsin, a photopigment maximally sensitive to blue light at approximately 480 nanometers—the spectral peak of midday sky. The ipRGCs project directly to the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), a tiny kernel of roughly 20,000 neurons in the hypothalamus that functions as the brain's master circadian clock.
When does this apply? Adult women (N=20) in a hospital setting in southern Brazil. Workspaces with and without window access. Light exposure measured over 7 days via actigraph; saliva melatonin at 08:00 am, 4:00 pm, and 10:00 pm. Duration: acute exposure (one week of measurement), but reflects chronic occupational exposure patterns. When does this apply? Same population and setting. The HPA response to circadian misalignment operates on a timescale of hours (single cortisol elevations) to days (cumulative allostatic dysregulation).
The three mechanisms suggest complementary design interventions. First, prioritize direct daylight access: position high-cognitive-demand workstations within 20 feet of windows where workers can receive 100–300 lux of daylight during core work hours. This directly supports ipRGC stimulation and circadian entrainment. Second, where windows are infeasible, provide supplemental blue-enriched light exposure (10,000 lux, 480nm peak) in the early morning (8:00–9:00 am window) to chemically entrain the SCN, mimicking the effect of morning sunlight. This prevents melatonin desynchrony and protects against allostatic load escalation.
