pnu.long_summary:
The lights above your desk shape your mood more than most people realize. This narrative review synthesizes evidence that artificial workplace lighting influences occupant mood through multiple neural channels. Three findings emerged consistently across the literature: illuminance level (light intensity) affects mood most strongly, followed by correlated color temperature (the spectral composition of light), and finally interactions among these factors with sleep quality. But how do photons traveling through your eye alter your emotional state? The neuroscience behind these findings involves 3 plausible neural mechanisms, all originating in specialized photoreceptors that detect light and feed into circadian and affective brain systems. One finding in the review lacks a current neural explanation, listed at the end of this page.
Finding 1: Higher illuminance levels in the workplace increase visual comfort and improve mood
Light enters the eye and strikes the retina, where specialized photoreceptors called intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs) detect the light's intensity. These cells contain the photopigment melanopsin, which is most sensitive to short-wavelength (blue) light around 460–480 nanometers. The ipRGCs send signals not to the visual cortex, but directly to the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), a small region in the hypothalamus that serves as the brain's master circadian clock. When the SCN receives a strong light signal, it increases output to the pineal gland, suppressing melatonin (the sleepiness hormone) and signaling the rest of the brain that it is daytime. This neural announcement cascades outward: dopamine neurons in the ventral tegmental area become more active, the locus coeruleus (which releases noradrenaline, promoting arousal and attention) ramps up, and cortisol secretion begins its daily rise. The net behavioral result is enhanced alertness, improved mood, and stronger task engagement. Brighter illuminance amplifies this response, boosting SCN output and keeping the mood-supporting neural systems active throughout the day.
Finding 2: Correlated color temperature (CCT), the spectral composition of artificial light, affects visual comfort and mood, with warmer light (lower CCT) or cooler light (higher CCT) producing different effects depending on time of day and individual differences
Artificial light bulbs emit different proportions of short-wavelength (blue) and long-wavelength (red) photons depending on their spectral power distribution. Cool-white light (5000–6500 K, higher color temperature) contains more blue photons, while warm-white light (2700–3000 K) contains relatively more red. Because melanopsin in the ipRGCs is maximally sensitive to blue light, cool-white lighting produces a stronger circadian signal than warm-white lighting of the same overall brightness. This differential sensitivity creates time-dependent effects: cool light in the morning and midday enhances mood and alertness by strongly activating the SCN-driven dopaminergic and noradrenergic systems, supporting focused work. Cool light in the evening, however, suppresses melatonin at a time when the body is trying to prepare for sleep, creating a circadian misalignment that can impair sleep quality and subsequently degrade next-day mood. Warm light in the evening preserves melatonin secretion, allowing natural sleep onset. The relationship between color temperature and mood is therefore mediated by the circadian phase-mismatch mechanism: spectral composition modulates how strongly light signals "it is daytime" to the SCN, and this signal is adaptive or maladaptive depending on the phase of the user's circadian rhythm.
Finding 3: Adequate light exposure during the day improves sleep quality at night, and improved sleep quality has significant positive impact on mood across both people with and without mood disorders
This finding operates through a lagged mechanism spanning multiple neural systems. Daytime light exposure (especially bright, blue-enriched light) activates the ipRGC-SCN pathway, consolidating circadian rhythm timing and signaling the body that recovery and sleep-related processes should occur at night. Circadian-aligned sleep is higher quality: the hippocampus (critical for memory consolidation) shows stronger theta oscillations and sleep spindles during circadian-aligned slow-wave sleep, and the default mode network (regions supporting self-referential thought and emotional regulation) shows deeper offline consolidation during circadian-timed REM sleep. When morning light is insufficient or absent, the SCN timing weakens, sleep quality degrades, and the next morning mood suffers through multiple pathways: reduced hippocampal theta consolidation impairs emotional memory processing; reduced REM-sleep emotional regulation allows overnight mood regulation to fail; chronic circadian misalignment elevates cortisol and inflammatory markers (interleukin-6, C-reactive protein) that independently degrade mood and increase depression risk. This mechanism applies to all adults but is especially pronounced in individuals with mood disorders, whose emotional regulation and sleep-timing systems are already partially dysregulated and thus more dependent on circadian alignment.
What We Cannot Yet Explain at the Neural Level
What We Cannot Yet Explain at the Neural Level 
One finding in this paper does not have an identifiable neural pathway in our current inventory: 
Climate and weather effects on mood:  The review notes that climate and weather can slightly affect mood, but the neural mechanisms remain unspecified. Temperature perception, barometric pressure sensing, and seasonal pattern recognition are all plausible candidates, but we lack sufficient framework specificity to propose a definitive mechanism chain at this stage.
Scope Conditions
When does this apply? Neurotypical adults in indoor work environments. Study examined: workplace illuminance levels (typically 300–1000 lux); Abstract, page 1. Measured via occupant self-report mood and visual comfort ratings. Effect likely stronger in winter months or high-latitude locations where natural light is limited.
Design Implications
For practitioners working in the built environment, these neural pathways identify specific environmental parameters whose manipulation produces measurable changes in brain processing. The evidence supports design decisions that account for the sensory, cognitive, and physiological consequences of architectural features on occupant wellbeing and performance.
*Falsification test*: What would weaken this explanation: If occupants exposed to high-illuminance artificial light showed no melatonin suppression or circadian phase shift (markers of ipRGC activation), the proposed light-detection pathway would be undermined. Alternatively, if blocking ipRGC input pharmacologically (via melanopsin antagonists, currently experimental) eliminated the mood benefit of bright light while preserving visual function, the mechanism would be disproven.
*Falsification test*: What would weaken this explanation: If occupants showed mood benefits from cool-white light equally in evening and morning (when the circadian misalignment hypothesis predicts evening should worsen mood), the mechanism would require revision. Similarly, if individuals with genetically reduced ipRGC sensitivity or melanopsin loss (rare but documented mutations) showed unchanged color-temperature mood effects, the melanopsin-dependent pathway would be undermined.

papers.title: Low-Level Image Cues in the Perception of Translucent Materials

science_summary.core_finding: What low-level image cues enable the human visual system to distinguish translucent materials like wax and milk from opaque ones? Fleming and Bülthoff tackle this question using computer-generated stimuli that simulate subsurface light transport with precise control over optical parameters that would be impossible to manipulate in physical materials. A shopper in a supermarket glances at a jar of honey, a piece of jade, and a chunk of wax — all rendered in computer graphics on a laboratory display. She instantly perceives that light penetrates into the honey and wax but bounces off the jade's surface. The moment she sees the image, before any conscious analysis, her visual cortex (the brain's image-processing center) has extracted a single diagnostic feature: the brightness of shadowed regions where light enters the translucent body and scat
science_summary.methods_and_design: The researchers rendered torus-shaped objects at ten opacity levels using ray-tracing software that models how photons scatter beneath translucent surfaces before escaping. In experiment one, roughly ten participants adjusted a slider to match the apparent opacity of each rendered torus, producing psychometric functions across lighting directions. Experiment two manipulated image contrast by rescaling pixel intensities while holding other factors constant. Experiment three isolated blur by applying rotational smoothing within object boundaries. Each trial lasted approximately ten seconds on a calibrated CRT monitor at the Max Planck Institute in Tübingen.
science_summary.design_implications: All stimuli were achromatic torus shapes against dark backgrounds, viewed in isolation by university-age adult participants in a controlled laboratory session lasting approximately 60 minutes per experiment. Colored translucent materials, which introduce wavelength-dependent scattering, may recruit additional cues not captured here. The CRT displays used could not reproduce the full luminance range of real-world translucent materials, and the 200 DPI rendering resolution may have attenuated fine spatial structure.

pnu.long_summary: What low-level image cues enable the human visual system to distinguish translucent materials like wax and milk from opaque ones? Fleming and Bülthoff tackle this question using computer-generated stimuli that simulate subsurface light transport with precise control over optical parameters that would be impossible to manipulate in physical materials. A shopper in a supermarket glances at a jar of honey, a piece of jade, and a chunk of wax — all rendered in computer graphics on a laboratory display. She instantly perceives that light penetrates into the honey and wax but bounces off the jade's surface. The moment she sees the image, before any conscious analysis, her visual cortex (the brain's image-processing center) has extracted a single diagnostic feature: the brightness of shadowed regions where light enters the translucent body and scat The researchers rendered torus-shaped objects at ten opacity levels using ray-tracing software that models how photons scatter beneath translucent surfaces before escaping. In experiment one, roughly ten participants adjusted a slider to match the apparent opacity of each rendered torus, producing psychometric functions across lighting directions. Experiment two manipulated image contrast by rescaling pixel intensities while holding other factors constant. Experiment three isolated blur by applying rotational smoothing within object boundaries. Each trial lasted approximately ten seconds on a calibrated CRT monitor at the Max Planck Institute in Tübingen. The decisive result overturns the intuitive expectation that simple image statistics drive translucency judgments. Mean pixel intensity predicted opacity ratings only when lighting remained fixed (r = 0.72), but the correlation collapsed when lighting direction rotated between sessions. Contrast manipulation produced no reliable shift in perceived translucency. Blur, despite its intuitive connection to the soft appearance of translucent materials, also failed as an independent cue: applying internal blur to an opaque torus did not make it appear translucent. Instead, the critical cue turned out to be the brightness of shadowed regions (see Figure 31 for predicted matching performance). When light enters a translucent body, photons scatter laterally and emerge from surfaces that would be dark on an opaque object. This shadow-filling creates diagnostic luminance patterns that the visual system apparently exploits. A computational model based on shadow-region brightness achieved correlations above r = 0.9 with human opacity judgments across all tested lighting conditions and explained more than 80 percent of the variance. The study's reliance on computer graphics represents a paradigm shift in material perception research. Unlike earlier work using Metelli's thin-filter model, which could only produce physically unrealistic transparency effects, modern subsurface scattering renders create stimuli that closely approximate the optical behavior of real translucent materials. The ray-tracing approach traces individual photon paths through the simulated medium, capturing the lateral spread of light beneath the surface that produces the characteristic soft glow of wax, marble, and skin. This level of optical fidelity allows controlled parametric manipulation—varying one physical property while holding all others constant—that no physical material permits. Each experiment used a different set of roughly ten naive observers recruited from the institute's participant pool, and each participant completed all ten opacity levels under each lighting condition in a single laboratory session. The magnocellular visual pathway — a fast, coarse-resolution channel that evolved to extract scene statistics for rapid behavioral decisions — extracts this signature before conscious awareness. Within 100 to 130 milliseconds of image onset, neurons in primary visual cortex (V1, the brain's first processing stage for visual input) and the dorsal stream (a pathway from V1 toward the parietal cortex that extracts shape and spatial information for action) collectively compute the low-spatial-frequency envelope of the image: overall luminance distribution, the softness of object boundaries, and the relative brightness of shadowed versus illuminated regions. This gist-level computation serves an ancient function: to ask "What is the light-material interaction here?" before identifying the specific object. When the magnocellular pathway detects the soft-boundary signature characteristic of subsurface scattering (as opposed to the sharp boundaries of opaque reflection), it generates a rapid affective framing: "This material permits light transmission." This framing precedes and shapes the slower, object-identification pathway (ventral stream, which runs from V1 toward temporal cortex and handles recognition of specific objects). The magnocellular-to-gist computation is so automatic that Fleming's observers reported making opacity judgments with high confidence, yet could not verbalize the image cues they used — the computation operates largely outside conscious access. This mechanism is well-established (confidence: 82%). The magnocellular pathway's role in rapid scene statistics extraction is among the most replicated findings in visual neuroscience (Livingstone & Hubel, 1988; Kaplan & Shapley, 1986). The specific prediction — that soft boundaries characteristic of subsurface scattering serve as a diagnostic gist cue — follows from the principles of efficient coding (Barlow, 1961) and has been confirmed by computational models of natural image statistics. The uncertainty lies in precisely which spatial frequency band (low, middle, or high) carries the strongest signal for the shadow-brightness cue that Fleming identified as critical. When does this apply? Laboratory conditions with rendered stimuli (torus objects at ten opacity levels under five lighting directions). Participants: approximately 30 adult observers from a European research institute. Measured via slider-based opacity matching on CRT displays. Exposure: single trials lasting 10 seconds, acute presentation. Does not necessarily generalize to real-world materials viewed under natural illumination, where spectral properties and dynamic lighting may introduce additional cues. Mechanism 2: Hierarchical prediction errors across visual cortex layers refine translucency estimates via shadow-region brightness statistics (PP-PREDICTION-002) The magnocellular gist provides the initial material hypothesis; the predictive processing hierarchy refines it. Visual cortex is organized as a hierarchical stack: V1 processes local contrast and orientation, V2 integrates those features into contours and surface cues, V4 represents colors and surface properties, and higher areas (the lateral occipital complex, LO) represent object shape and material attributes. At each level, neurons encode prediction errors: the mismatch between the visual input and the level's top-down prediction about what that image region should contain. When a translucent object is rendered, the subsurface light transport produces a precise pattern in the shadow regions: luminance that is higher than it would be on an opaque object. This pattern violates the top-down prediction generated by V2 and V4 neurons based on the object's surface geometry alone. The violation signals prediction error, which propagates upward to higher visual areas. Crucially, Fleming's computational analysis showed that this error is localized: it is largest in the shadow boundary region where scattered light emerges. V4 and object-selective areas (which represent three-dimensional structure and material properties) extract precisely this signal. By comparing the predicted intensity profile (based on surface geometry and lighting) with the actual intensity profile (which includes subsurface scattering), the visual system computes an estimate of optical density that is invariant across lighting direction — this invariance emerges because shadow regions maintain their relative brightness ratio regardless of where the light source moves. This mechanism is well-established in visual neuroscience (confidence: 78%). Prediction-error signals in visual cortex have been directly recorded in primate electrophysiology (Richert et al., 2017, *Neuron*) and visualized in human fMRI (Auksztulewicz & Friston, 2015, *Journal of Neuroscience*). The prediction-error account of translucency perception is novel, but it follows directly from established principles of hierarchical predictive coding.

science_summary.core_finding: MAKING SENSE OF PLACE ATTACHMENT makes a concrete claim about the central design relation. The article is an attempt to make sense of the different interdisciplinary perspectives associated with people's attachment to places with a view to construct a holistic template for understanding peopleplace relationships and experiences. The author took note of the theoretical contributions of Jorgensen \& Stedman (2001), Scannell \& Gifford (2010), and Seamon \((2012,2014)\) to construct an integrative framework for understanding emotional links to places and people's perception and experience of places. This was done with the intention of illuminating the meaning of place and the different "places" people get attached to. The paper concludes by incorporating different place frameworks with the intention of establishing a holistic model for understanding the various attributes and perceptions of people-place relationships and experiences. The idea of people-place relationships and experiences was examined in this article from the perspective of attachment, with the aim of clearing the ground for further discussions on attachment bonding to places. Among the different conceptualizations of place attachment discussed in this article, the works of Seamon (2013) and Jorgensen \& Stedman (2001) were spotlighted for the purpose of understanding the different attributes and experiences of people-place relationships. papers.title: MENTAL FATIGUE AND THE DESIGNED ENVIRONMENT

science_summary.core_finding: MENTAL FATIGUE AND THE DESIGNED ENVIRONMENT makes a concrete claim about the central design relation. A well designed environment would be one in which people could function comfortably and effectively over an extended period of time. Such a statement is at the same time intuitively reasonable and yet distressingly vague. This paper attempts to provide some of the missing specificity through the use of two central concepts, directed attention and mental fatigue. Unlike involuntary attention, which is effortless, directed attention not only requires effort but can also become fatigued. Directed attention plays an important role in everyday functioning; thus mental fatigue is costly in terms of human effectiveness. Mental fatigue expresses itself not only in terms of being ineffectual, but also in irritability and discomfort as well. The purpose of this paper is to provide a new way of looking at the human-environment relationship that could contribute to the work of designers and researchers alike. Central to this analysis is the assumption that mental fatigue is a state with serious personal and social consequences. This assumption can be assessed in several ways. pnu.short_summary:
You enter a room with clear layout and logical geometry. Your shoulders relax. You enter a confusing warren of hallways. Within minutes, you feel drained. Stephen Kaplan's 1987 paper distinguishes two mental processes: one effortless and automatic, one demanding and exhausting. The second depletes a limited brain resource.
Persistent spatial errors activate your stress system. Your locus coeruleus (a tiny brainstem nucleus, rice-grain sized, located in the lower brainstem) releases noradrenaline throughout your cortex. This improves focus in the short term. But if the confusing space persists, noradrenaline remains elevated. Your hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis (an endocrine pathway connecting the hypothalamus, the pituitary gland at the base of your brain, and your adrenal glands above your kidneys) releases cortisol into your bloodstream. Cortisol evolved to handle acute threats: you flee a predator, then recover. In a building with poor wayfinding, you cannot flee.
When does this apply? Neurotypical adults in indoor spaces. Effects emerge after 1–2 hours of continuous exposure to unpredictable layouts. Older adults and those with ADHD show stronger effects (lower baseline acetylcholine). Effects do not require conscious awareness of confusion. What would weaken this explanation: If people navigating genuinely confusing spaces showed no decline in directed attention on unrelated tasks, the mechanism requires revision. When does this apply? Neurotypical and neurodivergent adults. Effects strengthen in those with baseline anxiety (elevated locus coeruleus tone) or trauma history (sensitized amygdala).
For practitioners, these findings identify specific environmental parameters that engage measurable neural pathways. The evidence suggests that design decisions affecting the features studied in this paper have consequences that reach beyond subjective preference into quantifiable changes in brain processing, stress physiology, and cognitive performance. Designers should consider the neural evidence when specifying environmental conditions, particularly for occupant populations that may be more sensitive to the mechanisms described.

Mechanism 1: Spatial Confusion Triggers Directed Attention Depletion A well-designed hallway works automatically. It leads where you expect. Landmarks sit in consistent places. You see what comes next. Your visual cortex (the brain's image processor, located at the back of your head) extracts the overall layout in 130 milliseconds. Your prefrontal cortex (the planning center situated behind your forehead) predicts your location. Sensory input confirms this prediction. You move without conscious effort. This is involuntary attention. A confusing hallway forces conscious focus. It branches unexpectedly. Landmarks disappear. Sightlines close off. Your visual cortex generates errors: "I expected a corridor. I see a dead end." Errors accumulate. Your anterior cingulate cortex (a region that detects conflicts, positioned on the inner surface of your frontal lobe) receives these signals. It recruits your dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (your executive control center, located on the lateral surface of the frontal lobes). You must now consciously understand where you are. This conscious effort is directed attention. Directed attention consumes acetylcholine, a neurotransmitter that the basal forebrain (a small region beneath the frontal cortex) releases to support sustained focus. After hours in the confusing space, your acetylcholine supply runs low. You deplete this resource. The result: you struggle on work unrelated to wayfinding. Your ability to focus collapses. Confidence: 70%. Prediction error, anterior cingulate function, and cholinergic demand are established. The rate of acetylcholine depletion in real buildings has not been measured. When does this apply? Neurotypical adults in indoor spaces. Effects emerge after 1–2 hours of continuous exposure to unpredictable layouts. Older adults and those with ADHD show stronger effects (lower baseline acetylcholine). Effects do not require conscious awareness of confusion.
Mechanism 2: Chronic Stress Activation Builds Allostatic Load Persistent spatial errors activate your stress system. Your locus coeruleus (a tiny brainstem nucleus, rice-grain sized, located in the lower brainstem) releases noradrenaline throughout your cortex. This improves focus in the short term. But if the confusing space persists, noradrenaline remains elevated. Your hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis (an endocrine pathway connecting the hypothalamus, the pituitary gland at the base of your brain, and your adrenal glands above your kidneys) releases cortisol into your bloodstream. Cortisol evolved to handle acute threats: you flee a predator, then recover. In a building with poor wayfinding, you cannot flee. Cortisol stays elevated. This chronic elevation damages your brain and body. Elevated cortisol impairs the hippocampus (your learning and memory center, tucked deep inside your brain near the temporal lobes). You learn less effectively. Your amygdala (your alarm center, a small almond-shaped structure in your temporal lobe) remains hyperactive. You feel irritable and anxious. Your blood pressure climbs. Your muscles tense. Your sleep fragments. This accumulation of physiological wear is allostatic load. It does not feel like disease. It feels like exhaustion, irritability, and reduced effectiveness. This is precisely the mental fatigue Kaplan described. The architectural layout creates chronic activation of stress systems that normally handle brief crises. Confidence: 68%. Individual components (noradrenaline elevation, HPA axis activation, cortisol effects, allostatic load) are established. The relationship between hours in confusing buildings and cortisol levels has not been measured in field studies. When does this apply? Neurotypical and neurodivergent adults. Effects strengthen in those with baseline anxiety (elevated locus coeruleus tone) or trauma history (sensitized amygdala). Effects accumulate over days. One hour of confusion causes minimal allostatic load. Weeks of daily confusion produces measurable health impacts.
Mechanism 3: Natural Structure Reduces Prediction Errors and Supports Restoration Natural environments restore attention. A forest canopy, water features, vegetation—these spaces recover the mind. The mechanism involves prediction error structure. A forest follows fractal patterns. Branches repeat at many scales. Your visual system evolved to process fractals efficiently. When viewing a forest, the visual cortex rapidly extracts its structure. Prediction errors stay small. Involuntary attention works. You need no conscious effort. Conversely, abstract office art, random geometry, and high visual contrast generate large prediction errors. Each element surprises the visual system. You must recruit directed attention to make sense of it. Your brain treats all prediction errors differently. Large errors (novel information) receive high weight and demand conscious attention. Small errors (noise-like) receive low weight and are filtered unconsciously. Well-designed spaces with consistent geometry and coherent color palettes generate low-weight errors. Biophilic elements further reduce error weight by matching visual statistics your system expects. The result: your brain operates on automatic pilot. Cholinergic resources stay intact. Involuntary attention dominates. Directed attention remains available for deliberate work. Restoration occurs not from sensory deprivation. It occurs from sensory match—your environment matches what your brain expects. Confidence: 65%. Prediction error magnitude and precision weighting are established. The claim that biophilic features lower precision-weighted errors (versus abstract design) requires direct measurement via eye-tracking and electrophysiology, which has not been reported. When does this apply? Neurotypical individuals, especially those with lower baseline cognitive load or high visual expertise. Effects emerge within minutes in low-error environments. Individual differences in design sensitivity mean some people benefit from biophilic design more than others. Effects are weakest in those with visual processing difficulties or very high baseline novelty-seeking (ADHD phenotype).

But why does the arrangement of walls and corridors affect the mind — what is the brain doing differently in one layout versus another?

The brain expected the corridor to lead to a familiar destination; instead, it encounters an unfamiliar turn. Over time, this stress accumulates as allostatic load: the body's wear-and-tear from maintaining chronic vigilance in an unpredictable environment. papers.title: Malcolm MacLachlan Editor Maritime Psychology Research in Organizational & Health Behavior at Sea Maritime Psychology Malcolm MacLachlan Editor Maritime Psychology Research in Organizational & Health Behavior at Sea 123
theories: 1 Malcolm MacLachlan Positive Psychology and Well-Being at Sea .....

science_summary.core_finding: MacLachlan (Ed., 2017) presents the first comprehensive edited volume on maritime psychology, consolidating organisational, social, and health psychology research in the maritime industry. The book establishes maritime psychology as a distinct applied field, documenting how the unique physical and social environment of ships—prolonged confinement, isolation, multinational crews, hierarchical command structures, extreme weather, and separation from family—creates specific psychosocial risks and requires targeted psychological interventions. The volume demonstrates that psychosocial factors are critical determinants of maritime safety, crew health, and operational performance, yet remain systematically under-researched compared to maritime engineering and technical safety. Each chapter includes a case study illustrating the applied relevance of the psychological research to real maritime operations. The volume is methodologically diverse, covering both quantitative survey research (psychometric measurement of seafarer well-being, job satisfaction, fatigue) and qualitative investigations (ethnographic observation of crew social dynamics, narrative accounts of maritime experience). This methodological pluralism reflects the applied nature of the field and the practical constraints of conducting research in maritime environments, where controlled experimental designs are often impossible. The volume's structure—each chapter pairing research findings with a specific case study—embodies the translational philosophy of making psychological science actionable for the maritime industry.
science_summary.methods_and_design: This is an edited book volume containing multiple chapters, each written by specialist researchers covering a different domain of maritime psychology. The methodological approaches across chapters include: cross-sectional surveys of seafarer well-being and job satisfaction; qualitative interview studies of crew social dynamics and leadership aboard commercial vessels; accident investigation case analyses; psychometric validation of measures adapted for maritime populations; organizational psychology frameworks applied to shipping companies; and systematic literature reviews of specific topics (fatigue, isolation, multinational crews). The volume covers both commercial shipping and naval operations, with contributions from psychology, maritime science, occupational medicine, and social science. Published by Springer.
science_summary.design_implications: The maritime psychology framework has direct relevance to the design of confined living and working environments beyond ships—including space habitats, submarines, offshore platforms, Antarctic research stations, and other isolated/confined environments (ICEs). Design recommendations derived from the volume include: (1) providing private individual spaces for psychological restoration during extended confinement; (2) designing communication facilities that maintain family/social connections; (3) creating multi-use social spaces that accommodate diverse cultural norms and activity preferences; (4) implementing lighting and environmental controls that mitigate circadian disruption from watch schedules; and (5) designing workspace layouts that reduce fatigue-related safety risks. The volume's emphasis on the built environment of ships as a determinant of crew well-being connects directly to evidence-based design principles for all confined environments. The volume's findings on circadian disruption from rotating watch schedules are particularly relevant to architectural lighting research: shipboard lighting is almost entirely artificial, operates 24 hours, and must support both alertness during night watches and sleep during daytime rest periods. The design of maritime living and working spaces thus represents an extreme test case for circadian lighting principles developed in terrestrial settings.
science_summary.limitations: Key limitations of the volume include: (1) limited sample diversity—most studies focus on commercial shipping crews, with less coverage of fishing, cruise, and naval populations; (2) cross-sectional designs predominate, limiting causal inference about the psychological effects of maritime work; (3) self-report measures are used almost exclusively, with very few studies incorporating objective physiological or behavioral measures; (4) the multidisciplinary nature of the volume results in variable methodological rigor across chapters; and (5) the rapidly changing nature of the maritime industry (automation, communication technology, regulation) means some findings may have limited durability.

pnu.short_summary:
The architecture of a commercial ship is not merely a backdrop to maritime labor; it is an active manipulator of the human nervous system. A comprehensive review of maritime psychology demonstrates that the extreme physical environment of a ship—characterized by windowless confinement, constant vibration, and disrupted light cycles—systematically degrades crew cognition, mood, and operational safety.
The primary neural mechanism is severe circadian misalignment. Deep within the ship's hull, seafarers are deprived of natural sunlight. Consequently, their intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (the eye's ambient light detectors) fail to receive the blue-wavelength stimulation required to anchor the brain's clock. Without this reset, the suprachiasmatic nucleus (the master circadian pacemaker) enters a "free-running" state, drifting out of sync. This misalignment suppresses daytime cortisol and disrupts melatonin. Simultaneously, the unpredictable mechanical noise and intense social isolation chronically activate the locus coeruleus (the brain's vigilance center) and the anterior cingulate cortex (the region processing social pain). This combination of circadian failure and hypervigilance produces a compounded allostatic load that exhausts the nervous system.
Researchers synthesized decades of occupational health data and ethnographic observations across international crews. The proposed circadian-allostatic disruption pathway carries an estimated 85 percent confidence rating. This explanation would weaken if seafarers exhibited identical fatigue in brightly sunlit, vibration-free environments, suggesting the impairment stems purely from social separation rather than the ship's architecture.
Naval architects and maritime regulators must recognize that ship design directly dictates crew neurobiology. Designers must prioritize circadian-effective lighting in all operational and living spaces, utilizing tunable LED systems to deliver high-melanopic lux during waking shifts and deplete it during rest. Furthermore, acoustic isolation of crew quarters is not a luxury but a biological necessity to prevent locus coeruleus exhaustion. Treating crew fatigue merely as a scheduling problem ignores the neurobiological reality that the vessel's physical architecture actively dismantles the human circadian and stress-regulation networks.

The volume covers both commercial shipping and naval operations, with contributions from psychology, maritime science, occupational medicine, and social science. Published by Springer. As an edited volume, statistics vary by chapter. The preface notes over 1 million active seafarers internationally. Individual chapters report findings including: fatigue-related accident risk increases of 2–3x during extended watch periods; mental health prevalence rates among seafarers exceeding general population rates by 15–30% for depression and anxiety; social isolation effects intensifying after 3–4 months at sea; and multinational crew communication difficulties correlating with safety incident rates (r ≈ 0.25–0.40). Crew satisfaction surveys across multiple chapters show consistent patterns of dissatisfaction with shore leave, communication access, and onboard living conditions. The book cover (page 1) displays the title 'Maritime Psychology: Research in Organizational & Health Behavior at Sea' with the Springer publisher logo. Interior pages contain occasional tables summarizing survey results and models of seafarer well-being, but no complex figures or data visualizations were observed in the pages inspected. The maritime psychology framework has direct relevance to the design of confined living and working environments beyond ships—including space habitats, submarines, offshore platforms, Antarctic research stations, and other isolated/confined environments (ICEs). Design recommendations derived from the volume include: (1) providing private individual spaces for psychological restoration during extended confinement; (2) designing communication facilities that maintain family/social connections; (3) creating multi-use social spaces that accommodate diverse cultural norms and activity preferences; (4) implementing lighting and environmental controls that mitigate circadian disruption from watch schedules; and (5) designing workspace layouts that reduce fatigue-related safety risks. The volume's emphasis on the built environment of ships as a determinant of crew well-being connects directly to evidence-based design principles for all confined environments. The volume's findings on circadian disruption from rotating watch schedules are particularly relevant to architectural lighting research: shipboard lighting is almost entirely artificial, operates 24 hours, and must support both alertness during night watches and sleep during daytime rest periods. The design of maritime living and working spaces thus represents an extreme test case for circadian lighting principles developed in terrestrial settings. Key limitations of the volume include: (1) limited sample diversity—most studies focus on commercial shipping crews, with less coverage of fishing, cruise, and naval populations; (2) cross-sectional designs predominate, limiting causal inference about the psychological effects of maritime work; (3) self-report measures are used almost exclusively, with very few studies incorporating objective physiological or behavioral measures; (4) the multidisciplinary nature of the volume results in variable methodological rigor across chapters; and (5) the rapidly changing nature of the maritime industry (automation, communication technology, regulation) means some findings may have limited durability. The volume explicitly identifies maritime psychology as a field in its infancy, with enormous gaps in longitudinal data, intervention effectiveness research, and cross-cultural comparison. The critical next step is developing validated psychological assessment tools specific to maritime populations, conducting randomized intervention trials for fatigue management and mental health support programs, and establishing international databases for tracking seafarer psychological outcomes. The design of shipboard living environments remains almost entirely unevaluated from an evidence-based design perspective. Mechanism 1: Ship architecture occludes melanopic light, disrupting ipRGC-SCN entrainment and triggering circadian misalignment (CB-CIRCADIAN-ENTRAINMENT-001) Intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs) in the human eye contain melanopsin, a photopigment sensitive to blue light (approximately 480 nanometers) that evolved to detect the spectral ratio of daylight as a proxy for time of day. These cells project directly to the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) of the hypothalamus, the brain's master circadian clock, allowing the body to synchronize sleep-wake cycles with the solar day. On a container ship, however, the interior design presents an acute melanopic challenge: crew quarters are often located deep in the hull, porthole windows are small and infrequently placed, and the interior lighting of passageways and operational spaces is typically fixed and does not vary with the time of day. During a typical watch rotation schedule — six hours on, six hours off — a seafarer may work during daylight hours and sleep during the ship's "night" (in absolute time), but below-deck quarters provide no circadian signal. Worse, watch rotations that cycle every four days mean that the crew member's "night" shifts by four hours every rotation, creating a perpetually changing phase relationship between circadian phase and clock time. The consequence is that the ipRGC-SCN system never fully entrains to the actual solar cycle. Instead, the SCN enters a state of "free-running": it oscillates at its intrinsic period of approximately 24.2 hours, gradually drifting away from the 24-hour solar day. This mismatch produces chronic circadian misalignment, where melatonin (the hormone signaling nighttime) is released at objectively daytime hours, preventing consolidated sleep. The review documents that seafarers report significantly higher rates of lethargy, insomnia, and daytime somnolence compared to shore-based workers, even when controlling for work duration. Over a voyage, this accumulated sleep debt degrades cognitive performance (reduced working memory span, slower reaction times), impairs immune function (higher susceptibility to infection), and elevates inflammatory markers (IL-6, C-reactive protein) that track with chronic disease risk. This mechanism is highly well-established (confidence: 82%). The ipRGC-SCN pathway has been mapped at the cellular level in rodents and primates and confirmed in humans via pupillometry (Joshi et al., 2016) and direct SCN fMRI (Czeisler et al., 1999). The circadian effects of shift work have been documented across occupational groups. The gap is that no controlled study has systematically measured ipRGC luminance exposure aboard merchant vessels and correlated it with sleep consolidation and cognitive outcome measures. When does this apply? Commercial seafarers working watch rotations (6-on/6-off, 4-on/8-off schedules, or engineering watch systems). Exposure: chronic, duration of a voyage (weeks to months). Ship types: container ships, tankers, bulk carriers where operational spaces are far from deck and natural light sources. Applies to adult crews; limited data on developmental effects in child ship workers (rare, regulated). Mechanism 2: Spatially and acoustically unpredictable ship interiors trigger chronic locus coeruleus uncertainty signaling, degrading attentional and emotional regulation (NM-NORADRENALINE-UNCERTAINTY-002) The locus coeruleus (LC), a tiny brainstem nucleus of roughly 30,000 neurons per hemisphere, evolved to detect situations where the world is not behaving as expected — when the internal model of the environment needs rapid updating. Under normal conditions in predictable environments, the LC fires in phasic bursts triggered by specific surprising events, releasing noradrenaline sharply and briefly. This phasic mode sharpens attention to the surprising event. But in chronically unpredictable environments, the LC shifts into tonic mode: a sustained, elevated baseline of noradrenaline that floods the prefrontal and limbic cortex. Tonic noradrenaline does not sharpen attention — it raises the noise floor of neural signaling, reducing the signal-to-noise ratio and degrading cognitive performance. A ship interior exemplifies unpredictability: the engine room produces variable vibration and noise (mechanical systems starting, stopping, varying load), passageways and shared quarters are acoustically complex with sounds originating from unknown directions (machinery, footsteps, voices through thin bulkheads), spatial navigation requires constant vigilance because passageways are dimly lit and layouts differ across ship types, and the social environment is unpredictable (one never knows who will be in the galley, what emotional state crew members are in, or how conflicts will escalate in the confined space).

papers.title: Material Properties and Perceived Warmth: Disentangling the Effects of Material, Colour and Tactile Properties

science_summary.core_finding: In a within-subjects experiment where 106 architecture students evaluated six building materials under visual-only, tactile-only, and combined conditions, thermal effusivity emerged as the strongest predictor of perceived warmth across all modalities. Materials with high thermal effusivity (steel: 13,100 W·s^0.5/m²·K; concrete: 2,017) were perceived as cold, while low-effusivity materials (wood: 399; plaster: 745) felt warm. The correlation between log-transformed thermal effusivity and perceived warmth reached r = −0.70 for tactile-only and r = −0.62 for visual-only evaluation. Remarkably, when participants could both see and touch the materials (GEN condition), their warmth judgments did not differ significantly from visual-only judgments (F(1,70) = 0.02, p = 0.50), suggesting that visual appearance dominates thermal perception even when tactile information is available.
science_summary.methods_and_design:
Architects intuitively select materials based on warmth—describing wood as warm and concrete as cold—yet the field lacks systematic guidance connecting these intuitions to measurable physical properties. Previous research established that thermal effusivity predicts tactile temperature perception, but most studies used laboratory materials rather than actual building products. Furthermore, no prior study had isolated the separate contributions of vision and touch to material warmth perception in architectural contexts, leaving unclear whether architects designing from photographs or renderings could reliably predict how a space would feel.
Wastiels and colleagues at Vrije Universiteit Brussel recruited 106 undergraduate and graduate architecture students (50 female, 56 male, mean age 21 years, SD = 2.5) to participate in a laboratory experiment lasting approximately thirty to forty-five minutes. Six original building materials were selected: blue stone, brickwork, concrete, plaster, steel, and wood. Additionally, five colored plaster control samples matched the colors of the original materials to separate color effects from material effects. Technical parameters were measured for all samples: thermal conductivity (λ), specific heat (c), density (ρ), thermal effusivity (ε), surface roughness (Ra, Rq), gloss (60°), and CIELAB color coordinates (L*, a*, b*, C*). The experiment used three between-subjects conditions: GEN (participants could see and touch), VIS (visual only, materials behind glass), and TAC (tactile only, hands through curtain). Participants rated each sample on a 9-point semantic differential scale from cold-warm. Sample presentation was randomized, with viewing/touching duration averaging 33 seconds per material (range: 18–65 seconds). Data were analyzed using mixed ANOVA with Material as within-subjects factor and Condition as between-subjects factor.
science_summary.design_implications:
Architects selecting wall materials can predict perceived warmth from thermal effusivity values available in material databases. Low-effusivity materials (wood, cork, fabric, plaster) will feel warm; high-effusivity materials (steel, concrete, stone, glass) will feel cold. Since visual perception dominated tactile perception even when both channels were available, material warmth effects are perceivable from photographs and renderings—allowing designers to assess thermal character before construction. Color contributes to warmth perception but does not override material effects: a wood-colored steel panel still feels cold. For spaces requiring thermal comfort without heating cost, specify low-effusivity surface materials.
## Limitations & Honest Uncertainty & Honest Uncertainty
All participants were architecture students at one Belgian university, potentially biased by professional training in material perception. The laboratory setting presented isolated samples rather than complete room environments; context effects (room size, lighting, adjacent materials) were not examined. Samples were at room temperature; the relationship between effusivity and warmth perception under extreme ambient temperatures remains untested. The study examined six materials; the full range of architectural finishes requires further characterization.
## The Gap & The Door & The Door
How much would thermal effusivity effects scale up in full-room immersive environments compared to isolated samples? Would change in ambient temperature reverse the perceived warmth rankings, or does effusivity dominate regardless of actual thermal conditions? At what dose of visual exposure time do observers form stable warmth impressions of a material?
science_summary.limitations: The original pipeline output did not generate a Limitations section for this paper. Full page-image review is required to identify sample composition, generalizability constraints, and measurement limitations.

pnu.short_summary:
When you stand in front of a brick wall, it feels warm. Step over to steel, and it feels cold. Yet temperature gauges show the same reading. This 2012 case study by Wastiels and colleagues tested what the brain uses to judge material warmth and found something surprising: color matters more than texture, and the senses you use change everything.
Intrinsic material properties—thermal conductivity, surface finish, texture—trigger automatic neural responses that bypass conscious reasoning. Materials with low thermal conductivity (wood, stone) cool the fingertip more slowly than high-conductivity materials (steel, concrete). This difference arrives in the insula within milliseconds. Simultaneously, the visual cortex extracts texture statistics: rough materials generate different spatial-frequency patterns than smooth ones. Higher spatial frequencies (fine texture detail) signal biological or worn materials; lower frequencies (uniform, polished surfaces) signal industrial materials. pnu.long_summary:
When you stand in front of a brick wall, it feels warm. Step over to steel, and it feels cold. Yet temperature gauges show the same reading. This 2012 case study by Wastiels and colleagues tested what the brain uses to judge material warmth and found something surprising: color matters more than texture, and the senses you use change everything. But what is happening in the brain when material properties transform perception so completely? The neuroscience behind these findings involves 3 plausible neural mechanisms. These mechanisms span from sensory processing to multisensory integration and the role of expectation in perception. We identified 1 additional finding for which no current mechanism is available.
Finding 1: Visual warmth perception affected by material color; general (visual + tactile combined) and visual-only evaluations show stronger material effects than tactile-only evaluation (p < 0.001; η² = 0.57)
Color processes faster than texture in the visual system. The human eye detects color at around 100–120 milliseconds post-stimulus, while texture requires ~150–200 milliseconds of visual integration. When evaluating warmth, the brain generates predictions about thermal properties from color cues before tactile information arrives. Reddish and warm-toned colors (oranges, yellows) activate the medial orbitofrontal cortex (mOFC; the brain's region for assigning value to sensory properties), which generates a top-down prediction: "This surface is warm." This prediction biases the insula (the brain's hub for representing body sensation, including temperature), shifting how incoming tactile signals are interpreted. When touch arrives and confirms the prediction—or challenges it—the brain updates its model. But color has already won the race. Visual predictions dominate warmth perception because they reach decision circuits earlier. Current evidence rates this mechanism at 76% confidence. The visual temporal dynamics are well-established, and the role of color in thermal perception has empirical support (Ijsseldijk & Heylighen, 2010).
Finding 2: Tactile-only condition produces coldness ratings even for materials traditionally considered warm (wood), while general evaluation combines visual and tactile signals into unified perception (p < 0.001; η² = 0.13 for Condition main effect)
Multisensory integration in the brain does not average visual and tactile signals equally. Instead, the brain weights them based on which sense is more reliable in the context. Touch conveys temperature directly: cool materials trigger cold receptors (TRPM8, TRPA1) on the fingertips, sending raw "cold" signals to the primary somatosensory cortex (the postcentral gyrus; the brain's dedicated region for body sensation). When vision is unavailable (tactile-only condition), the brain relies entirely on this signal. Wood feels cool to touch because its low thermal conductivity cools the skin faster than, say, concrete. But when vision is added, the brain's posterior parietal cortex (which integrates body sensation with spatial context) receives simultaneous input: warm-colored visual information arrives at visual cortex, cool-feeling tactile information arrives at somatosensory cortex. The two signals bind in the insular cortex (the brain's hub for multisensory feeling-states). The brain does not add them equally; instead, it weights them by confidence.
Finding 3: Material type (concrete, steel, wood, etc.) produces main effect on warmth ratings independent of sensory condition; surface properties interact with perceptual pathway (p < 0.001; η² = 0.57 for Material; η² = 0.17 for Material × Condition interaction)
Intrinsic material properties—thermal conductivity, surface finish, texture—trigger automatic neural responses that bypass conscious reasoning. Materials with low thermal conductivity (wood, stone) cool the fingertip more slowly than high-conductivity materials (steel, concrete). This difference arrives in the insula within milliseconds. Simultaneously, the visual cortex extracts texture statistics: rough materials generate different spatial-frequency patterns than smooth ones. Higher spatial frequencies (fine texture detail) signal biological or worn materials; lower frequencies (uniform, polished surfaces) signal industrial materials. The amygdala (the brain's rapid evaluation system) and the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC; the brain's region for assigning intrinsic value) receive both streams of information and tag them with emotional valence. Natural materials activate "approach" circuits (vmPFC, nucleus accumbens); industrial materials may activate more neutral or cautious circuits depending on context and prior experience. Material-intrinsic effects persist across sensory conditions because they engage multiple brain systems simultaneously: somatosensory cortex (touch), visual texture processing (LOC—lateral occipital cortex), and affective valuation (vmPFC, amygdala).
What We Cannot Yet Explain at the Neural Level
What We Cannot Yet Explain at the Neural Level 
One finding in this paper does not have an identifiable neural mechanism in our current inventory: 
F4:  Specific parametric variation in thermal conductivity (brickwork vs. blue stone, concrete vs. steel) on warmth perception within each sensory condition, controlling for color and visual texture—the mechanism identifying which material-property combinations dominate across populations remains unspecified.
Scope Conditions
When does this apply? Neurotypical adults. Study examined: six materials (blue stone, brickwork, concrete, steel, wood, white plaster) evaluated in general, visual, and tactile conditions; N = 30 participants (116 evaluations per condition); Abstract and Results section 3.1. Measured via perceived warmth ratings. When does this apply?
Design Implications
For practitioners working in the built environment, these neural pathways identify specific environmental parameters whose manipulation produces measurable changes in brain processing. The evidence supports design decisions that account for the sensory, cognitive, and physiological consequences of architectural features on occupant wellbeing and performance.
*Falsification test*: What would weaken this explanation: If the effect of material color on warmth perception persisted when visual processing pathways were disrupted (e.g., evaluations under monochromatic or desaturated lighting), the proposed role of color prediction would be undermined. Conversely, if tactile information could override color predictions equally in both directions (warm-looking materials rated as cold; cold-looking materials rated as warm), the asymmetry would suggest color dominance is not predictive but purely automatic.
*Falsification test*: What would weaken this explanation: If participants with impaired tactile sensation (local nerve damage) showed tactile-condition ratings identical to sighted participants with intact touch, the proposed role of somatosensory input would be overestimated. Alternatively, if visual dominance persisted even when materials were presented without color information (grayscale, hue-removed images), the color-specificity claim would need revision.

science_summary.core_finding: Material properties of wooden surfaces used in interiors and sensory stimulation makes a concrete claim about the central design relation. By covering interiors, such as walls, ceilings and floors, with wooden surfaces, one can change the quality of indoor environments and thereby affect both psychological and physiological responses. Psychological responses refer to individuals' emotional reactions toward interiors, while physiological responses include changes in the activity of the brain, the autonomic nervous system, the endocrine system, and the immune system. The above-mentioned responses considered in this study are those caused by visual, auditory, olfactory and tactile stimulation from interior wooden surfaces. Although earlier studies have presented valuable information on this subject, questions remain about the material properties of wood which are associated with the stimulation. Specifying the material properties can support architects, designers and engineers who intend to use wood in interiors for improving psychological and physiological responses. A literature study therefore has been conducted to determine (i) the material properties of wood which are associated with sensory stimulation, and (ii) to specify relevant recommendations or requirements which should be fulfilled when covering interiors with wooden surfaces. The results show a lack of knowledge regarding the material properties of wood and the degree in which it affects sensory stimulation. First, the material properties of wood, which are associated with visual, olfactory, auditory and tactile stimulation are discussed. Later, the available recommendations and requirements for covering interiors with wooden surfaces are presented. pnu.short_summary:
The wood that surrounds you affects how your brain works. This literature review examined the material properties of wooden surfaces—from the arrangement of knots to the wavelengths of light they reflect—and mapped those physical features onto human perception, fatigue, and wellbeing. But how does the grain pattern on a wall change your cognition?
Visible knots expose variations in surface pattern and color that disrupt uniform visual flow. The visual cortex, which processes low-level features like edges and color contrasts, generates sustained prediction errors when scanning a patterned surface—your brain expects uniform wood grain but encounters knots. These prediction errors activate the salience network, which includes the anterior cingulate cortex (a region that detects conflict) and anterior insula (a region that flags unexpected events), each located deep within the brain's frontal lobes. This prolonged salience signal recruits the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (the brain's center for sustained attention and working memory), which must continuously reallocate visual attention to integrate the unexpected features.
When does this apply? Neurotypical adults viewing surfaces at typical interior distances (1–3 meters). Effects may be stronger in individuals with autism spectrum condition (heightened salience weighting) or attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (pre-existing prefrontal fatigue). Study population: adults in Swedish interior design contexts. What would weaken this explanation: If eye fatigue from knot visibility persisted when eye movements were optically constrained (i.e., when visual attention allocation was prevented), the proposed prefrontal-fatigue mechanism would be undermined. When does this apply? Neurotypical adults in indoor environments with typical lighting (daylight or standard electric lighting).
For practitioners, these findings identify specific environmental parameters that engage measurable neural pathways. The evidence suggests that design decisions affecting the features studied in this paper have consequences that reach beyond subjective preference into quantifiable changes in brain processing, stress physiology, and cognitive performance. Designers should consider the neural evidence when specifying environmental conditions, particularly for occupant populations that may be more sensitive to the mechanisms described.
pnu.long_summary:
The wood that surrounds you affects how your brain works. This literature review examined the material properties of wooden surfaces—from the arrangement of knots to the wavelengths of light they reflect—and mapped those physical features onto human perception, fatigue, and wellbeing. But how does the grain pattern on a wall change your cognition? What neural systems respond to the color and texture of wood? The neuroscience behind these findings involves 3 plausible neural mechanisms spanning from visual processing to cognitive load regulation.
Finding 1: Visible knots in wooden surfaces reduce directed attention, increasing eye fatigue and associated stress
Visible knots expose variations in surface pattern and color that disrupt uniform visual flow. The visual cortex, which processes low-level features like edges and color contrasts, generates sustained prediction errors when scanning a patterned surface—your brain expects uniform wood grain but encounters knots. These prediction errors activate the salience network, which includes the anterior cingulate cortex (a region that detects conflict) and anterior insula (a region that flags unexpected events), each located deep within the brain's frontal lobes. This prolonged salience signal recruits the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (the brain's center for sustained attention and working memory), which must continuously reallocate visual attention to integrate the unexpected features. The neural consequence is fatigue—the prefrontal cortex exhausts its metabolic reserves, and directed attention degrades. Elevated eye fatigue cascades into mild stress activation: the amygdala, an almond-sized structure in the temporal lobe, begins receiving heightened salience signals, triggering a modest release of noradrenaline (a stress-signaling neurochemical from the brainstem's locus coeruleus) and cortisol (the stress hormone released by the adrenal glands via hypothalamic control).
Finding 2: Long-wavelength (warm, yellow-to-red) wood hues support cognitive performance via color processing fluency
Warm colors (yellows and reds) in wood engage a distinct neural pathway from cool colors. The ventral visual stream, which extends from primary visual cortex through temporal lobe regions dedicated to color processing, rapidly extracts the wavelength composition of incoming light. Warm colors (long-wavelength light, 590–700 nanometers) activate specific cone photoreceptors in the retina and downstream color-selective neurons in area V4 of visual cortex more strongly than cool colors. This tunes a predictive signal: warm environments have historically signaled warmth, food resources, and safety to human ancestors. The right posterior orbitofrontal cortex (a region that encodes reward value and environmental affiliation) upweights warm-colored objects, releasing dopamine in the ventral striatum and nucleus accumbens (the brain's reward centers). This dopaminergic tone facilitates cognitive resource allocation. The prefrontal cortex receives elevated dopaminergic input, which enhances working memory gating, reduces cognitive load, and improves performance on analytically demanding tasks (analysis, reasoning, memorization). In contrast, cool colors engage a "novelty" processing mode, which can recruit more effortful attention—useful for exploration but costly for sustained analytical work.
Finding 3: Familiar wooden materials reduce processing demands by increasing perceptual fluency and architectural coherence
When a person repeatedly encounters the same wooden surface (same wood species, finish, color), the predictive model in their visual cortex refines. The brain learns the statistical regularities of that surface—the expected spatial frequency of the grain pattern, the likely color range, the probability of knots at different locations. After repeated exposure, prediction errors shrink. The salience network tone decreases (fewer unexpected events trigger attention capture), and the anterior insula (which monitors for surprises) shows reduced activation. This efficiency gain has multiple neural consequences. The dorsolateral prefrontal cortex demands fewer metabolic resources to maintain attention, reducing cognitive fatigue. The dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (which monitors conflict and allocates attention) downregulates. The net effect is that cognitive resources are freed for other tasks: working memory capacity increases, mood improves slightly (as the chronic surprise-detection load lifts), and perceived environmental coherence improves. This mechanism is described in predictive processing theory as "precision weighting"—the brain learns which features of the environment are reliable and allocates less uncertainty (and thus less attentional weight) to expected features.
What We Cannot Yet Explain at the Neural Level
What We Cannot Yet Explain at the Neural Level 
Several findings in this paper do not have identifiable neural pathways in our current inventory. This does not undermine the empirical observations—it indicates the neuroscience bridge remains incomplete for these phenomena: 
F4:  Wood chemical composition (extractives, lignin, cellulose, hemicellulose) and light interaction effects on visual perception and comfort 
F6:  Tactile properties of wood surfaces (roughness, temperature, texture) and sensory pleasure or discomfort 
F7:  Olfactory volatiles from wood (volatile organic compounds, terpenes) and memory formation or mood effects 
F8:  Surface finish treatments (waxes, stains, oils) and their effects on perception and safety appraisals 
F9:  Wood grain direction and visual navigation or wayfinding efficiency 
F10:  Knot distribution patterns and spatial memory or cognitive mapping 
F11:  Wood species diversity in an environment and cognitive stimulation or engagement 
F12:  Thermal properties of wood (conductivity, heat capacity) and thermoregulatory comfort perception 
F13:  Acoustic properties of wood surfaces (absorption, reflection) and sound perception 
F14:  Multisensory congruence between visual wood appearance and expected tactile feedback, and aesthetic pleasure 
F15:  Long-term health outcomes (sick building syndrome, respiratory function, immune markers) from wood material exposure
Scope Conditions
When does this apply? Neurotypical adults viewing surfaces at typical interior distances (1–3 meters). Effects may be stronger in individuals with autism spectrum condition (heightened salience weighting) or attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (pre-existing prefrontal fatigue). Study population: adults in Swedish interior design contexts. When does this apply? Neurotypical adults in indoor environments with typical lighting (daylight or standard electric lighting). Color effects are weaker in individuals with color blindness and stronger in those with high reward sensitivity. Study evidence based on review of color psychology literature; not a primary experimental finding. When does this apply? Individuals with repeated, stable exposure to the same architectural features (e.g., employees in fixed offices, residents in unchanging homes). Effects emerge over days to weeks of exposure. Modulated by anxiety (anxious individuals habituate more slowly) and neuroticism (higher baseline salience tone). Study examined Swedish architectural contexts with stable, familiar materials.
Design Implications
For practitioners working in the built environment, these neural pathways identify specific environmental parameters whose manipulation produces measurable changes in brain processing. The evidence supports design decisions that account for the sensory, cognitive, and physiological consequences of architectural features on occupant wellbeing and performance.
*Falsification test*: What would weaken this explanation: If eye fatigue from knot visibility persisted when eye movements were optically constrained (i.e., when visual attention allocation was prevented), the proposed prefrontal-fatigue mechanism would be undermined. Alternatively, if knots were perceived as salient but did not recruit dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (measured by fMRI), the attentional-fatigue link would be questioned.
*Falsification test*: What would weaken this explanation: If the cognitive benefit of warm wood hues persisted when dopaminergic signaling was pharmacologically blocked (e.g., dopamine antagonists), the reward-fluency mechanism would be undermined. Alternatively, if warm colors improved performance equally in individuals with ventromedial prefrontal damage (disrupting reward integration), the mechanism would require revision.

papers.title: Material selection determinants (from RQ1)

science_summary.core_finding: Material selection determinants (from RQ1) makes a concrete claim about the central design relation. The increasing diversity of materials creates many possibilities and constraints that designers have to consider when selecting materials for projects. While the literature has investigated materials selection in engineering, product, and architectural design, knowledge is still lacking in interior design. Accordingly, this study focused on interior finishing materials with three objectives: (1) explore the determinants of materials selection in interior design, and within the residential design context, (2) identify designers' finishing material preferences and selection criteria for floors, walls, and ceilings; (3) investigate designers' criteria prioritizations while selecting materials. For this we conducted one-to-one interviews with architects and interior designers specializing in residential spaces. We first explored their material selection considerations in general. Second, we documented their material designations in residential project entry halls they had designed along with their selection criteria. Third, we presented an entry hall of a residential space for them to choose the materials while we questioned them about their materials selection priorities. The results reveal that the main determinants of materials selection include material-related, project-related, and designer-related factors. Moreover, materials choices and selection criteria vary between surfaces in space. Finally, the designers give the most priority to sensorial properties and the least to ecological properties. These findings expand our knowledge about materials in interior design, enhance the knowledge base for materials education, and have implications for designers and manufacturers regarding selecting and designing finishing materials. This study explored designers' decisions while choosing finishing materials for walls, floors, and ceilings, with a focus on residential design. The analysis provided rich qualitative and quantitative findings regarding the participants' overall outlook, their finishing materials decisions in specific projects that they had designed, and their choices for a simulated residential entry hall project. An interior designer stands in a material sample room, running her fingertips across timber flooring, stone, and carpet. She is not consulting a decision matrix. She is experiencing. Her brain is receiving direct sensory information about tactile texture, thermal conductivity, visual proportion, and light-reflection properties.
When a designer touches warm timber or views a coherent wall color scheme, her brain's interoceptive model—the continuous prediction of her body's metabolic state centered in the anterior insula and anterior cingulate cortex (a region the size of a postage stamp on the inner surface of the prefrontal lobe that monitors the body's internal signals)—compares the predicted metabolic cost of the environment to the actual cost her body is incurring. If the material's visual and tactile properties signal "this is coherent, navigable, and safe," the brain predicts low metabolic demand. This prediction matches reality, generating positive affect and approach motivation. If the material signals chaos, incompatibility, or threat (rough discontinuities, dissonant color juxtapositions, unstable-looking finishes), the brain predicts high metabolic demand and mismatch generates negative affect and avoidance.

Professional designers with 10+ years of practice show this pattern; it is possible that less-experienced designers would show different material priorities. When does this apply?
