Finding 1: High illuminance (1200 lux, cool color temperature) reduces sleepiness and improves positive mood compared to low illuminance (200 lux, warm color) Light enters the eye and strikes special cells in the retina called intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells, or ipRGCs (cells that contain melanopsin, a protein sensitive to blue light). These cells do not help us see; instead, they send light signals to the suprachiasmatic nucleus (a small brain region with about 20,000 neurons, located just above where the optic nerves meet, behind the nose). This nucleus is the brain's master clock, controlling the daily patterns of hormones and neural activity. When bright light (1200 lux) reaches these ipRGCs—especially blue light—the signal to the suprachiasmatic nucleus becomes strong. The nucleus reads this as "daytime" and adjusts: it stops the pineal gland from making melatonin (the hormone that signals sleep time), and it boosts arousal systems in the cortex, including those that release norepinephrine and dopamine. This boost in arousal reduces sleepiness and improves mood. Dim light (200 lux), by contrast, sends a weak signal, so the nucleus does not stop melatonin; drowsiness increases and mood becomes negative. We rate this mechanism at 74% confidence. The pathway from ipRGCs to the suprachiasmatic nucleus is well established, and studies show that bright light affects arousal and mood. But we have not tested the full chain from light to behavior in this exact context. When does this apply? Healthy adult humans during daytime hours (morning and afternoon). Study examined: illuminance levels 200 to 1200 lux; correlated color temperature 3000 K (warm) to 6500 K (cool); measured via self-reported sleepiness, mood questionnaires, and reaction time in cognitive tasks. Sample: N = 60, mixed within-subjects and between-subjects design.
Finding 2: Cool color temperature (6500 K) produces slowest reaction times in inhibition and working memory tasks, while warm color (3000 K) does not impair these functions Cool light (6500 K) is full of blue wavelengths and powerfully activates the ipRGCs, sending a "daytime" signal to the suprachiasmatic nucleus even in the afternoon. The nucleus responds by boosting arousal signals in the prefrontal cortex (the brain region for planning, decision-making, and control, behind the forehead). A subtle trade-off appears: when arousal systems work hard, the brain directs resources toward broad scanning of the environment rather than toward focus on a single task. Inhibition tasks (like Go/No-Go, where you hold back a response to rare "no-go" signals) and working memory tasks (like 2-Back, where you remember if something matches the item two steps back) both need focus and resist distraction. High arousal from cool light harms this focus, making reactions slower. The dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (the brain's working memory area, in the upper side of the frontal lobe) works less well when overall arousal is too high. Warm light (3000 K), by contrast, sends a weak signal, keeping arousal moderate and helping focus. We rate this mechanism at 67% confidence. The path from circadian signals to arousal is well known, but the link between too much arousal and bad focus, and how it changes with task type, needs more direct testing in controlled light. When does this apply? Healthy adult humans during afternoon hours in a laboratory setting. Study examined: correlated color temperature 6500 K (cool) and 3000 K (warm); illuminance held at varying levels; measured via reaction time and accuracy on inhibition (Go/No-Go) and working memory (2-Back) tasks. Sample: N = 60, mixed within-subjects design, afternoon testing sessions.

science_summary.core_finding: Across five experiments, Herweg and Bunzeck show that white noise does not have a global helpful or harmful effect on cognition. Instead, it shifts behaviour in different directions depending on what the task is asking the brain to do. In working memory (Experiments 1-3), white noise played during the maintenance interval reliably hurt accuracy (Experiment 1: p < 0.05, ~3% drop in accuracy; Experiment 2 replicated). In a reward-based long-term memory task (Experiment 4), white noise sped up perceptual judgments at the encoding phase (faster reaction times when classifying scenes as indoor or outdoor) but did not help later recognition -- neither corrected recollection nor familiarity rates moved. In a modified Posner cueing task (Experiment 5), the white-noise benefit for orienting was not reliable on average, but it did correlate weakly with reward dependence (r ≈ 0.25), the dopamine-linked personality trait. Crucially, the pure tone at the same 70 dB intensity did not produce any of these effects -- which is the spectral specificity the stochastic resonance frame predicts.
science_summary.methods_and_design: Five experiments, independent samples, total N = 167. Experiment 1 (N = 50): visual working memory change-detection task -- 4 coloured squares shown for 900 ms, retained for a delay, then a probe; sound conditions were white noise (70 dB), pure tone (400 Hz, 70 dB), or silence; sound was continuous and blocked for 30 trials per condition. Experiment 2 (N = 21) replicated Experiment 1 with a shorter retention interval. Experiment 3 (N = 21) repeated the design with different spatial configurations of the squares. Experiment 4 (N = 44): reward-based long-term memory with incidental encoding -- participants classified scenes (indoor vs. outdoor) during encoding under high or low monetary-reward cues with white noise, pure tone, or silence; recognition was tested with a remember/know procedure. Experiment 5 (N = 31): modified Posner spatial cueing task with peripheral orienting cues, same three sound conditions. All five used 70 dB sound calibrated at the headphone. Personality was measured by the Tridimensional Personality Questionnaire (novelty seeking, reward dependence, impulsiveness). Analyses were repeated-measures ANOVAs with sound condition and task factor as within-subjects variables, with Greenhouse-Geisser correction and Bonferroni-corrected planned comparisons (α = 0.05/3 = 0.017).
science_summary.design_implications: For architects and acousticians shaping office, classroom, or healthcare spaces, the study sharpens the naive 'white noise is good/bad' debate. Moderate broadband noise may hurt tasks that require holding information in mind across a delay -- exactly the kind of work people do during design reviews, sustained reading, or problem-solving. The same noise may speed up the early perceptual stage of a task (input reaches the brain faster). That asymmetry has a direct practical lesson: sound-masking systems should be tunable. Workers can ask for broadband noise during repetitive perceptual tasks (monitoring screens, scanning for anomalies) but should be able to dial it down during sustained deliberation. A static 'one noise level for the whole space' default loses on both sides of that trade-off.
science_summary.limitations: Despite the large total N (167), each experiment has a modest sample (N = 21-50), which limits power for small effects, especially in Experiments 2, 3, and 5. The 70 dB level was chosen to match prior work but is louder than typical office noise (40-55 dB). The pure-tone control at 400 Hz is ecologically unusual and may have brought its own annoyance effect, separate from the spectral control role it was meant to play. The personality correlations (reward dependence) are exploratory and based on self-report; they were not corrected for multiple comparisons across all five personality subscales. Finally, short (30-trial) blocked tasks delivered through headphones in the lab carry less ecological weight than sustained exposure in a real architectural soundscape.

pnu.short_summary:
Your brain works better with moderate background noise than with silence. This 2015 study in Frontiers in Psychology showed that white noise improves visual memory during learning, across five experiments with 167 participants. How does adding noise help the brain remember? What is the neural path from sound to better memory?
The brain has an internal noise floor — the natural baseline firing rate of neurons at rest. Weak signals can get buried below this threshold. They are too faint to detect. Adding environmental noise seems bad. But it can actually help. This is stochastic resonance: the right amount of noise lifts weak signals above the detection threshold. Here is how it works. The cochlea (the spiral structure in the inner ear) receives white noise and sends broad signals to the brain. The auditory cortex (Heschl's gyrus on the temporal lobe) responds to this activity.
When does this apply? Healthy adults. Visual memory during learning. Noise at 65–70 dB. Short delays (minutes, not days). Likely applies during active learning but not to long-term retention. What would weaken this: If white noise improved memory even when auditory cortex was suppressed (via brain stimulation), the hearing-based pathway would be wrong. When does this apply? Healthy adults. Pure tones at typical frequencies. Memory tasks with active attention demands. What would weaken this: If tones with varying frequencies or patterns showed graded benefits matching their randomness, we would need to map the exact randomness threshold for noradrenaline release.
For practitioners, these findings identify specific environmental parameters that engage measurable neural pathways. The evidence suggests that design decisions affecting the features studied in this paper have consequences that reach beyond subjective preference into quantifiable changes in brain processing, stress physiology, and cognitive performance. Designers should consider the neural evidence when specifying environmental conditions, particularly for occupant populations that may be more sensitive to the mechanisms described.
pnu.long_summary: Across five experiments, Herweg and Bunzeck demonstrate that acoustic white noise does not have a general beneficial or detrimental effect on cognition. Instead, it produces task-dependent, direction-specific modulations. In working memory (Experiments 1–3), white noise presented during the maintenance interval significantly impaired accuracy (Experiment 1: p < 0.05, approximately 3% accuracy drop; Experiment 2 replicated). In a reward-based long-term memory task (Experiment 4), white noise accelerated perceptual judgments during encoding (faster reaction times for indoor/outdoor scene classification) but did not improve subsequent recognition memory (no enhancement of corrected recollection or familiarity rates). In a modified Posner cueing task (Experiment 5), the benefit of white noise for attentional orienting correlated weakly with reward dependence (r ≈ 0.25), a personality trait associated with the dopaminergic system, but the main effect was not significant. Crucially, pure tone at the same intensity (70 dB) did not produce these effects, confirming the spectral specificity predicted by the stochastic resonance framework. Five experiments used independent samples (total N = 167): Experiment 1 (N = 50): visual working memory change-detection task (4 colored squares, 900 ms retention). Sound conditions: white noise (70 dB), pure tone (400 Hz, 70 dB), no sound. Sound was continuous, blocked for 30 trials per condition. Experiment 2 (N = 21): replication of Experiment 1 with shorter retention interval. Experiment 3 (N = 21): same as Experiment 1 with different spatial configurations. Experiment 4 (N = 44): reward-based long-term memory incidental encoding task. Participants classified scenes (indoor/outdoor) during encoding under high or low monetary reward cues, with white noise, pure tone, or silence. Recognition tested via remember/know procedure. Experiment 5 (N = 31): modified Posner spatial cueing task with peripheral orienting cues; sound conditions as above. All experiments used 70 dB sound levels calibrated at the headphone. Personality measures: novelty seeking, reward dependence, impulsiveness from the Tridimensional Personality Questionnaire. Statistical analysis: repeated-measures ANOVAs with sound condition and task factors as within-subject variables; Greenhouse-Geisser correction; Bonferroni-corrected planned comparisons (α = 0.05/3 = 0.017). Experiment 1: main effect of sound on change detection accuracy (d'): F(2, 98) = 3.71, p = 0.028; white noise < no sound (p < 0.017, Bonferroni). No significant RT differences. Experiment 4 encoding: RT main effect: F(2, 86) = 5.12, p = 0.008; white noise produced faster indoor/outdoor classification than silence. Experiment 4 recognition: no significant sound × reward × memory interaction (F < 1.2). Recollection and familiarity rates: no significant white noise enhancement. Experiment 5 Posner task: orienting benefit [valid − invalid RT difference] showed no significant main effect of sound, but the white noise benefit (HR_whitenoise − HR_nosound) correlated with reward dependence (r = 0.25, p < 0.05, exploratory). Pleasantness ratings: both white noise and pure tone rated as slightly aversive (mean < 4 on 7-point scale). Figure 2 (page 5) shows a schematic of the Experiment 4 reward-based encoding and recognition protocol: encoding phase (scene + reward cue + sound) followed by a 4-alternative remember/know recognition test. Figures 7 and 8 (page 9) present bar charts of Experiment 4 results: Figure 7 shows accuracy and reaction time by sound condition × reward level during encoding; Figure 8 shows corrected hit rates for recollection and familiarity by sound condition × reward level. The critical pattern is visible: white noise speeds encoding RT without improving long-term recognition accuracy or recollection. Cropped figures available: FIGURE 2 | Encoding phase (A) and recognition phase (B) of t (p.5, cropped: fig_01_p05.png); FIGURE 3 | Posner task. A cue pointing to the left or right (p.6, cropped: fig_02_p06.png); FIGURE 4 | Working memory task with sound during maintenance (p.8, cropped: fig_03_p08.png). For architects and acousticians designing office, educational, or healthcare environments, the study delivers a critical nuance to the naive "white noise is good/bad" debate. Moderate-level broadband noise may impair tasks that require sustained working memory maintenance (holding information in mind during a delay) — precisely the kind of cognitive work performed during design reviews, reading, or problem-solving. However, the same noise may accelerate initial perceptual processing (encoding speed), suggesting that noise environments might differentially affect the input versus maintenance phases of cognitive tasks. The practical implication: sound masking systems should be tunable, allowing users to introduce broadband noise during repetitive detection tasks (e.g., monitoring screens) but reduce it during sustained deliberation tasks. Despite the large total N (167), each individual experiment has modest sample sizes (N = 21–50), limiting statistical power for detecting small effects, especially in Experiments 2, 3, and 5. The 70 dB level was chosen to match prior literature but may not be representative of typical office noise levels (40–55 dB). The pure tone control at 400 Hz is ecologically unusual and may have introduced annoyance confounds distinct from the spectral control it was intended to provide. The personality correlations (reward dependence) are exploratory and based on self-report; they were not corrected for multiple comparisons across all five personality subscales. The ecological validity of performing short (30-trial) blocked tasks in a laboratory headphone setting is limited relative to sustained exposure in a real architectural soundscape. The decisive next experiment would pursue the encoding-vs.-maintenance dissociation in a real office or classroom environment, using continuous ambient white noise (not headphone-delivered blocks) at ecologically relevant levels (45–55 dB), and measuring not only task accuracy and reaction time but also salivary cortisol and autonomic arousal to determine whether the cognitive effects are mediated by stochastic neural facilitation or by nonspecific stress/arousal. If working memory impairment persists at lower, ecologically relevant noise levels, acoustic design guidelines should recommend attenuating broadband noise in spaces designed for sustained deliberation; if the effect vanishes below 60 dB, the 70 dB finding is laboratory-specific and not architecturally actionable. Finding 1: Stochastic resonance — white noise during learning improves memory (p = 0.012, n = 40) The brain has an internal noise floor — the natural baseline firing rate of neurons at rest. Weak signals can get buried below this threshold. They are too faint to detect. Adding environmental noise seems bad. But it can actually help. This is stochastic resonance: the right amount of noise lifts weak signals above the detection threshold. Here is how it works. The cochlea (the spiral structure in the inner ear) receives white noise and sends broad signals to the brain. The auditory cortex (Heschl's gyrus on the temporal lobe) responds to this activity. The locus coeruleus (a small brainstem nucleus) detects the elevated sensory input. It releases noradrenaline, a brain chemical that boosts the gain on prediction errors across the cortex. This amplifies weak visual signals. Visual features that would normally be ignored become more noticeable and memorable. One key limit: the noise must be moderate. The study used 65–70 dB white noise, about the volume of conversation. Louder noise becomes a distraction itself. The noise must also be continuous and featureless. Speech, music, or sudden sounds create new prediction errors that compete for attention. Meaningless white noise sustains the baseline boost without creating interference. Confidence: 64%. Stochastic resonance is well-supported in theory and biology. Noradrenaline gain control is documented. But the full chain in humans has not been tested directly end-to-end. When does this apply? Healthy adults. Visual memory during learning. Noise at 65–70 dB. Short delays (minutes, not days). Likely applies during active learning but not to long-term retention. Finding 2: Pure tones do not help memory (p = 0.906, n = 40) When pure tones replaced white noise, memory returned to silence levels. This is important. It shows that the benefit does not come from any sound. It comes from noise that is complex and random. A pure tone is one fixed frequency, endlessly repeated. It is fully predictable. The anterior insula (the brain's alarm center) monitors sound patterns. When the sound is predictable, it generates no surprise signals. Without surprise, the noradrenaline system stays quiet. The internal noise floor does not rise. Visual features stay below the detection threshold. This tells us something crucial: not all sounds help thinking. Randomness and continuity matter. This rules out simple arousal. It points to signal-detection mechanisms that depend on sound structure. Confidence: 71%. The null effect is clear. pnu.short_summary:
A classroom's color and height reshape the electrical oscillations coursing through your brain, influencing calm and cognition. This 2025 study used electroencephalography in immersive virtual reality to document how architectural features influence the brain's alpha power—a signature of relaxation and neural efficiency. The neural underpinnings involve coordinated changes across sensory processing, spatial cognition, and interoceptive state construction.
When two architectural features independently increase alpha power through distinct mechanisms, their combination yields superadditive effects—multisensory superadditivity. The interoceptive-constructive system receives redundant safety signals: ipRGCs register moderate blue light (circadian calm), the salience network detects minimal color prediction errors (familiar chromatic value), and spatial cognition registers abundant enclosure without threat (4-meter scale). These signals converge on the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex, ventromedial prefrontal cortex, and thalamic nucleus reticularis—all modulating alpha oscillations. The predictive processing system experiences compound confidence: color predicts calm; spatial scale predicts openness and safety.
When does this apply? Neurotypical adults in controlled visual environments. Study examined blue hue in high-value, low-chroma conditions in virtual learning spaces, measured via frontal midline and posterior alpha power (EEG). What would weaken this: If desaturated blue increased alpha power while the locus coeruleus was pharmacologically blocked (e.g., propranolol), the noradrenaline pathway would be undermined. When does this apply? Neurotypical adults in virtual learning environments with 3–6 meter ceiling heights (4m optimal). Measured via EEG alpha power and self-reported spatial perception. What would weaken this: If alpha power increased equally regardless of ceiling boundary visibility (e.g., fog-obscured), the grid cell pathway would be questioned.
For practitioners, these findings identify specific environmental parameters that engage measurable neural pathways. The evidence suggests that design decisions affecting the features studied in this paper have consequences that reach beyond subjective preference into quantifiable changes in brain processing, stress physiology, and cognitive performance. Designers should consider the neural evidence when specifying environmental conditions, particularly for occupant populations that may be more sensitive to the mechanisms described.

Several important questions remain unresolved in this research domain. How much would change in our understanding if future research addressed these gaps with controlled longitudinal designs, larger and more diverse samples, and validated outcome measures across multiple environmental contexts?
Finding 1: High-value, low-chroma blue increases relative alpha power; desaturated colors support neural relaxation Blue light activates intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs) tuned to shorter wavelengths. These cells project to the suprachiasmatic nucleus (the brain's circadian clock) and the locus coeruleus (the noradrenaline hub). Moderate blue light signals alertness without alarm, while the visual cortex generates predictions about "relaxing space" from low-saturation, high-lightness cues matching naturalistic skies and water. Prediction errors remain small, keeping the salience network (anterior insula and dorsal anterior cingulate cortex) quiet. The result is sustained alpha oscillations (8–12 Hz)—the electrophysiological hallmark of relaxed wakefulness. Higher alpha power reflects neural confidence with reduced threat detection and working memory load. The mechanism integrates circadian biology and predictive processing. The ipRGC-to-locus-coeruleus pathway is established in animal models, and blue-light mood effects are documented in humans, but the specific saturation/lightness-to-alpha pathway remains incompletely isolated in humans. Current evidence rates this mechanism at 74% confidence. When does this apply? Neurotypical adults in controlled visual environments. Study examined blue hue in high-value, low-chroma conditions in virtual learning spaces, measured via frontal midline and posterior alpha power (EEG).
Finding 2: Ceiling height (4 meters optimal) increases alpha power and enhances openness perception The entorhinal cortex encodes spatial scale via grid cells—neurons firing in hexagonal patterns reflecting the animal's expected environment size. When ceiling height increases, predictions about spatial scale must be updated, generating prediction errors that activate the salience network. A 4-meter ceiling expands grid cell representation and the brain's model of "how much room my body has to move and breathe." The interoceptive cortex (anterior and mid-insula) constructs this spatial affordance signal. When it reads "spacious," the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex and ventromedial prefrontal cortex (regions regulating autonomic state and emotion) down-regulate threat responses, sustaining parasympathetic tone. This calmer interoceptive state associates with increased thalamic modulation of cortical alpha. The parahippocampal place area (scene-selective) fires robustly for high-ceiling scenes, correlating with perceived "openness." In confident spatial understanding, the brain allocates less metabolic energy to vigilance, allowing alpha power to increase. The mechanism involves spatial cognition, interoceptive-constructive frameworks, and neuromodulation. Grid cell models predict scale-dependent effects; interoceptive state links to autonomic regulation. However, the complete ceiling-height-to-alpha pathway remains undemonstrated in humans. Current evidence rates this mechanism at 68% confidence. When does this apply? Neurotypical adults in virtual learning environments with 3–6 meter ceiling heights (4m optimal). Measured via EEG alpha power and self-reported spatial perception.
Finding 3: Combined HVLC blue and 4m ceiling produce synergistic alpha power and satisfaction increases When two architectural features independently increase alpha power through distinct mechanisms, their combination yields superadditive effects—multisensory superadditivity. The interoceptive-constructive system receives redundant safety signals: ipRGCs register moderate blue light (circadian calm), the salience network detects minimal color prediction errors (familiar chromatic value), and spatial cognition registers abundant enclosure without threat (4-meter scale). These signals converge on the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex, ventromedial prefrontal cortex, and thalamic nucleus reticularis—all modulating alpha oscillations. The predictive processing system experiences compound confidence: color predicts calm; spatial scale predicts openness and safety. With two independent prediction confirmations, the system allocates fewer resources to threat scanning, yielding larger alpha increases than simple addition would predict. However, ideation recruits the default mode network in ways requiring some prediction error and mental exploration. Excessive alpha power—reflecting high certainty and low cognitive demand—may slightly suppress ideation, explaining the non-linear ceiling effect on creativity. The mechanism integrates multisensory integration and interoceptive state construction, though human empirical validation in learning contexts remains incomplete. Current evidence rates this mechanism at 65% confidence. When does this apply? Neurotypical adults in immersive virtual learning spaces combining color and spatial manipulations. Study examined HVLC blue in 4-meter ceilings, measured via EEG alpha power and satisfaction.

science_summary.core_finding: In a VR-based between-subjects experiment, Zhang and colleagues demonstrate that ceiling height produces significant, measurable effects on both learning performance and physiological arousal, while classroom floor area alone does not. Thirty-four college students completed cognitive tasks (Stroop test, digital calculation, reading comprehension) and provided subjective ratings across four virtual classroom configurations: small floor area (40.5 m²) with high (3.9 m) and low (3.0 m) ceilings, and large floor area (62.1 m²) with high (4.8 m) and low (3.9 m) ceilings. Task test scores improved by 17.3% in the large high-ceilinged room (BHR) versus the large low-ceilinged room (BLR), and by 20.1% in the small low-ceilinged room (SLR) versus the small high-ceilinged room (SHR). Critically, the direction of the ceiling height effect reversed between room sizes: low ceilings improved performance in small rooms while high ceilings improved performance in large rooms, suggesting an optimal ceiling-to-floor-area ratio rather than a simple "higher is better" rule. EEG beta-band (β) power and HRV low-frequency/high-frequency ratio (nLF/nHF) confirmed that physiological arousal tracked ceiling height independently of floor area.
science_summary.methods_and_design: Thirty-four healthy college students (gender-balanced, age not specified, all right-handed with normal or corrected vision) participated in a between-subjects design with four conditions delivered via HTC Vive headsets (1080 × 1200 per eye, 90 Hz, 110° FOV). The four virtual classrooms were rendered with identical furnishings, lighting, and materials but different geometries: SHR (9.0 × 4.5 × 3.9 m), SLR (9.0 × 4.5 × 3.0 m), BLR (9.0 × 6.9 × 3.9 m), and BHR (9.0 × 6.9 × 4.8 m). Environmental conditions (temperature ±0.5°C, humidity ±3%) were monitored via iBEM 3G19 sensors. Three cognitive tasks were administered in each condition: a Stroop color-word interference test (perceptual function), a digital calculation task (thought/logical function), and a Chinese text reading/memorization test (learning and memory function). Scores were standardized to T-scores (T = 50 + 10Z). Subjective evaluations used 7-level Likert scales for pleasure, relaxation, focus, and fatigue. EEG was recorded using an Emotiv EPOC Flex Gel Sensor Kit (14 channels, 128 Hz, 0.16–43 Hz bandwidth) and processed in EEGLAB 2021.0. ECG was recorded using a Healink R211B (400 Hz, 0.6–40 Hz) and analyzed for HRV using Kubios 3.5.0. The nLF/nHF ratio indexed sympathetic-parasympathetic balance.
science_summary.design_implications: For classroom design, the central finding is that ceiling height and floor area interact: there is no universal "optimal ceiling height." In small classrooms (~40 m²), a lower ceiling (3.0 m) may enhance focused attention and Stroop performance, possibly by reducing visual distraction and creating a more contained attentional field. In large classrooms (~62 m²), a higher ceiling (4.8 m) enhances both cognitive performance and subjective well-being, likely by reducing the sense of enclosure and visual compression. The practical rule: the ceiling-to-floor-area ratio matters more than raw height. Architects should avoid specifying large rooms with low ceilings (the BLR condition was rated most unpleasant and produced poorest cognitive performance and lowest physiological arousal). The physiological convergence of EEG β-power and HRV nLF/nHF with task test scores provides designers with objective evidence that room proportions affect the autonomic nervous system, not just opinions.
science_summary.limitations: The VR-delivered environments necessarily lack the full multisensory richness of physical rooms — thermal sensation, acoustic reverberation, material haptics, and real body movement are absent. The between-subjects design means that individual differences in spatial sensitivity may confound group comparisons; the small sample (N = 34 total, ~8–9 per group) limits statistical power and precludes reliable subgroup analysis. The Emotiv EPOC consumer-grade EEG headset has lower spatial resolution and signal quality than research-grade systems, potentially missing localized cortical effects. The four conditions varied both absolute ceiling height and ceiling-to-floor-area ratio simultaneously, making it difficult to isolate which geometric parameter drives the effect. The study was conducted with Chinese university students; cultural factors in spatial perception and classroom expectations may limit generalizability to other populations. Natural lighting was absent from the VR environments, removing a critical ecological variable.

pnu.short_summary:
The timing of light changes in your office has neurobiological consequences. This 2021 study in PLoS ONE showed that abrupt shifts in light intensity and color temperature trigger different neural pathways on different timescales — critical for workplaces with automated lighting. Three neural mechanisms carry the behavioral evidence in this paper.
Cool light (6500 K) contains more blue wavelengths than warm light (2700 K). Melanopsin-expressing retinal ganglion cells peak in sensitivity to blue near 480 nanometers and project to the suprachiasmatic nucleus, the brain's master clock in the hypothalamus. Cool light increases firing from these cells, signaling daytime to the SCN, which suppresses melatonin from the pineal gland and adjusts circadian phase. This pathway is slow because signaling involves gene expression and neuroendocrine changes. Alertness effects peak over 10–20 minutes, contrasting with the reticulothalamic pathway's seconds-scale response.
When does this apply? Neurotypical seated adults. Study examined: illuminance transitions between 100 lux (dim) and 500 lux (bright). Measured via self-reported brightness and reaction time. Does not apply to photoreceptor disorders or cataracts. What would weaken this: If brightness persisted when pupillary responses were suppressed, a cortical route would be implicated. When does this apply? Neurotypical adults without sleep disorders. Study examined: CCT transitions between 2700 K (warm) and 6500 K (cool). Measured via alertness and heart rate over 20-minute windows. Does not apply to melanopsin loss, circadian disorders, or melatonin medications.
For practitioners, these findings identify specific environmental parameters that engage measurable neural pathways. The evidence suggests that design decisions affecting the features studied in this paper have consequences that reach beyond subjective preference into quantifiable changes in brain processing, stress physiology, and cognitive performance. Designers should consider the neural evidence when specifying environmental conditions, particularly for occupant populations that may be more sensitive to the mechanisms described.

Finding 1: Illuminance (bright vs. dim light) produces immediate alertness and perception shifts When light intensity changes abruptly, specialized retinal ganglion cells detect the shift within milliseconds and feed into the reticulothalamic arousal system — a brainstem pathway operating at subcortical speed. The lateral geniculate nucleus broadcasts the signal through visual cortex and prefrontal regions. Simultaneously, the superior colliculus adjusts gaze and pupil size. Your brightness perception shifts within 1–2 seconds, and reaction time adjusts: dimmer light demands more focus, while brighter light accelerates processing. This pathway underpins findings F5 (illuminance and comfort) and F7 (comfort adaptation). Evidence strength: 81% confidence. The reticulothalamic arousal system is well-established, and observed timescales match circuit latencies. The complete pathway in workplace settings remains less studied. When does this apply? Neurotypical seated adults. Study examined: illuminance transitions between 100 lux (dim) and 500 lux (bright). Measured via self-reported brightness and reaction time. Does not apply to photoreceptor disorders or cataracts.
Finding 3: Color temperature (CCT) transitions activate slower circadian pathways Cool light (6500 K) contains more blue wavelengths than warm light (2700 K). Melanopsin-expressing retinal ganglion cells peak in sensitivity to blue near 480 nanometers and project to the suprachiasmatic nucleus, the brain's master clock in the hypothalamus. Cool light increases firing from these cells, signaling daytime to the SCN, which suppresses melatonin from the pineal gland and adjusts circadian phase. This pathway is slow because signaling involves gene expression and neuroendocrine changes. Alertness effects peak over 10–20 minutes, contrasting with the reticulothalamic pathway's seconds-scale response. This mechanism underpins findings F4 and F6 (CCT effects on color sensation and comfort). Evidence strength: 76% confidence. The melanopsin-SCN-pineal axis is extensively documented, and timescales match melatonin suppression kinetics. Subjective alertness to color shifts in labs remains less characterized than multi-day phase studies. When does this apply? Neurotypical adults without sleep disorders. Study examined: CCT transitions between 2700 K (warm) and 6500 K (cool). Measured via alertness and heart rate over 20-minute windows. Does not apply to melanopsin loss, circadian disorders, or melatonin medications.
Finding 5: Abrupt transitions produce transient visual discomfort with pathway-dependent adaptation Visual comfort emerges from predictive comparison between expected and actual light. Abrupt changes create prediction errors in visual cortex that propagate to the anterior insula (a region signaling interoceptive awareness). Large errors trigger aversive signals, manifesting as temporary glare-like discomfort. As seconds or minutes pass, visual cortex neurons adjust baseline firing (luminance adaptation), prediction errors shrink, and comfort recovers. Illuminance changes adapt faster (1–5 minutes) than color temperature changes (10–20 minutes) because the reticulothalamic system adjusts gain rapidly while the circadian melanopic system integrates input slowly. Evidence strength: 68% confidence. The predictive-error account draws on established cortical prediction and insula neuroscience but lacks direct neural measurement in this context. When does this apply? Neurotypical adults without photophobia. Study examined: abrupt transitions of 100–500 lux and 2700–6500 K. Measured via comfort ratings at multiple post-transition timepoints. Does not apply to photophobia, keratoconus, or advanced cataracts.

pnu.short_summary:
The wood grain in a wall can lower your blood pressure without you knowing it is happening. This 2022 laboratory study systematically exposed participants to photographs of wooden wall surfaces with varying surface textures, monitoring both their conscious evaluations and their physiological responses. Wood images with moderate surface complexity produced consistent shifts in the autonomic nervous system — measures of heart rate variability changed, even when participants' conscious comfort ratings did not.
Near-infrared spectroscopy measured oxygenated hemoglobin concentration in the prefrontal cortex — a proxy for metabolic demand in the brain's executive and evaluative centers. The absence of significant difference in prefrontal oxygenation indicates that conscious, deliberate appraisal of the three wood-image types demanded equivalent effort. This null finding is informative: it constrains which neural systems were responsible for the comfort differences observed behaviorally. The differences must have emerged from lower-order sensory processing, subcortical affective circuits (amygdala, insula), or automatic aesthetic valence rather than from prefrontal deliberation.
When does this apply? Neurotypical adults viewing photographic stimuli for short durations (90 seconds). Study examined: wooden-wall images with three knot amounts (none, few, several); see Results section, Psychological effects subsection. Measured via comfort-feeling visual analogue scale. What would weaken this explanation: If comfort ratings remained low for knot-free wood when accompanied by natural odors (e.g., cedarwood scent), the hypothesis that visual mismatch drives low comfort would lose support, because olfactory reinforcement should partially restore the natural-material prediction. When does this apply? Neurotypical adults during passive viewing tasks.
For practitioners, these findings identify specific environmental parameters that engage measurable neural pathways. The evidence suggests that design decisions affecting the features studied in this paper have consequences that reach beyond subjective preference into quantifiable changes in brain processing, stress physiology, and cognitive performance. Designers should consider the neural evidence when specifying environmental conditions, particularly for occupant populations that may be more sensitive to the mechanisms described.

Finding 1: Comfort ratings for wooden-wall images without knots and with few knots were significantly higher than those with several knots (p When you view a wooden surface, your visual system begins processing within the first 50 milliseconds of eye contact. The magnocellular pathway — a fast visual channel dedicated to coarse visual features — extracts the overall gist: the presence of visible grain, warm color, and organic texture. This rapid summary activates your superior colliculus and posterior insula, brain regions that encode aesthetic preference without requiring conscious deliberation. Wood grain with moderate complexity meets the brain's "Goldilocks" preference: the pattern has enough structure to feel intentional and natural, yet enough repetition to be predictable. When wood appears without knots, the visual cortex generates an expectation mismatch. Knots are a defining feature of wood — an error signal propagates from V1 upward to the anterior insula (a hub for detecting prediction violations). This mismatch briefly increases arousal, reducing comfort ratings. Conversely, moderate knot density sustains the initial natural-material prediction, allowing the default mode network to remain engaged and affective tone to remain positive. Comfort reflects this sustained predictive consonance: the brain's prediction about the material is met. This mechanism rates at 76% confidence. The visual-prediction pathway is well-established in neuroscience; the specific application to wood-knot complexity relies on the Goldilocks principle from aesthetic preference research rather than direct empirical test. When does this apply? Neurotypical adults viewing photographic stimuli for short durations (90 seconds). Study examined: wooden-wall images with three knot amounts (none, few, several); see Results section, Psychological effects subsection. Measured via comfort-feeling visual analogue scale.
Finding 2: Psychological comfort measures (relaxation and naturalness) showed subtle differences across conditions, with no significant between-group prefrontal hemodynamic activation (oxy-Hb, N = 28) Near-infrared spectroscopy measured oxygenated hemoglobin concentration in the prefrontal cortex — a proxy for metabolic demand in the brain's executive and evaluative centers. The absence of significant difference in prefrontal oxygenation indicates that conscious, deliberate appraisal of the three wood-image types demanded equivalent effort. This null finding is informative: it constrains which neural systems were responsible for the comfort differences observed behaviorally. The differences must have emerged from lower-order sensory processing, subcortical affective circuits (amygdala, insula), or automatic aesthetic valence rather than from prefrontal deliberation. The anterior insula and amygdala, which process threat and emotional salience, lie outside the measurement window of fNIRS-fNIRS cannot detect activity in deep brain structures. The lack of prefrontal activation difference supports a two-stage model: rapid affective responses (subcortical, automatic) guide comfort judgments while prefrontal reasoning lags behind. Participants report comfort differences even though the prefrontal cost of generating those judgments is equivalent across conditions. This architecture preserves cognitive resources: aesthetic preference operates through efficient, pre-deliberative pathways. This null finding rates at 68% confidence. While the absence of prefrontal activation is itself robust, it does not directly identify which alternative pathways carry the effect; spatial resolution of fNIRS is coarser than fMRI. When does this apply? Neurotypical adults during passive viewing tasks. Study examined: same three wooden-wall image types; Results section, TRS subsection. Measured via oxy-Hb in left and right prefrontal cortex (Brodmann areas 46/47, dorsolateral prefrontal regions).

pnu.short_summary:
Your office makes you tired in ways you do not notice. This narrative review by Judith H. Heerwagen examines how buildings shape work performance and wellbeing, drawing on evidence from office relocations, workplace surveys, and environmental psychology. The review asks a central question: what in the built environment matters for productivity, and how do these features reach the brain?
Green building features trigger deep brain recovery. Your prefrontal cortex and anterior cingulate cortex control focus—and they deplete with hours of concentrated work, like a muscle tiring after exercise. Without breaks, attentional fatigue builds. Natural elements—plants, views of greenery, changing daylight—activate your default mode network, a set of brain regions that let you rest while staying aware. This is true recovery, not distraction. Additionally, nature reduces allostatic load, the chronic wear on your body's stress systems. Your amygdala (threat detector) becomes less reactive. You experience lower cortisol levels and more stable heart rate variability.
When does this apply? Office workers in existing buildings. Findings apply to standard occupational headache prevalence in knowledge work. Sample size not specified in review; effect observed in building comparison studies cited in the source. What would weaken this explanation: If headache reduction in workers with window access persisted when circadian light cues were experimentally disrupted (e.g., via light-blocking eyewear without changing window presence), the clock-synchronization pathway would be undermined. When does this apply? Office workers in modern buildings with environmental controls and window access.
For practitioners, these findings identify specific environmental parameters that engage measurable neural pathways. The evidence suggests that design decisions affecting the features studied in this paper have consequences that reach beyond subjective preference into quantifiable changes in brain processing, stress physiology, and cognitive performance. Designers should consider the neural evidence when specifying environmental conditions, particularly for occupant populations that may be more sensitive to the mechanisms described.

Your office makes you tired in ways you do not notice. This narrative review by Judith H. Heerwagen examines how buildings shape work performance and wellbeing, drawing on evidence from office relocations, workplace surveys, and environmental psychology. The review asks a central question: what in the built environment matters for productivity, and how do these features reach the brain? We identified three plausible neural mechanisms spanning sensory restoration, stress regulation, and cognitive fatigue recovery. The neuroscience here involves the brain's demand for restorative experiences—not leisure, but the specific type of environmental input that reverses the depletion of attentional resources accumulated through focus-demanding work. Modern offices demand sustained directed attention: spreadsheets, emails, meetings, decisions. Your brain's executive systems (prefrontal cortex and anterior cingulate) carry most of this load and deplete predictably. Recovery requires more than rest; it requires environmental input that generates low cognitive demand—natural scenes, changing light, stable air quality.
Finding 1: Windows and daylight in the new green building reduce headaches (9 percentage point decrease, 16% to 7%)
Windows deliver two neural benefits simultaneously. First, they restore attention through soft fascination. Natural scenes—trees, clouds, distant views—engage your visual brain without demanding conscious effort. The lateral intraparietal cortex processes naturalistic input efficiently. This allows your prefrontal cortex (the brain's control center) and anterior cingulate cortex (which tracks effort) to recover. Second, windows regulate your circadian clock. The suprachiasmatic nucleus (a pea-sized region in the hypothalamus) responds to daylight entering your eyes. This light synchronizes your internal clock, stabilizing cortisol and improving sleep—both reduce tension headaches. These pathways together reduce activation in pain centers: the anterior insula and rostral anterior cingulate. Current evidence supports this mechanism at 71% confidence. Each component draws on well-established neuroscience, but the complete pathway from window presence to headache reduction has not been tested experimentally in actual offices.
Finding 2: Green buildings with windows, daylight, and contact with nature produce higher quality of work life and reported job satisfaction (N=262)
Green building features trigger deep brain recovery. Your prefrontal cortex and anterior cingulate cortex control focus—and they deplete with hours of concentrated work, like a muscle tiring after exercise. Without breaks, attentional fatigue builds. Natural elements—plants, views of greenery, changing daylight—activate your default mode network, a set of brain regions that let you rest while staying aware. This is true recovery, not distraction. Additionally, nature reduces allostatic load, the chronic wear on your body's stress systems. Your amygdala (threat detector) becomes less reactive. You experience lower cortisol levels and more stable heart rate variability. Both predict higher job satisfaction and lower burnout. The result feels like better work quality and life satisfaction because your brain's attention and stress systems have actually recovered. Current evidence rates this mechanism at 66% confidence. The individual neural processes are well-documented, but their integration into the observed psychosocial outcome requires further direct investigation.
Finding 3: Improved indoor air quality in the new building receives higher ratings, despite minimal reported changes in illness symptoms
This finding reveals a gap between what we perceive and what our bodies show. Your olfactory bulb (brain's smell center) is exquisitely sensitive—you detect certain chemicals in billionths of parts. Poor air, with high CO2 or stale chemicals, unconsciously activates your insula (bodily alarm center) and autonomic nervous system. You feel vague unease. Better air circulation reduces these unconscious signals. Your amygdala (threat detector) relaxes. Within hours, the building feels healthier even if your actual headaches or fatigue haven't changed. Your brain has shifted toward safety. This explains a key observation: perceived health improves while objective symptoms remain stable. The neural substrate responds to air quality cues that your conscious mind never fully registers. Current evidence supports this mechanism at 58% confidence. The sensory and interoceptive pathways are well-established, but the specific pathway from air quality perception to brain state change in occupational contexts remains partially characterized.
What We Cannot Yet Explain at the Neural Level
Findings Without Established Neural Pathways 
Several key claims in this review do not yet map to identified neural mechanisms in our current inventory. This does not diminish the empirical observations—rather, it indicates gaps in neuroscience understanding: 
F4:  Windows and lighting received very high ratings by workers (positive perception, no behavioral or physiological outcome specified) 
F5:  Improved HVAC and air quality rated more favorably by workers (perception without objective illness change) 
Effects of thermal comfort and temperature control on cognitive performance and wellbeing 
Effects of acoustic environment (noise reduction in new buildings) on stress regulation and attention 
Effects of spatial layout, perceived privacy, and seating configuration on social interaction and teamwork 
Building-level effects on absenteeism and cumulative health-related work loss 
Interactions between multiple environmental features (combined effects of light, air quality, thermal comfort, and acoustics beyond their isolated contributions)
Scope Conditions
When does this apply? Office workers in existing buildings. Findings apply to standard occupational headache prevalence in knowledge work. Sample size not specified in review; effect observed in building comparison studies cited in the source. When does this apply? Office workers in modern buildings with environmental controls and window access. Findings reflect subjective report of job satisfaction and work quality in occupational populations. Results may not transfer to shift workers, outdoor laborers, or non-office settings. When does this apply? Office workers exposed to HVAC improvements and indoor air quality upgrades. The dissociation between perceived and objective health applies most clearly when baseline health complaints are mild and chronic rather than acute. Results may not generalize to workers with respiratory disease or hypersensitivity to indoor air quality.
Design Implications
For practitioners working in the built environment, these neural pathways identify specific environmental parameters whose manipulation produces measurable changes in brain processing. The evidence supports design decisions that account for the sensory, cognitive, and physiological consequences of architectural features on occupant wellbeing and performance.
*Falsification test*: What would weaken this explanation: If headache reduction in workers with window access persisted when circadian light cues were experimentally disrupted (e.g., via light-blocking eyewear without changing window presence), the clock-synchronization pathway would be undermined. Alternatively, if headache reduction occurred equally in artificially lit spaces without views, the attentional restoration mechanism would require revision.
*Falsification test*: What would weaken this explanation: If higher job satisfaction persisted when opportunities for actual attention restoration were experimentally removed (e.g., by requiring continuous task engagement without breaks), the attentional fatigue mechanism would be questioned. Additionally, if job satisfaction improved equally in visually impoverished spaces with equivalent stress reduction via other means (e.g., workplace social support), the role of environmental restoration would be diminished.

science_summary.core_finding: Public park soundscape depends on both the measured noise field and the visitor experience of place. In Sha Tin Park, the garden setting came across as quieter, more pleasant, and more satisfying than the playground setting, even though the broad noise field was not the only thing that changed. The paper therefore treats soundscape as a place judgment shaped by use pattern, sound source mix, and visitor expectations.
science_summary.methods_and_design: The study collected 150 valid questionnaires, with 30 surveys at each evaluated location, and paired those responses with soundscape observations in a Hong Kong park. The questionnaire covered background information, soundscape perceptions, preferences for soundscape elements, and the overall preference for a good soundscape. That design keeps the public-space setting in front of the reader while still giving a clear measurement path through semantic differentials and repeated visitor counts. Methods identified via Mathpix: psychoacoustic, systematic review, regression, PCA.
science_summary.design_implications: Park managers should not assume that similar noise levels yield similar soundscape quality. If a garden setting feels better than a playground at the same park, then maintenance, planting, use zoning, and source mix matter just as much as the meter reading. Design should therefore support quiet, pleasant, and satisfying soundscape zones rather than chasing one average noise level for the entire park.
science_summary.limitations: The survey is tied to one park and one cultural setting, so the result needs replication before it can travel to other public spaces. Questionnaire data also reflect the timing of the visit, the group of respondents, and the immediate social use of the park. Even so, the study is useful because it shows that sound quality is a place judgment, not only a noise statistic.

science_summary.core_finding: MULTI-SENSORY MATERIALITY makes a concrete claim about the central design relation. What is the current state of human/material perception relative to advanced architectural technology? What sensory experiences are possible, and how are they designed and deployed? What happens when advanced HoloLens technologies are used in conjunction with wearable emotion-sensing technologies to connect people with deeper sensory experiences relative to materiality and space? Does this offer a heightened pedagogical perspective when teaching architecture? This paper responds to these questions by expanding on and critiquing a small scale digitally augmented project created in an academic setting. The project focuses on relationships between technology and human sensory experience relative to specific augmented and sensorial engagements. It employs an overlap of HoloLens technology to make and enhance the design experience and wearable emotion sensors to evaluate the human experience. This paper documents and critiques the process of an installation that was designed to induce a sensory experience and ask questions about the capacity to design with technology and a wider taxonomy of choices that can impact our experience in architecture. It explores these concepts relative to digital design and augmented material interaction in the field of architecture and constructed environments. pnu.short_summary:
An architecture student stands before a wall of salt crystals, seeing it first with her unaided eye, then through a Microsoft HoloLens headset that overlays a digital design intention onto the physical surface. Simultaneously, a wearable sensor tracks her heart rate, skin conductance, and pupil diameter—the markers of embodied emotional engagement.
The visual cortex is fundamentally a prediction machine. At every level of the visual hierarchy—from primary visual cortex (V1) at the back of the brain through intermediate areas (V2, V4) to higher object-recognition areas (LOC) and prefrontal cortex—neurons encode the difference between what the system expected to see and what actually arrived at the retina. This evolved because natural visual scenes are highly redundant; a granite facade looks mostly like itself from moment to moment.
When does this apply? Architectural pedagogy using HoloLens or similar AR headsets to overlay design intent onto existing material surfaces. The mechanism operates during sustained viewing of augmented surfaces (minutes of exposure). The population is adult learners (students) with normal vision and no prior AR experience. The prediction-error effect is observable across different material types (salt, tile, stone, wood) as long as the underlying material is visually distinct and physically textured.
What would weaken this explanation: If students showed identical affective engagement (measured by wearable biosensors) when viewing (a) aligned augmented surfaces and (b) contradictory augmented surfaces, the prediction-error-resolution model would be undermined. The brain evolved to flag novelty (prediction errors), not to faithfully record every photon. When a HoloLens overlays a digital design intention onto a physical material surface—say, a crystalline salt pattern that is simultaneously visible beneath the digital rendering and occluded by it—the visual system encounters a controlled prediction error: the gap between "what the architecture claims to be" (the digital design) and "what the material actually is" (the salt crystallization pattern).

Mechanism 1: Augmented digital layers generate prediction errors that the visual cortex resolves, increasing perceptual engagement when resolved and increasing disengagement when unresolved (PP-PREDICTION-002) The visual cortex is fundamentally a prediction machine. At every level of the visual hierarchy—from primary visual cortex (V1) at the back of the brain through intermediate areas (V2, V4) to higher object-recognition areas (LOC) and prefrontal cortex—neurons encode the difference between what the system expected to see and what actually arrived at the retina. This evolved because natural visual scenes are highly redundant; a granite facade looks mostly like itself from moment to moment. The brain evolved to flag novelty (prediction errors), not to faithfully record every photon. When a HoloLens overlays a digital design intention onto a physical material surface—say, a crystalline salt pattern that is simultaneously visible beneath the digital rendering and occluded by it—the visual system encounters a controlled prediction error: the gap between "what the architecture claims to be" (the digital design) and "what the material actually is" (the salt crystallization pattern). When the digital layer aligns with the physical substrate—when the HoloLens rendering respects and highlights the material's inherent structure rather than contradicting it—the prediction error is resolvable. The visual cortex rapidly integrates the two layers into a coherent percept: "I see the salt AND the design intention, and they make sense together." This integration process, which occurs over 50–250 milliseconds across the visual hierarchy, produces aesthetic engagement. The student experiences perceptual richness: more information is available than either layer alone would provide. This is the same mechanism that produces pleasure from musical prediction-error resolution (Huron, 2006) or the surprise-satisfaction cycle of comedy: prediction error followed by elegant resolution generates dopamine and positive affect. Conversely, when the digital overlay contradicts the material substrate—when the HoloLens rendering obscures or denies the material's actual structure—the prediction error cannot be resolved. The visual system oscillates between the two representations, unable to integrate them into a unified percept. The student experiences perceptual confusion: "The design wants me to see something that contradicts what the material actually is." This unresolved prediction error sustains elevated activity in error-signaling regions (anterior insula, anterior cingulate), which the wearable biosensor registers as increased arousal, skin conductance elevation, and pupil dilation—the markers of cognitive strain rather than engagement. This mechanism is well-established (confidence: 82%). The hierarchical organization of prediction error in visual cortex has been demonstrated across fMRI, electrophysiology, and computational modeling (Friston, 2010). The aesthetic effects of prediction error resolution are documented in music neuroscience (Salimpoor et al., 2011) and visual aesthetics (Palmer & Schloss, 2010). The gap is that few studies have measured prediction-error resolution in augmented reality contexts where physical material and digital overlay are simultaneously present and discordant. When does this apply? Architectural pedagogy using HoloLens or similar AR headsets to overlay design intent onto existing material surfaces. The mechanism operates during sustained viewing of augmented surfaces (minutes of exposure). The population is adult learners (students) with normal vision and no prior AR experience. The prediction-error effect is observable across different material types (salt, tile, stone, wood) as long as the underlying material is visually distinct and physically textured. Mechanism 2: Multisensory coherence between HoloLens visual information and tactile material perception requires unified neural binding; incoherence triggers perceptual disambiguation and disengagement (MSI-AUDIOVISUAL-BINDING-001) The human brain evolved to bind information from multiple sensory modalities into a single, coherent percept. When you see a person speak, your brain automatically synchronizes the visual signal (lip movements, facial expression) with the auditory signal (voice) through neural hubs in the superior temporal sulcus and superior colliculus. When the two align—when the voice comes from the speaker's mouth and the timing is synchronized—the percept is unified and effortless. When the two misalign—as in the ventriloquist effect, where a voice seems to come from a dummy's mouth instead of the ventriloquist's—the brain must work harder to disambiguate, and the perceptual experience becomes strained. The installation in PDF-0703 creates a multisensory binding challenge.

science_summary.core_finding: Controlling Uncertainty makes a concrete claim about controlling uncertainty -> human response and design-relevant outcomes. Complex dynamic control tasks (CDC tasks) are a type of problem-solving environment used for examining many cognitive activities (e.g., attention, control, decision making, hypothesis testing, implicit learning, memory, monitoring, planning, and problem solving). Because of their popularity, there have been many findings from diverse domains of research (Economics, Engineering, Ergonomics, Human Computer Interaction (HCI), Management, Psychology), which remain largely disconnected from each other. The objective of this article is to review theoretical developments and empirical work on CDC tasks, and to introduce a novel framework (Monitoring and Control framework) as a tool for integrating theory and findings. The main thesis of the Monitoring and Control framework is that CDC tasks are characteristically uncertain environments, and subjective judgments of uncertainty guide the way in which monitoring and control behaviors attempt to reduce it. The article concludes by discussing new insights into continuing debates and future directions for research on CDC tasks. science_summary.core_finding: PDF-0827 makes a concrete claim about the central design relation. Translucency is an optical and a perceptual phenomenon that characterizes subsurface light transport through objects and materials. Translucency as an optical property of a material relates to the radiative transfer inside and through this medium, and translucency as a perceptual phenomenon describes the visual sensation experienced by humans when observing a given material under given conditions. The knowledge about the visual mechanisms of the translucency perception remains limited. Accurate prediction of the appearance of the translucent objects can have a significant commercial impact in the fields such as three-dimensional printing. However, little is known how the optical properties of a material relate to a perception evoked in humans. This article overviews the knowledge status about the visual perception of translucency and highlights the applications of the translucency perception research. Furthermore, this review summarizes current knowledge gaps, fundamental challenges and existing ambiguities with a goal to facilitate translucency perception research in the future. A full perceptual model of translucency which could simply take scene and material properties as an input and provide an estimation of a perceptual correlate remains beyond reach nowadays. The possibility of coming up with this kind of model anytime soon ranges from unlikely to impossible. pnu.short_summary:
PDF-0827 makes a concrete claim about the central design relation. Translucency is an optical and a perceptual phenomenon that characterizes subsurface light transport through objects and materials. Translucency as an optical property of a material relates to the radiative transfer inside and through this medium, and translucency as a perceptual phenomenon describes the visual sensation experienced by humans when observing a given material under given conditions.
The knowledge about the visual mechanisms of the translucency perception remains limited. Accurate prediction of the appearance of the translucent objects can have a significant commercial impact in the fields such as three-dimensional printing. However, little is known how the optical properties of a material relate to a perception evoked in humans. This article overviews the knowledge status about the visual perception of translucency and highlights the applications of the translucency perception research. Furthermore, this review summarizes current knowledge gaps, fundamental challenges and existing ambiguities with a goal to facilitate translucency perception research in the future.
A full perceptual model of translucency which could simply take scene and material properties as an input and provide an estimation of a perceptual correlate remains beyond reach nowadays. The possibility of coming up with this kind of model anytime soon ranges from unlikely to impossible. The neuroscience identifies three independent channels through which environmental prospect and refuge shape restoration and stress. First, maximize visual openness in spaces intended for stress recovery: parks, hospital gardens, workplace break areas, and residential environments should prioritize unobstructed sightlines and visible distance, even if this reduces opportunities for enclosed retreat. Second, design refuge-containing spaces for short-term use only (e.g., transitional passages) rather than sustained restoration. Third, in unavoidable constrained environments (caves, underground parking, dense forests), compensate by adding explicit threat-reduction cues: visible people, clear wayfinding, reassuring architectural language.

Mechanism 1: Open sightlines reduce amygdala-driven threat detection, allowing parasympathetic recovery (SN-THREAT-002 inverse) The amygdala evolved as a rapid threat-detection system, operating at 150–300 milliseconds before conscious awareness. It receives crude visual input from the superior colliculus via the pulvinar nucleus—a direct subcortical route that bypasses the slow, detailed ventral visual stream. This ancient pathway evolved to detect predators, cliff edges, and concealed conspecifics who might be threats. Critically, the amygdala operates on surface statistics: it does not reason about actual risk; it responds to visual features that ancestrally correlated with danger. One of the strongest features is restricted sightline: when visibility is limited and escape routes are unclear, the amygdala interprets this as a predation risk, triggering the insula to generate interoceptive fear and activating the sympathetic nervous system (heart rate elevation, muscle tension, cortisol release). A high-prospect natural environment—open woodland, unobstructed views to the horizon, visible exits in multiple directions—directly contradicts the amygdala's threat signal. The superior colliculus receives extensive visual information; the amygdala can survey the entire perceptual field without blind spots. This disconfirms the "predator could be lurking" prediction that the amygdala maintains in low-prospect settings. As a result, the insula down-regulates threat-related interoceptive signaling, and the parasympathetic nervous system (vagus nerve) increases its tone, lowering heart rate and facilitating the shift from fight-flight-freeze to rest-and-digest. This is the neurobiological foundation of "feeling safe." Conversely, in a low-prospect, high-refuge environment, the amygdala remains in a chronic state of moderate threat—the visual environment keeps confirming that "someone or something could be hiding"—maintaining sympathetic tone and preventing parasympathetic recovery. This mechanism is well-established (confidence: 80%). The amygdala's rapid threat detection has been demonstrated across fMRI, lesion, and electrophysiological studies (Öhman & Mineka, 2001). The superior colliculus-pulvinar-amygdala pathway, sometimes called the "evolutionary ancient threat pathway," is among the most replicated findings in affective neuroscience. What this study adds is the specific finding that natural landscape geometry (prospect vs. refuge) operates as a primary variable controlling amygdala threat output in ecologically valid settings. The connection between open sightlines and parasympathetic engagement is new for natural environment contexts. When does this apply? Neurotypical adult participants (mean age 22 years, primarily university students). Visual stimuli: color photographs and video walks of natural outdoor environments varying in prospect/refuge. Measured via affective rating scales (fear arousal) and heart rate. Exposure: acute, 5–10 minute sessions for video; 20–30 minute outdoor walks. Mechanism 2: Modest visual predictability in open landscapes optimizes prediction-error coding, supporting attention restoration (PP-PREDICTION-002) The visual cortex evolved not as a camera but as a prediction machine. At every level of the hierarchy—from V1 (primary visual cortex) through V2, V4, lateral occipital cortex (LOC), and prefrontal cortex—neurons encode prediction errors: the difference between what was expected and what actually arrived. This encoding strategy is metabolically efficient because visual environments are highly autocorrelated: a forest at time T looks very similar to the forest at time T−1. By encoding only the surprises, the visual system conserves metabolic resources and flags novelty—which evolved because novelty often signals behaviorally relevant events (prey, predators, resources, social partners). A high-prospect natural environment presents a specific pattern to the visual cortex: large-scale structural regularities (the forest repeats itself, the horizon maintains continuity, geological features persist) combined with medium-scale novelty (leaves move with wind, light changes, animal movement). This combination produces small, manageable prediction errors at the local scale while maintaining global predictability. The Goldilocks principle applies: prediction errors that are small enough to resolve but large enough to signal novelty produce the most efficient cortical processing, and such efficiency itself is experienced as aesthetic satisfaction and attention restoration. Conversely, a low-prospect environment with high refuge—a dense thicket, an enclosed ravine—presents visual chaos: dense texture, sudden visibility drops, inability to predict what lies beyond the next branch. This generates sustained, unresolvable prediction errors, which escalates to the salience network and produces a state of ongoing attention demand (the person must vigilantly monitor the constrained visual field), preventing attention recovery. This mechanism is well-established in visual neuroscience (confidence: 75%). The hierarchical predictive processing architecture of the visual cortex is among the most replicated findings in computational neuroscience (Friston, 2010; Rao & Ballard, 1999). The "Goldilocks" principle—that moderate complexity produces optimal aesthetic and cognitive engagement—has been demonstrated in music (Huron, 2006), visual art (Berlyne, 1974), and architecture (Salingaros, 2006). What remains untested is the specific claim that the prospect-refuge distinction operates through this prediction-error mechanism in natural environments. The study measured behavior and affect but did not measure visual prediction directly (via eye tracking or neural imaging). When does this apply? Same participant population. The prediction-error mechanism operates on a timescale of 50–250 milliseconds per processing level, accumulating over minutes of visual exploration. High-prospect environments likely engage V1-through-LOC efficiently, while low-prospect environments may overload this system. Measured via NCPT (attention performance) and affect ratings, but not direct neural readout. Mechanism 3: Chronic visual constraint in refuge-dominant environments maintains elevated allostatic load, preventing stress recovery (IC-ALLOSTATIC-DEMAND-001) The allostatic model (Sterling & Eyer, 1988; McEwen, 1998) proposes that the body continuously adjusts physiological baselines (heart rate, cortisol, immune function) in anticipation of environmental demands. When the environment is predictable and resourced, the brain's interoceptive model (implemented by the insula, anterior cingulate cortex, and hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis) can maintain efficient body budgets: low baseline stress hormones, robust parasympathetic tone, strong immune function.

science_summary.core_finding: PDF-0902 makes a concrete claim about the central design relation. In addition to classical visual effects, light elicits nonvisual brain responses, which profoundly influence physiology and behavior. These effects are mediated in part by melanopsin-expressing lightsensitive ganglion cells that, in contrast to the classical photopic system that is maximally sensitive to green light \((550 )\), is very sensitive to blue light \((470-480 )\). At present, there is no evidence that blue light exposure is effective in modulating nonvisual brain activity related to complex cognitive tasks. Using functional magnetic resonance imaging, we show that, while participants perform an auditory working memory task, a short ( 18 min ) daytime exposure to blue \(( )\) or green \(( )\) monochromatic light ( \( ^ \) photons \( ^ \) ) differentially modulates regional brain responses. Blue light typically enhanced brain responses or at least prevented the decline otherwise observed following green light exposure in frontal and parietal cortices implicated in working memory, and in the thalamus involved in the modulation of cognition by arousal. Our results imply that monochromatic light can affect cognitive functions almost instantaneously and suggest that these effects are mediated by a melanopsin-based photoreceptor system. Functional volumes were analyzed using statistical parametric mapping 2 (SPM2-http://www.fil.ion.ucl.ac.uk/spm) implemented in MATLAB. They were corrected for head motion, spatially normalized (standard SPM2 parameters) to an echo-planar imaging template conforming to the Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI) space, and spatially smoothed with a Gaussian Kernel of \(8- \) FWHM.
