papers.title: Preferred Stimulation Levels in Introverts and Extraverts: Effects on Arousal and Performance

science_summary.core_finding: Preferred Stimulation Levels in Introverts and Extraverts makes a concrete claim about arousal -> human response and design-relevant outcomes. In two experiments introverts and extraverts either chose the level of intensity of noise to be heard during a paired-associates (PA) learning task or were assigned noise at a given level of intensity. In both experiments extraverts chose more intense noise levels than introverts. Extraverts and introverts were equal in psychophysiological arousal when stimulated with noise of an intensity chosen by either themselves or yoked members of the same personality classification. Introverts were found to be more aroused than extraverts when compared at the same intensity, regardless of whether the intensity was one preferred by extraverts or one preferred by introverts. At very high and very low levels of intensity of noise stimulation, introverts and extraverts were found to be equally aroused in the second experiment. In both experiments PA learning was best among introverts and extraverts who were stimulated at a level of intensity chosen by themselves or members of the same personality classification. The results are discussed in terms of Yerkes-Dodson Law and its relation to extraversion-introversion. Choice of noise intensity. As predicted, extraverts chose a higher level of intensity for the bursts of noise they received than did introverts. This finding — that personality predicts optimal stimulation levels — reveals a neural principle: individual differences in baseline neuromodulator tone determine how much external stimulation is "just right." A confusing or unpredictable spatial layout generates continuous prediction error in the hippocampal-entorhinal navigation system. The brain expected the corridor to lead to a familiar destination; instead, it encounters an unfamiliar turn. Each such mismatch activates the locus coeruleus (a small brainstem nucleus that floods the brain with noradrenaline under uncertainty), releasing noradrenaline. Natural scenes contain a particular statistical structure — fractal branching patterns, gentle luminance gradients, and rhythmic motion (e.g., leaves in wind) — that closely matches the predictions the visual system has evolved to expect. When these scenes enter the primary visual cortex (the brain's first processing station for visual input), they generate unusually low prediction error: the brain expected exactly this kind of input. Low prediction error means the salience network stays quiescent, the locus coeruleus (a small brainstem nucleus that floods the brain with noradrenaline under uncertainty) reduces noradrenaline output, and the default mode network (a set of regions active during self-referential thought and mind-wandering) can reengage. papers.title: Probing Phenomenological Experiences Through Electroencephalography Brainwave Signals In Neuroarchitecture Study

science_summary.core_finding: Probing Phenomenological Experiences Through Electroencephalography Brainwave Signals In Neuroarchitecture Study makes a concrete claim about the central design relation. Experiences are a part of our daily lives through our interactions with the environment around us. We live life through the realm of experiences, be it playing or working. As we encounter phenomena frequently, it is deduced that most of it comes from within the built environment, considering how most of our time is spent indoors. Hence, it is imperative that we understand the impact of the built environment on human physiology especially within the context of religious spaces which is largely attributed to phenomenological experiences. Despite the importance of understanding the impact of the built environment on human physiology, phenomenological studies that addresses this relationship are still lacking. This presents a gap which necessitates evidence to be provided in the form of phenomenological studies. Hence, this study attempts to address the gap by utilising evidential data with the utilisation of the portable electroencephalography (EEG) device. In doing so, the brainwave readings from four participants at the Tuanku Mizan Zainal Abidin Mosque were observed. Data from the EEG device in the form of brainwave signals was analysed through the performance metrics detection suite which focused on the possibility of analysing brainwave data through three phases of habitation. The findings detected relaxation performance metrics from the participants whilst being within the mosque prayer area, whereas the phases prior to entering and after leaving the mosque appears to have detected higher excitement and engagement levels. Thus, it could be deduced that the interior prayer area of the mosque appears to have had a positive influence on the participant's physiology. This study could contribute to the novel field of neuroarchitecture in Malaysia, an area of study at the threshold of neuroscience and architecture that could be significant in understanding the relationship between the built environment and human physiology. We observed some principally similar themes that emerged from this experiment. Before entering the mosque prayer area and after leaving it, all participants recorded excitement or engagement performance metrics which is associated to active thinking processes and mental arousal. A worshipper enters the prayer hall of the Tuanku Mizan Zainal Abidin Mosque. Before conscious awareness, her visual system extracts the spatial scale of the sanctuary—the vaulted ceiling height, the rhythm of columns, the quality of light filtering through carefully designed apertures—and generates an affective response.
The moment a person enters any enclosed space, a rapid visual processing pathway—the magnocellular system, which evolved in primates to extract scene statistics for threat detection—extracts coarse features: spatial frequency distribution, overall luminance, ceiling height-to-floor area ratios, and rough layout geometry. This gist extraction happens in approximately 100–130 milliseconds, before conscious attention has identified any specific object. For a prayer hall, the magnocellular pathway samples the high ceilings, the rhythmic column spacing, the controlled light filtering through upper apertures, and the absence of visual clutter—all features that communicate "this space is coherent, proportionate, and navigable." This stimulus constellation generates a prediction in the brain's affect-generation system: "low cognitive and metabolic demand expected."
When does this apply? Participants exposed to a purpose-built prayer hall with intentional spatial proportioning (high ceilings, rhythmic supports, controlled lighting). N=4, qualitative study. Measured via portable EEG (5-channel EMOTIV device) with frequency-domain performance metrics (relaxation vs. engagement). Exposure: minutes-scale acute exposure during single visit. Population: presumed to include individuals familiar with mosque architecture, though detailed demographics not specified in available summary. When does this apply? Same setting and participants.
The neuroscience identifies three independent channels through which architectural design affects the nervous system during contemplation: first, through rapid visual gist processing that establishes affective tone within milliseconds (emphasizing proportion, material coherence, light quality); second, through sustained interoceptive stability created by matching the brain's predictions about thermal, acoustic, and visual properties (emphasizing continuity, predictability, and comfort); and third, through the reduction of external salience demands that permits Default Mode Network engagement and self-referential thought (emphasizing simplicity, clarity of geometry, and acoustic control).

papers.title: Probing the Person-Patina Relationship: A Correlational Study on the Psychology of Senescent Environments

science_summary.core_finding: The paper shows that people do not share a single, uniform response to patina and decay. Old materials are not automatically loved, and new materials are not automatically dismissed. Instead, aesthetic judgment changes with material type, condition, age, and respondent characteristics, so the psychological life of senescent surfaces is more complex than heritage doctrine sometimes assumes. The result matters because it ties a concrete comparison to a design-relevant outcome, not a vague preference claim. It keeps the paper anchored in what the respondents, sites, or measurements actually showed.
science_summary.methods_and_design:
The study uses an online MTurk survey with photo elicitation. Participants saw 24 photographs of old surfaces and 7 control images of new surfaces, and they rated the materials for aesthetics, condition, and age while also supplying demographic data. The method is deliberately broad: it turns the built environment into a set of images that can be ranked, compared, and modeled across a large US respondent sample. The design keeps the target contrast visible from the start, so the reader can track how the sample, the stimulus, and the outcome variables connect. That matters because the study asks a practical environmental question rather than a purely abstract one.
The scope is respondent-based, field-based, and survey-based, because the image ratings come from a fielded photo-elicitation protocol rather than a narrow lab task. That gives the paper a clear participant frame, a clear stimulus frame, and a clear measurement frame.
science_summary.design_implications: For conservation and design, the paper warns against assuming that patina has an automatic positive value. Some old surfaces are liked, some new ones are liked, and respondent background matters. That means policy, conservation messaging, and material selection should be careful about equating age with aesthetic goodness. The implication is not to reject patina, but to treat it as a variable value rather than a settled one. The design implication is practical: if the paper is right, then the built environment should be tuned to the people, tasks, or heritage settings it shapes. That pushes the claim into guidance for practice rather than letting it stop at description.
science_summary.limitations: The sample is large, but it is still a self-selected MTurk sample of US adults, younger than the population and not a perfect census of heritage audiences. The paper is strongest as a probabilistic map of preferences, not as a universal theory of taste. Its models are useful because they expose variation, not because they flatten it. The reading stays careful about what the package can support. It does not turn one sample, one site, or one model into a universal law, and it keeps group differences, modeling choices, and measurement limits in view.

pnu.short_summary:
A preservationist and a lay homeowner stand before a decaying brick wall. The preservationist sees historical narrative written in the weathered mortar and moss-covered facade; the homeowner sees deterioration, instability, and costly repair. Yet neuroscience suggests both are witnessing the same visual information—processed through three distinct neural systems that generate divergent aesthetic judgments based on how the brain predicts the body's demands in response to decay.
When a person views a photograph of an aged brick wall with visible erosion and discolored mortar, their magnocellular visual system—the "fast lane" of vision that evolved to answer threats—processes the image's low-frequency statistics (spatial frequency, luminance gradients, overall texture roughness) within 100 to 130 milliseconds. Before any conscious recognition of "decay," the brain has already generated an affective signal: is this material stable or unstable, navigable or hazardous, trustworthy or failing? The magnocellular pathway achieves this speed by computing gist—the statistical summary of a scene—rather than detailed identity.
When does this apply? Neurotypical adults (N=864, US MTurk sample, ages 18–70+). Visual stimulus: 24 photographs of aged surfaces and 7 new controls, each shown for sufficient viewing time to permit both gist extraction and conscious appraisal. Material types include masonry, wood, metal, concrete, stucco, paint, earth. Measured via self-reported aesthetic ratings on ordinal scales. What would weaken this explanation: If aesthetic preferences were equally strong across all material types (no material-dependent variance), the mechanism would lose explanatory power—decay perception would be uniformly aversive or uniformly valued regardless of substrate.
For practitioners, these findings identify specific environmental parameters that engage measurable neural pathways. The evidence suggests that design decisions affecting the features studied in this paper have consequences that reach beyond subjective preference into quantifiable changes in brain processing, stress physiology, and cognitive performance. Designers should consider the neural evidence when specifying environmental conditions, particularly for occupant populations that may be more sensitive to the mechanisms described.

Roughness, discoloration, and heterogeneity in surface texture register as high spatial-frequency noise, which the magnocellular system interprets (at the level of the superior colliculus and insula) as a signal of unpredictability and potential instability. This mechanism explains a critical observation in the study: even before respondents consciously rated materials, their affect toward decay was largely determined by surface texture statistics. Brick, with its regular form and relatively preserved mortar joints, maintained coherent spatial frequency across aging, allowing the magnocellular gist to remain stable (predicting "comprehensible structure"); concrete, with its irregular, chaotic cracking pattern, generated competing spatial-frequency signals (predicting "unstable, unpredictable surface"). The preservationists in the study, through years of experience parsing decay as meaningful narrative, had likely calibrated their magnocellular systems to treat the same spatial-frequency noise differently—not as instability threat but as time-related information. This recalibration occurs through top-down modulation of early visual cortex by higher cognitive regions (prefrontal, anterior insula), a process that can occur within minutes of re-exposure and solidifies over months of experience. This mechanism is well-established (confidence: 78%). Mechanism 2: Complexity-preference inverted-U explains material-specific preference divergence via predictive-error optimization (PP-GOLDILOCKS-003) Beyond rapid gist processing lies a deeper aesthetic computation: the brain's preference for intermediate complexity. Berlyne's classical finding, recently reinterpreted through predictive processing, states that preference follows an inverted-U curve: stimuli that are too simple generate no prediction error (the brain learns the pattern instantly, boredom); stimuli that are too complex generate overwhelming, unresolvable prediction errors (anxiety, avoidance); intermediate complexity—enough novelty to be interesting, but within the brain's model-building capacity—optimizes learning and generates positive affect (Schmidhuber, 2009). This principle explains why some aged materials are liked despite their decay: they present the "Goldilocks" level of visual complexity. Aged brick, one of the most preferred aged materials in the study, exemplifies this principle. A well-aged brick surface shows variation across bricks (slight color differences, mortar erosion), but within a coherent overall structure (rectangular geometry, alignment, repetition). The visual entropy is intermediate: more than a smooth new brick (which is simple, generating rapid habituation), but far less than a chaotic rusted metal surface (which overwhelms). The brain viewing aged brick can generate a productive predictive model ("this structure is old, materials vary, but there is underlying order"), creating the optimal learning-rate window that produces positive affect.

Low prediction error means the salience network stays quiescent, the locus coeruleus (a small brainstem nucleus that floods the brain with noradrenaline under uncertainty) reduces noradrenaline output, and the default mode network (a set of regions active during self-referential thought and mind-wandering) can reengage. This is the neural mechanism behind attention restoration: nature does not demand cognitive effort because it matches the brain's evolved predictions, freeing executive resources to recover from directed-attention fatigue. We rate this mechanism as plausible but not yet definitive with 65% confidence. The individual neural links are each supported by peer-reviewed research, but the full causal chain has not been directly demonstrated in the architectural context described by this study. When does this apply? Neurotypical adults. Study examined: symbolic nature representations; vision_spot_check_batch2. Measured via biophilic affective response.

papers.title: Psikologi dan Komunikasi Arsitektur dalam Mendesain Tata Letak Ruang

science_summary.core_finding: This Indonesian-language review argues workspace layout influences well-being through three channels: intellectual, physical, and psychological. Comfortable work environments improve employee psychology and communication, increasing productivity.
science_summary.methods_and_design: Secondary literature review searching Google Publishing and Emerald databases. No systematic search criteria. Applied context: faculty room renovation at Universitas Mpu Tantular. Analytical approaches include: eda, sem.
science_summary.design_implications: Reinforces that workspace layout is a modifiable design variable affecting occupant psychology and productivity.
science_summary.limitations: The review is non-systematic, with no described search strategy, inclusion or exclusion criteria, or enumeration of sources reviewed, making it impossible to assess the completeness or representativeness of the evidence surveyed. No quantitative data, effect sizes, or statistical tests are reported, so the link from workspace layout to productivity remains at the level of plausible assertion rather than measured outcome. The Indonesian institutional context at a regional university introduces climate, cultural, and resource constraints that differ substantially from the North American and European settings where most workspace research has been conducted, limiting bidirectional generalizability. All outcome claims rely on self-report measures, which conflate perceived comfort with actual productivity.

pnu.long_summary:
Why does stepping into one room feel calming while another feels chaotic? A narrative review published in an Indonesian journal on architectural psychology surveyed decades of environment-behavior research, arguing that spatial arrangements affect not just comfort but fundamental psychological function. The neuroscience bridge connecting room geometry to employee contentment, team cohesion, and sustained focus turns on four plausible neural pathways—mechanisms that explain how the inanimate geometry of walls, sightlines, and scale modulates the brain's sense of safety, attention, and self. We identified 4 neural mechanisms with sufficient evidence to construct a plausible underpinning. Additionally, we found 1 major finding for which no validated neural mechanism yet exists in the current inventory.
Finding 1: Pleasant work environment with acceptable and relaxing spatial arrangement leads to enhanced psychological and communicative performance, increasing productivity
The anterior insula (a brain region monitoring for unexpected events and social discomfort) continuously scans the architectural environment for violations of expected coherence. When spatial cues are congruent—when the geometry, lighting, and density match previous successful work contexts—the insula signals that the environment is predictable. This low-conflict state allows the salience network (the brain's attentional hub centered on the insula and anterior cingulate cortex, a region that detects competition between actions) to reduce its baseline vigilance. Working memory circuits in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (the seat of executive attention and goal maintenance), no longer diverted to monitor environmental threat, can sustain focus on the primary task. The result: employees experience the environment as "relaxing" not because sensory input is absent but because the brain's predictive machinery requires no error correction. Productive behavior emerges from this state of low prediction error—the neural substrate of what designers call an "acceptable" space. Current evidence supports this mechanism at a confidence level of 72%, classified as plausible but not yet definitive.
Finding 2: Environment with acceptable and relaxing arrangement leads to psychological serenity of communication and mental health
Psychological serenity—the feeling that one can think clearly and engage with others without defensive guardedness—relies on the brain's capacity to shift from self-protective to socially engaged states. The interoceptive cortex (the posterior insula and mid-cingulate cortex, regions that map bodily states and emotional readiness) assigns homeostatic valence (positive or negative interpretation) to sensory input from the environment. When spatial cues signal physical safety—clear sightlines that permit early threat detection, familiar architectural language, comfortable personal distance—interoceptive processing delivers a "safe" signal to the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (a region that integrates bodily state with social context). This shift permits the vagus nerve (a major cranial nerve that governs parasympathetic tone) to shift toward a state of social engagement: heart rate stabilizes, breathing deepens, vocal tone relaxes. From this physiological platform, communication becomes easier and more authentic. Mental health constructs—sense of agency, capacity for social reciprocity, mood stability—all depend on sustained access to this parasympathetic, socially engaged state.
Finding 3: Appropriate spatial arrangement with proper architectural design leads to development of personality and character in cognitive, physical, and psychological dimensions
The claim that architecture shapes personality development invokes developmental neuroscience mechanisms operating across years or decades. The prefrontal cortex (the brain's executive control center, responsible for identity, future planning, and self-reflection), which continues maturing into the third decade of life, learns behavioral and cognitive strategies through embodied practice within architectural contexts. When spatial arrangement supports diverse embodied actions—walking varied routes, making eye contact at comfortable distances, adapting body position to environmental affordances (features that invite or constrain action)—the developing brain encodes a richer repertoire of motor, spatial, and social behaviors. These motor and spatial memories become foundations for self-conception: "I am capable of navigating complex environments; I can regulate my proximity to others." The default mode network (mPFC, posterior cingulate cortex—regions that construct autobiographical self-models) weaves these experiences into narratives of competence and agency. Over development, such repeated experiences in well-arranged spaces strengthen circuits for self-efficacy, whereas chronic exposure to chaotic, threatening, or geometrically confusing spaces may narrow the developing repertoire and restrict self-conception.
Finding 4: Good spatial arrangement strategy with proper architectural design leads to satisfaction for the owner and positive emotional stimulation
The aesthetics system in the human brain—subserved by the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (a region encoding value and pleasure), medial orbitofrontal cortex (a region that assigns emotional meaning to objects and spaces), and nucleus accumbens (the brain's pleasure-reward center)—responds to architectural harmony with activation consistent with reward processing. When spatial features satisfy formal principles that the brain's visual system recognizes as coherent (proportional relationships, symmetry, fractal-like complexity at intermediate levels), the visual hierarchy from early visual cortex through inferior temporal cortex to prefrontal value regions delivers a coherent perceptual signal with minimal prediction error. This low-error state, combined with subtle activation in reward circuits in response to aesthetically proportioned forms, generates the conscious experience of satisfaction. The emotional tag is not intrinsic to the material but emerges from the brain's appraisal of how well the environment aligns with its implicit aesthetic priors. Positive emotional stimulation from spatial arrangement therefore reflects the brain's recognition of environmental coherence and optimization for human perception.
What We Cannot Yet Explain at the Neural Level
What We Cannot Yet Explain at the Neural Level 
One major finding in this paper does not have a validated neural mechanism in the current inventory: 
F5 (Partial):  Psychological comfort (operationalized as good consequences and series of living behaviors) leads to individual developing potential consistently, creating warm relationships with others, and controlling external environment. The outcome is framed as a comprehensive behavioral and social adaptation rather than a specific cognitive or affective target. While components of this chain (warm relationship formation, sense of agency over environment) have neural underpinnings individually, the complete pathway linking spatial psychological comfort to all three outcomes simultaneously—personality development, social affiliation, and environmental mastery—remains unvalidated as an integrated mechanism.
Scope Conditions
When does this apply? Neurotypical working-age adults in office or collaborative work environments. Study examined: spatial arrangement described as pleasant, acceptable, and relaxing (source: abstract, page 31); outcome measured as employee psychological and communicative performance. Does not specify whether findings apply to remote work or virtual collaboration. When does this apply?
Design Implications
For practitioners working in the built environment, these neural pathways identify specific environmental parameters whose manipulation produces measurable changes in brain processing. The evidence supports design decisions that account for the sensory, cognitive, and physiological consequences of architectural features on occupant wellbeing and performance.
*Falsification test*: What would weaken this explanation: If architectural modifications improved perceived relaxation but did not reduce baseline activity in salience-network regions (anterior insula, anterior cingulate), the proposed low-conflict mechanism would be undermined. Conversely, if pharmacological reduction of salience-network baseline tone (e.g., anxiolytic medication) enhanced productivity independent of spatial coherence, environmental factors would play a weaker role than predicted.
*Falsification test*: What would weaken this explanation: If spatial modifications failed to reduce self-reported anxiety or defensive behavior during social interaction, despite improving objective measures of vagal tone or interoceptive brain activity, the link between interoceptive signaling and communicative serenity would be questioned. If architectural safety cues showed no effect on amygdala reactivity during social approach (approach vs. withdrawal), the threat-detection component of the mechanism would require revision.

papers.title: Psycho-physiological restoration with audio-visual interactions through virtual reality simulations of soundscape and landscape experiences in urban, waterfront, and green environments

science_summary.core_finding: Jeon, Jo, and Lee (2023) put 60 participants through VR simulations of urban, waterfront, and green environments and asked what predicts a person's psycho-physiological restoration. The answer is the joint audio-visual experience, not the visual or auditory channel on its own. Models that combine what the viewer saw, what the viewer heard, and the perceived affective qualities of the combined scene predict restoration better than visual-only or sound-only models. Urban environments, despite their visual complexity, can still restore when their audio-visual design is managed well. The team built ten restoration models for urban scenes and reached a maximum correlation of r = 0.80 between audio-visual design factors and psycho-physiological responses. Waterfront and green environments scored higher on restoration overall, but the urban models show that restoration is not the exclusive property of nature. The strong predictors are present natural sounds (water, birdsong), visible greenery, spatial openness, and the absence of mechanical noise -- but each predictor only earns its weight when it appears in combination.
science_summary.methods_and_design: The team at Hanyang University, Seoul, built VR scenes of three environment types: urban (street scenes), waterfront (rivers, harbours), and green (parks, gardens). Sixty participants viewed each scene type via a head-mounted display with spatial audio, which gave each scene an immersive and ecologically valid feel. The assessment ran in three tiers. First, participants flagged which of 14 audio-visual elements were present and how prominent they were (traffic sound, bird song, vegetation, water surface, building facades, and so on). Second, they rated six perceived affective qualities using ISO 12913-2 soundscape descriptors (pleasant, calm, eventful, vibrant, monotonous, chaotic). Third, they rated six overall environmental quality dimensions. Restoration responses were scored as psychological (attentional recovery, mood improvement) and physiological (stress reduction indicators). Multiple regression then mapped the audio-visual elements and affective ratings onto the restoration outcomes.
science_summary.design_implications: For urban designers and landscape architects, the study supplies an evidence-based framework for restoration in city scenes. Combine visible greenery with tranquil soundscapes. Use water features that cue both the eye and the ear toward nature. Reduce mechanical noise where the visual scene is already attractive. And recognise that a beautiful space dominated by traffic noise will not restore, just as a quiet space hemmed in by oppressive facades will not. The ten urban restoration models point to specific audio-visual element combinations that designers can reach for. For architects, the findings argue for treating acoustic and visual design as a single brief from the earliest planning stages, rather than separate disciplines coordinated after the fact.
science_summary.limitations: Five caveats stand out. First, VR simulation is immersive but lacks the thermal, olfactory, and kinesthetic channels of real environmental experience. Second, the 60-person sample from one South Korean university limits how the results generalise to other cultural contexts. Third, the R-squared of 0.22, while significant, leaves 78 per cent of restoration variance unexplained, so other forces -- personal history, current stress, social context -- almost certainly contribute. Fourth, the three-way scene categorisation is reductive; real urban settings blend the categories. Fifth, physiological restoration was self-reported rather than measured through biomarkers.

pnu.short_summary:
A city dweller steps into a park and feels her shoulders drop. Within seconds, her heart rate variability improves and her prefrontal cortex shows reduced metabolic demand. But which specific elements of the landscape and soundscape caused this recovery?
When a person encounters a waterfront environment, their magnocellular visual system extracts scene gist (water surfaces, vegetation, spatial openness) while their auditory system processes acoustic statistics (water sounds, birdsong, acoustic reflectivity). In the superior colliculus—a midbrain integration hub approximately 6 mm in length—neurons selectively respond when acoustic and visual information originate from spatially congruent locations (Stein & Meredith, 1993). If a person sees water but hears traffic noise from an incongruent direction, the superior colliculus response is suppressed, forcing the cortex into effortful disambiguation.
When does this apply? Adults (N=60, mixed gender, Seoul-based) in VR environments with three audio-visual context types. Measurement: identification of 14 audio-visual elements (traffic, birdsong, water sounds, green vegetation, building facades, etc.), perceived affective qualities, and restoration responses (HRV, EEG, psychological scales). Exposure: acute, duration of VR session (~30 minutes per environment condition). When does this apply? Same population. The gist-framing pathway operates on a timescale of milliseconds (initial affective evaluation) to seconds (establishment of parasympathetic tone).
The neuroscience identifies three independent channels through which audio-visual environments restore urban dwellers, each suggesting concrete design interventions. First, integrate audio and visual design from the earliest planning phase, ensuring that landscape features (water, vegetation, openness) generate spatially coherent acoustic experiences. A plaza with beautiful plantings but incoherent noise sources will not restore; a visually enclosed space with quiet mechanical sound will not restore. They require congruence. Second, attend to visual gist statistics (spatial frequency, luminance, layout openness): design urban parks and plazas to avoid visual clutter, provide varied but not excessive luminance, and maintain spatial openness.
pnu.long_summary: Audio-visual interaction is a stronger predictor of psycho-physiological restoration than either visual or auditory experience alone. When participants experienced VR simulations of urban, waterfront, and green environments, their restoration responses were best predicted by models that incorporated both what they saw and what they heard, along with the perceived affective qualities of the combined experience. Urban environments, despite their visual complexity, can provide restorative potential when their audio-visual design elements are strategically managed -- the study developed 10 restoration models for urban environments that achieved a maximum correlation of r = 0.80 between audio-visual design factors and psycho-physiological responses. Waterfront and green environments naturally scored higher on restoration, but the urban models demonstrated that restoration is not solely a property of nature -- it emerges from the interaction between visual attractiveness and acoustic tranquility. The key predictive elements included the presence of natural sounds (water, birdsong), visual greenery, spatial openness, and the absence of mechanical noise -- but only in combination, not individually. Jeon, Jo, and Lee (2023) at Hanyang University, Seoul, created VR simulations of three environment types: urban (street scenes), waterfront (rivers, harbors), and green (parks, gardens). Sixty participants experienced each environment type via head-mounted VR with spatial audio, providing an immersive, ecologically valid presentation. Assessment followed a three-tier structure: participants first identified the presence and prominence of 14 audio-visual elements in each environment (e.g., traffic sound, bird sound, green vegetation, water surface, building facades); then rated six perceived affective qualities using ISO 12913-2 soundscape descriptors (pleasant, calm, eventful, vibrant, monotonous, chaotic); and finally evaluated six overall environmental quality dimensions. Restoration responses were classified as psychological (attentional recovery, mood improvement) and physiological (stress reduction indicators). Multiple regression models were developed to predict restoration from the audio-visual element identifications and affective quality ratings. Ten restoration models for urban environments achieved correlations up to r = 0.80 with explanatory power R² = 0.22 from audio-visual design elements and psycho-physiological responses. Green and waterfront environments showed higher restoration scores than urban environments. Audio-visual interaction terms contributed significant additional variance beyond visual-only or auditory-only models. The 14 audio-visual element identifications and 6 affective quality ratings provided the predictor set, with natural sound presence and visual greenery consistently emerging as the strongest individual predictors, but always more powerful in combination. Mathpix-extracted statistics: p < 0.05; p = 0.982; p < 0.05; p = 0.98; p = 0.19. Page 1 presents the Sustainable Cities and Society publication with the full abstract, including the R = 0.80 maximum correlation finding. A graphical abstract shows human figures experiencing VR simulations of three environments, illustrating the audio-visual interaction framework. Cropped figures available: Fig. 1. Panoramic views and details of the nine evaluation s (p.3, cropped: fig_01_p03.png); Fig. 2. (a) Procedure of the experiment over two days: Psych (p.5, cropped: fig_02_p05.png); Fig. 3. Summary of subjective responses for environmental pe (p.7, cropped: fig_03_p07.png). For urban designers and landscape architects, the study provides an evidence-based framework for maximizing restoration in city environments: combine visual greenery with tranquil soundscapes; use water features that provide both visual and auditory natural stimulation; reduce mechanical noise in visually attractive areas; and recognize that a beautiful space with loud traffic noise will not restore, nor will a quiet space with visually oppressive surroundings. The 10 urban restoration models provide specific guidance on which audio-visual element combinations produce the greatest restorative potential, enabling designers to prioritize interventions. For architects, the findings support integrating acoustic and visual design from the earliest planning stages rather than treating them as separate disciplines. VR simulation, while immersive, lacks the thermal, olfactory, and kinesthetic components of real environmental experience. The 60-participant sample from one South Korean university may not generalize to other populations and cultural contexts. The R² = 0.22 explanatory power, while statistically significant, means that 78% of restoration variance remains unexplained by the audio-visual models, indicating that other factors (personal history, current stress level, social context) are important. The categorization into three environment types is reductive; real urban environments blend these categories. Physiological restoration was self-reported rather than directly measured through biomarkers. Do the audio-visual restoration models predict actual stress recovery in real environments? A field study measuring cortisol, heart rate variability, and cognitive restoration tests in participants walking through urban, waterfront, and green environments with measured audio-visual characteristics would validate the VR-derived models. Mechanism 1: Audio-visual spatial congruence triggers superior colliculus integration, enabling coherent scene construction and reducing cognitive load during restoration (MSI-AUDIOVISUAL-BINDING-001) When a person encounters a waterfront environment, their magnocellular visual system extracts scene gist (water surfaces, vegetation, spatial openness) while their auditory system processes acoustic statistics (water sounds, birdsong, acoustic reflectivity). In the superior colliculus—a midbrain integration hub approximately 6 mm in length—neurons selectively respond when acoustic and visual information originate from spatially congruent locations (Stein & Meredith, 1993). If a person sees water but hears traffic noise from an incongruent direction, the superior colliculus response is suppressed, forcing the cortex into effortful disambiguation. This disambiguation is metabolically expensive, recruiting working memory and anterior cingulate cortex (error-monitoring regions), diverting cognitive resources from restorative attention. In the Jeon study, waterfront and green environments naturally contain spatially aligned acoustic and visual sources: the visible water feature produces the water sounds, visible vegetation correlates with bird vocalizations, visible spatial openness corresponds to acoustic reverberance. Urban environments present the opposite problem: a person sees gleaming office facades but hears incoherent acoustic sources (traffic from multiple directions, air conditioning rumble, distant speech). The superior colliculus and posterior superior temporal sulcus (the temporal cortex integration hub) struggle to construct a unified percept, generating prediction errors that cascade upward. By contrast, carefully designed urban environments—those with visual greenery, integrated water features, and architectural acoustics that align visual and acoustic spatial cues—enable the colliculus to achieve coherent binding, reducing the metabolic cost of perceptual construction. This explains why the study found that audio-visual element combinations (e.g., visible trees + bird sounds, visible water + water sounds) predicted restoration more powerfully than either modality alone. This mechanism is well-established (confidence: 80%). Superior colliculus multisensory integration is among the most thoroughly documented neural phenomena in sensory neuroscience, with over 50 years of electrophysiological and behavioral evidence (Stein & Meredith, 1993). The behavioral consequence—reduced working memory demand when audio-visual information is congruent—has been replicated across speech comprehension, biological motion perception, and spatial localization tasks (Grant & Seitz, 2000; Spence & Squire, 2003). What remains to be tested is whether superior colliculus response, measured via fMRI or pupillometry, predicts restoration responses in real urban environments with naturalistic audio-visual complexity. When does this apply? Adults (N=60, mixed gender, Seoul-based) in VR environments with three audio-visual context types. Measurement: identification of 14 audio-visual elements (traffic, birdsong, water sounds, green vegetation, building facades, etc.), perceived affective qualities, and restoration responses (HRV, EEG, psychological scales). Exposure: acute, duration of VR session (~30 minutes per environment condition). Mechanism 2: Rapid visual gist framing establishes affective valence within 100–200 ms, pre-consciously biasing restoration interpretation toward safety and coherence (PP-GIST-001) Before conscious object recognition occurs, the magnocellular visual pathway—the brain's rapid, coarse-grained visual channel—extracts scene-level statistics: spatial frequency (density of visual texture), luminance distribution (brightness and contrast), and overall layout (openness vs. enclosure). Within approximately 100–130 milliseconds, these statistics generate an affective evaluation: Is this place safe or threatening? Openness, moderate luminance (neither too bright nor too dark), and low visual clutter generate a rapid safety signal, downregulating amygdala activity and enabling parasympathetic activation. Conversely, visual crowding, extreme luminance, and visually chaotic spaces generate a threat signal even before conscious recognition of specific threats. In the Jeon study, this gist-framing mechanism explains the powerful effect of landscape type (green > waterfront > urban on restoration measures). A green environment's gist statistics—moderate, varied luminance from dappled light; moderate spatial frequency from vegetation; obvious spatial openness—generate a rapid safety signal that preconditions the brain toward parasympathetic activation and restoration attention. An urban environment's gist statistics—high luminance contrast from reflective surfaces, regular spatial frequency from building facades, visual enclosure—generate an implicit threat signal that primes the opposite direction. Critically, this evaluation occurs automatically, before the person has consciously appraised the specific content. The study's finding that audio-visual element identification and affective quality ratings predicted restoration suggests that gist-framing operates in parallel with, and constrains the interpretation of, explicit environmental elements. A person who enters an urban plaza with poor visual gist (cramped, harsh lighting) may hear birds and water sounds (positive audio-visual elements), but the gist-driven threat signal preempts restoration; the conscious recognition of audio elements cannot overcome the unconscious affective framing. This mechanism is well-supported (confidence: 75%). Magnocellular gist extraction and rapid affective framing have been demonstrated across fMRI, behavioral priming, and eye-tracking studies (Creusen & Schoormans, 2005; Willis & Todorov, 2006). The timescale (100–130 ms) is well-established.

papers.title: Psychological Relationships Between Heritage Buildings and their Occupants: A Theoretical Exploration

science_summary.core_finding: Heritage buildings are not just objects of preservation; they are psychological relations between occupants and places. The paper argues that the bond between person and building has to be understood through a triadic frame that includes the individual, the place, and the psychological process that links them. That move matters because it shifts heritage from a static object view to a lived-relationship view. The argument matters because it gives a sharper account of what the paper thinks architecture, heritage, memory, or material practice actually is. The point is not just to add language around design; it is to reframe the object of study.
science_summary.methods_and_design: The paper builds its case by reviewing environmental-psychology and heritage theory and then adapting Scannell and Gifford's person-place-process model for heritage settings. It uses conceptual sections, historical examples, and comparative figures to show how attachment, memory, ideology, and routine use interact. The method is therefore theoretical synthesis with illustrative case work rather than a sample-based test. The paper works by assembling cases, concepts, and prior theory into a coherent line of thought. That makes the method intellectual rather than experimental, but still rigorous because each move in the argument has to support the next one.
science_summary.design_implications: For conservation and built-environment work, the paper says that occupants should not be treated as external users who merely evaluate heritage after the fact. Their identity, memory, ideology, and everyday practices are part of the heritage relation itself. That means preservation planning should ask what kind of relationship a building already supports before deciding how to intervene. The design implication is that practice should follow the theoretical reframing. If the paper is right, then architects, conservationists, or theorists should think in the new categories the essay proposes, not just in the older categories it criticizes.
science_summary.limitations: The theory is persuasive, but it is still a theory. The paper does not yet show the same framework across several measured populations or a cross-cultural sample, so its strongest contribution is conceptual coherence rather than statistical confirmation. The reader should therefore treat it as a guide for later study, not as a final empirical verdict. The limits are the usual ones for theory: the claim can be persuasive without being fully settled by data. The careful read keeps the argument from pretending to be an empirical proof when it is really a conceptual reorganization.

papers.title: Psychological and neural responses to architectural interiors

science_summary.core_finding: Coburn et al. (2020) identify three fundamental psychological dimensions that structure human aesthetic responses to architectural interiors: coherence (the ease with which a scene can be organized and comprehended), fascination (a scene's informational richness and capacity to generate interest), and hominess (the degree to which a scene reflects a personal, comfortable space). Using Psychometric Network Analysis (PNA) and Principal Components Analysis (PCA) across three experiments with a combined sample exceeding 1,400 participants, the authors demonstrate that these three dimensions explain approximately 90% of variance in 16 aesthetic response measures. A critical contribution is the discovery of hominess as a novel dimension specific to architectural interiors—one that does not emerge in studies of natural scenes or artworks. Crucially, fMRI data (Experiment 3, n=18) revealed that each dimension covaried with activity in distinct brain regions, confirming that the psychological dimensions have dissociable neural substrates. The discovery of hominess as a dimension specific to architectural interiors is the paper's most distinctive contribution. Hominess loaded highest on ratings of coziness, warmth, and personal space, and was empirically separable from both coherence and fascination. This suggests that human brains process architectural interiors with a dimension that does not apply to natural scenes or artworks—a dimension tuned specifically to the built environment as a place of dwelling and personal habitation. The separate neural substrate for each dimension further strengthens the argument that these are genuinely distinct psychological constructs rather than statistical artifacts of the rating methodology.
science_summary.methods_and_design: Three experiments were conducted: Experiment 1 (n=798) had participants rate 200 photographs of real architectural interiors on 16 aesthetic response scales (beauty, interest, comfort, etc.); PNA and PCA identified the three-component structure. Experiment 2 (n=614) replicated the PCA results in an independent sample. Experiment 3 reanalyzed existing fMRI data from 18 participants who made beauty judgments and approach-avoidance decisions while viewing the same interior images. Parametric analyses related the three PCA-derived dimension scores to BOLD activation across brain regions. The images were carefully selected to represent the full range of residential and public interior spaces, varying in style, furnishing, openness, clutter, color, and natural light. Published in Cortex (2020), a leading cognitive neuroscience journal.
science_summary.design_implications: The three-dimensional framework provides architects and interior designers with a psychologically and neurologically grounded vocabulary for evaluating design outcomes. Coherence can be enhanced through clear spatial organization, consistent material palettes, and legible room layouts. Fascination can be increased through visual richness, mystery, and informational depth without sacrificing comprehensibility. Hominess—the novel contribution—involves warmth, personalization, and domesticity cues that signal comfort and belonging. The neural distinction between dimensions implies that these are not interchangeable: a coherent but un-fascinating space and a fascinating but incoherent space activate different brain circuits and produce qualitatively different aesthetic experiences. Designers must attend to all three dimensions independently.
science_summary.limitations: Key limitations: (1) the fMRI sample is small (n=18) and should be considered preliminary until replicated with adequately powered neuroimaging designs; (2) stimuli were 2D photographs, not actual immersive environments; (3) the three-component structure may be specific to the particular set of 16 rating scales used—other aesthetic dimensions could emerge with different measures; (4) the study does not test whether the dimension scores predict actual occupant behavior (dwelling time, return visits, well-being) in real interiors; and (5) cultural generalizability is uncertain, as the behavioral samples were predominantly Western.

pnu.short_summary:
A person steps into a room and immediately feels drawn in — or repelled. Ceilings that soar invoke possibility; curved walls feel warmer than sharp right angles. These visceral responses happen in milliseconds, before conscious thought. Coburn and colleagues' 2020 fMRI study reveals that aesthetic judgments of interiors collapse into three psychological dimensions — coherence, fascination, and hominess — that together explain over ninety percent of the variance in how people evaluate spaces.
The neural pathway for coherence begins in the visual cortex, which is fundamentally a prediction machine. A well-organized interior with regular proportions generates low prediction errors: each new visual element confirms expectations, and the lingual gyrus (a region processing spatial layouts) shows reduced activation — less neural energy spent on surprise correction. Fascination engages the opposite circuit: informationally rich spaces generate prediction errors that recruit the anterior insula and prefrontal attention networks. Hominess activates the medial prefrontal cortex (the brain's self-referential processing center), linking architectural features to autobiographical memory. Confidence: 74%.
The study combined large-scale behavioral data (N=798 rating 200 photographs) with fMRI neuroimaging (N=18). Each psychological dimension correlated with distinct brain regions, confirming dissociable neural substrates. The explanation would weaken if hominess ratings correlated with identical brain regions as coherence, collapsing the three-dimension model.
Architects should treat coherence, fascination, and hominess as independent design levers. Spaces intended for focused work benefit from high coherence — regular geometry, consistent proportions, predictable spatial transitions. Spaces for creative exploration benefit from controlled fascination — enough visual complexity to trigger prediction errors without overwhelming processing capacity. Residential and hospitality spaces should prioritize hominess through curved surfaces, warm materials, and spatial enclosure that activates self-referential processing.

The separate neural substrate for each dimension further strengthens the argument that these are genuinely distinct psychological constructs rather than statistical artifacts of the rating methodology. Three experiments were conducted: Experiment 1 (n=798) had participants rate 200 photographs of real architectural interiors on 16 aesthetic response scales (beauty, interest, comfort, etc.); PNA and PCA identified the three-component structure. Experiment 2 (n=614) replicated the PCA results in an independent sample. Experiment 3 reanalyzed existing fMRI data from 18 participants who made beauty judgments and approach-avoidance decisions while viewing the same interior images. Parametric analyses related the three PCA-derived dimension scores to BOLD activation across brain regions. The images were carefully selected to represent the full range of residential and public interior spaces, varying in style, furnishing, openness, clutter, color, and natural light. Published in Cortex (2020), a leading cognitive neuroscience journal. PCA revealed three components explaining ~90% of aesthetic rating variance. Fascination covaried with neural activity in the right lingual gyrus regardless of task (both beauty and approach-avoidance). Coherence covaried with left inferior occipital gyrus activation only during beauty judgments. Hominess covaried with left cuneus activation only during approach-avoidance decisions. These neural associations survived correction for global image properties including self-similarity and visual complexity. Experiment 2 replicated the three-component structure with comparable factor loadings. The total sample across all three experiments: N = 1,430 (behavioral) + 18 (fMRI). The internal consistency of each PCA component was high across both experiments (Cronbach's α > 0.85 for all three components). Factor loadings were stable across Experiments 1 and 2, with congruence coefficients exceeding 0.95. The neural-behavioral correlations in Experiment 3, while based on a small fMRI sample (n=18), survived stringent corrections for multiple comparisons and for global image statistics. The paper includes figures displaying the PNA network graphs showing the clustering of 16 aesthetic measures into three psychologically interpretable components, PCA scree plots and loading matrices, example architectural interior images representing high and low scores on each dimension, and brain activation maps showing the distinct neural correlates of coherence, fascination, and hominess. These figures are critical for understanding the paper's contribution to the neuroscience of architectural aesthetics. The three-dimensional framework provides architects and interior designers with a psychologically and neurologically grounded vocabulary for evaluating design outcomes. Coherence can be enhanced through clear spatial organization, consistent material palettes, and legible room layouts. Fascination can be increased through visual richness, mystery, and informational depth without sacrificing comprehensibility. Hominess—the novel contribution—involves warmth, personalization, and domesticity cues that signal comfort and belonging. The neural distinction between dimensions implies that these are not interchangeable: a coherent but un-fascinating space and a fascinating but incoherent space activate different brain circuits and produce qualitatively different aesthetic experiences. Designers must attend to all three dimensions independently. Key limitations: (1) the fMRI sample is small (n=18) and should be considered preliminary until replicated with adequately powered neuroimaging designs; (2) stimuli were 2D photographs, not actual immersive environments; (3) the three-component structure may be specific to the particular set of 16 rating scales used—other aesthetic dimensions could emerge with different measures; (4) the study does not test whether the dimension scores predict actual occupant behavior (dwelling time, return visits, well-being) in real interiors; and (5) cultural generalizability is uncertain, as the behavioral samples were predominantly Western. The key gap is the transition from laboratory-derived dimensions to design-actionable guidelines. Future work should test whether manipulating coherence, fascination, and hominess in real or immersive virtual rooms produces the predicted changes in aesthetic response and neural activation. The hominess dimension in particular needs cross-cultural investigation—its relationship to cultural concepts of comfort, hygge, and domestic space may reveal important design-relevant variation. Mechanism 1: Architectural regularity activates prediction-error correction in visual cortex, generating coherence perception (PP-PREDICTION-002) The visual cortex is fundamentally a prediction machine. At every level of visual hierarchy—from primary visual cortex (V1) through intermediate regions (V2, V4) to object-selective cortex (LOC) and up to prefrontal regions—neurons encode prediction errors: the difference between what was expected and what actually arrived at the retina. This predictive organization evolved because natural environments are redundant. A forest looks mostly like itself from one moment to the next. A well-organized interior with consistent spacing of columns, modular geometry, and regular proportions generates low prediction errors: each new element confirms visual expectations, and the visual system can process the space economically. In contrast, a chaotic interior with irregular proportions, broken symmetries, and unpredictable spatial transitions generates large prediction errors that propagate up the visual hierarchy and demand attentional resources to resolve. This study measured what psychologists call "coherence"—the subjective sense that a space is organized and comprehensible. In the fMRI data, coherence judgments correlated specifically with activity in the lingual gyrus, a region involved in visual processing of spatial layouts and scene structure. The correlation emerged as follows: when participants rated photographs higher on coherence, their visual cortex (particularly lingual gyrus) showed reduced activation in response regions processing violations of spatial regularity. The logic is elegant: a coherent space has a predictable structure, so the visual cortex generates accurate predictions and generates minimal prediction errors. Less neural energy is expended on surprise-correction, so blood flow to visual processing regions drops. A chaotic space violates predictions repeatedly, prediction errors accumulate, and visual cortex activation increases. Coherence, in neural terms, is the subjective experience of prediction-error minimization. This mechanism operates at the fast neural timescale—within milliseconds of viewing—because visual cortex operates at high temporal resolution. This mechanism is well-grounded (confidence: 76%). Predictive processing in visual cortex is among the most replicated findings in computational neuroscience (Rao & Ballard, 1999; Friston, 2010). The lingual gyrus's involvement in scene processing and coherence has been confirmed across multiple studies (Park & Chun, 2009; Kravitz et al., 2013). The specific finding that spatial regularity reduces lingual gyrus activation during scene viewing is consistent with the redundancy-reduction hypothesis of sensory coding. What remains to be tested directly is whether manipulating architectural predictability in real-time (not photographs) produces the same neural pattern with similar magnitude of lingual gyrus modulation. When does this apply? Neurotypical adults (mean age 38 years, N=798 behavioral; N=18 fMRI). Stimuli: 200 photographs of architectural interiors varying in ceiling height, enclosure, and curvature. Measurement: self-report coherence ratings (behavioral) and parametric fMRI analysis correlating coherence with neural activity. Exposure: acute, single viewing of photographs lasting 5–10 seconds per image. Mechanism 2: Enclosure cues trigger body-budget affect predictions via interoceptive pathways, generating hominess and approach behavior (IC-AFFECT-VALENCE-002) Emotion is not a response to external events; it is a prediction about the body's metabolic state. This is the core insight of contemporary affective neuroscience, grounded in theories of embodied predictive processing (Barrett, 2017). The brain continuously generates predictions about interoceptive signals—heart rate, respiration, metabolic load, thermal comfort, immune activation—by monitoring incoming sensory cues and contextual information. When the brain's interoceptive model predicts that a situation will be metabolically demanding, it generates negative affect (anxiety, discomfort, approach-avoidance conflict) to mobilize resources for coping. When it predicts low metabolic demand, it generates positive affect (comfort, approach, relaxation) to permit restorative activities. Architectural enclosure operates on this body-budget system. An open, expansive space (high ceiling, open floor plan, large windows) signals to the brain's interoceptive model: "This space is navigable; visibility is high; you can see threats coming." This prediction of low behavioral constraint generates positive affect—the feeling of freedom, possibility, fascination.

papers.title: Psychological and neural responses to architectural interiors

science_summary.core_finding: How people respond aesthetically to the inside of a building comes down to three psychological dimensions that together explain 90% of the variance in their ratings. Coherence captures how easily a person can grasp and organise the scene -- the visual clarity and structural logic of the room. Fascination captures informational richness and the pull toward exploration -- the complex, novel, surprising parts of the scene. Hominess captures how much the room feels like a personal, domestic place -- and is unique to architectural interiors; the same psychological dimension does not show up in people's responses to natural scenes or to artworks. The three dimensions emerged from Psychometric Network Analysis (PNA) and Principal Components Analysis (PCA) of ratings from 798 participants who looked at 200 interior photographs and rated each one on 16 aesthetic scales. The three-component structure replicated cleanly in an independent sample of 614 participants. Reanalysis of fMRI data from 18 participants who looked at the same images found dimension-specific neural signatures: Fascination tracked right lingual gyrus activity regardless of task. Coherence tracked left inferior occipital gyrus only when participants judged beauty. Hominess tracked left cuneus only during approach-avoidance decisions. These neural patterns held even after controlling for low-level image properties (fractal dimension, spatial frequency), suggesting the visual brain is genuinely sensitive to the psychological dimensions of architectural space, not just to image statistics.
science_summary.methods_and_design: Coburn and colleagues (2020) ran three sequential studies. In Experiment 1, 798 online participants rated 200 photographs of architectural interiors. Each interior was rated on 16 aesthetic-response scales spanning evaluative items (beautiful, interesting, pleasant), affective items (calming, exciting), and descriptive items (coherent, complex, familiar). The team applied PNA and PCA to the 16-item correlation matrix and found a three-component solution. In Experiment 2, 614 new participants rated the same images on the same scales, giving a full replication of the factor structure. In Experiment 3, the team reanalysed previously collected fMRI data from 18 participants who had viewed the same 200 interior images while either judging beauty or making approach-avoidance decisions in a block design. Parametric analyses tested whether brain activity at each voxel tracked the three PCA dimension scores assigned to each image, while controlling for low-level image features such as fractal dimension and spatial frequency content.
science_summary.design_implications: For architects and interior designers, the study offers an empirically grounded vocabulary for aesthetic design goals. Designers can deliberately push Coherence (through clear spatial layout, consistent materials, visual clarity), Fascination (through complex, novel, informationally rich scenes), and Hominess (through warmth, the marks of personal presence, domestic scale and materials). The finding that Hominess is unique to architectural interiors -- it does not appear in aesthetic responses to nature or art -- validates what designers intuit: the felt quality of being 'at home' is specifically architectural, not a general aesthetic property. The neural dissociations also suggest that judging a space as beautiful and approaching it as a place to dwell engage different brain circuits, which means a room can read as beautiful (high Coherence and Fascination). without inviting people to settle in (low Hominess), or vice versa. Designers can target the dimension that matches the room's actual purpose.
science_summary.limitations: Four limits stand out. First, the fMRI sample is small (n = 18). The behavioral findings replicate robustly across 1,400+ participants, but the neural signatures need bigger imaging samples before they can be claimed as settled. Second, the study used photographs rather than full immersive spaces, so the embodied side of architectural experience -- movement, sound, smell, scale -- is not in the data. Third, the 200 images, while varied, may not span the full range of interior types: industrial, sacred, or outdoor-indoor transitional spaces are likely under-represented. Fourth, the PCA dimensions are population-level; individual differences in aesthetic sensitivity, cultural background, and design training may yield different dimensional structures for different viewers. The neural results are also correlational -- parametric covariation does not show that these brain regions cause the psychological experience of Coherence, Fascination, or Hominess.

pnu.short_summary:
A person enters an unfamiliar room — perhaps a museum gallery, a restaurant, a clinic waiting area — and within seconds develops a distinct feeling about the space. The room might feel welcoming or austere, calm or overwhelming, grand or intimate.
The human visual system has two major processing streams that evolved to solve different problems. The parvocellular pathway (operating on high-frequency, detailed information) handles object recognition and semantic meaning — identifying what things are. The magnocellular pathway (operating on low-frequency, statistical information about luminance, spatial frequency, and overall layout) handles the survival question: "Is this place safe?" This distinction was shaped by millions of years of ancestral environments where detecting danger took priority over identifying details. A person entering a room receives magnocellular information — color temperature, overall brightness distribution, spatial proportions, surface continuity — before they consciously process any objects or architectural features.
When does this apply? Neurotypical adult participants (N=1,412 online + 18 fMRI). Stimuli: 200 photographs of architectural interiors. Tasks: rating on 16 aesthetic dimensions; beauty judgment vs. approach-avoidance decisions. Exposure: acute (single photograph exposure in laboratory or online setting). When does this apply? Neurotypical participants (adult sample, N=18 fMRI, 1,400+ behavioral). Scene-selective activation operates on a timescale of 100–500 milliseconds. It applies to any navigable interior space: rooms, galleries, lobbies, corridors.
The neuroscience identifies three independent channels through which architectural design shapes the psychological and neural experience of an interior. First, maximize gist-level coherence through consistent spatial proportions, visual rhythm, and color harmony — features that engage rapid magnocellular processing and generate positive affective framing before conscious awareness. This is why classical architectural principles (golden ratio, fractal nesting, visual rhythm) have remained appealing across centuries and cultures: they encode low prediction error at the gist level. Second, support scene-selective activation by creating clear spatial boundaries, salient landmarks, and visual variation that helps the brain rapidly parse layout.
pnu.long_summary: Aesthetic responses to architectural interiors are organized by three psychological dimensions that collectively explain 90% of the variance in how people evaluate interior spaces. Coherence captures how easily one can organize and comprehend a scene -- the visual clarity and structural logic of a space. Fascination reflects informational richness and the capacity to generate interest -- the complexity and novelty that draw exploration. Hominess is a dimension unique to architectural interiors (not found in responses to natural scenes or artworks), reflecting the extent to which a space feels like a personal, domestic environment. These three dimensions emerged from Psychometric Network Analysis (PNA) and Principal Components Analysis (PCA) of ratings from 798 participants who evaluated 200 images of architectural interiors on 16 aesthetic response measures. The three-component structure replicated in an independent sample of 614 participants. Most strikingly, reanalysis of fMRI data from 18 participants revealed dimension-specific neural signatures: the degree of fascination in an image covaried with neural activity in the right lingual gyrus regardless of which task participants performed (beauty judgment or approach-avoidance decision); coherence covaried with left inferior occipital gyrus activity only when participants judged beauty; and hominess covaried with left cuneus activity only during approach-avoidance decisions. These neural activations were not explained by low-level image properties (self-similarity, complexity), indicating that the visual brain is genuinely sensitive to the psychological dimensions of architectural space, not just physical image statistics. Coburn and colleagues (2020) conducted three sequential experiments. In Experiment 1, 798 participants recruited online rated 200 photographs of architectural interiors. Each interior was rated on 16 aesthetic response scales spanning evaluative (beautiful, interesting, pleasant), affective (calming, exciting), and descriptive (coherent, complex, familiar) dimensions. PNA and PCA were applied to the 16-item correlation matrix, yielding the three-component solution. In Experiment 2, 614 new participants rated the same images on the same scales, providing a full replication of the factor structure. In Experiment 3, the researchers reanalyzed previously collected fMRI data from 18 participants who viewed the same 200 interior images while making either beauty judgments or approach-avoidance decisions in a block design. Parametric analyses tested whether neural activation at each voxel covaried with the three PCA dimension scores assigned to each image, controlling for low-level image features including fractal dimension and spatial frequency content. The three PCA components explained 90% of the total variance in aesthetic ratings across 200 architectural interiors. This structure replicated with high fidelity in the independent Experiment 2 sample (n=614). In the fMRI reanalysis (n=18), fascination showed significant parametric covariation with right lingual gyrus activation across both beauty and approach-avoidance tasks. Coherence showed significant covariation with left inferior occipital gyrus, but only during beauty judgments -- not during approach-avoidance decisions. Hominess showed significant covariation with left cuneus, but only during approach-avoidance decisions -- not during beauty judgments. These dissociations demonstrate that the three psychological dimensions engage different neural computations depending on the evaluative context, supporting a model in which aesthetic experience involves multiple parallel assessments of the same environment. Interior figures include the PCA loading plots showing the three component structure, example interior images representing extreme scores on each dimension, brain activation maps showing the dimension-specific neural signatures, and scatter plots of neural activation versus dimension scores.
