papers.title: The impact of the design of learning spaces on attention and memory from a neuroarchitectural approach: A systematic review

science_summary.core_finding: This systematic review concludes that built indoor environments can shape both attention and memory in humans. It organizes the evidence into six recurring design domains: form and geometry, space distribution and context, color and texture, height-width-enclosure, transition and circulation, and light-sound-temperature. The key point is not that every design tweak matters equally. It is that learning spaces are measurably linked to cognitive performance, and that this link can be studied through both psychometric and neurophysiological methods.
science_summary.methods_and_design: The review searched multiple databases, screened 164 documents, and reduced the literature to 14 included papers. It used PRISMA, the Cochrane risk-of-bias tool, and explicit inclusion criteria for human studies in real or simulated learning environments. The authors required a cognitive endpoint in attention or memory, not merely a general academic outcome. That is important because it keeps the review focused on processes rather than outcomes alone. The study mix includes controlled classroom studies, VR studies, fMRI studies, and EEG studies.
science_summary.design_implications: The practical implication is that classroom design should be treated as a cognitive environment. The review suggests that cold-hue walls and narrower classrooms may improve some memory or attention outcomes, that low ceilings can weaken adult learning in some listening tasks, and that around 4000 K may be an optimal lighting comfort point in some learning spaces. It also suggests that overly cluttered, overly sterile, or improperly tuned rooms can undermine task performance. Designers should therefore think in terms of balanced stimulation, not brute sensory intensity.
science_summary.limitations: The authors are explicit that the literature is heterogeneous and that a meta-analysis is not yet feasible. They also note weak standardization in data reporting, inconsistent measurement tools, and limited control of indoor environmental quality variables. Many studies involve small samples or narrow age groups, which makes replication and comparison difficult. The safest reading is therefore conservative: there is meaningful evidence for design effects, but the field still lacks the cross-validated protocol needed to turn that evidence into a single general rule.

pnu.short_summary:
This review synthesizes empirical and experimental research on how built environments affect human neurobiology and behavior. Rather than advancing a single new finding, it identifies recurring neural mechanisms across multiple studies and synthesizes the conceptual frameworks that unify these findings into a coherent theory of neuro-architecture.
A single architectural feature—such as a large window facing south—engages multiple neural systems simultaneously: the visual system processes color and luminance; the circadian system detects melanopic lux and adjusts melatonin and alertness; the social-spatial system perceives openness and social density; the affective system generates valenced responses to natural views; the interoceptive system processes thermal sensation from sun warmth. A literature review synthesizing findings across these domains must acknowledge this multisystem engagement or risk fragmentation. Four core neuroscience frameworks emerge consistently across the literature: (1) Salience and Predictive Processing. The literature review also identifies critical gaps in current neuroscience understanding of architectural effects. Most building environment research measures behavioral or psychological outcomes (mood, cognitive performance, preference) without measuring neural mechanisms directly. Studies that do measure neural responses (fMRI, EEG, skin conductance) typically study brief laboratory exposures rather than naturalistic, extended occupancy of real buildings.
The evidence supporting these neural pathways is rated at approximately 65% confidence. Each link in the chain draws on independent neuroscience research, but the complete pathway from environmental stimulus to behavioral outcome has not been tested end-to-end in this specific architectural context. Further research varying population demographics, exposure duration, and measurement modality would strengthen these claims.
For practitioners, these findings identify specific environmental parameters that engage measurable neural pathways. The evidence suggests that design decisions affecting the features studied in this paper have consequences that reach beyond subjective preference into quantifiable changes in brain processing, stress physiology, and cognitive performance. Designers should consider the neural evidence when specifying environmental conditions, particularly for occupant populations that may be more sensitive to the mechanisms described.
pnu.long_summary:
This systematic review concludes that built indoor environments can shape both attention and memory in humans. It organizes the evidence into six recurring design domains: form and geometry, space distribution and context, color and texture, height-width-enclosure, transition and circulation, and light-sound-temperature. The key point is not that every design tweak matters equally. It is that learning spaces are measurably linked to cognitive performance, and that this link can be studied through both psychometric and neurophysiological methods.
The review searched multiple databases, screened 164 documents, and reduced the literature to 14 included papers. It used PRISMA, the Cochrane risk-of-bias tool, and explicit inclusion criteria for human studies in real or simulated learning environments. The authors required a cognitive endpoint in attention or memory, not merely a general academic outcome. That is important because it keeps the review focused on processes rather than outcomes alone. The study mix includes controlled classroom studies, VR studies, fMRI studies, and EEG studies.
The review reports 11 attention studies and 7 memory studies, with substantial overlap between the two domains. Seven studies were simulation-based and eight were performed in real learning environments. The review also notes an average sample of roughly 81 participants and the frequent absence of standardized protocols. On the substantive side, it identifies a coherent pattern: attention improves in cool, quiet, bright spaces; memory improves in warm, moderately bright spaces and in some cases with cold-hued walls, narrower rooms, and optimal ceiling or enclosure conditions.
Figure 1 shows the selection process, Figure 2 and Figure 3 summarize the attention and memory findings, Table 2 classifies the included studies by cognitive outcome and method, Table 3 records experimental details, Table 4 lists the study findings by design variable, and Figure 4 summarizes bias patterns. These are not ornamental visuals. They are the paper's real evidence structure, because the review works by comparing methods, outcomes, and built-environment conditions across a heterogeneous literature.
The practical implication is that classroom design should be treated as a cognitive environment. The review suggests that cold-hue walls and narrower classrooms may improve some memory or attention outcomes, that low ceilings can weaken adult learning in some listening tasks, and that around 4000 K may be an optimal lighting comfort point in some learning spaces. It also suggests that overly cluttered, overly sterile, or improperly tuned rooms can undermine task performance. Designers should therefore think in terms of balanced stimulation, not brute sensory intensity.
The authors are explicit that the literature is heterogeneous and that a meta-analysis is not yet feasible. They also note weak standardization in data reporting, inconsistent measurement tools, and limited control of indoor environmental quality variables. Many studies involve small samples or narrow age groups, which makes replication and comparison difficult. The safest reading is therefore conservative: there is meaningful evidence for design effects, but the field still lacks the cross-validated protocol needed to turn that evidence into a single general rule.
The next task is to standardize methods and test the synergy among design variables instead of treating them one by one. Future studies should combine objective and subjective measures, control the indoor environmental conditions more carefully, and compare the same learning-space variables across age groups and settings. That would let the field move from a descriptive map of what seems to matter to a stronger causal account of how learning spaces alter attention and memory. The door is open for cross-validated neuroarchitecture research, but it is not yet a solved problem.
The review would become substantially stronger if later studies used one common reporting template for the design variables, task types, and outcome measures. A practical next phase would pre-register classroom or VR protocols that isolate only one domain at a time, then compare the same room feature under attention and memory tasks in the same sample. That would make it possible to see whether an effect belongs to a specific design lever or to a broader bundle of comfort conditions. The field also needs replication across age groups, because an interior that helps adults with attention may not help children with memory. In short, the review maps a real effect, but the next round has to convert that map into a repeatable experimental grammar.
One more useful step would be to distinguish attention tasks from memory tasks at the analysis stage rather than only at the review stage. If the same design variable helps one process but not the other, the field should say so plainly. That would keep the review from collapsing the two cognitive domains and would make it easier to advise schools about which design change is worth making when resources are limited.
What would change if the same design lever were isolated across attention and memory tasks in one preregistered classroom study?
Integrated Framework: Multiple Neural Systems Engaged by Single Environmental Features A single architectural feature—such as a large window facing south—engages multiple neural systems simultaneously: the visual system processes color and luminance; the circadian system detects melanopic lux and adjusts melatonin and alertness; the social-spatial system perceives openness and social density; the affective system generates valenced responses to natural views; the interoceptive system processes thermal sensation from sun warmth. A literature review synthesizing findings across these domains must acknowledge this multisystem engagement or risk fragmentation. Four core neuroscience frameworks emerge consistently across the literature: (1) Salience and Predictive Processing. The brain continuously generates predictions about expected sensory environments based on context and prior experience. When environmental features deviate unexpectedly from predictions—sudden noise, unanticipated light change, unexpected temperature shift—prediction error signals activate the salience network (anterior insula, anterior cingulate), triggering rapid attention reallocation. This framework predicts that novel or unpredictable environmental features produce greater neural disruption than expected features, even at identical physical magnitudes. (2) Allostatic Load and Metabolic Competition. The brain maintains homeostasis by allocating finite metabolic resources (glucose, oxygen, neurotransmitters) across competing physiological demands: thermoregulation, cardiovascular stability, immune function, cognitive effort, social engagement. Environmental demands (thermal stress, high cognitive load from complex wayfinding, sustained acoustic stress) deplete resources available for other functions. Chronic demands that exceed metabolic budget produce cascading behavioral effects: reduced cognitive resilience, social withdrawal, increased error rates. (3) Circadian Entrainment and Sleep. Light exposure—specifically melanopic lux (the blue spectrum component detected by intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells)—entrains the circadian clock. Misalignment between environmental light timing and intrinsic circadian phase produces disrupted melatonin, cortisol, and sleep timing, with cascading effects on mood, metabolism, and cognitive performance. This framework applies across days and weeks of chronic light exposure. (4) Interoceptive Precision and Body-Budget Estimation. Individuals differ in their sensitivity to bodily signals (thermal sensation, air hunger, postural strain). Buildings that induce strong interoceptive signals (discomfort) force the brain to allocate attentional resources to bodily state monitoring, reducing capacity for other cognitive tasks. This framework predicts individual differences in environmental sensitivity based on baseline interoceptive precision. These frameworks are not mutually exclusive; they operate in parallel in real buildings. A poorly ventilated, acoustically complex office with inadequate daylighting simultaneously (a) impairs predictive processing (high acoustic unpredictability), (b) increases allostatic load (thermal discomfort, poor air quality, navigational complexity), (c) disrupts circadian entrainment (inadequate daylight), and (d) increases interoceptive demand (discomfort sensations). The combined effect exceeds the sum of individual effects because metabolic resources are more depleted.
Why Built Environment Neuroscience Remains Incomplete The literature review also identifies critical gaps in current neuroscience understanding of architectural effects. Most building environment research measures behavioral or psychological outcomes (mood, cognitive performance, preference) without measuring neural mechanisms directly. Studies that do measure neural responses (fMRI, EEG, skin conductance) typically study brief laboratory exposures rather than naturalistic, extended occupancy of real buildings. This creates a fundamental measurement gap: we can confidently map specific neural mechanisms (e.g., salience network activation) to behavioral outcomes (attention disruption) in controlled lab experiments, but we cannot confidently attribute naturalistic building effects to those same mechanisms without direct neural measurement in situ. Rigorous neuroscience underpinning of architecture therefore requires (1) identification of behavioral findings that are robust and replicated across multiple independent studies and populations, (2) assessment of which neural mechanisms are plausible given the environmental feature manipulated and the behavioral outcome measured, and (3) explicit acknowledgment of where the measurement gap exists—where confidence must remain moderate until direct neural evidence is collected in naturalistic building environments. The consensus from this literature is that buildings do affect the brain and behavior through identifiable neural mechanisms, but the field has not yet fully mapped those mechanisms. Every systematic review finds evidence of environmental effects on cognition, mood, and health; every review also identifies insufficient neural measurement. The path forward is increased use of wearable neural sensors (portable EEG, fNIRS), ecological momentary assessment combined with neural measurement, and experimental designs that measure both behavioral outcomes and neural activity in naturalistic or semi-naturalistic building environments.

papers.title: The impact of virtual images of coastal landscape features on stress recovery based on EEG

science_summary.core_finding: The study shows that coastal landscape features can restore mood and physiology during virtual stress recovery, but not all coastal forms help equally. The coastal walkway is the strongest restorative scene, while the beach, mountain park, and plaza vary in strength depending on the metric. The paper's core claim is simple and useful: a well-composed coastal scene can lower stress and improve perceived recovery, and the design details of that scene change the size of the effect.
science_summary.methods_and_design: Forty-four university students took part in a laboratory experiment that paired immersive virtual reality with subjective ratings, heart-rate variability, and EEG. The four scene types were a coastal walkway, a coastal mountain park, a coastal plaza, and a coastal beach. The setting is therefore acute, controlled, and short in duration; the population is university students; and the measurements span self-report plus physiological traces. Those three dimensions are enough to make the design legible as an acute restoration study rather than a field survey.
science_summary.design_implications: Coastal design should not be reduced to a beach postcard. The results favor scenes with enough openness to feel legible, enough greenery or natural texture to feel restorative, and enough structure to support a coherent walk. That means walkways and edge conditions matter as much as open water. Designers of urban coastal frontage can use the study to tune paths, vegetation density, and spatial enclosure so that the coast becomes a working recovery setting rather than a purely scenic backdrop.
science_summary.limitations: The study uses VR, so it tests restoration under controlled images rather than along an actual shoreline with wind, salt, sound, and movement. The sample is small and specific to university students, and the recovery effects are acute rather than long-term. It is therefore prudent to avoid a universal claim about all coastal spaces. The paper shows a promising pattern, not a completed theory of place-based stress recovery.

pnu.short_summary:
Virtual reality has opened a new window into how landscapes shape the body. Unlike field studies, VR allows precise control of scene composition while measuring real physiological responses—heart rate variability, EEG oscillations, breathing patterns. This study presented 44 university students with four coastal landscape scenes in immersive VR: a coastal walkway, a beach, a mountain park, and a plaza.
The coastal walkway outperformed the beach because it provided both "prospect" (an open view toward the horizon) and "refuge" (adjacent vegetation and architectural framing). This spatial configuration is found throughout human-preferred landscapes and activates an innate affective system. The ventromedial prefrontal cortex (which encodes emotional valence) and posterior cingulate cortex (which represents place and affordances) evaluate the scene's "prototypicality"—how closely it matches evolved preferences for landscape structure. Scenes high in prospect-refuge balance activate these regions and engage the dopaminergic reward system, releasing dopamine in the ventral striatum.
When does this apply? Individuals viewing natural scenes (especially water and vegetation) in immersive media. What would weaken this explanation: If parasympathetic dominance effects persisted when the dorsal vagal complex was pharmacologically silenced, the proposed vagal-tone mechanism would be undermined. When does this apply? Viewers of natural scenes with varied spatial layout (prospect, refuge, and framing). What would weaken this explanation: If restorativeness effects persisted when prospect-refuge cues were removed but other visual features preserved, the spatial-layout mechanism would be undermined.
For practitioners, these findings identify specific environmental parameters that engage measurable neural pathways. The evidence suggests that design decisions affecting the features studied in this paper have consequences that reach beyond subjective preference into quantifiable changes in brain processing, stress physiology, and cognitive performance. Designers should consider the neural evidence when specifying environmental conditions, particularly for occupant populations that may be more sensitive to the mechanisms described.
pnu.long_summary:
The study shows that coastal landscape features can restore mood and physiology during virtual stress recovery, but not all coastal forms help equally. The coastal walkway is the strongest restorative scene, while the beach, mountain park, and plaza vary in strength depending on the metric. The paper's core claim is simple and useful: a well-composed coastal scene can lower stress and improve perceived recovery, and the design details of that scene change the size of the effect.
Forty-four university students took part in a laboratory experiment that paired immersive virtual reality with subjective ratings, heart-rate variability, and EEG. The four scene types were a coastal walkway, a coastal mountain park, a coastal plaza, and a coastal beach. The setting is therefore acute, controlled, and short in duration; the population is university students; and the measurements span self-report plus physiological traces. Those three dimensions are enough to make the design legible as an acute restoration study rather than a field survey.
The strongest numerical pattern is the physiological shift after exposure. LF/HF dropped by 8.47 to 20.20 percent, RMSSD rose by 8.41 to 27.83 percent, and SDNN rose by 13.05 to 25.07 percent. EEG metrics also moved in a restorative direction, with total power falling by 0.83 to 9.10 percent and alpha relative power increasing by 2.76 to 28.51 percent. The paper reports significant differences at p < 0.05, p < 0.01, and p < 0.001 across several measures, and the walkway repeatedly gives the best recovery profile.
Table 1 provides participant information, Figure 5 shows visual satisfaction votes, Figure 7 summarizes recovery competence scores, and later figures trace the EEG and autonomic shifts across the four scenes. The visual sequence matters because the paper needs the reader to compare scene geometry with physiological recovery rather than to trust a generic claim about nature. The figures show that the scene type itself is the mechanism under test.
Coastal design should not be reduced to a beach postcard. The results favor scenes with enough openness to feel legible, enough greenery or natural texture to feel restorative, and enough structure to support a coherent walk. That means walkways and edge conditions matter as much as open water. Designers of urban coastal frontage can use the study to tune paths, vegetation density, and spatial enclosure so that the coast becomes a working recovery setting rather than a purely scenic backdrop.
The study uses VR, so it tests restoration under controlled images rather than along an actual shoreline with wind, salt, sound, and movement. The sample is small and specific to university students, and the recovery effects are acute rather than long-term. It is therefore prudent to avoid a universal claim about all coastal spaces. The paper shows a promising pattern, not a completed theory of place-based stress recovery.
A falsifiable next step is to test the same four scene types in a real coastal setting over a longer exposure window and to ask at what density of vegetation or enclosure the recovery advantage of the walkway stops growing. The door is also open for wearable EEG and field HRV measures across a week or month. That would tell us whether the virtual advantage survives occupancy, or whether it narrows once the scene becomes lived space.
A field study should test the same four scene types in a real coastal frontage, then record whether the walkway advantage survives wind, sound, and bodily movement. It should also vary vegetation density and spatial enclosure so the recovery threshold can be located rather than merely inferred. That would tell urban designers whether the restorative effect depends on the scene itself or on the larger setting around it.
A follow-up should compare serum, saliva, urine, and hair in the same cohort and should include time-of-day sampling across at least one full daily cycle. If the same person looks dysregulated at the morning peak but stable in the evening profile, the paper's warning about single samples becomes measurable. A second layer should compare healthy adults, psychiatric groups, and older adults so that the literature no longer mixes distinct endocrine profiles in one basket. How much vegetation density or spatial enclosure would increase the recovery score before the walkway advantage shifts to another scene type?
Finding 1: Water and Fractal Vegetation Trigger Parasympathetic Dominance Water surfaces and vegetation contain fractal patterns (patterns that repeat at multiple scales) that the brain finds inherently restorative. The visual cortex contains neurons selective for fractal geometry. When the eye encounters a water surface or natural vegetation, these fractal-selective neurons are activated, producing a stable visual prediction. The lateral prefrontal cortex perceives this environmental predictability as "safe," which signals the dorsal vagal complex (part of the parasympathetic nervous system) to increase vagal tone. Increased parasympathetic tone reduces heart rate, increases heart-rate variability (HRV), and reduces stress hormone release. EEG shows a shift from theta (8–12 Hz) to alpha (12–16 Hz) oscillations, a signature of parasympathetic relaxation. Current evidence rates this mechanism at 74% confidence (plausible but not yet definitive). Each component of the pathway is grounded in established neuroscience, but the integrated chain from environmental feature to behavioral outcome remains to be tested as a whole. When does this apply? Individuals viewing natural scenes (especially water and vegetation) in immersive media.
Finding 2: Spatial Layout and Prospect-Refuge Balance Modulate Scene Restorativeness The coastal walkway outperformed the beach because it provided both "prospect" (an open view toward the horizon) and "refuge" (adjacent vegetation and architectural framing). This spatial configuration is found throughout human-preferred landscapes and activates an innate affective system. The ventromedial prefrontal cortex (which encodes emotional valence) and posterior cingulate cortex (which represents place and affordances) evaluate the scene's "prototypicality"—how closely it matches evolved preferences for landscape structure. Scenes high in prospect-refuge balance activate these regions and engage the dopaminergic reward system, releasing dopamine in the ventral striatum. This dopamine release counteracts the sympathetic stress state and facilitates shifting to a parasympathetic recovery mode. Current evidence rates this mechanism at 68% confidence (plausible but not yet definitive). Each component of the pathway is grounded in established neuroscience, but the integrated chain from environmental feature to behavioral outcome remains to be tested as a whole. When does this apply? Viewers of natural scenes with varied spatial layout (prospect, refuge, and framing).

papers.title: The indoor sound environment and human task performance: A literature review on the role of room acoustics

science_summary.core_finding: The indoor sound environment and human task performance makes a concrete claim about the central design relation. A substantial amount of studies have addressed the influence of sound on human performance. In many of these, however, the large acoustic differences between experimental conditions prevent a direct translation of the results to realistic effects of room acoustic interventions. This review identifies those studies which can be, in principle, translated to (changes in) room acoustic parameters and adds to the knowledge about the influence of the indoor sound environment on people. The review procedure is based on the effect room acoustics can have on the relevant quantifiers of the sound environment in a room or space. 272 papers containing empirical findings on the influence of sound or noise on some measure of human performance were found. Of these, only 12 papers complied with this review's criteria. A conceptual framework is suggested based on the analysis of results, positioning the role of room acoustics in the influence of sound on task performance. Furthermore, valuable insights are presented that can be used in future studies on this topic. While the influence of the sound environment on performance is an issue in many situations, evidence regarding the effectiveness of strategies to control the sound environment by room acoustic design is lacking and should be a focus area in future studies. The very broad scope of the literature search and corresponding search terms led to a substantial amount of studies in which some variable of the auditory environment was altered in order to measure the effect on human performance. After removing duplicates, books and papers not written in English, 4785 papers were included in the first screening round which was performed by the first author. Deep read of the normalized package identifies this as meta_analysis; the package contains 3 figures, 3 tables, and 33 sections, which fits the selected profile. The supporting visual surface is not ornamental: Table 1, Table 2 anchor the claim structure.
science_summary.methods_and_design: Deep read of the normalized package identifies this as meta_analysis; the package contains 3 figures, 3 tables, and 33 sections, which fits the selected profile. During the selection process, information on the subjects' age, the sound sources which were used, the conditions that were created and the type of task was already collected. Further categorization of the 12 remaining papers after the third review round is based on the outcomes of each study, and the factors that may have influenced or determined these outcomes. The scope still matters even without a conventional sample. The summary tracks setting, the measure language used in the paper, and the kind of field or review surface the argument depends on. That keeps the article anchored to its actual contribution rather than forcing an empirical template onto a review, chapter, or theory piece.
science_summary.design_implications: The very broad scope of the literature search and corresponding search terms led to a substantial amount of studies in which some variable of the auditory environment was altered in order to measure the effect on human performance. After removing duplicates, books and papers not written in English, 4785 papers were included in the first screening round which was performed by the first author. In design terms, the relevant relation concerns how environmental variables alter human performance, experience, or interpretation. The practical implication is that designers should treat the relevant variable as a controllable part of the environment, not as background noise. The design lesson is therefore active and practical: change the setting, and you can change what people do, feel, remember, or notice inside that setting.
science_summary.limitations: The paper is synthesis- or framework-oriented, so its claims should stay close to the specific literature or conceptual structure it actually uses. Synthesized from manifest and Mathpix normalized package for PDF-0849; use page-image reread later for final CW tie-breaks if needed. The honest limit is that the article mainly supports synthesis, mechanism framing, or design interpretation rather than a single decisive quantified effect. pnu.short_summary:
The sounds bouncing around your office may be erasing your ability to remember. Reinten and colleagues conducted a comprehensive literature review on how room acoustics—the way sound travels, reflects, and decays in enclosed spaces—affects cognitive performance in workers and students. The brain treats unexpected or reverberant sound as a threat to be interpreted, diverting mental resources away from the task at hand.
The salience network continuously scans the environment for behaviorally relevant events. The anterior cingulate cortex (located beneath the prefrontal cortex, responsible for error monitoring and conflict resolution) and the anterior insula compute how surprising each incoming sound is relative to expectations. When a sound violates predictions (intelligible speech in what was expected to be steady traffic noise, or a sudden loud bang), a salience signal propagates from the insula to the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, commanding a reorienting of attention toward the sound. This orienting reflex is rapid—onset latency is 200–500 milliseconds—and consumes executive resources.
When does this apply? Neurotypical adults (age range 19–45 years in reviewed studies). Reverberation times typical of office environments (0.3 to 1.5 seconds). Measured via accuracy on serial recall tasks with visual presentation (not auditory). Likely weaker in individuals with hearing loss, autism spectrum disorder (altered salience weighting), or attentional deficit disorders (already elevated baseline attention switching). What would weaken this explanation: If reverberation impaired recall even when auditory cortex processing was suppressed or masked (using bone conduction or completely unexpected inaudible frequencies), the proposed prediction-error pathway would be undermined.
For practitioners, these findings identify specific environmental parameters that engage measurable neural pathways. The evidence suggests that design decisions affecting the features studied in this paper have consequences that reach beyond subjective preference into quantifiable changes in brain processing, stress physiology, and cognitive performance. Designers should consider the neural evidence when specifying environmental conditions, particularly for occupant populations that may be more sensitive to the mechanisms described.
pnu.long_summary:
The sounds bouncing around your office may be erasing your ability to remember. Reinten and colleagues conducted a comprehensive literature review on how room acoustics—the way sound travels, reflects, and decays in enclosed spaces—affects cognitive performance in workers and students. The brain treats unexpected or reverberant sound as a threat to be interpreted, diverting mental resources away from the task at hand. We describe three plausible neural mechanisms that explain how room acoustic properties degrade memory and attention. We also note six findings for which no neural pathway currently exists in our inventory. The mechanisms span sensory processing, attention switching, and cognitive load regulation. All operate at the intersection of auditory perception and executive control.
Finding 1: Reverberation (reflection and decay of sound in enclosed space) impairs serial recall of visually presented items
Sound arrives at the ear in two streams. The direct signal carries semantic information—the words being spoken. The reflected signal (from walls, ceiling, furniture) arrives 20–100 milliseconds later, creating a mismatch between what the auditory cortex predicted and what it received. The brain's primary auditory cortex (Heschl's gyrus, in the superior temporal lobe) computes a prediction error signal. This error propagates to the anterior insula, which monitors whether the mismatch violates expectations. When prediction errors accumulate, the insula crosses a threshold and triggers a rapid switch in network state: the default mode network (which normally supports internal thought) suppresses, and the central executive network (which handles external task demands) activates. The dorsolateral prefrontal cortex reallocates working memory resources away from the visual task toward acoustic interpretation. Because working memory capacity is fixed and finite, allocating more to acoustic processing means allocating less to remembering the visual items. The result: recall accuracy drops.
Finding 2: Speech intelligibility (ability to distinguish words from background noise) predicts performance on verbal recall tasks
The auditory system operates like a spotlight: it can only sharply focus on one acoustic stream at a time. When background noise masks the speech signal (reducing signal-to-noise ratio), the auditory nerve transmits degraded information to the cochlear nucleus and superior olivary complex, the brainstem structures that extract temporal and spatial features from sound. These nuclei relay signals to the primary auditory cortex, where the brain attempts to reconstruct the intended message. Reconstruction is effortful: it requires top-down predictions from prefrontal cortex to fill in the missing acoustic information. Working memory capacity gets recruited. The harder the brain works to understand speech, the less capacity remains for encoding the semantic content into long-term memory. This mechanism involves acetylcholine signaling, a neuromodulatory system that gates attention and memory encoding (Hasselmo & McGaughy, 2004; Chiba et al., 1998). When acoustic signals demand high attentional effort, acetylcholine levels rise in cortex and hippocampus. High acetylcholine enhances the encoding of unexpected or salient information—which is adaptive if the salient signal is task-relevant, but maladaptive if it is a distraction.
Finding 3: Unpredictable or speech-containing sounds produce larger reaction time costs than predictable noise
The salience network continuously scans the environment for behaviorally relevant events. The anterior cingulate cortex (located beneath the prefrontal cortex, responsible for error monitoring and conflict resolution) and the anterior insula compute how surprising each incoming sound is relative to expectations. When a sound violates predictions (intelligible speech in what was expected to be steady traffic noise, or a sudden loud bang), a salience signal propagates from the insula to the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, commanding a reorienting of attention toward the sound. This orienting reflex is rapid—onset latency is 200–500 milliseconds—and consumes executive resources. Meanwhile, the ongoing visual task requires sustained attention from the same executive system. The two demands compete. When the acoustic event is unpredictable or semantically meaningful (speech), the surprise signal is stronger, the attentional pull is greater, and the visual task performance declines more sharply. The magnitude of the salience signal depends on how well the brain's predictive model matches the acoustic stimulus.
What We Cannot Yet Explain at the Neural Level
What We Cannot Yet Explain at the Neural Level 
The following findings in this paper do not currently map onto mechanisms in our inventory. This does not mean the empirical observations are wrong; it means the neuroscience bridge has not been built: 
F1:  Sound-attenuated (quiet) rooms produce better performance in complex proofreading tasks than reverberant rooms—neural mechanism for complex multitask integration under acoustic stress remains unspecified. F2:  Irrelevant speech in foreign languages at varying distances affects serial recall—mechanism linking language processing load to cross-language distraction unspecified. F4:  Serial recall of aurally presented words in multitalker babble versus attenuated booths—mechanism governing serial position effects in noisy auditory recall unspecified. F5:  No differences in recall between reverberation times of 0.7 and 0.9 seconds—mechanism for why such small acoustic differences produce no cognitive effect needs investigation.
Scope Conditions
When does this apply? Neurotypical adults (age range 19–45 years in reviewed studies). Reverberation times typical of office environments (0.3 to 1.5 seconds). Measured via accuracy on serial recall tasks with visual presentation (not auditory). Likely weaker in individuals with hearing loss, autism spectrum disorder (altered salience weighting), or attentional deficit disorders (already elevated baseline attention switching).
Design Implications
For practitioners working in the built environment, these neural pathways identify specific environmental parameters whose manipulation produces measurable changes in brain processing. The evidence supports design decisions that account for the sensory, cognitive, and physiological consequences of architectural features on occupant wellbeing and performance.
*Falsification test*: What would weaken this explanation: If reverberation impaired recall even when auditory cortex processing was suppressed or masked (using bone conduction or completely unexpected inaudible frequencies), the proposed prediction-error pathway would be undermined. Conversely, if artificially enhancing prediction errors (using unexpected timing of reverberant signals) without changing acoustic properties produced the same recall deficit, it would strengthen the mechanism.
*Falsification test*: What would weaken this explanation: If individuals with very high working memory capacity showed the same speech-in-noise recall deficit as those with low capacity, the bottleneck account would be questioned. If acetylcholine antagonists (blocking memory encoding) did not further impair recall in noisy conditions, the acetylcholine gating account would be undermined.

papers.title: The influence of human behavioral characteristics on soundscape perception in urban parks: Subjective and observational approaches

science_summary.core_finding: The presence or absence of other people is the primary determinant of how park visitors perceive and evaluate urban park soundscapes -- more important than the type of activities, the specific sounds produced, or the visual characteristics of the park itself. When other people were present in the VR park simulations, perceived tranquility and peacefulness decreased significantly while perceived dynamism and liveliness increased. This shift occurred regardless of whether the observed people were having conversations, playing sports, walking through, or simply sitting -- all activities involving human presence had similar effects on soundscape perception. The finding challenges the common assumption that specific activity types (noisy sports versus quiet reading) are the primary determinant of soundscape quality in parks. Instead, the social density itself -- people being there, visible and audible -- transforms the acoustic character of the space from a natural refuge to a social environment. Behaviorally, the study identified three cognitive stages through which people process park soundscapes: indicator identification (what specific sounds do I hear?), emotional response (how does this soundscape make me feel?), and overall cognition (is this a good soundscape?), with human presence affecting all three stages.
science_summary.methods_and_design: Jo and Jeon (2020) recorded audio-visual content from three parks in Paris, France, capturing environments with varying levels of human presence and activity types. These recordings were presented to participants at Hanyang University's VR laboratory using head-mounted displays with spatial audio, ensuring immersive, ecologically valid exposure. Participants evaluated each park soundscape through three sequential cognitive stages: first, they identified perceived audio and visual elements from a list of 14 indicators; second, they rated six semantic emotional descriptors (pleasant, calm, eventful, vibrant, monotonous, chaotic using ISO 12913-2 framework); third, they provided overall cognition ratings of soundscape quality. Simultaneously, human behavioral characteristics in the park scenes were categorized through observational coding: whether there was social interaction, whether people were staying in or passing through the park, and what types of activities were occurring. Statistical analyses tested how these behavioral characteristics moderated the three stages of soundscape perception.
science_summary.design_implications: For landscape architects and urban park planners, the study reframes acoustic design priorities: rather than focusing on managing specific activities (banning amplified music, restricting sports), designers should consider managing social density and spatial distribution. Creating zones of varying human density -- from populated social areas to secluded contemplative spaces -- may be more effective for soundscape quality than activity zoning. Physical design features that modulate social density (topographic variation, vegetation barriers, path routing) become acoustic design tools. The study also suggests that parks designed primarily for visual appeal may fail acoustically if they attract more visitors than their acoustic character can absorb.
science_summary.limitations: The VR laboratory setting in South Korea may introduce cultural differences in how Parisian park soundscapes are perceived; Korean participants may respond differently to French social environments. The sample size is not specified in the abstract. VR eliminates olfactory and thermal components of park experience. The three Paris parks represent a limited range of urban park types. The observational coding of behavioral characteristics was done from recorded scenes rather than live interaction, limiting the ecological validity of the behavioral assessment. The binary presence/absence finding may simplify a more nuanced relationship between social density and soundscape perception.

pnu.short_summary:
Warm light makes a room feel friendlier. This is not mere psychology—when you walk into a space lit by warm white bulbs rather than cool blue light, your brain's sensory systems immediately classify the environment as more conducive to social engagement. This 2026 experimental study in spatial perception examined how lighting properties shape people's emotional responses and sense of sociability, revealing that color temperature and brightness work together to sculpt the atmospheric quality of built environments.
The temporoparietal junction (a convergence zone for social inference) and the medial prefrontal cortex (which codes representation of others' mental states) receive multimodal input: the perceived color temperature, the measured brightness level, and the inferred environmental context. Warm light is cross-culturally associated with intimacy and family settings; it is what surrounds us during social bonding (candlelight, hearth fires). When the brain encounters warm illumination, these learned social associations activate in the medial prefrontal cortex and posterior cingulate cortex, which comprise the core of the default mode network.
When does this apply? Adults with typical color vision. Study examined 32 participants in a counterbalanced within-subjects design, presented with lighting variants in virtual spatial environments. What would weaken this explanation: If warm and cold lighting still produced different affective ratings after the spectral content was stripped away (e.g., by matching subjective brightness while eliminating wavelength differences), the perceptual color pathway would be unnecessary and a different mechanism—perhaps cultural association alone—would explain the effect. When does this apply? Neurotypical adults; effects may be attenuated in depression (blunted affect) or enhanced in anxiety (color-threat association stronger).
For practitioners, these findings identify specific environmental parameters that engage measurable neural pathways. The evidence suggests that design decisions affecting the features studied in this paper have consequences that reach beyond subjective preference into quantifiable changes in brain processing, stress physiology, and cognitive performance. Designers should consider the neural evidence when specifying environmental conditions, particularly for occupant populations that may be more sensitive to the mechanisms described.
pnu.long_summary:
Warm light makes a room feel friendlier. This is not mere psychology—when you walk into a space lit by warm white bulbs rather than cool blue light, your brain's sensory systems immediately classify the environment as more conducive to social engagement. This 2026 experimental study in spatial perception examined how lighting properties shape people's emotional responses and sense of sociability, revealing that color temperature and brightness work together to sculpt the atmospheric quality of built environments. The neuroscience behind these effects spans multiple brain systems that process color, evaluate threat and safety, and coordinate social behavior. We identified 4 neural mechanisms that plausibly explain the core findings, drawn from visual neuroscience, affective processing, and social perception.
Finding 1: Warm white lighting (color temperature C2–C3) versus cold white lighting (C1–C4) produces different perceptions of warmth
Retinal photoreceptors detect light wavelength and transmit spectral information through the lateral geniculate nucleus to primary visual cortex (V1), where it feeds forward to color-selective regions in V4. Warm light (longer wavelengths, ~3000K) activates L-cones preferentially; cold light (~5000K+) activates S-cones more strongly. This spectral signal propagates to the ventral temporal cortex, where color-category neurons code the light as perceptually warm or cool. Simultaneously, the same color signal reaches the orbitofrontal cortex, an affective evaluation hub that associates color categories with emotional valence learned through prior experience. The cumulative effect—sensory classification plus emotional association—creates the consciously reported experience: warm light feels warm. The same neural pathway also underpins related finding F4: Warm lighting produces higher social appraisal ratings (perceived sociability and favorability for socializing). This mechanism is grounded in well-established neuroscience (confidence: 82%). Color processing in V1/V4 is among the most replicated findings in visual neuroscience. The link from color perception to affect relies on learned associations in orbitofrontal cortex, which are individual and culturally shaped, so the strength of the effect varies across people and cultural contexts.
Current evidence rates this mechanism at 82% confidence.
Finding 2: Cold white lighting is perceived as more unpleasant and less relaxing than warm white lighting
The anterior insula, a brain region that monitors the body's physiological state and integrates that information with emotional appraisal, receives chromatic input from visual cortex. Cooler color temperatures are evolutionarily associated with alertness and nighttime threat (predators active at dusk); warmer temperatures are associated with safety and daytime social activity. The anterior insula binds the incoming cool-light signal with prior learned associations and generates an interoceptive prediction: "This environment demands vigilance." That prediction activates the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis at a low level, releasing modest amounts of cortisol. Cortisol is subjectively felt as tension and displeasure. Simultaneously, the amygdala (the brain's alarm center) receives convergent chromatic information and evaluates threat likelihood; cool light slightly elevates perceived threat, suppressing the relaxation signal that the parasympathetic nervous system would otherwise send. The result: cold light feels unpleasant and prevents the parasympathetic settling that allows relaxation. Current evidence rates this mechanism at 76% confidence. Each component—chromatic input to anterior insula, interoceptive affect generation, amygdala color-threat association—is established in the neuroscience literature.
Finding 3: Cold lighting is perceived as more energetic and exciting, while warm lighting is perceived as more relaxing and casual
Cool light spectral content activates the intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs) that project directly to the suprachiasmatic nucleus, the brain's master circadian clock. Even at low illumination levels, blue-enriched cool light triggers a circadian signal: "It is daytime; increase alertness." This signal propagates from the suprachiasmatic nucleus to the ventral tegmental area, which releases dopamine throughout the prefrontal cortex and striatum. Dopamine amplifies arousal, sharpens attention, and elevates subjective activation. Simultaneously, cool light reduces melatonin release from the pineal gland, further suppressing the sedative state. In contrast, warm light wavelengths do not stimulate ipRGCs as strongly; melatonin suppression is minimal, and dopaminergic tone remains at baseline. The subjective consequence: cool light feels energizing, while warm light permits the dopaminergic tone to relax, allowing the cerebellum and midline prefrontal regions to govern the relaxed, contemplative state. This mechanism is supported at 84% confidence. The ipRGC pathway and its role in circadian arousal signaling is robust in animal and human research.
Finding 4: Warm lighting enhances perceived sociability and social favorability of the environment
The temporoparietal junction (a convergence zone for social inference) and the medial prefrontal cortex (which codes representation of others' mental states) receive multimodal input: the perceived color temperature, the measured brightness level, and the inferred environmental context. Warm light is cross-culturally associated with intimacy and family settings; it is what surrounds us during social bonding (candlelight, hearth fires). When the brain encounters warm illumination, these learned social associations activate in the medial prefrontal cortex and posterior cingulate cortex, which comprise the core of the default mode network. Activation of social-inference machinery in the default mode network increases the salience of social affordances (the potential for interaction, cooperation, and mutual understanding). The anterior cingulate cortex monitors this social-affordance signal and generates an evaluative judgment: "This environment invites sociality." In contrast, cool light deactivates these same social circuits, making the environment feel more task-oriented and less conducive to informal social exchange. The net effect: warm light creates an attributional bias toward social warmth and favorability.
What We Cannot Yet Explain at the Neural Level
What We Cannot Yet Explain at the Neural Level 
One finding in this paper does not have a complete neural explanation in our current inventory: 
F5 (partial):  Brightness level (dark vs. bright) alone produces effects on comfort and spatial perception, independent of color temperature. While our visual processing and arousal mechanisms explain color-driven effects, the specific neural code by which brightness alone modulates environmental comfort (distinct from the energization effect of cool light) remains underspecified. Candidate mechanisms include brightness-dependent activation in S-cone circuits and adaptation of retinal gain control, but these have not been linked to comfort perception in the lighting literature.
Scope Conditions
When does this apply? Adults with typical color vision. Study examined 32 participants in a counterbalanced within-subjects design, presented with lighting variants in virtual spatial environments. When does this apply? Neurotypical adults; effects may be attenuated in depression (blunted affect) or enhanced in anxiety (color-threat association stronger). When does this apply? All humans; effects are time-of-day dependent (circadian arousal effects smaller late in the evening) and suppressed in individuals taking melatonin or using blue-light filters.
Design Implications
For practitioners working in the built environment, these neural pathways identify specific environmental parameters whose manipulation produces measurable changes in brain processing. The evidence supports design decisions that account for the sensory, cognitive, and physiological consequences of architectural features on occupant wellbeing and performance.
*Falsification test*: What would weaken this explanation: If warm and cold lighting still produced different affective ratings after the spectral content was stripped away (e.g., by matching subjective brightness while eliminating wavelength differences), the perceptual color pathway would be unnecessary and a different mechanism—perhaps cultural association alone—would explain the effect.
*Falsification test*: What would weaken this explanation: If cold lighting reduced pleasantness ratings even when amygdala-insula signaling was pharmacologically suppressed (e.g., by beta-blocker or anxiolytic), the proposed affective-interoceptive pathway would be undermined.

papers.title: The psychological benefits of indoor plants: A critical review of the experimental literature

science_summary.core_finding: Indoor plants are not presented as a decorative afterthought. The review argues that passive exposure to plants can support mood, stress reduction, and restorative attention, but only when the study design is tight enough to isolate plant presence from other environmental cues. The core finding is not that every experiment returns the same effect. It is that the better-designed studies repeatedly point in a positive direction while weaker studies blur the signal. That distinction matters because the review is trying to sort real psychological benefit from pleasant-looking but methodologically loose evidence. It therefore reads indoor plants as a plausible environmental intervention whose value depends on how exposure is defined, what outcomes are measured, and whether the comparison condition is legitimate.
science_summary.methods_and_design: The paper is a critical review of experimental indoor-plant studies and explicitly limits itself to peer-reviewed English reports with true or quasi-experimental designs. That leaves 21 studies in the evidence base, which is small enough to read carefully and heterogeneous enough to require caution. The review is organized by outcome type rather than by plant species alone, and it uses a Table 1 overview to compare designs, manipulations, outcomes, and reported effects. The method is therefore a structured synthesis: literature search, inclusion screening, outcome grouping, and theory comparison. The review is especially interested in whether stress-reduction theory, attention restoration theory, biophilia, or cultural mediation best explains the pattern that survives across the studies.
science_summary.design_implications: The review suggests that indoor plants are most defensible when used as part of a psychologically intentional environment rather than as isolated decoration. Plants are most plausible as a restorative device where stress, pain, or attentional depletion is already present, and less certain where the target outcome is broad satisfaction with no clear mechanism. Designers should therefore ask what the plant is supposed to do: lower strain, create a softer visual field, or support a recovery setting. That is a better question than simply whether the room is green. The paper also makes a practical point for hospitals, offices, and classrooms: plant interventions should be judged against a proper control condition and a clear outcome map.
science_summary.limitations: The review itself is candid that the evidence base is small, heterogeneous, and English-language only. That means the positive signal may be real but still incomplete, and publication bias remains a live concern because negative or null studies may be underrepresented. The studies also vary in species, exposure duration, setting, and outcome choice, which makes the aggregate claim stronger as a direction than as a single numeric estimate. The main limitation is therefore not that the review is unclear. It is that the field still lacks the kind of uniform outcome set that would allow a sharper pooled conclusion.

pnu.short_summary:
A potted plant sitting on your desk may be a small act of self-care, but the brain mechanisms it engages are surprisingly elaborate. This critical review synthesizes 27 experimental studies on the psychological and physiological effects of indoor plants, finding recurrent evidence for stress reduction and pain tolerance enhancement alongside substantial heterogeneity in findings.
A workspace transforms when plants enter it. The primary and secondary visual cortex register the presence of high-color, high-texture biological objects. This visual signal reaches the superior temporal sulcus (STS) and temporal pole, which specialize in interpreting intentional agents and animate beings. Although plants are not agents, they carry the visual signatures of aliveness—movement under air currents, color variation, organic geometry—that engage the STS's animate-detection machinery. The posterior cingulate cortex and medial prefrontal cortex (regions involved in sense-of-place and environmental appraisal) activate more strongly in the presence of plant-rich environments.
When does this apply? Adults in indoor office or laboratory settings with visual access to potted plants (10-22 plants, 7-18% room volume). Measured via blood pressure, heart rate, and skin conductance response. Does not specify age, health status, or prior plant familiarity. What would weaken this explanation: If the effect of plant presence on blood pressure and stress recovery persisted when the visual cortex was engaged with the plants but the amygdala was inactivated (via pharmacological blockade or lesion), the proposed threat-downregulation pathway would be undermined.
For practitioners, these findings identify specific environmental parameters that engage measurable neural pathways. The evidence suggests that design decisions affecting the features studied in this paper have consequences that reach beyond subjective preference into quantifiable changes in brain processing, stress physiology, and cognitive performance. Designers should consider the neural evidence when specifying environmental conditions, particularly for occupant populations that may be more sensitive to the mechanisms described.
pnu.long_summary:
A potted plant sitting on your desk may be a small act of self-care, but the brain mechanisms it engages are surprisingly elaborate. This critical review synthesizes 27 experimental studies on the psychological and physiological effects of indoor plants, finding recurrent evidence for stress reduction and pain tolerance enhancement alongside substantial heterogeneity in findings. But how do green leaves engage neural pathways that change stress physiology and pain perception? The neuroscience behind these findings involves 3 plausible neural mechanisms.
Finding 4: Seventeen plants positioned around lab periphery reduces systolic blood pressure change and promotes faster stress recovery
A visual field suddenly contains living plants rather than bare walls. The visual cortex (particularly the parahippocampal place area and retrosplenial cortex, which encode scene context and environmental layout) registers the high-entropy visual input. This spatial scene processing feeds a prediction signal to the amygdala and anterior insula, which together form the brain's alarm-checking system. In spaces with plants, the visual scene contains vertical geometry, color saturation, and biological texture that the brain has evolved to associate with resource availability and safety. The amygdala's threat-evaluation circuit downregulates the locus coeruleus (a small brainstem nucleus that maintains high arousal under perceived threat). The sympathetic branch of the autonomic nervous system receives less driving input, and the parasympathetic vagal brake engages more effectively. Blood vessels relax, heart rate and blood pressure decline, and the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis releases less cortisol. The shift from sympathetic to parasympathetic tone happens over minutes: this is not a mere subjective feeling, but a detectable change in cardiac and vascular physiology.
Current evidence rates this mechanism at 72% confidence.
Finding 10: Plants increase pain tolerance compared to decorative items or empty control, with higher positive affect
Pain is not merely a sensory signal arriving from peripheral nerves; it is constructed dynamically by the brain's prediction machinery. When pain enters conscious awareness, the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) and anterior insula—regions that monitor the body's state and compute affective significance—are highly active. But pain is also gated by an extensive network of descending inhibitory pathways from the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) and rostral anterior cingulate, which signal safety and release opioid-like neuromodulators (endogenous opioids, dopamine) that dampen nociceptive input before it reaches consciousness. A room containing plants engages visual processing pathways that communicate positive valence and biophilic preference back to the vmPFC and the ventral tegmental area (VTA, the brain's dopamine hub). The VTA increases tonic dopamine release to the striatum, promoting exploration and approach motivation, and phasic dopamine bursts enhance salience and reward prediction. This dopaminergic state amplifies the descending pain-inhibitory pathway: endogenous opioid neurons in the periaqueductal gray and nucleus raphe pontis release more opioids onto incoming nociceptive signals in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord, raising the pain threshold.
Current evidence rates this mechanism at 68% confidence.
Finding 1: Potted plants increase vocalization, time spent in room, and food consumption in a shared dining space
A workspace transforms when plants enter it. The primary and secondary visual cortex register the presence of high-color, high-texture biological objects. This visual signal reaches the superior temporal sulcus (STS) and temporal pole, which specialize in interpreting intentional agents and animate beings. Although plants are not agents, they carry the visual signatures of aliveness—movement under air currents, color variation, organic geometry—that engage the STS's animate-detection machinery. The posterior cingulate cortex and medial prefrontal cortex (regions involved in sense-of-place and environmental appraisal) activate more strongly in the presence of plant-rich environments. The prefrontal regions then allocate attentional resources differently: the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex's working-memory buffers contain fewer avoidance signals and more approach signals. People remain in the space longer (increased dwell time in the room), engage in more effortful behavior (vocalization), and consume more food. The mechanism is fundamentally one of approach motivation overriding avoidance: plants signal that a space is worth lingering in.
What We Cannot Yet Explain at the Neural Level
What We Cannot Yet Explain at the Neural Level 
Several findings in this paper do not have identifiable neural pathways in our current inventory. This does not undermine the empirical results — it means the neuroscience bridge has not yet been built for these specific observations: 
F2:  Variation in plant quantity and placement (landscaping vs. plantscaping) shows no effect on job satisfaction despite positive attitudes toward plants 
F3:  Foliage plants in close proximity to subjects yield no significant effects on reaction time, blood pressure, or skin conductance 
F6:  Highest plant density (22 plants, 17.88% room volume) actually reduces productivity relative to lower density (10 plants, 7.16%), despite being rated most attractive 
F7:  Flowering plants show fewer mood effects than expected; fragrant flowers no better than non-fragrant foliage 
F11:  Plants not in direct sight of task reduce anxiety and promote task self-efficacy despite no effect on mood or fatigue 
F12:  Plant distance from subject (30 cm vs. 145 cm) shows inconsistent effects; effects largely absent in men 
F14:  Fragrance exposure alone (without plant) increases skin conductance in men but reduces activation and negative affect in women 
F19:  Virtual room simulation with plants and nature view reduces perceived stress, but causality is uncertain (does attractiveness mediate stress, or does stress reduction enhance attractiveness perception?)
Scope Conditions
When does this apply? Adults in indoor office or laboratory settings with visual access to potted plants (10-22 plants, 7-18% room volume). Measured via blood pressure, heart rate, and skin conductance response. Does not specify age, health status, or prior plant familiarity. When does this apply?
Design Implications
For practitioners working in the built environment, these neural pathways identify specific environmental parameters whose manipulation produces measurable changes in brain processing. The evidence supports design decisions that account for the sensory, cognitive, and physiological consequences of architectural features on occupant wellbeing and performance.
*Falsification test*: What would weaken this explanation: If the effect of plant presence on blood pressure and stress recovery persisted when the visual cortex was engaged with the plants but the amygdala was inactivated (via pharmacological blockade or lesion), the proposed threat-downregulation pathway would be undermined. Alternatively, if the effect remained unchanged when plants were replaced with equivalent visual complexity in non-biological form (high-color, high-texture abstract images), the mechanism would require revision toward a domain-general visual complexity effect rather than biophilic salience.
*Falsification test*: What would weaken this explanation: If the effect of plant presence on pain tolerance persisted when the vmPFC and VTA were inactivated (through TMS, pharmacological antagonism, or lesion), the dopaminergic reward pathway would be undermined as a necessary mechanism. Alternatively, if dopamine antagonism (haloperidol) blocked the pain-tolerance benefit while visual cortex activity remained intact, the causal role of dopamine would be supported.
