papers.title: Towards a Sustainable Indoor Lighting Design: Effects of Artificial Light on the Emotional State of Adolescents in the Classroom

science_summary.core_finding: Baeza Moyano, San Juan Fernández, and González Lezcano (2020) review the non-visual effects of artificial light—particularly the blue-enriched light emitted by LED luminaires and electronic device screens—on the emotional state and circadian rhythms of adolescents in classroom environments. The paper's central finding is that while the absolute irradiance of blue light from screens and LED luminaires is far lower than that from sunlight (by orders of magnitude), even small amounts of blue-spectrum light received during evening and nighttime hours can have measurable effects on melatonin suppression and circadian phase-shifting. The authors argue that the rapid, unregulated adoption of LED lighting in educational settings creates an urgent need for lighting standards that account for non-visual biological effects, particularly given the heightened sensitivity of adolescent circadian systems. The paper's most provocative finding is the paradox of LED adoption: LEDs are promoted as sustainable lighting technology because of their energy efficiency and long lifespan, yet their spectral flexibility allows manufacturers to produce light with high blue-spectrum content that may be biologically inappropriate for evening and nighttime use. The authors argue that sustainability in lighting must be redefined to include human biological sustainability—not just energy sustainability—and that lighting regulations must evolve from purely photometric standards (lux, CRI) to include melanopic and circadian impact metrics.
science_summary.methods_and_design: This is a systematic review article published in the MDPI journal Sustainability. The authors analyze published studies on: (1) the spectral composition and irradiance of LED luminaires used in homes and educational centers; (2) the melanopic sensitivity function and its relationship to retinal ganglion cell activation; (3) the dose-response relationship between evening blue light exposure and melatonin suppression; (4) the circadian effects of light from laptops, tablets, and smartphones on adolescent sleep; and (5) existing lighting regulations and their adequacy for addressing non-visual effects. The review covers both laboratory photometry studies measuring spectral power distributions of commercial LEDs and field studies measuring adolescent sleep quality and circadian timing in relation to lighting exposure.
science_summary.design_implications: The review has direct implications for classroom and educational facility lighting design: (1) LED luminaire spectral specifications should include melanopic equivalent daylight illuminance (M-EDI), not just photopic lux; (2) classroom lighting should incorporate tunable-white LEDs that reduce blue-spectrum content during afternoon and evening classes; (3) schools with extended hours (after-school programs, evening classes) should implement circadian-aware lighting schedules; (4) screen policies for adolescents should consider the cumulative blue-light exposure from both room lighting and personal devices; and (5) regulatory frameworks need updating to address the non-visual biological effects of LED adoption in educational settings. The paper explicitly calls for sustainable indoor lighting design that accounts for both visual performance and circadian health.
science_summary.limitations: Important limitations include: (1) the dose-response relationship between blue light exposure and adolescent circadian disruption remains imprecisely characterized, with large inter-individual variation; (2) most melatonin suppression studies use controlled laboratory conditions that may overestimate effects in real-world settings with room lighting and screen use combined; (3) long-term health consequences of chronic low-level circadian disruption in adolescents are largely inferred from adult epidemiological data; (4) the review focuses primarily on European and North American lighting standards, with limited coverage of other regulatory contexts; and (5) the rapid technological evolution of LED products means specific spectral data may become outdated quickly.

pnu.short_summary:
The artificial lighting in a classroom does more than illuminate desks; it actively dictates an adolescent's emotional regulation and cognitive capacity. A 2020 review of sustainable lighting design reveals that poor spectral tuning—specifically the timing and intensity of blue-enriched LED light—systematically disrupts student circadian rhythms. These lighting misalignments destabilize the endocrine system, impairing sleep and degrading daytime mood.
The neural pathway centers on the brain's extreme sensitivity to spectral light composition. During the school day, standard warm-temperature lighting fails to provide sufficient blue-wavelength stimulation. Consequently, intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells fail to fully activate the suprachiasmatic nucleus (the master circadian clock). The brain interprets this warm light as dusk, blunting alertness. Conversely, evening exposure to blue-enriched screens aggressively signals the suprachiasmatic nucleus that it is midday. The clock responds by instructing the pineal gland to suppress melatonin production. This delayed melatonin release prevents sleep onset and guarantees chronic circadian misalignment, increasing overall allostatic load.
Researchers synthesized data tracking the dose-response relationship between LED spectral composition and melatonin suppression in adolescents. The proposed circadian-photoentrainment pathway is exceptionally well-documented, carrying an 88 percent confidence rating. This explanation would weaken if adolescents demonstrated the exact same delayed sleep onset and emotional dysregulation when exposed exclusively to long-wavelength (red/amber) light in the evening, which would indicate the disruption is caused by general visual stimulation rather than specific melanopic suppression.
Architects must redefine "sustainable lighting" to include human biological sustainability, not just energy efficiency. Installing generic LED luminaires without regard for spectral tuning sabotages adolescent neurobiology. Classrooms require dynamic, tunable lighting systems that deliver high-intensity, blue-enriched light during morning hours to anchor the circadian clock, transitioning to warmer spectrums in the afternoon. Treating lighting purely as an engineering problem ignores the reality that light is an endocrine intervention fundamentally shaping the developing brain.
pnu.long_summary: Baeza Moyano, San Juan Fernández, and González Lezcano (2020) review the non-visual effects of artificial light—particularly the blue-enriched light emitted by LED luminaires and electronic device screens—on the emotional state and circadian rhythms of adolescents in classroom environments. The paper's central finding is that while the absolute irradiance of blue light from screens and LED luminaires is far lower than that from sunlight (by orders of magnitude), even small amounts of blue-spectrum light received during evening and nighttime hours can have measurable effects on melatonin suppression and circadian phase-shifting. The authors argue that the rapid, unregulated adoption of LED lighting in educational settings creates an urgent need for lighting standards that account for non-visual biological effects, particularly given the heightened sensitivity of adolescent circadian systems. The paper's most provocative finding is the paradox of LED adoption: LEDs are promoted as sustainable lighting technology because of their energy efficiency and long lifespan, yet their spectral flexibility allows manufacturers to produce light with high blue-spectrum content that may be biologically inappropriate for evening and nighttime use. The authors argue that sustainability in lighting must be redefined to include human biological sustainability—not just energy sustainability—and that lighting regulations must evolve from purely photometric standards (lux, CRI) to include melanopic and circadian impact metrics. This is a systematic review article published in the MDPI journal Sustainability. The authors analyze published studies on: (1) the spectral composition and irradiance of LED luminaires used in homes and educational centers; (2) the melanopic sensitivity function and its relationship to retinal ganglion cell activation; (3) the dose-response relationship between evening blue light exposure and melatonin suppression; (4) the circadian effects of light from laptops, tablets, and smartphones on adolescent sleep; and (5) existing lighting regulations and their adequacy for addressing non-visual effects. The review covers both laboratory photometry studies measuring spectral power distributions of commercial LEDs and field studies measuring adolescent sleep quality and circadian timing in relation to lighting exposure. Key quantitative findings synthesized in the review: blue light irradiance from LED luminaires is 2–5× lower than from traditional daylight; screen irradiance from laptops and tablets at typical viewing distances produces approximately 1–10 lux at the cornea in the blue spectrum (460–490 nm); melatonin suppression begins at blue-light exposures as low as 10–30 lux at the retina; adolescents show delayed circadian phase (DLMO) of 30–60 minutes following 2 hours of evening screen exposure; and current European lighting standards (EN 12464-1) do not specify melanopic lux limits for educational environments. The review synthesizes data from approximately 50 published studies. Additional data synthesized: adolescent melatonin onset (DLMO) occurs approximately 1-2 hours later than in adults, making adolescents particularly vulnerable to further circadian delay from evening blue light; LED luminaires with correlated color temperature (CCT) above 4000K contain 30-50% more blue-spectrum energy in the 460-490nm melanopic sensitivity peak than comparable 3000K luminaires; and total daily blue-light dose from combined room and screen exposure in typical adolescent schedules exceeds recommended limits for evening exposure in approximately 40% of the exposure scenarios modeled in the reviewed studies. The paper contains no photographs or complex data visualization figures in the pages inspected. It is a text-based review with occasional reference to spectral power distribution curves and circadian sensitivity functions from cited studies. The review has direct implications for classroom and educational facility lighting design: (1) LED luminaire spectral specifications should include melanopic equivalent daylight illuminance (M-EDI), not just photopic lux; (2) classroom lighting should incorporate tunable-white LEDs that reduce blue-spectrum content during afternoon and evening classes; (3) schools with extended hours (after-school programs, evening classes) should implement circadian-aware lighting schedules; (4) screen policies for adolescents should consider the cumulative blue-light exposure from both room lighting and personal devices; and (5) regulatory frameworks need updating to address the non-visual biological effects of LED adoption in educational settings. The paper explicitly calls for sustainable indoor lighting design that accounts for both visual performance and circadian health. Important limitations include: (1) the dose-response relationship between blue light exposure and adolescent circadian disruption remains imprecisely characterized, with large inter-individual variation; (2) most melatonin suppression studies use controlled laboratory conditions that may overestimate effects in real-world settings with room lighting and screen use combined; (3) long-term health consequences of chronic low-level circadian disruption in adolescents are largely inferred from adult epidemiological data; (4) the review focuses primarily on European and North American lighting standards, with limited coverage of other regulatory contexts; and (5) the rapid technological evolution of LED products means specific spectral data may become outdated quickly. The critical unmet need is field-based research measuring objective circadian markers (salivary melatonin, actigraphy-derived sleep timing) in real classrooms with different LED spectral profiles. Randomized crossover trials comparing student alertness, academic performance, and sleep quality under conventional versus circadian-optimized LED lighting would provide the evidence base needed to reform educational lighting standards. The adolescent population is particularly important given their naturally delayed circadian phase and vulnerability to further phase-shifting by evening light exposure. Mechanism 1: Artificial light misalignment disrupts ipRGC-SCN-pineal circadian entrainment, explaining impaired sleep onset and mood dysregulation (CB-CIRCADIAN-ENTRAINMENT-001) Light enters the eye and reaches the retina, where a specialized population of neurons — intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs) — detect the spectral composition of incoming light. Unlike rods and cones, which mediate conscious vision, ipRGCs contain melanopsin, a photopigment maximally sensitive to blue light (approximately 480 nanometers). These cells project directly to the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), a region of the hypothalamus approximately the size of a pinhead that functions as the brain's master circadian clock. The SCN does not care about visual detail; it cares about one thing: the ratio of blue to amber light. Blue-rich light signals that the sun is high overhead (midday); amber light signals dawn or dusk. This signal enables the SCN to synchronize the body's distributed clocks (in the liver, pancreas, adipose tissue, muscle) with the 24-hour solar cycle. Artificial classroom lighting violates this system at two levels. First, during school hours, indoor fluorescent and LED lighting — even at high illuminance (400–800 lux) — typically delivers a spectral distribution skewed toward longer wavelengths (warmer color temperatures, 2700–4000 K), because designers optimized for human visual comfort rather than circadian photometry. ipRGCs detect this relative lack of blue and interpret it as late afternoon or dusk, sending a signal to the pineal gland to begin releasing melatonin — but the adolescent's school day is only half over. Second, in the evening, adolescents typically use smartphones, tablets, and computers with blue-enriched screens (5000–6500 K) or are exposed to blue-enriched LED lighting in homes. This blue-at-night exposure directly suppresses melatonin, further delaying sleep onset. The result is a chronic misalignment: the adolescent's endogenous circadian period (which in adolescence naturally drifts 1–3 hours later than in adults, a phenomenon called the adolescent circadian phase delay) is further delayed by evening light exposure and inadequately resynchronized by daytime lighting that lacks sufficient melanopic stimulation. Over days to weeks, this misalignment produces measurable effects. Sleep onset latency increases (the adolescent lies awake longer); sleep quality deteriorates (more arousals, reduced slow-wave sleep); daytime alertness declines (the SCN, desynchronized from the light-dark cycle, cannot maintain high arousal during morning classes). Emotional regulation depends critically on the prefrontal cortex's ability to modulate limbic reactivity, and this modulation is impaired when circadian-dependent arousal systems are dysregulated — hence the mood decline observed in adolescents under chronic circadian misalignment. This mechanism is well-established (confidence: 82%), supported by controlled laboratory studies of light exposure, longitudinal classroom studies, and genetic studies of SCN function. What remains uncertain is the minimum melanopic lux (or illuminance at 480 nm equivalent) required in classroom settings to maintain daytime circadian phase, and whether individual differences in ipRGC sensitivity or photoreceptor density create variability in response to the same lighting environment. When does this apply? Adolescents ages 13–19, particularly during the circadian phase-delay window (ages 14–18). Lighting conditions: typical classroom illumination (400–800 lux, 3000–4000 K) plus evening screen exposure (5000–6500 K for 2–4 hours before bed). Measurement: sleep-onset latency via actigraphy or polysomnography; circulating melatonin via saliva or blood sampling; mood via self-report questionnaires (PANAS, ESM). Exposure duration: weeks to months of school calendar. Mechanism 2: Chronic unpredictable lighting (flicker, variation in color temperature, mismatch to circadian timing) elevates tonic cortisol via the HPA axis, producing allostatic load (AL-CHRONIC-PE-001) The hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis (HPA) is the brain's hormonal stress-response system. When a threat is detected — or when the brain receives prediction errors it cannot explain — the hypothalamus releases corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH), which triggers the pituitary to release adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), which signals the adrenal glands to release cortisol into the bloodstream. In acute conditions (a 20-minute encounter with a predator), this is adaptive: cortisol mobilizes glucose, sharpens attention, and suppresses non-essential functions like digestion and reproduction.

papers.title: Towards multi-sensory design: Placemaking through immersive environments – Evaluation of the approach

science_summary.core_finding: Immersive multisensory environments can support placemaking when designers use them to test how people experience visual, aural, and kinesthetic cues together. The paper treats VR as a design-evaluation tool, not as a decorative add-on, and it argues that the place experience gains force when users can interact with the scene.
science_summary.methods_and_design: Three workshops in an urban design context drew n = 10-20 participants per workshop, and the participants were professionals or students from architecture and urban design backgrounds. The study used surveys, activity tracking, and VR prototype testing to see how the multisensory design approach performed across different settings and sessions. Analytical approaches include: sem, Likert, EEG, case study, questionnaire.
science_summary.design_implications: Designers can use multisensory VR to ask how users read place before a build is locked in. That is useful for placemaking, because the method makes intangible sensory cues visible and lets a team compare alternatives while the project is still flexible.
science_summary.limitations: The project is an early prototype and the evaluation sits inside a specific urban-design workshop setting. The local record should therefore keep the claim close to the prototype, the workshop sessions, and the reported limitations rather than claiming that multisensory VR is already a finished design standard.

pnu.short_summary:
When you step into a virtual place—designed not just to be seen but felt through sound and movement—your brain starts a conversation with itself. This design research study explored how a multi-sensory immersive environment can engage architecture professionals and students in meaningful placemaking, examining which sensory elements matter most and how temporal dynamics reshape spatial understanding.
The integration of aural and kinesthetic information with visual design activates the default mode network (a set of brain regions including medial prefrontal cortex, posterior cingulate cortex located at the back of the brain below the splenium, and angular gyrus where temporal and parietal lobes meet) in a way that purely visual-only representation does not. The default mode engages during autobiographical thinking and the construction of a narrative self—how you position yourself within a remembered or imagined scene.
When does this apply? Young to middle-aged adults (75% aged 18–34, 10% aged 45–54, mean professional experience mixed). Study examined: immersive VR environment with synchronized visual, aural, and kinesthetic elements; evaluation during 10–15 minute exploration sessions. Measured via Likert scale effectiveness and engagement ratings. What would weaken this explanation: If engagement ratings remained equally high when auditory or proprioceptive signals were temporally desynchronized from visual input (e.g., audio delayed by 500 ms, or movement tracking disabled), the proposed multisensory binding mechanism would be undermined. When does this apply?
For practitioners, these findings identify specific environmental parameters that engage measurable neural pathways. The evidence suggests that design decisions affecting the features studied in this paper have consequences that reach beyond subjective preference into quantifiable changes in brain processing, stress physiology, and cognitive performance. Designers should consider the neural evidence when specifying environmental conditions, particularly for occupant populations that may be more sensitive to the mechanisms described.
pnu.long_summary:
When you step into a virtual place—designed not just to be seen but felt through sound and movement—your brain starts a conversation with itself. This design research study explored how a multi-sensory immersive environment can engage architecture professionals and students in meaningful placemaking, examining which sensory elements matter most and how temporal dynamics reshape spatial understanding. But what happens in the brain when sensory channels are integrated in this way, and why does adding sound and movement to visual design create stronger engagement? The neuroscience behind these findings involves 3 plausible neural mechanisms, spanning from multisensory binding to aesthetic experience. Several findings in the paper—particularly those involving qualitative participant preferences and navigational engagement—currently lack identified neural pathways in our mechanism inventory.
Finding 1: Multisensory design approach (visual + aural + kinesthetic integration) leads to higher engagement and effectiveness ratings (38–43% rated as 6–7 on 7-point scale, N=21)
The immersive environment presents visual information through head-mounted display (generating retinal input), aural information through spatial audio (activating bilateral auditory cortex, the primary auditory processing region in the superior temporal lobe), and kinesthetic information through body movement in the VR space (engaging proprioceptive pathways in the posterior parietal cortex, which integrates body-position signals). The superior colliculus (a small brainstem structure coordinating multisensory attention) receives converging signals from each modality and computes their temporal and spatial alignment. When the timing of visual, auditory, and proprioceptive events matches within a critical window—typically 100–200 milliseconds—the posterior parietal cortex binds these signals into a unified percept, creating the impression of a coherent place rather than three separate streams. This multisensory binding activates the medial prefrontal cortex (a region involved in self-referential processing and autobiographical memory, located behind the forehead), which encodes the experience as "a place where I was present," rather than a collection of isolated stimuli.
Finding 2: Brief familiarization (2-minute demonstration) with VR navigation leads to minimal reported fatigue, dizziness, or nausea (0 adverse reports, N=21)
Vestibular mismatch—the conflict between visual motion signals from the VR display and inner-ear motion signals from the user's actual body position—normally triggers the chemoreceptor trigger zone in the brainstem (a region sensitive to toxins and motion signals), activating the vomiting center and producing motion sickness symptoms. However, when users receive explicit warning that motion will be discordant, the anterior insula (a brain region monitoring body state and prediction errors, located deep within the lateral sulcus) pre-adjusts its expectations. This predictive recalibration, supported by the cerebellum (a structure at the base of the brain that learns to predict sensory consequences of action), dampens the mismatch signal and suppresses the nausea response. A 2-minute demonstration provides sufficient time for this cerebellar learning to occur. The spatial mapping from controller input to visual output becomes encoded in the cerebellum's forward models—internal simulations that predict the sensory outcome of movement. Once encoded, the brain can anticipate and suppress prediction errors before they reach conscious awareness, preventing the cascade that leads to motion sickness.
Finding 3: Multi-sensory design approach compared to baseline spatial representation leads to greater sense of place, presence, and design utility (qualitative consensus among 8 architecture professionals, N=21 total)
The integration of aural and kinesthetic information with visual design activates the default mode network (a set of brain regions including medial prefrontal cortex, posterior cingulate cortex located at the back of the brain below the splenium, and angular gyrus where temporal and parietal lobes meet) in a way that purely visual-only representation does not. The default mode engages during autobiographical thinking and the construction of a narrative self—how you position yourself within a remembered or imagined scene. When the multisensory environment includes temporal structure (the ability to revisit locations, hear ambient soundscapes evolve, feel architectural mass through movement), the hippocampus (a seahorse-shaped structure deep in the temporal lobe essential for spatial memory) can bind these diverse signals into a coherent environmental model that feels like "a place I know" rather than "an image I saw." For architecture professionals in particular, this matters because their cognitive task involves imagining not just static forms but inhabited spaces—how bodies move through and experience a design.
What We Cannot Yet Explain at the Neural Level
What We Cannot Yet Explain at the Neural Level 
Several findings in this paper do not have identifiable neural pathways in our current inventory. This does not undermine the empirical results—it means the neuroscience bridge has not yet been built for these specific observations: 
Participant demographics (age, gender, professional background)  and their relationship to design engagement or effectiveness ratings. The paper documents demographic variation but makes no explicit causal claims. Prior VR experience (67% prior exposure)  as a moderator of engagement. The mechanism linking prior exposure to reduced cognitive load or increased comfort is not yet specified at the neural level.
Scope Conditions
When does this apply? Young to middle-aged adults (75% aged 18–34, 10% aged 45–54, mean professional experience mixed). Study examined: immersive VR environment with synchronized visual, aural, and kinesthetic elements; evaluation during 10–15 minute exploration sessions. Measured via Likert scale effectiveness and engagement ratings. When does this apply? Young to middle-aged adults with mixed VR experience (67% had prior VR exposure). Study examined: 2-minute guided demonstration followed by self-directed 10–15 minute exploration in multi-sensory VR environment. Measured via open-ended participant report of fatigue, dizziness, nausea symptoms. When does this apply? Primarily architecture professionals and students familiar with design representation (8 of 21 participants: 3 construction managers, 5 architects). Study examined: immersive multi-sensory virtual environment representing a real place, with temporal continuity and navigational agency. Measured via Likert-scale evaluation and open-ended interview feedback on design utility and sense of place.
Design Implications
For practitioners working in the built environment, these neural pathways identify specific environmental parameters whose manipulation produces measurable changes in brain processing. The evidence supports design decisions that account for the sensory, cognitive, and physiological consequences of architectural features on occupant wellbeing and performance.
*Falsification test*: What would weaken this explanation: If engagement ratings remained equally high when auditory or proprioceptive signals were temporally desynchronized from visual input (e.g., audio delayed by 500 ms, or movement tracking disabled), the proposed multisensory binding mechanism would be undermined. Alternatively, if engagement were equally strong in a purely visual-only version of the environment, multisensory integration would not be the primary driver.
*Falsification test*: What would weaken this explanation: If nausea rates remained low with zero demonstration time (immediate unguided exploration), or if they spiked dramatically with visual-vestibular desynchronization that violates cerebellar predictions even in experienced VR users, the forward-model explanation would require revision. Additionally, if nausea were equally absent in passive observation (no movement) versus active navigation, vestibular mismatch would not be the limiting factor.

papers.title: Towards standardization in soundscape preference assessment

science_summary.core_finding: Towards standardization in soundscape preference assessment makes a concrete claim about the central design relation. The study of soundscapes involves diverse fields of practice, diverse approaches and diverse disciplinary interests. The field overlaps with the much larger and established field of environmental noise management, and also intersects, to various degrees, with other areas of acoustics such as sound quality, human acoustic comfort in buildings, and music-and also with non-acoustic fields such as wilderness and recreation management, urban and housing design, and landscape planning and management. Working Group 54 of ISO/TC 43/SC 1 has been formed with a remit of standardization for perceptual assessment of human sound preference (in outdoor space) using questionnaires. The working group began its work in 2009, with considerable and wide-ranging discussion amongst its members. This paper makes a range of observations, and sometimes suggestions, on matters pertinent to eventual definition of the soundscape; on outcomes of interest arising from experience of a soundscape; on the role of context in assessment; on sound sources in different places; and on relevant lessons for soundscape assessment from experience of questionnaire measurement of noise annoyance. It represents a personal view, though informed by a range of opinions from the Working Group meeting and from literature. For standardization, there is a need to develop a common language of concepts and terms regarding the outdoor acoustic environment that can provide a foundation for communication across different academic disciplines and across different professional areas with an interest in soundscapes. This paper makes a range of observations and suggestions to this end including: - An adequate term for the entity on which soundscape studies focus is the acoustic environment (or less preferably sonic environment) of any place. pnu.short_summary:
A walk through a public park engages more than casual listening. The acoustic environment you encounter is a perceptual construct shaped by your brain's predictions and learned preferences. This 2011 ISO Working Group 54 paper proposes standardized methods for assessing soundscape quality, moving beyond noise-reduction paradigms to ask: how do people actually perceive and prefer the acoustic environments they inhabit?

papers.title: Traditional noise control approach (decibel-based metrics, sound reduction focus)

science_summary.core_finding: Traditional noise control approach (decibel-based metrics, sound reduction focus) makes a concrete claim about the central design relation. The focus of the building industry and research is shifting from delivering satisfactory spaces to going beyond what is merely acceptable with a wave of new research and practice dedicated to exploring how the built environment can support task performance and enhance people's health and well-being. The present study addresses the role of acoustics in this paradigm shift. Indoor soundscape research has recently emerged as an approach that brings a perceptual perspective on building and room acoustics in order to shape built environments that "sound good" according to building occupants' preference and needs. This paper establishes an initial discussion over some of the open questions in this field of research that is still in an embryonic stage. A thematic analysis of structured interviews with a panel of experts offered a range of perspectives on the characterization, management, and design of indoor soundscapes and health-related outcomes. The discussion pointed out the importance of both perceptual and multisensory research and integrated participatory design practices to enable a holistic view regarding the complex building-user interrelations and the design of just cities. Soundscape methodologies tailored to the peculiarities of indoor soundscapes can help to measure and predict the human perceptual response to the acoustic stimuli in context, thus reducing the risk of mismatches between expected and real building experiences. This perceptual perspective is expected to widen the scientific evidence for the negative and positive impacts of the acoustic environment on human health, well-being, and quality of life. This will support prioritizing the role of acoustics in building design and challenge many current design practices that are based on a noise control approach. The interviews were first recorded and then transcribed verbatim. pnu.short_summary:
Your brain responds to the sounds around you in ways that shape how well you work, how you feel, and how you connect with others. This 2020 narrative review synthesizes emerging research on how buildings should sound from a human health perspective, moving beyond simple noise reduction to embrace perceptual acoustic quality.
Removing negative sounds differs from adding positive sounds because they engage different brain systems. When you hear birdsong or water in your office, the ventral tegmental area (a midbrain region) releases dopamine. The sound is safer and more pleasant than expected. This dopamine signal creates positive feeling in the orbitofrontal cortex (which assigns value to what you hear). With repeated listening, your brain learns these associations and sustains the positive feeling. Positive soundscapes do more than add pleasant sounds. They quiet the brain's alarm system.
When does this apply? Neurotypical adults and children in indoor built environments. Applies to offices, residential buildings, institutional spaces. The mechanism scales from moment-to-moment perception to long-term satisfaction with acoustic environment. What would weaken this explanation: If participants consistently judged identical acoustic signals as equally pleasant or unpleasant regardless of visual context, architectural setting, or prior experience, the multisensory-contextual pathway would be undermined. When does this apply? Neurotypical and many neurodivergent adults. Reward prediction responses to nature sounds are robust across cultures, though preferred sound sources vary individually and culturally.
For practitioners, these findings identify specific environmental parameters that engage measurable neural pathways. The evidence suggests that design decisions affecting the features studied in this paper have consequences that reach beyond subjective preference into quantifiable changes in brain processing, stress physiology, and cognitive performance. Designers should consider the neural evidence when specifying environmental conditions, particularly for occupant populations that may be more sensitive to the mechanisms described.

papers.title: Transformation of the office: territorial behaviour and place attachment in shared desk design

science_summary.core_finding: Transformation of the office makes a concrete claim about the central design relation. Purpose - The purpose of this paper is to present an environmental psychological case study regarding an office design change. The employees of the researched company had the chance to decide whether to stay in the classic open office set-up or to switch to a shared desk supplemented by a one-day-a-week home office possibility. The authors examined the development of participants' territorial behaviour and place attachment. Design/methodology/approach - The given organizational situation is a quasi-experimental design; the variables were examined via questionnaire in a longitudinal model. Quantitative measurement was supplemented with focus group discussions. Findings - The degree of personalization (a type of territorial behaviour) decreased significantly not only among those who lost their permanent workstations - as we expected - but also in the entire population. Workplace attachment stagnated for the entire population, but workstation attachment showed a significant decrease among those who switched to the shared desk. Research limitations/implications - The limitations and the advantages are also followed by the nature of a case study: high ecological validity with relatively low sample size. Practical implications - Redesigning an office is never just an economic or interior design issue, but a psychological one. This paper provides practical environmental psychological insights into implementing office designs without permanent individual workstations. Originality/value - This paper presents the environmental psychological background of shared desk design implementation. The authors point out the significance of repressing personalization behaviour and as per the authors' knowledge, they are the first to introduce the concept of workstation attachment. The development of territorial behaviour was examined along all the subtypes. The distribution of the scale is asymmetric, extending to the right and significantly differing from the normal, so we applied nonparametric tests. When you lose your personal desk at work, something shifts in how you use the space. This study of a Hungarian office redesign found that employees who moved from assigned workstations to shared desks reduced their personalization—adding photos, plants, or mementos—not only at their old locations but throughout the entire office.

When you occupy a permanent desk, your brain encodes that location as part of an extended identity system—a workspace intrinsically linked to "you." This integration occurs through insula-mediated interoceptive prediction: the posterior insula and medial prefrontal cortex jointly predict which bodily and environmental features belong within your sense of self. Personalization acts as a visible assertion of this extended identity; by decorating your space, you strengthen the neural association between that location and your autobiographical self.
When does this apply? Neurotypical adults in office environments. Study examined office redesign from assigned to shared workstations in a Budapest organization (N = 176); measured via self-reported personalization behaviors and territorial marking questionnaire (Altman 1975). Effects observed in both those who lost permanent stations and the broader population, suggesting social transmission of environmental prediction error. What would weaken this explanation: If personalization levels remained low even when shared desks were assigned new permanent owners (restoring territorial control), the proposed mechanism would be questioned. When does this apply?

Finding 1: Transition from personal workstation to shared desk reduces identity-oriented personalization (p = 0.001, Cramér's V = 0.34, N = 176) The brain's default mode network (a collection of interconnected cortical regions including medial prefrontal cortex, posterior cingulate, and temporoparietal junction) constructs a sense of self in relation to physical space. When you occupy a permanent desk, your brain encodes that location as part of an extended identity system—a workspace intrinsically linked to "you." This integration occurs through insula-mediated interoceptive prediction: the posterior insula and medial prefrontal cortex jointly predict which bodily and environmental features belong within your sense of self. Personalization acts as a visible assertion of this extended identity; by decorating your space, you strengthen the neural association between that location and your autobiographical self. Transition to shared desk design severs this territorial control. The anterior insula (the brain's hub for detecting threats to bodily and social integrity) registers the loss of predictability: your designated location no longer exists. This mismatch activates the salience network, which reorients attention to the unpredictability of the shared environment. Simultaneously, the posterior cingulate cortex and medial prefrontal cortex—neural substrates of self-referential thought—reduce the strength of encoding between "self" and any particular location, because no location now reliably belongs to you. The result: reduced motivation to personalize, both at the former desk (identity already severed) and throughout the office (overall territorial control eroded). This effect spreads to the entire population, not just those who lost desks, suggesting a social transmission of the territorial threat signal: colleagues observe the new affordances and adjust their self-environmental predictions accordingly. The evidence for this pathway is plausible but not yet definitive (confidence: 72%). Each component draws on independent neuroscience research. The integrated chain from territorial loss to reduced self-extension in physical space, however, has not been tested end-to-end in this specific workplace context. When does this apply? Neurotypical adults in office environments. Study examined office redesign from assigned to shared workstations in a Budapest organization (N = 176); measured via self-reported personalization behaviors and territorial marking questionnaire (Altman 1975). Effects observed in both those who lost permanent stations and the broader population, suggesting social transmission of environmental prediction error. Finding 2: Workplace attachment stagnates under shared desk design; workstation attachment decreases among those who switched Place attachment—the emotional and cognitive bond between person and location—emerges from a cascade of predictive learning. When you occupy the same desk daily, your brain's hippocampus (a seahorse-shaped structure critical for episodic memory) creates a stable spatial map of that location. The entorhinal cortex (a neighboring region housing grid cells for geometric representation) encodes the spatial relationships between your desk and surrounding landmarks. Over time, these spatial representations integrate with your sense of where "you" belong through connections between hippocampus and medial prefrontal cortex, creating lasting emotional attachment. This attachment is reinforced by successful prediction: your brain predicts what you will see, hear, and feel at your desk, and those predictions are routinely confirmed. In shared desk environments, prediction fails at a fundamental level.

papers.title: Transport Reviews Wayﬁnding: A simple concept, a complex process

science_summary.core_finding: Wayfinding appears simple — you want to get from here to there — but the process conceals a remarkable complexity. This review pulls together research from transportation engineering, environmental psychology, spatial cognition, architecture, neuroscience, and computer science to show that wayfinding involves the continuous interplay of three processes: decision-making (forming a plan of action), decision execution (transforming the plan into appropriate behavior at the right time and place), and information processing (perceiving and interpreting environmental cues that feed the other two processes). The central conclusion is that no existing model successfully integrates all of these factors, and that the rapid spread of mobile navigation technology may be transforming the very cognitive processes that researchers have spent decades trying to understand.
science_summary.methods_and_design: This is a narrative review drawing on literature spanning from Kevin Lynch's The Image of the City in 1960 through 2012. The review does not report formal systematic search methods, PRISMA protocols, or inclusion-exclusion criteria. Instead, it organizes an extensive multi-disciplinary literature thematically, covering motivations for studying wayfinding, individual differences, environmental factors, cognitive mapping, spatial ability, modeling approaches, technology impacts, and future directions across built environment contexts including airports, hospitals, transit systems, and urban centers. The review was conducted as part of the Airports of the Future project funded by the Australian Research Council Linkage scheme and draws on extensive field observation in airport terminal settings.
science_summary.design_implications: For architects and transport planners, the review consolidates practical knowledge: visual access and spatial differentiation are consistently supported as predictors of wayfinding success. Signage helps but cannot compensate for fundamentally confusing spatial layouts. For airport designers specifically, the Visibility Index provides a quantifiable design criterion. The review suggests that buildings should be designed so that key destinations are visible from major decision points, reducing cognitive load and the need for external wayfinding aids throughout the navigation process.
science_summary.limitations: The review lacks formal systematic methodology — there is no search protocol, no inclusion-exclusion flow diagram, no quality assessment of individual studies, and no quantitative synthesis across the literature. The coverage reflects the authors' disciplinary focus on transportation and airport design, with less attention to wayfinding in outdoor urban environments, wilderness settings, or virtual environments. The gender differences section presents conflicting evidence without fully resolving whether observed spatial ability differences are primarily biological or culturally mediated. The review's conclusions about technology impacts are necessarily speculative given the early state of mobile navigation research in 2012.

pnu.long_summary:
Getting from one place to another looks effortless from the outside. But inside the brain, wayfinding engages a coordinated dance of memory systems, spatial codes, emotional regulation, and gender-specific neural strategies. This review of wayfinding research points to four plausible neural mechanisms that explain how humans navigate built environments—and why some people do it better than others. The neuroscience involves spatial cognition (how the brain encodes maps and routes), emotional regulation (how anxiety disrupts that encoding), and neuromodulatory control (how gender-linked neurochemistry shapes preferred navigation strategies). We identified 4 findings with solid neural support and 4 additional findings for which the mechanism remains open—listed at the end of this page.
Finding 1: Wayfinding decomposition into four sequential operations (orientation → route selection → route control → destination recognition) engages a hierarchical chain of spatial and cognitive processes
When you arrive at a train station and must navigate to your gate, your brain executes a sequence that cognitive scientists named in the 1970s: first, you orient yourself by identifying your location (the hippocampus and nearby entorhinal cortex construct a spatial map from visible landmarks). Second, you select a route by holding candidate paths in working memory—a task centered in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex that integrates stored knowledge of airport layouts with real-time perceptual input. Third, you execute the route while monitoring your position continuously, a process driven by the posterior parietal cortex and striatum, which track your heading and distance traveled. Fourth, you recognize your destination when landmarks match your expectation—another hippocampal operation that compares incoming sensory patterns to learned memories. These operations are not independent. The hippocampus generates predictions about which landmarks you should encounter at each step, and the anterior cingulate cortex signals when prediction errors arise—a mismatch between expected and observed location.
Finding 2: Spatial anxiety impairs navigational accuracy and spatial problem-solving, particularly in women
Higher spatial anxiety correlates with worse navigation performance. The pathway is neuroendocrine. When a wayfinder feels uncertain about their location, the amygdala interprets this mismatch as a threat, triggering activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, which releases cortisol and other glucocorticoids. Chronically elevated cortisol has a direct pharmacological effect: it binds to glucocorticoid receptors in the prefrontal cortex and hippocampus, impairs working memory capacity, and disrupts the consolidation of new spatial memories. The person becomes trapped in a paradox—anxiety about navigation triggers a hormonal cascade that makes spatial memory and executive function worse, confirming the initial fear and amplifying anxiety further. Women show elevated resting cortisol and heightened amygdala responsivity to uncertain situations, a pattern shaped by gonadal hormones and partly by socialization. This amplifies the anxiety-performance coupling. Men show equivalent levels of spatial anxiety when explicitly threatened, but baseline anxiety about spatial tasks is lower in men across most studies, dampening the allostatic load.
Finding 3: Men preferentially rely on distal environmental cues (distant landmarks, hill lines, cardinal directions) while women preferentially rely on proximal cues (nearby objects, intersections, street networks)
The brain encodes space using two partially dissociable systems. The posterior parietal cortex and dorsal striatum compute egocentric coordinates—directions and distances relative to the body. The medial temporal lobes (hippocampus and entorhinal cortex) compute allocentric coordinates—abstract maps where locations have fixed relationships independent of the observer's position. Distal cues like hill lines and cardinal directions (north, south) feed preferentially into allocentric systems, which support global route planning and sense of direction. Proximal cues like street intersections and nearby buildings feed into egocentric systems, which support local obstacle avoidance and turn-by-turn guidance. Men show stronger functional connectivity between the parietal cortex and retrosplenial cortex (a region encoding global cognitive maps), predicting allocentric preference. Women show stronger recruitment of the caudate nucleus (a striatal region supporting egocentric, route-following behavior), predicting proximal-cue preference. These differences emerge from a combination of gonadal hormone effects on neural development (particularly testosterone's amplification of spatial system maturation in males) and practice patterns shaped by social norms.
Finding 4: Mental rotation and spatial visualization abilities show robust male advantage, mediated by testosterone-sensitive neural regions
Mental rotation—mentally spinning a 3D object—recruits the right parietal cortex, right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, and networks supporting visuospatial working memory. Men score significantly higher on mental rotation tests. Testosterone, present at higher concentrations in males during key developmental windows, promotes the structural development of these networks: increased dendritic branching, longer axons, and stronger synaptic density in parietal and frontal regions associated with spatial reasoning. The effect is not simply motivational—administering testosterone to women elevates mental rotation scores, while testosterone antagonists lower men's scores in experimental settings. The functional consequence is that men construct more stable 3D mental models of space and can more rapidly compare multiple spatial configurations. This advantage is largest on tasks involving dynamic rotation and smallest on tasks involving static memory of spatial layouts. The advantage emerges around puberty as testosterone levels rise and persists into adulthood, though it can be partially reduced by spatial training in women.
What We Cannot Yet Explain at the Neural Level
What We Cannot Yet Explain at the Neural Level 
Several findings in this review do not have identifiable neural pathways in our current mechanism inventory. This does not undermine the behavioral observations—it means the neuroscience bridge remains incomplete: 
F2:  Successful wayfinding system criteria (location recognition at start, destination recognition at arrival, reorientation capacity) 
F3:  Gender differences in spatial abilities emerge across multiple domains (why is the male advantage so consistent across mental rotation, navigation, and dynamic spatial ability?) 
F5:  The specific neural basis for accuracy improvements when directional information is explicitly provided versus inferred from landmarks 
F6 (partial):  Why women's proximal-cue preference (when combined with lower baseline spatial confidence) produces faster disorientation in novel environments
Scope Conditions
When does this apply? Neurotypical adults navigating unfamiliar indoor environments (airports, hospitals, transportation hubs). Primarily applies to first-time navigation or high-uncertainty routes where active spatial memory is engaged. When does this apply? Neurotypical adults, with stronger effects in women. Applies to novel or ambiguous navigation contexts where wayfinder confidence is low and error feedback increases perceived threat. When does this apply? Neurotypical adults. Shows robust gender effects. Applies to navigation in novel large-scale environments where global organization (distal cues) and local turning (proximal cues) can be dissociated.
Design Implications
For practitioners working in the built environment, these neural pathways identify specific environmental parameters whose manipulation produces measurable changes in brain processing. The evidence supports design decisions that account for the sensory, cognitive, and physiological consequences of architectural features on occupant wellbeing and performance.
*Falsification test*: What would weaken this explanation: If the four-step decomposition remained behaviorally valid but neuroimaging showed these operations recruiting distinct neural systems that do not interact (e.g., if each step could be performed without access to hippocampal output), the integrated chain account would need revision. Alternatively, if the temporal ordering of these steps varied substantially across individuals without affecting wayfinding success, the universality of the four-step model would be questioned.
*Falsification test*: What would weaken this explanation: If pharmacological cortisol blockade or anxiolytic drugs (that target the amygdala without affecting stress hormone signaling) produced equivalent improvements in navigational accuracy, the neuroendocrine pathway would be questioned in favor of a purely attentional account. Alternatively, if gender differences in spatial anxiety disappeared in cultures with different gender socialization patterns while neural architecture remained stable, the biological determinism implied here would require modification.

Neuroscience References for Further Reading

papers.title: Trends in research related to Shinrin-yoku (taking in the forest atmosphere or forest bathing) in Japan

science_summary.core_finding: A 15-minute walk through a Japanese cedar forest shifts the autonomic nervous system toward parasympathetic dominance, lowers blood pressure, and reduces prefrontal cortex activity as measured by near-infrared spectroscopy. These convergent physiological signatures form the empirical backbone of shinrin-yoku, the Japanese practice of forest bathing that Tsunetsugu, Park, and Miyazaki have spent over a decade documenting through controlled field experiments and targeted laboratory olfaction studies.
science_summary.methods_and_design: The review synthesizes results from the authors' own program of research under Japan's Therapeutic Effects of Forests project, launched in 2004. Field studies conducted in actual forests used portable heart rate variability (HRV) monitors to separate sympathetic from parasympathetic contributions, near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) headbands to measure prefrontal cerebral blood flow, and salivary cortisol sampling for neuroendocrine stress markers. Complementary laboratory studies isolated individual forest volatile compounds, including alpha-pinene, limonene, and cedrol, delivering them at controlled concentrations (e.g., 10 and 500 microliters per 30 liters of air) through nose-positioned emitters while monitoring blood pressure and subjective mood via semantic differential scales.
science_summary.design_implications: The dose-response findings for individual forest volatiles offer a molecular design vocabulary for biophilic architecture: low-concentration alpha-pinene exposure via natural wood surfaces might produce the relaxation response that high-concentration exposure reverses. Architects specifying interior wood finishes and ventilation strategies could calibrate volatile emission rates to maintain concentrations within the parasympathetic-promoting range. The NIRS results also suggest that forest-like environments reduce prefrontal cognitive load, relevant for designing recuperative spaces in hospitals and offices.
science_summary.limitations: The review draws almost exclusively on the authors' own research program, creating a narrow evidence base that lacks independent replication from other laboratories or cultural contexts. The field studies compared forest to urban walking, confounding environment type with physical activity level, temperature, humidity, and ambient sound. The olfactory studies used artificial delivery systems at fixed positions, which may not replicate the variable, fluctuating scent exposure that occurs during actual forest walking where wind, temperature, and breathing rate modulate volatile intake. The absence of standardized effect sizes across the reviewed studies prevents quantitative synthesis.

pnu.short_summary:
When you walk through a cedar forest for twenty minutes, your nervous system changes. Your blood pressure falls. Your body stops bracing. But why does a forest have these powers? This 2010 literature review by Tsunetsugu, Park, and Miyazaki synthesizes a decade of Shinrin-yoku research, showing that brief forest exposure produces measurable shifts in physiology—but the neural mechanisms underlying these changes have only recently become clear.
The forest enters through every sensory channel simultaneously. When you walk among trees, the visual system encounters a world organized by fractal branching patterns—trunks splitting into limbs, limbs into twigs, all following a self-similar geometry that repeats across scales. This fractal structure is less jarring than the sharp lines and abrupt edges of buildings, and the predictive processing system (located throughout visual cortex, from V1 onwards) encounters fewer large prediction errors. Simultaneously, the olfactory bulb receives volatile organic compounds called phytoncides, released by trees, which activate the olfactory epithelium and send direct signals to the amygdala (the brain's alarm center for threat) and to the piriform cortex (which encodes odor identity and context).
When does this apply? Healthy adults without anxiety disorders or trauma history. Study population: mostly healthy Japanese university students (N = 288 total, 12 per site). Measured via salivary cortisol, blood pressure, heart rate variability, and prefrontal cortex activity via near-infrared spectroscopy. When does this apply? Healthy adults. Study examined: forest environments versus urban centers and abstract controls. Participants walked for 20 minutes or viewed scenes for 15 minutes seated. Measured via near-infrared spectroscopy, blood pressure, and heart rate.
What would weaken this explanation: If forest exposure reduced salivary cortisol and blood pressure even when olfactory input was blocked (by nasal plug or perfumed air), the proposed phytoncide-amygdala pathway would lose support. When the amygdala detects no danger—only the steady chemical signature of vegetation—it quiets its output to the rest of the brain.
pnu.long_summary:
When you walk through a cedar forest for twenty minutes, your nervous system changes. Your blood pressure falls. Your body stops bracing. But why does a forest have these powers? This 2010 literature review by Tsunetsugu, Park, and Miyazaki synthesizes a decade of Shinrin-yoku research, showing that brief forest exposure produces measurable shifts in physiology—but the neural mechanisms underlying these changes have only recently become clear. The neuroscience behind forest bathing involves 3 plausible neural mechanisms, spanning from autonomic regulation to how the brain interprets visual scenes. We identified 2 findings for which no mapped mechanism exists — described at the end of this page.
Finding 1: Forest walking increases parasympathetic nervous system activity and decreases sympathetic activity compared to urban environments
The forest enters through every sensory channel simultaneously. When you walk among trees, the visual system encounters a world organized by fractal branching patterns—trunks splitting into limbs, limbs into twigs, all following a self-similar geometry that repeats across scales. This fractal structure is less jarring than the sharp lines and abrupt edges of buildings, and the predictive processing system (located throughout visual cortex, from V1 onwards) encounters fewer large prediction errors. Simultaneously, the olfactory bulb receives volatile organic compounds called phytoncides, released by trees, which activate the olfactory epithelium and send direct signals to the amygdala (the brain's alarm center for threat) and to the piriform cortex (which encodes odor identity and context). When the amygdala detects no danger—only the steady chemical signature of vegetation—it quiets its output to the rest of the brain. The hypothalamus (the master control center for hormone release and autonomic balance) responds by down-regulating the locus coeruleus (a small brainstem nucleus that floods the brain with noradrenaline during stress), allowing parasympathetic tone to increase.
Finding 3: Viewing forest scenery decreases blood pressure and prefrontal cortex activity more than viewing urban or abstract scenes
The moment you see a forest, your brain begins computing a rapid estimate of the scene's structure—what researchers call the scene "gist." This happens in under 200 milliseconds, before conscious awareness. Low-spatial-frequency information (the broad outlines of light and shadow, the overall color palette) travels via the magnocellular pathway in the visual system to the prefrontal cortex (the brain's decision-making and impulse-control center), which makes a fast prediction: "This is a place where nothing will harm me. There are no sharp edges, no sudden drops, no crowds, no locked doors." This initial affective frame—safety, predictability, openness—is communicated to the amygdala (the brain's alarm center) via direct connections. At the same time, high-spatial-frequency information (fine detail) takes a slower route through visual cortex. If this detailed information confirms the initial prediction, the prefrontal cortex relaxes. The anterior cingulate cortex (a region that monitors for conflict and mismatch) finds no error to report.
Finding 4: Individual differences in personality type (Type A vs. Type B) modulate the magnitude of autonomic recovery during nature exposure
The same forest produces different responses in different people. In the laboratory, Type A individuals (those characterized by impatience, competitive drive, and chronic time urgency) show a smaller decrease in heart rate when viewing displeasure-inducing images compared to Type B individuals. This difference originates in the anterior insula (the brain's headquarters for sensing the body's internal state) and its connections to the amygdala and prefrontal cortex. Type A individuals have a chronically elevated baseline activation in these regions—their brains are wired to treat more situations as potentially demanding or threatening. The insula, in effect, "turns up the volume" on autonomic arousal signals. When Type A individuals then view nature, the downregulation still occurs, but it begins from a higher baseline. Their vagal tone increases, but not to the same degree as in Type B individuals who began from lower baseline arousal. This pattern suggests that the forest activates the same recovery mechanism in everyone, but individual differences in personality and stress reactivity determine how far the system can swing back toward parasympathetic dominance.
What We Cannot Yet Explain at the Neural Level
What We Cannot Yet Explain at the Neural Level 
The remaining findings in this paper do not have identifiable neural pathways in our current inventory. This does not invalidate the empirical observations—it means the neuroscience bridge has not yet been constructed: 
F5:  Wood interior design with 45% wood surface ratio increases comfort ratings and "vigorous" mood more than other wood ratios. (Neural mechanism linking wood material properties to preference and affect requires further research in material-perception neuroscience.) 
F2 (partial):  Sakura (cherry blossom) scenery produces less "soothing" perception and more "awakening" effect compared to forest imagery. (This differential effect may involve reward-system novelty coding, but the mechanism is not yet established in the literature.)
Scope Conditions
When does this apply? Healthy adults without anxiety disorders or trauma history. Study population: mostly healthy Japanese university students (N = 288 total, 12 per site). Measured via salivary cortisol, blood pressure, heart rate variability, and prefrontal cortex activity via near-infrared spectroscopy. When does this apply? Healthy adults. Study examined: forest environments versus urban centers and abstract controls. Participants walked for 20 minutes or viewed scenes for 15 minutes seated. Measured via near-infrared spectroscopy, blood pressure, and heart rate. When does this apply? Healthy adults with measurable Type A/Type B personality variation. Study population: Japanese adults viewing nature versus stress-inducing images in lab settings. Measured via heart rate, heart rate variability, and cardiac output.
Design Implications
For practitioners working in the built environment, these neural pathways identify specific environmental parameters whose manipulation produces measurable changes in brain processing. The evidence supports design decisions that account for the sensory, cognitive, and physiological consequences of architectural features on occupant wellbeing and performance.

Similarly, if the autonomic shift persisted when visual input was occluded but smell was intact, the fractal-visual mechanism would be less central to the effect.
*Falsification test*: What would weaken this explanation: If viewing a photograph of a forest produced the same reduction in prefrontal activity and blood pressure as walking in an actual forest, the olfactory component would be less important than the visual mechanism alone. If forest scenes with edited-out natural clutter (artificially clean, high-contrast filtered images) produced the same effect, this would suggest the predictive-processing mechanism is robust to simplification. Conversely, if adding random visual noise to forest scenes eliminated the effect, this would support the prediction-error hypothesis.

Hospital lighting shapes the nervous system of the people who work there. This thesis examines natural light integration in 450 healthcare facility spaces and finds that most staff experience dissatisfaction with current lighting — yet more than half report symptoms that improve when they leave the building.
The visual cortex extracts spatial structure from the retinal image using hierarchical predictive processing. When a room receives natural daylight, the sun's movement creates predictable patterns of light and shadow that the visual system learns to forecast. The superior colliculus and visual cortex together build an internal model of how shadows will move across surfaces as time passes. However, when staff work in spaces lit only by fixed artificial sources, they receive no solar-angle cues. If they then encounter moving shadows (from other people, passing clouds visible through occasional windows, or flickering from ventilation shifts), the visual system experiences an unpredictability violation: the brain expected a stable light field but instead encounters dynamic change.

When does this apply? Healthcare workers in artificially lit indoor environments.
For practitioners, these findings identify specific environmental parameters that engage measurable neural pathways. pnu.long_summary:
Hospital lighting shapes the nervous system of the people who work there. This thesis examines natural light integration in 450 healthcare facility spaces and finds that most staff experience dissatisfaction with current lighting — yet more than half report symptoms that improve when they leave the building. But how does the absence of daylight degrade wellbeing? The answer involves mechanisms spanning from the eye to the brain's deepest stress-response systems, operating silently while staff care for patients. The neuroscience behind these findings involves 3 plausible neural mechanisms, spanning from circadian rhythm disruption to chronic allostatic load.
Finding 1: Most healthcare workspaces (>50%) fail to meet illuminance standards, leading to symptom improvement when staff leave the facility (52% report symptom relief away from the hospital)
Insufficient natural light bypasses the intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs) that detect daylight wavelengths and normally drive circadian entrainment. These cells project directly to the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), the brain's master clock, which then synchronizes peripheral oscillators throughout the body through outputs to the hypothalamus and pineal gland. When hospital indoor lighting replaces daylight, the SCN receives degraded phase signals and receives them at wrong times of day. This desynchronization between the SCN's internal rhythm and external environmental time produces circadian misalignment — a state where the body's hormone rhythms (melatonin, cortisol, body temperature) no longer align with the 24-hour solar day. Chronic misalignment activates the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis persistently, elevating basal cortisol and suppressing melatonin production. The body interprets this mismatch as a sustained threat, triggering systemic inflammation and accelerated cellular aging. Staff removed from this artificial environment escape the desynchronizing signal — their ipRGCs receive the true solar time cue, the SCN realigns, and hormonal rhythms re-synchronize within hours to days.
Current evidence rates this mechanism at 82% confidence.
Finding 2: Staff express low satisfaction with current lighting (only 8% highly satisfied) and dissatisfaction with multiple lighting characteristics (70% unhappy with at least one aspect), indicating persistent visual and affective stress
The anterior insula — the brain's interoceptive hub that monitors internal body state — integrates information from the salience network about whether the visual environment meets the body's predictive needs. When hospital lighting is insufficient or misaligned with circadian expectations, photoreceptors in the eye transmit weak or temporally scrambled signals. The superior colliculus and pulvinar nucleus relay these degraded visual cues to the salience network, triggering a prediction error in the anterior insula: the brain expected to receive temporal and spectral information that matches daylight, but instead receives artificial, flat, time-independent illumination. This persistent mismatch between predicted (daylight) and actual (electric light) keeps the insula in a state of heightened sensitivity. The anterior cingulate cortex, which monitors affective valence and assigns negative weight to unmet expectations, then propagates this negative signal throughout the default mode network, producing the conscious experience of dissatisfaction. Over hours and days, this chronic low-level prediction error accumulates into allostatic load — the physiological wear of sustained arousal.
Finding 3: Unwanted shadows and visual disturbances are rated as more bothersome than direct glare (shadow discomfort 3.16 vs. glare 2.58 on average rating scale, p<0.001), suggesting spatial attention capture by unpredictable contrast patterns
The visual cortex extracts spatial structure from the retinal image using hierarchical predictive processing. When a room receives natural daylight, the sun's movement creates predictable patterns of light and shadow that the visual system learns to forecast. The superior colliculus and visual cortex together build an internal model of how shadows will move across surfaces as time passes. However, when staff work in spaces lit only by fixed artificial sources, they receive no solar-angle cues. If they then encounter moving shadows (from other people, passing clouds visible through occasional windows, or flickering from ventilation shifts), the visual system experiences an unpredictability violation: the brain expected a stable light field but instead encounters dynamic change. This prediction error activates the posterior parietal cortex and the temporal parietal junction, drawing visuospatial attention toward the shadow source. The anterior insula and anterior cingulate cortex assign negative salience to the unexpected change, and sustained attention capture disrupts task focus.
What We Cannot Yet Explain at the Neural Level
What We Cannot Yet Explain at the Neural Level 
Several aspects of this paper's findings do not have fully characterized neural pathways in our current inventory. This does not undermine the empirical observations — it means the neuroscience bridge is still under construction: 
Parameterized illuminance effects:  The paper documents variation in illuminance from 14 to 788 lux across hospital spaces, but the precise neural threshold at which circadian signaling shifts from degraded to adequate is not defined in this context. Workplace-specific stress symptom patterns:  While the paper identifies 52% reporting symptom improvement away from work, the study does not specify which symptoms (fatigue vs. headache vs. mood disturbance) map to which neural circuits in healthcare workers specifically.
Scope Conditions
When does this apply? Healthcare workers in facilities with suboptimal daylighting. Study examined: n=450 hospital rooms measured; 52% of personnel (n=108) reported symptoms improving away from the facility. Measured via self-reported symptom change upon leaving the workplace. When does this apply? Healthcare workers in artificially lit indoor environments. Study examined: n=450 respondents; 8% high/very high satisfaction, 70% dissatisfied with one or more lighting characteristics (source, level, or glare/shadow). Measured via structured satisfaction questionnaire. When does this apply? Healthcare workers in mixed artificial and natural light environments. Study examined: n=450 respondents rated shadow and glare disturbances on a Likert scale; unwanted shadow rated significantly higher (3.16) than glare (2.58), p<0.001. Measured via structured discomfort questionnaire.
Design Implications
For practitioners working in the built environment, these neural pathways identify specific environmental parameters whose manipulation produces measurable changes in brain processing. The evidence supports design decisions that account for the sensory, cognitive, and physiological consequences of architectural features on occupant wellbeing and performance.
*Falsification test*: What would weaken this explanation: If staff symptoms improved equally in facilities that received artificial bright light exposure timed to match solar schedule (chronotherapy), the core circadian mechanism would remain intact but the necessity of natural light specifically would be undermined. Conversely, if symptoms failed to improve in workers moved to high-daylight environments despite identical HPA-suppressing medications, the mechanism would require revision.
*Falsification test*: What would weaken this explanation: If workers in dimly lit facilities reported equally high satisfaction after receiving real-time feedback about predicted circadian benefit (cognitive reframing alone), the affective prediction error mechanism would be undermined. Alternatively, if increasing illuminance without changing spectral composition (adding more fluorescent light) eliminated dissatisfaction, the daylight-specificity component would be questioned.

Humanistic concerns about children’s environments matter. One of these concerns is about the impacts of children's living spaces quality on their social-spatial behaviours.
