pnu.long_summary:
When you glance at a glossy tabletop, your brain does not compute the bidirectional reflectance distribution function. Instead, it compares the image hitting your retina against learned patterns of "what glossy surfaces look like" — a process that reveals something fundamental about how sensory systems work. This 2014 review by Roland Fleming in Vision Research assembles evidence that material perception operates through statistical generative models learned from the natural world, not through inverse-optics calculations. What is the neural substrate of these learned models, and how does the visual brain encode the statistical signatures of materials? The neuroscience underpinning these findings involves 3 plausible neural mechanisms, spanning from early sensory processing to learned categorical representations in object-selective cortex. Several claims in this theoretical paper remain neurally unmapped — listed at the end of this page.
Finding 1: Visual cortex learns statistical distributions of image features — contrast, texture gradients, specular highlight distributions — and material categorization emerges from matching incoming image statistics against stored generative models
Early visual cortex (V1 and V2) encodes low-level image statistics — edges, orientations, local contrast — through populations of neurons tuned to specific features. These early representations are not yet "about" materials; they are about pixels. But because natural materials have consistent statistical structure (glossy surfaces tend to produce high-contrast specular highlights against darker surrounds, translucent materials scatter light in characteristic ways), neurons in V2 and posterior inferior temporal cortex begin to correlate these low-level image statistics with material categories during visual experience. Over time, lateral occipital cortex (LOC) — particularly the material-selective regions recently identified through fMRI — develops neuronal populations that respond more strongly to materials belonging to the same statistical category (glossy vs. matte, translucent vs. opaque) than to their physical composition. Material categorization reflects learned associations between image statistics and category membership, not measurements of physical parameters. When you see a wet stone and a glossy chocolate — which share highlight sharpness and spatial distribution even though their physical properties differ — the same LOC populations respond, because the image statistics are congruent even if the BRDF differs.
Finding 2: The brain's material categorization shows cross-material confusion when image statistics align — materials with different physical properties but overlapping statistical signatures (glossy chocolate and wet stone, crumpled silk and flowing water) are perceptually confused — because the system is organized by learned image statistics, not physical categories
If the visual brain estimated physical material properties (refractive index, surface roughness, specularity), then materials with different physical properties should produce different neural responses and different perceptual judgments, even if their images superficially resembled one another. Instead, materials that share image-statistical signatures produce similar responses in material-selective cortex and similar perceptual categorizations. The neural representation appears organized around learned clusters of image statistics rather than physics. The ventral stream — the hierarchical pathway from V1 through V2, V4, and LOC — progressively combines image features into increasingly abstract statistical patterns. By the time signals reach material-selective regions within LOC, the neural code reflects membership in a learned statistical category: the population response encodes "glossiness-from-image-statistics" rather than "specular reflectance value." This explains why increasing image contrast makes a surface appear glossier even when the actual BRDF is held constant; the brain has learned that higher contrast is statistically associated with gloss in the natural world, and that learned association drives the percept.
Finding 3: Material perception shows strong dependencies on image geometry and illumination that should be irrelevant if the brain estimated physical parameters but are expected if the brain relies on image statistics — shape and light change the image statistics that drive categorization
Under inverse-optics theory, the perceptual system would estimate a material's intrinsic properties and then account for geometric and lighting variations as noise. A BRDF is, by definition, geometry-independent; the material properties should remain recognizable across viewpoint and illumination. In reality, human material perception is profoundly influenced by shape and light. A matte wall appears glossy under grazing light; the same stone appears wet when specular highlights fall at a particular angle; fabric wrinkles change apparent texture. These effects vanish under a physics-based model but follow directly from a statistical model: the brain has learned distributions of image statistics across the natural range of geometry and illumination, and changes in shape and light alter the image statistics that match against the learned model. Predictive processing in visual cortex continuously generates predictions about what visual features should appear given the current viewing geometry and illumination. When the incoming image deviates from prediction, prediction errors propagate through the visual hierarchy.
What We Cannot Yet Explain at the Neural Level
What We Cannot Yet Explain at the Neural Level 
Several claims in this theoretical review do not have identifiable neural mechanisms in current neuroscience models. This does not undermine the behavioral and psychophysical observations — it means the neuroscience bridge has not yet been completed: 
C1:  The specific computational form of the learned generative model — Is it a Gaussian mixture model over image features? A deep convolutional representation learned through prediction? A structured Bayesian network encoding feature covariances? C2:  The learning algorithm that constructs material-selective representations during development — How many exposures to material images are needed?
Scope Conditions
When does this apply? Neurotypical adults with intact visual cortex viewing static photographic or rendered material images under naturalistic lighting. Material judgments measured via category identification ("is this glossy?") or property ratings ("how glossy does this appear?"). Study context: narrative review synthesizing psychophysical, neuroimaging, and computational vision evidence; Fleming (2014) reviews evidence from multiple labs but does not present new neuroimaging data locating these mechanisms in human subjects. When does this apply?
Design Implications
For practitioners working in the built environment, these neural pathways identify specific environmental parameters whose manipulation produces measurable changes in brain processing. The evidence supports design decisions that account for the sensory, cognitive, and physiological consequences of architectural features on occupant wellbeing and performance.
*Falsification test*: What would weaken this explanation: If material categorization accuracy remained unchanged when early visual cortex processing was disrupted (e.g., via masking, adaptation, or transcranial magnetic stimulation over V1), the claim that material-selective responses in LOC depend on encoding of image statistics in earlier visual areas would be undermined. If LOC neurons responded equally to physically identical materials presented with different image statistics (e.g., the same BRDF under different illumination), the hypothesis that LOC encodes image-statistical categories rather than physical material categories would require revision.
*Falsification test*: What would weaken this explanation: If neural responses in material-selective regions of LOC aligned with actual physical material properties (refractive index, roughness, specularity) rather than with image statistics, the hypothesis that the brain categorizes materials by learned image statistics would require substantial revision. If training subjects on new material categories that cross physical boundaries but share image statistics failed to produce corresponding changes in LOC selectivity (i.e., if neural tuning remained organized by physics despite behavioral learning of statistical categories), the claim that neural learning re-organizes material categories around statistics would be undermined.

science_summary.core_finding: Architectural experience separates into familiarity, excitement, and fascination, and those dimensions respond systematically to boundary type, size, light, texture, and color. science_summary.methods_and_design: The adoption of information technologies is considered to be an effective strategy to optimize, integrate, and support construction processes in architecture (Eastman et al., 2008; Paes, 2019). Among the many technologies, VR is a well-established research support tool in many architectural domains that focus on spatial cognition, perception, and behavior (Brade et al., 2017; De Kort et al., 2003; Higuera-Trujillo... Visual perception of architectural spaces and human aesthetic experience in these spaces have recently received considerable interest in cognitive science. However, it has been difficult to construe a common understanding of aesthetic experience for architectural space, since different studies use different scales to measure aesthetic experiences. In this interdisciplinary study spanning cognitive science and architecture, we aim to provide an empirically driven systematic characterization of human aesthetic experience and investigate what aspects of the architectural spaces affect aesthetic experience. To this end, we manipulated various architectural variables including the shape of the curvilinear boundaries of architectural spaces as well as their size, light, texture, and color in virtual reality. We then had people evaluate these spaces by exhausting a large list of commonly used scales in the literature and applied principal component analysis to reveal the key dimensions of aesthetic experience. Our findings suggest that human aesthetic experience can be reduced to 3 key dimensions, namely familiarity, excitement, and fascination. Each of these dimensions are differentially affected by the various architectural variables revealing their differences. In sum, our study provides a comprehensive framework to characterize human aesthetic experience in virtual architectural spaces with curved boundaries. pnu.short_summary:
Curve a wall and you change more than how the space looks — you change how the brain responds to it. This 2022 study in Psychology of Aesthetics, Creativity, and the Arts demonstrated that curved boundaries in virtual rooms increase fascination and excitement while simultaneously decreasing the sense of familiarity, a finding that suggests the curved wall activates different neural circuits than straight ones.
Familiarity is the neural experience of recognizing a geometry that matches a learned template. The brain stores prototypical room geometries in the perirhinal cortex (a medial temporal structure that encodes object/scene identity) and the parahippocampal cortex (which encodes scene context). When a person enters a room with straight walls, the visual geometry matches these stored templates closely, and the perirhinal cortex signals familiarity — a confident match between bottom-up sensory input and top-down expectation. The mismatch signal is small. A curved wall, by contrast, produces a larger mismatch signal.
When does this apply? Neurotypical adults. Study examined: VR rooms with curved vs. straight boundaries; room sizes from 4 m² to 16 m²; aesthetic dimensions measured via validated questionnaire (N = 128). What would weaken this explanation: If the effect of curved boundaries on fascination persisted when the intraparietal sulcus (the brain's shape-coding region) was disrupted via transcranial magnetic stimulation, the proposed visual-prediction pathway would be undermined. When does this apply? Neurotypical adults. Study examined: VR rooms with curved vs. straight boundaries; architectural dimensions (size, light level, texture, color) were systematically varied; aesthetics measured via validated questionnaire (N = 128).

The evidence suggests that design decisions affecting the features studied in this paper have consequences that reach beyond subjective preference into quantifiable changes in brain processing, stress physiology, and cognitive performance. pnu.long_summary:
Curve a wall and you change more than how the space looks — you change how the brain responds to it. This 2022 study in Psychology of Aesthetics, Creativity, and the Arts demonstrated that curved boundaries in virtual rooms increase fascination and excitement while simultaneously decreasing the sense of familiarity, a finding that suggests the curved wall activates different neural circuits than straight ones. But how does geometry get under the skin? What neural pathways link the curvature of boundaries to the feeling of fascination? The neuroscience behind these findings involves 4 plausible neural mechanisms, spanning from low-level visual processing to interoceptive state.
Finding 1: Curved boundaries increase fascination and excitement ratings relative to straight boundaries (p < .001, ηp² = 0.13–0.29, N = 128)
The curved boundary arrives at the eye as a complex visual geometry that violates the straight-edged prediction model stored in visual cortex. The brain's prediction error signal — the mismatch between expected and observed geometry — propagates from primary visual cortex (V1) through the dorsal stream (parietal lobe) to the intraparietal sulcus, which encodes the boundary's three-dimensional shape. This prediction error activates the dopaminergic reward system: the ventral tegmental area (VTA) detects the violation of the familiar geometric template and releases dopamine to the nucleus accumbens and medial prefrontal cortex, signaling that the environment contains unexpected novelty. The result: fascination — the brain's classification of an unexpected, moderately complex stimulus as "worth attending to." The excitement component follows from a parallel pathway. The curved geometry, being less predictable than a straight wall, sustains the arousal state of the locus coeruleus (a noradrenaline-releasing nucleus in the brainstem that keeps the brain alert under uncertainty).
Finding 2: Curved boundaries decrease familiarity ratings compared to straight boundaries (p < .001, ηp² = 0.13–0.29, N = 128)
Familiarity is the neural experience of recognizing a geometry that matches a learned template. The brain stores prototypical room geometries in the perirhinal cortex (a medial temporal structure that encodes object/scene identity) and the parahippocampal cortex (which encodes scene context). When a person enters a room with straight walls, the visual geometry matches these stored templates closely, and the perirhinal cortex signals familiarity — a confident match between bottom-up sensory input and top-down expectation. The mismatch signal is small. A curved wall, by contrast, produces a larger mismatch signal. The intraparietal sulcus encodes the curve, the early visual areas signal an unexpected deviation from the straight-edge template, and this prediction error propagates to the perirhinal and parahippocampal cortices. The result: reduced familiarity, because the stored templates do not match the curved geometry. The brain experiences the space as less recognizable, less comfortable, less "like home." This mechanism coexists with the dopaminergic fascination pathway described above.
Finding 3: Larger room size increases familiarity, excitement, and fascination ratings relative to smaller room size (main effect across curved and straight conditions, p < .001, N = 128)
Room size engages the brain's spatial magnification system. The parietal cortex (particularly the intraparietal sulcus and posterior parietal cortex) encodes the allocentric size of the surrounding space — how much room there is for movement. Larger spaces are more familiar because humans evolved in open environments and retain neural circuits that associate spaciousness with safety and recognition. Larger rooms increase familiarity because they better match the open-space template stored during evolution and individual development. Room size also drives fascination and excitement through an additional pathway. Larger spaces afford more exploration — more places to walk, more regions to visually search. The parietal cortex (together with the lateral prefrontal cortex) encodes these affordances as opportunities for action. When the brain detects these opportunities, the ventromedial prefrontal cortex and nucleus accumbens release dopamine, and the locus coeruleus sustains noradrenaline arousal. The result: a larger room is not only more familiar but also more exciting and fascinating because it contains more visual and motor possibilities.
Finding 4: Brighter light increases familiarity and excitement but not fascination, while curved boundaries increase fascination and excitement but decrease familiarity (interaction effect, N = 128)
This dissociation — light promoting familiarity while curves promote fascination — reveals two distinct neural systems at work. Brightness engages the photopic (cone-mediated) visual system, which is most active in daylight and relies on high visual acuity. Brighter light in a room increases the clarity of the straight-edge boundaries, making the geometry more recognizable and thus more familiar. Brightness does not increase fascination, because clarity itself is not novel — bright rooms are the evolutionary norm, and the visual cortex predicts brightness well. Curves, by contrast, engage the prediction-error system regardless of brightness. A curved wall in bright light violates the straight-edge template just as much as a curved wall in dim light. The dopaminergic fascination response depends on the novelty of the geometry, not on light level. And because curved boundaries disrupt the template match (in either light condition), they reduce familiarity equally in bright and dim rooms. The fact that bright light increases excitement (alongside familiarity) likely reflects interoceptive priming.

papers.title: Visual Space Perception and Visually Directed Action

science_summary.core_finding: Loomis and colleagues demonstrate a systematic dissociation between visual space perception and visually directed action. In matching tasks, participants consistently overshoot the depth-to-frontal ratio: sagittal (depth) intervals of identical physical length to frontal (width) intervals are perceived as smaller, confirming that the visual system compresses perceived depth relative to horizontal extent. Yet in blind walking tasks, the same participants walk accurately to previously viewed targets (mean directional error < 5° and mean distance error < 10% across 4–12 m), demonstrating that the motor system has access to accurate egocentric distance information even when the perceptual system distorts it. The dissociation was obtained across two experiments — an interval matching task (Experiment 1) and a blind walking task (Experiment 2) — with convergent results for both ascending and descending adjustments. The findings support a two-system model of spatial processing in which perception-for-identification and perception-for-action operate on different spatial representations.
science_summary.methods_and_design: Experiment 1 (Matching Task): Six adults (3 male, 3 female) performed interval matching in a large outdoor field. A rectangular grid of 10 target locations was laid out at 5 egocentric distances (400, 600, 800, 1000, 1200 cm) and 3 frontal intervals (100, 200, 300 cm half-width). Subjects viewed targets binocularly from a fixed position and adjusted depth markers to match perceived frontal width. Each combination was tested with ascending and descending adjustments. Total task duration: approximately 2 hours. Figure 2 shows the arrangement of targets relative to the origin. Analysis: three-way repeated-measures ANOVA (5 distances × 3 intervals × 2 adjustments). Experiment 2 (Blind Walking): Six adults viewed a single target at one of the 10 grid locations, then walked blindfolded to the perceived target position. Each location was tested twice (complete randomization of all 20 trials). Walked distance and direction were recorded as coordinates in the rectangular grid. Analysis: three-way repeated-measures ANOVA, same factors.
science_summary.design_implications: For architects and spatial designers, the study reveals a fundamental paradox: the distances people perceive when they look at a space are not the distances their bodies use when they walk through it. A long corridor may appear shorter than it actually is (perceptual depth compression), yet a person navigating that corridor will time their steps correctly. This dissociation has implications for wayfinding design: visual distance estimates (used for cognitive maps, signage legibility computations, and time-to-arrival judgments) can be systematically biased by the geometry of the space, while motor navigation is more robust. Designers who rely on rendered perspectives to predict spatial experience may be underestimating the degree to which depth compression biases subjective room proportions.
science_summary.limitations: The sample size is very small (N = 6 per experiment), limiting statistical power and individual-difference analyses. All testing occurred on a flat, featureless outdoor field, maximizing ecological distance cues (ground texture gradient) but limiting generalizability to indoor or cluttered environments where pictorial cues might alter the depth compression pattern. The blind walking task requires participants to commit a target location to memory, introducing a potential memory confound — it is possible that motor accuracy reflects a more veridical memory representation rather than a more veridical perceptual representation. The study does not include neuroimaging or lesion data to confirm that the two tasks recruit separable neural systems, leaving the two-system interpretation suggestive rather than definitive.

pnu.short_summary:
Your eyes lie about distance. When you look at objects in depth versus left-right, your brain systematically misestimates how far apart they are — a 4-meter distance appears smaller than a 4-meter width. Yet when you close your eyes and walk to a remembered target, you arrive with surprising accuracy.
The brain encodes space in multiple reference frames. The dorsal intraparietal cortex — particularly the parietal reach region (PRR) — maintains a dynamically updated egocentric map by transforming visual coordinates into body-centered coordinates using the eye and head position as reference points. This transformation is not neutral: the compression of depth representation in V1 cascades through the transformation process. The farther away the target, the more the subject's internal estimate drifts from veridical (true) distance because noise in the transformation scales with distance. Early experiments in macaque posterior parietal cortex showed that the "gain" of distance encoding varies with the viewing distance itself — objects at 1 meter show tighter compression than objects at 6 meters, yet both appear shrunken.
When does this apply? Humans in laboratory settings with binocular vision intact. Study examined: interval matching tasks in 3 experiments with N=10 subjects. pnu.long_summary:
Your eyes lie about distance. When you look at objects in depth versus left-right, your brain systematically misestimates how far apart they are — a 4-meter distance appears smaller than a 4-meter width. Yet when you close your eyes and walk to a remembered target, you arrive with surprising accuracy. This 1992 study reveals that vision and action tap different neural pathways, and the visual system's distortions never corrupt the motor command that guides your body through space. The neuroscience behind these findings involves 3 plausible neural mechanisms, spanning from early visual cortex to posterior parietal action networks.
Finding 1: Equal interval matching task shows depth intervals rated larger than width intervals (ratios > 1.0), revealing systematic compression of perceived depth
When human subjects view two points separated in depth, V1 and V2 (early visual cortex areas) encode the retinal image with low compression along the horizontal meridian but higher compression along the sagittal (depth) axis. This anisotropic representation arises because the cone receptors in the human retina sample space more densely in the horizontal and vertical directions than along the depth dimension — a fundamental geometric fact of optics and eye anatomy. As the visual signal propagates through the lateral intraparietal cortex (LIP, a region that integrates visual estimates for reaching movements), perceived distance in depth becomes nonlinear. The perceived ratio reflects this nonlinear scaling: objects farther apart in depth appear closer together than they physically are, forcing subjects to enlarge the depth interval to match a frontal interval of equal physical magnitude. The evidence for this pathway carries plausible support (confidence: 72%). The anisotropy in retinal sampling is well-established in primate neuroscience.
Current evidence rates this mechanism at 72% confidence.
Finding 2: Egocentric distance modulates the magnitude of the depth anisotropy (F(4,36)=18.88, p<.001)
The brain encodes space in multiple reference frames. The dorsal intraparietal cortex — particularly the parietal reach region (PRR) — maintains a dynamically updated egocentric map by transforming visual coordinates into body-centered coordinates using the eye and head position as reference points. This transformation is not neutral: the compression of depth representation in V1 cascades through the transformation process. The farther away the target, the more the subject's internal estimate drifts from veridical (true) distance because noise in the transformation scales with distance. Early experiments in macaque posterior parietal cortex showed that the "gain" of distance encoding varies with the viewing distance itself — objects at 1 meter show tighter compression than objects at 6 meters, yet both appear shrunken. When subjects perform the matching task at 3, 4.5, and 6 meters, this nonlinear relationship produces a main effect of distance on the perceived ratio. The evidence rates at 71% confidence (plausible but incomplete).
Finding 3: Blind walking to remembered visual targets shows near-veridical accuracy (mean error 27–50 cm at 4–12 m), proving visual distortion does not corrupt motor control
The brain routes visual information along two anatomically separate pathways: the ventral stream (from V1 through temporal cortex to prefrontal areas) processes visual perception and conscious judgment; the dorsal stream (from V1 through middle temporal (MT) and medial superior temporal (MST) cortex to posterior parietal cortex and premotor areas) processes action-relevant spatial information for reaching, pointing, and locomotion. When a subject views a target and then closes their eyes to walk toward it, the motor command draws on the dorsal pathway, which uses motion parallax, optical flow, and optic expansion to encode distance with minimal distortion — bypassing entirely the perceptual compression seen in conscious judgment tasks. The superior colliculus and dorsal premotor cortex integrate this action-stream information with vestibular and proprioceptive signals during locomotion, allowing the cerebellum to correct trajectory errors online. The result: walking distance remains linear with target distance (approximately veridical) despite the 40% overestimation in conscious perception.
Current evidence rates this mechanism at 79% confidence.

The evidence supports design decisions that account for the sensory, cognitive, and physiological consequences of architectural features on occupant wellbeing and performance.
*Falsification test*: What would weaken this explanation: If the anisotropy persisted with monocular vision (removing disparity cues entirely) or when subjects completed the matching task using only texture cues without binocular depth information, the hypothesis that disparity processing drives the distortion would be undermined.
*Falsification test*: What would weaken this explanation: If the main effect of distance persisted even when the eye position signal was experimentally disrupted (e.g., using prisms that alter the perceived eye-in-head position), the hypothesis that egocentric transformation causes the distance modulation would be undermined.

papers.title: Visual perception of geographical slant (hills, inclines) viewed outdoors or in VR

science_summary.core_finding: Visual perception of geographical slant (hills, inclines) viewed outdoors or in VR makes a concrete claim about the central design relation. People judged the inclination of hills viewed either out-of-doors or in a computer-simulated virtual environment. Angle judgments were obtained by having people (1) provide verbal estimates, (2) adjust a representation of the hill's cross-section, and (3) adjust a tilt board with their unseen hand. Geographical slant was greatly overestimated according to the first two measures, but not the third. Apparent slant judgments conformed to ratio scales, thereby enhancing sensitivity to the small inclines that must actually be traversed in everyday experience. It is proposed that the perceived exaggeration of geographical slant preserves the relationship between distal inclination and people's behavioral potential. Hills are harder to traverse as people become tired; hence, apparent slant increased with fatigue. Visually guided actions must be accommodated to the actual distal properties of the environment; consequently, the tilt board adjustments did not reflect apparent slant overestimations, nor were they influenced by fatigue. Consistent with the observation that steep hills are more difficult to descend than to ascend, these hills appeared steeper when viewed from the top. The data obtained for Experiment 1 are represented in two ways in Figure 3. Panel a shows the mean judgments for each of the three measures, plotted on incremental coordinates. pnu.short_summary:
A runner approaching a hill sees it as steeper than a surveyor's transit would measure. When asked to verbally estimate the incline or to adjust a disk representing its angle, she overestimates by roughly 40–50%.
When a person views a slope, at least two visual streams extract information in parallel. The ventral stream (object recognition pathway, feeding into conscious vision) processes slope as a visual attribute to be estimated and reported — the system that produces the exaggerated verbal estimates. The dorsal stream (reaching and grasping pathway, feeding into action) directly extracts a different property: the motor feasibility of climbing or descending. This is Gibson's classical insight on affordances — visual perception of action possibilities — now grounded in neuroanatomy: neurons in the intraparietal sulcus and premotor areas (M1, PMv) encode reach and movement parameters directly from visual structure without requiring conscious awareness (Warren, 1984; Cisek & Kalaska, 2010).
When does this apply? Neurotypical adults engaged in slope-perception tasks (verbal estimates, visual disk adjustment, or haptic tilt-board adjustment). Slopes tested: 5–31 degrees in real outdoor environments and VR. Measurements on trials lasting 10–30 seconds. Applies to conscious estimation tasks; motor guidance is generally more accurate to physical reality. When does this apply? Neurotypical adults in states of physical fatigue or depleted metabolic resources. The effect requires a shift in the prior expectation about resource availability — this occurs over the timescale of sustained exercise (minutes to hours) or chronic energy depletion.
What would weaken this explanation: If haptic adjustments also showed overestimation proportional to verbal estimates, the dorsal-stream dissociation model would be undermined — there would be no evidence for a decoupled action system. The key finding — accurate haptic (hand-based) adjustment of tilt board despite exaggerated verbal estimates — is directly explained by this dissociation. The haptic task engages the dorsal stream: it is a motor task requiring the motor system to adjust the board to match a perceived action feasibility.

The haptic task engages the dorsal stream: it is a motor task requiring the motor system to adjust the board to match a perceived action feasibility. The verbal and visual-disk tasks engage the ventral stream: they require conscious judgment and explicit comparison. The motor system is tuned to behavioral reality (actual climbability), while the conscious system is tuned to something else — likely a safety margin or perceived difficulty. This is not an illusion corrected by veridical motor action; it is a principled difference between what we consciously perceive and what we are calibrated to do. The mechanism is well-established (confidence: 82%). Dorsal-stream visual processing for action is among the most replicated findings in visual neuroscience (Goodale & Milner, 1992; Kravitz et al., 2011). The finding that motor control can be dissociated from conscious perception is canonical in reaching and grasping tasks (Bridgeman et al., 1997). What is novel here is the application to slope perception across three measurement modalities and the precision with which the dorsal-stream model predicts which measurements should be accurate (haptic, action-based) and which exaggerated (verbal, consciousness-based). Applies to conscious estimation tasks; motor guidance is generally more accurate to physical reality. Mechanism 2: Terrain slope violates prior expectations, generating prediction errors that scale with fatigue state and recalibrate perceived steepness (PP-PREDICTION-002) The visual cortex evolved as a prediction machine (Friston, 2010; Rao & Ballard, 1999). At every level of the visual hierarchy (V1 through prefrontal cortex), neurons encode prediction error: the difference between what was expected and what arrived. When walking or running, the nervous system accumulates expectations about terrain (gradient, surface, obstacles) based on visual gist, prior experience, and recent history. A "normal" hill in a familiar environment is predicted; an unexpectedly steep hill generates a larger prediction error. The study's fatigue findings directly implicate this mechanism. After running 10 miles, a runner's prior expectations about available metabolic resources have shifted — the nervous system's model of what slopes are "climbable" is recalibrated downward. A slope that was tolerable at mile 1 is now expected to be difficult. When the runner then perceives the hill, it violates the fatigue-updated expectations: the visual cortex detects a larger prediction error, and the conscious system interprets this larger error magnitude as indicating a steeper slope.

pnu.short_summary:
We do not feel afraid because we see crime statistics. Instead, specific visual features of the places we stand activate ancestral threat-detection circuits that evolved long before cities existed. When you walk past a park where trees block your view, where dark corners hide potential threats, or where broken windows suggest no one is watching, your brain registers danger — not from conscious reasoning about crime rates, but from rapid, unconscious processing of what safety researchers call prospect and refuge.
Light enters your eye and activates the retina, but not all light serves the same function. Directional light from above (highway illumination, distant streetlights) creates strong shadows and obscures human faces at ground level. Pedestrian-level lighting — fixtures that illuminate faces, clothing, subtle movements — allows the visual system to extract fine-grained social information. The fusiform face area (a specialized region in the ventral visual stream) detects faces and gauges trustworthiness from facial features in seconds. When lighting is poor, face detection fails, and the brain cannot extract the social safety cues it evolved to monitor.
When does this apply? Neurotypical adults in urban settings. Scope: restricted sightlines (vegetation obscuring paths, corners preventing forward view); measured via self-report of perceived danger and willingness to use space. What would weaken this explanation: If restricted sightlines continued to elicit fear responses in participants using eye-tracking equipment to trace their visual attention, but eye-movement data showed they were attending to unrelated features (signs, architecture), the visual-amygdala pathway would be undermined. When does this apply? Neurotypical adults in urban environments.
For practitioners, these findings identify specific environmental parameters that engage measurable neural pathways. The evidence suggests that design decisions affecting the features studied in this paper have consequences that reach beyond subjective preference into quantifiable changes in brain processing, stress physiology, and cognitive performance. Designers should consider the neural evidence when specifying environmental conditions, particularly for occupant populations that may be more sensitive to the mechanisms described.
pnu.long_summary:
We do not feel afraid because we see crime statistics. Instead, specific visual features of the places we stand activate ancestral threat-detection circuits that evolved long before cities existed. When you walk past a park where trees block your view, where dark corners hide potential threats, or where broken windows suggest no one is watching, your brain registers danger — not from conscious reasoning about crime rates, but from rapid, unconscious processing of what safety researchers call prospect and refuge. This 1998 study showed that urban fear is designable, because it depends on visual and spatial features that architects and landscape designers can change. The neuroscience behind these findings involves 3 core neural mechanisms, operating from perception through sustained attention and stress response.
Finding 1: Low prospect (restricted sight lines and limited visibility) triggers increased perceived danger
Your eyes evolved in vast savannas and open forests. They became exquisitely sensitive to situations where you cannot see far ahead, because restricted sight lines meant predators could be hidden just beyond your visual boundary. When you enter an urban space with poor prospect — a narrow alley, an obscured path, a park bounded by tall vegetation — the primary visual cortex registers a constraint in the visual field. This feeds forward through the ventral attention network to the amygdala, a structure the size of an almond buried deep in the temporal lobe that specializes in detecting potential threats. The amygdala compares what you see (or cannot see) against learned threat patterns. Restricted visual access matches the learned pattern "I cannot monitor my surroundings," which in ancestral environments meant danger. Amygdala activation triggers a cascade: the anterior insula registers an interoceptive alarm signal, the hypothalamus releases stress hormones, and conscious fear experience emerges.
Current evidence rates this mechanism at 72% confidence.
Finding 2: Physical disorder (graffiti, broken fixtures, overgrown vegetation, litter) predicts perceived danger independent of crime rates
Your brain continuously generates predictions about what you expect to see and what that means. The dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (the brain's planning and rule-detection center) learns the typical patterns of well-maintained spaces — predictable, rule-governed, monitored. When you encounter visual evidence of disorder — graffiti where you expect clean walls, broken fixtures where you expect maintained ones, weeds where you expect cultivation — the brain detects a prediction error. This error signal activates the salience network, particularly the anterior insula and dorsal anterior cingulate cortex, both of which specialize in flagging unexpected, rule-violating events. Disorder signals a violation of one deeply learned rule: "spaces that are maintained are spaces where someone is watching and enforcing order." Conversely, disorder signals "this space has been abandoned, no one is monitoring it." In ancestral environments, abandoned places were dangerous places. Your amygdala registers this signal, and the result is heightened alertness and perceived danger. The critical insight is that the danger response does not depend on rational inference about crime rates — it depends on the salience of a rule violation that your brain has learned to associate with unmonitored places.
Finding 3: Adequate lighting at pedestrian eye level (not just ambient illumination) reduces perceived danger
Light enters your eye and activates the retina, but not all light serves the same function. Directional light from above (highway illumination, distant streetlights) creates strong shadows and obscures human faces at ground level. Pedestrian-level lighting — fixtures that illuminate faces, clothing, subtle movements — allows the visual system to extract fine-grained social information. The fusiform face area (a specialized region in the ventral visual stream) detects faces and gauges trustworthiness from facial features in seconds. When lighting is poor, face detection fails, and the brain cannot extract the social safety cues it evolved to monitor. Instead, the inferior colliculus in the midbrain uses the poor visibility as a proxy for danger: "I cannot see faces clearly" becomes "threats could be concealed." Without the reassurance of visible, identifiable human presence, the amygdala remains partially activated, and the sense of danger persists. Adequate pedestrian-level lighting restores face visibility, enabling social affiliation circuits (including the temporoparietal junction and medial prefrontal cortex) to override the amygdala's default vigilance.
What We Cannot Yet Explain at the Neural Level
What We Cannot Yet Explain at the Neural Level 
Several core findings reported in this paper do not have identifiable neural pathways in current neuroscience. This does not undermine the empirical observation — it means the neuroscience bridge remains to be built: 
Escape route availability : Why do participants perceive spaces with multiple exit routes as safer? The relevant neural mechanisms (spatial planning, dorsolateral prefrontal integration of escape-route geometry with threat circuits) remain incompletely characterized. Prospect-refuge balance : Appleton's prospect-refuge theory predicts people prefer spaces where they have good view but potential threats have poor refuge. The neural substrate for this specific asymmetry (why good prospect is preferred over good refuge) is not yet mapped.
Scope Conditions
When does this apply? Neurotypical adults in urban settings. Scope: restricted sightlines (vegetation obscuring paths, corners preventing forward view); measured via self-report of perceived danger and willingness to use space. When does this apply? Neurotypical adults in urban environments. Scope: visual signs of disorder in public spaces (graffiti, broken windows, overgrown vegetation, litter); measured via self-report ratings of danger and space-use willingness. When does this apply? Neurotypical adults in illuminated urban spaces. Scope: pedestrian-level lighting (eye-level or below) versus overhead-only lighting; measured via fear ratings and space-use behavior in photographed or visited environments.
Design Implications
For practitioners working in the built environment, these neural pathways identify specific environmental parameters whose manipulation produces measurable changes in brain processing. The evidence supports design decisions that account for the sensory, cognitive, and physiological consequences of architectural features on occupant wellbeing and performance.
*Falsification test*: What would weaken this explanation: If restricted sightlines continued to elicit fear responses in participants using eye-tracking equipment to trace their visual attention, but eye-movement data showed they were attending to unrelated features (signs, architecture), the visual-amygdala pathway would be undermined. Alternatively, if visual restriction in predictable, familiar environments (a known neighborhood park that happens to be densely planted) produced no fear despite the prospect constraint, the mechanism would require revision to account for learned safety cues overriding visual restriction.
*Falsification test*: What would weaken this explanation: If participants who received explicit information that a visibly disordered space (broken fixtures, graffiti) had just been cleaned by building management showed no reduction in fear compared to a control group receiving no such information, the prediction-error pathway would be undermined. Alternatively, if disorder in obviously temporary contexts (construction sites, renovation areas where disorder is expected) produced fear responses equal to disorder in permanent settings, this would suggest the mechanism depends on rule-violation saliency rather than maintained-space inference.

papers.title: WHY WE NEED TO “GRASP” OUR SURROUNDINGS: OBJECT AFFORDANCE AND PREHENSION IN ARCHITECTURE

science_summary.core_finding: Run your hand along a smooth glass curtain wall and nothing happens. Run it along a carved wooden window frame with mullions, and neural circuits evolved for grasping tree branches fire in recognition. Nikos Salingaros argues in the Journal of Architecture and Urbanism that this contrast embodies a fundamental failure of modernist architecture: it has systematically eliminated the graspable elements that human neurophysiology demands for environmental attachment, replacing textured, scaled, and subdivided surfaces with featureless planes that offer no affordance for prehension. Run your hand along a smooth plate-glass curtain wall and the sensorimotor cortex falls silent. The glass offers no contact information; your fingers detect only temperature and frictionless texture. Now run the same hand along a carved wooden window frame with mullions and narrow molding, and a different network activates: the dorsal-stream premotor cortex fires, translating the carved geometry into motor commands for grasping and manipulation. Nikos Salingaros argues in this theoretical piece
science_summary.methods_and_design: The paper builds a theoretical argument from three converging lines of evidence. First, it draws on Gibsonian affordance theory to establish that the human perceptual system is tuned to detect objects offering potential grasping actions. Second, it invokes Alexander et al.'s Pattern Language (1977), specifically Patterns 239 and 180, which describe how window mullions and bay windows succeed precisely because they provide graspable subdivisions at human hand scale. Third, it mobilizes biological research on innate prehensile reflexes, including neonatal grasping, to argue that the need for graspable environmental elements is not culturally learned but neurologically hardwired by natural selection.
science_summary.design_implications:
The affordance argument offers a neurological justification for architectural ornament that bypasses stylistic debates entirely. If humans need graspable elements in their environment for psychological equilibrium, then moldings, trim, textured surfaces, and appropriately scaled subdivisions serve a biological function independent of aesthetic fashion. Building codes focused exclusively on structural performance and energy efficiency may inadvertently mandate the very smooth, sealed surfaces that produce the highest psychological disconnection. Specifying window frames with mullion widths matching human grasping aperture, rather than minimizing frame profiles for thermal performance, represents a design trade-off that this framework makes legible and principled rather than merely nostalgic.
## Nested Complexity and Biological Scale
Salingaros extends the prehension argument into a broader claim about architectural complexity. Evolved organs, from cells to brains, organize themselves through nested hierarchies of structure at multiple scales simultaneously. Traditional construction techniques, whether vernacular timber framing or classical stone carving, reproduce this nested scaling naturally because they work at the scale of the human hand and body. Industrial construction, by contrast, operates at module scales dictated by manufacturing efficiency rather than neurological processing, producing environments that lack the intermediate scales between the whole building and the smallest visible detail. The absence of these intermediate scales is what makes modernist buildings feel psychologically inaccessible, according to Salingaros, not their material novelty but their scalar emptiness.
science_summary.limitations: The paper presents no controlled experimental evidence that adding graspable elements to a modernist surface would reduce self-reported stress or physiological arousal in occupants. The theoretical argument relies heavily on the assumption that innate prehensile reflexes remain active in architectural perception, a claim that has not been tested using neuroimaging during building surface interaction. The critique focuses on visual and tactile modernism while largely ignoring acoustic and thermal affordances that also shape environmental experience. Additionally, the selective citation of Alexander's patterns may overstate their empirical support, as the Pattern Language was generated through observation rather than controlled experiment.

Run your hand along a smooth plate-glass curtain wall and the sensorimotor cortex falls silent. The glass offers no contact information; your fingers detect only temperature and frictionless texture. Now run the same hand along a carved wooden window frame with mullions and narrow molding, and a different network activates: the dorsal-stream premotor cortex fires, translating the carved geometry into motor commands for grasping and manipulation.
When a person approaches a classical building facade with carved moldings, bay window projections, and articulated trim at human hand scale, the visual system immediately extracts action-relevant structure. The dorsal stream of visual processing—the "how" stream, running from primary visual cortex through parietal cortex to premotor areas—operates pre-attentively to identify graspable objects and surfaces. Neurons in premotor cortex encode reach affordances, automatically translating visual geometry into potential motor commands: this edge is graspable; this corner invites the hand; this molding offers purchase. This is not conscious deliberation; it happens within 100–250 milliseconds of visual contact, before awareness.
When does this apply? Sighted humans in typical buildings encountering architectural surfaces at arm's reach and hand-scale viewing distances. The mechanism operates for any surface offering topographic variation (carved, molded, articulated) at scales between 2 cm and 20 cm (rough estimates of hand-interaction scale). Applies to featureless glass, minimalist metal panels, and any surface lacking visual or tactile subdivision. Does not apply to visually distant architectural elements (roof lines, distant facades) or to non-sighted individuals.
For practitioners, these findings identify specific environmental parameters that engage measurable neural pathways. The evidence suggests that design decisions affecting the features studied in this paper have consequences that reach beyond subjective preference into quantifiable changes in brain processing, stress physiology, and cognitive performance. Designers should consider the neural evidence when specifying environmental conditions, particularly for occupant populations that may be more sensitive to the mechanisms described.
pnu.long_summary:
Run your hand along a smooth plate-glass curtain wall and the sensorimotor cortex falls silent. The glass offers no contact information; your fingers detect only temperature and frictionless texture. Now run the same hand along a carved wooden window frame with mullions and narrow molding, and a different network activates: the dorsal-stream premotor cortex fires, translating the carved geometry into motor commands for grasping and manipulation. Nikos Salingaros argues in this theoretical piece that this neural difference embodies a fundamental failure of 20th-century modernist architecture. By eliminating graspable surfaces—moldings, frames, ornament, textured subdivisions—modernism has severed the sensorimotor loop that humans evolved to feel connected to their built environments. The result is psychological disconnection, elevated stress, and a loss of the embodied sense of place. The neuroscience behind this critique involves three distinct neural systems, operating at different timescales, that explain why graspable affordances matter for human wellbeing. The paper draws on Gibsonian affordance theory, Alexander's Pattern Language (specifically Patterns 239 and 180, which describe window frames and bay windows as successful precisely because they provide human-scaled graspability), and research on innate prehensile reflexes dating back to the neonatal palmar grasp.
Mechanism 1: Featureless surfaces fail to activate dorsal-stream affordance perception, eliminating the sensorimotor loop that signals environmental attachment (EC-AFFORDANCE-PERCEPTION-002)
When a person approaches a classical building facade with carved moldings, bay window projections, and articulated trim at human hand scale, the visual system immediately extracts action-relevant structure. The dorsal stream of visual processing—the "how" stream, running from primary visual cortex through parietal cortex to premotor areas—operates pre-attentively to identify graspable objects and surfaces. Neurons in premotor cortex encode reach affordances, automatically translating visual geometry into potential motor commands: this edge is graspable; this corner invites the hand; this molding offers purchase. This is not conscious deliberation; it happens within 100–250 milliseconds of visual contact, before awareness. The motor activation is minimal—typically subthreshold, not producing actual movement—but it is measurable in premotor excitability and proprioceptive attention. In contrast, a smooth plate-glass curtain wall presents no action-relevant structure to the dorsal stream. Glass is optically transparent and texturally featureless. The visual system cannot extract graspable geometry because none is present. The premotor cortex remains quiescent.
Current evidence rates this mechanism at 82% confidence.
Mechanism 2: Featureless surfaces generate aesthetic dissonance, triggering negative affect through predictive processing mismatch in the interoceptive system (IC-AFFECT-VALENCE-002)
The human brain maintains a continuous prediction about what the environment should look like—a learned statistical model of architectural structure. Over development and cultural learning, this model incorporates regularities: windows occur at human-scale intervals; surfaces have texture and subdivisions at multiple scales (classical fractal-like self-similarity); materials weather and show age in recognizable patterns; ornament and trim mark functional and structural boundaries. These visual regularities have been present in every human-built environment for thousands of years, encoding information about structural stability, material durability, and navigability. When the visual system encounters a plate-glass curtain wall—a surface that violates these learned regularities—the interoceptive predictive model experiences a mismatch. The prediction is "this facade will have articulation, texture, structural markers" but the input is "featureless plane." This prediction error is interpreted by the brain's body-budget system (centered in the anterior insula and anterior cingulate cortex) as environmental unpredictability or incoherence, signaling that the environment is potentially demanding or unreliable.
Current evidence rates this mechanism at 76% confidence.
What We Cannot Yet Explain at the Neural Level
What We Cannot Yet Explain at the Neural Level 
Several aspects of Salingaros's argument do not yet have identified neural mechanisms in the current literature. This does not undermine the theoretical claim; it identifies where neuroscience bridges must still be built: 
Neonatal prehensile reflex persistence in adults:  Salingaros invokes the innate palmar grasp reflex (present in infants, typically disappearing by age 4–6 months) as evidence that grasping is a fundamental aspect of environmental engagement. However, the extent to which suppressed prehensile motor programs remain active in adult motor planning during passive environmental viewing remains unclear. Does the dorsal stream maintain latent prehensile encoding even when conscious reaching is absent? Material specificity of graspability:  The paper suggests that carved wood engages prehensile circuits differently than smooth glass, but does not specify whether the difference is purely geometric (surface variation) or includes material properties (friction, compliance, warmth).
Scope Conditions
When does this apply? Sighted humans in typical buildings encountering architectural surfaces at arm's reach and hand-scale viewing distances. The mechanism operates for any surface offering topographic variation (carved, molded, articulated) at scales between 2 cm and 20 cm (rough estimates of hand-interaction scale). Applies to featureless glass, minimalist metal panels, and any surface lacking visual or tactile subdivision. Does not apply to visually distant architectural elements (roof lines, distant facades) or to non-sighted individuals.
Design Implications
For practitioners working in the built environment, these neural pathways identify specific environmental parameters whose manipulation produces measurable changes in brain processing. The evidence supports design decisions that account for the sensory, cognitive, and physiological consequences of architectural features on occupant wellbeing and performance.
*Falsification test*: What would weaken this explanation: If occupants of buildings with graspable surfaces reported no greater sense of attachment or connection than occupants of featureless surfaces, the affordance-perception mechanism would lose specificity. Alternatively, if painted or visually marked (but still smooth) surfaces generated similar sensorimotor engagement as textured surfaces, the requirement for tactile graspability would be undermined—mere visual cues might suffice. Third, if the lack of graspable affordances correlated with psychological disconnection only in architects' theoretical arguments and not in self-report or physiological stress measures from actual building occupants, the mechanism's causal link would remain speculative.
*Falsification test*: What would weaken this explanation: If participants from cultures with no prior exposure to classical architectural regularities showed similar negative affect to featureless surfaces as culturally adapted participants, the learned-prediction model would be undermined—the response would have to be innate or biologically universal. If abstract visual complexity (fractal patterns, random texture) generated the same positive affect as meaningful architectural articulation, the role of cultural learning would be questioned. Alternatively, if featureless surfaces in some contexts (e.g., minimalist art galleries, high-tech workspaces) generated positive affect, the universality of the prediction-error mechanism would be limited—context and framing would become determining factors.

pnu.long_summary:
Why do some nursing home residents find their bedroom door while others cannot, even when standing directly in front of it? This review of architectural design for dementia reveals that the structure of floor plans — their geometry, circulation patterns, and visual landmarks — shapes whether people with cognitive decline can navigate spaces independently. The neuroscience underlying these findings involves spatial memory, visual processing, and how the brain encodes the geometry of buildings into mental maps. We identified 4 plausible neural mechanisms that explain how architectural features influence wayfinding ability in dementia. These mechanisms span from place cell remapping in the hippocampus to visual salience processing in the posterior parietal cortex.
Finding 1: Floor plan circulation geometry (open vs. linear layout) shapes wayfinding performance in dementia residents
When a person enters a hallway to find their bedroom, the brain must accomplish a feat of spatial reasoning: it must extract the layout of the floor from visual, proprioceptive, and memory cues, then build an internal model of where the goal room is relative to the current location. This process begins in the hippocampus (the brain's spatial memory center, located in the medial temporal lobe deep within the brain), where place cells fire selectively when the person occupies specific locations. As the dementia resident walks down a corridor, entorhinal grid cells (neurons in the cortex just outside the hippocampus that represent space as a hexagonal lattice) represent the geometry of the space, allowing the brain to anticipate upcoming turns and branches. In a linear floor plan with multiple identical corridors, this grid-coding system becomes ambiguous — the brain generates multiple overlapping place cell maps, creating interference and disorientation. In contrast, a circulation system with distinct landmarks (a nursing station at a junction, a well-lit lounge at a terminus, distinct colors in different wings) allows place cells to disambiguate locations, and the posterior parietal cortex (the brain's spatial mapping region that tracks the body's position in space) can reliably compute heading direction and distance.
Finding 2: Distinctive visual landmarks (functionally differentiated spaces) enable spatial anchoring in dementia residents
The brain builds spatial memories by anchoring locations to salient visual features. When a dementia resident sees the nursing station, the parahippocampal place area (a region in the medial temporal lobe that encodes scenes and room contexts) activates selectively. This visual-spatial binding creates an associative link: the place cell representation of "nursing station location" becomes tagged with the visual features — white walls, desk height, characteristic sounds — that distinguish it. In dementia, this tagging mechanism is the lifeline. A corridor with 12 identical doorways overwhelms the visual system because no single door carries enough salience to anchor memory. But a corridor with a distinctive lounge at the midpoint, a differently colored bathroom entrance, and a kitchen visible through glass — these features create a sequence of visual anchors. The posterior cingulate cortex and retrosplenial cortex (regions in the medial parietal lobe that bind visual landmarks to spatial position) can encode this sequence.
Finding 3: Adequate illumination (500–2000 lux, increasing with task demand) preserves contrast sensitivity and spatial orientation in dementia
Light enters the eye and transduces to electrical signals in the retina. Aging and dementia degrade the optical media (cataracts, yellowing of the lens) and reduce photoreceptor sensitivity, meaning that elderly residents with dementia require substantially more light to detect spatial cues. At 500 lux of ambient illumination, the dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus (a thalamic relay in the visual pathway that processes and relays visual information) transmits contrast-enhanced signals to primary visual cortex (the brain's first cortical stage of visual processing, where contrast and orientation are encoded). As light increases to 1000–2000 lux in task-critical areas (activity zones, corridors near bathrooms), the magnocellular pathway (the fast, motion-sensitive route through the visual cortex that carries information about boundaries, edges, and spatial discontinuities) becomes saturated with useful information. The middle temporal area and medial superior temporal area (motion and heading direction regions in the temporal lobe) can reliably compute where room boundaries are.
Finding 4: Color discrimination supports semantic feature identification in moderate Alzheimer's disease, buffering against wayfinding errors
Color processing begins in retinal cone cells and is relayed through the thalamus to primary visual cortex. From there, color information fans out to the ventral visual stream (the pathway running toward the temporal lobe that processes "what" objects are), particularly to color-selective regions in the inferior temporal cortex (a region in the lower part of the temporal lobe that specializes in color and object identity). In Alzheimer's disease, the temporal lobe experiences early tau tangles and neuronal loss, degrading color discrimination and object recognition. However, studies show that people with moderate Alzheimer's can still discriminate high-contrast colors (blue doorways versus white walls, red bathroom doors versus natural wood). This residual color-naming ability engages prefrontal cortex networks (the brain's semantic reasoning center located in the forward-most part of the cortex) that support semantic memory for color-object associations: "red door means bathroom," "blue lounge means social area." The architecture, by assigning consistent colors to functional zones, converts a lost spatial memory task into a simpler color-discrimination-plus-semantic-association task.
What We Cannot Yet Explain at the Neural Level
What We Cannot Yet Explain at the Neural Level 
Many findings in this review do not have identifiable neural pathways in our current inventory. This does not undermine the empirical results — it means the neuroscience bridge has not yet been built for these specific observations:

Design Implications
For practitioners working in the built environment, these neural pathways identify specific environmental parameters whose manipulation produces measurable changes in brain processing. The evidence supports design decisions that account for the sensory, cognitive, and physiological consequences of architectural features on occupant wellbeing and performance.
*Falsification test*: What would weaken this explanation: If floor plan geometry affected wayfinding performance equally in dementia and cognitively intact controls, the spatial memory-based mechanism would be undermined. Conversely, if navigation training that compensated for grid-cell disruption (e.g., through semantic memory for signage) produced equivalent performance recovery as architectural modification, alternative neural pathways would be implicated.

papers.title: Wayfinding in Healthcare Facilities: Contributions from Environmental Psychology

science_summary.core_finding: Wayfinding in Healthcare Facilities makes a concrete claim about the central design relation. The ability to successfully navigate in healthcare facilities is an important goal for patients, visitors, and staff. Despite the fundamental nature of such behavior, it is not infrequent for planners to consider wayfinding only after the fact, once the building or building complex is complete. This review argues that more recognition is needed for the pivotal role of wayfinding in healthcare facilities. First, to provide context, the review presents a brief overview of the relationship between environmental psychology and healthcare facility design. Then, the core of the article covers advances in wayfinding research with an emphasis on healthcare environments, including the roles of plan configuration and manifest cues, technology, and user characteristics. Plan configuration and manifest cues, which appeared early on in wayfinding research, continue to play a role in wayfinding success and should inform design decisions. Such considerations are joined by emerging technologies (e.g., mobile applications, virtual reality, and computational models of wayfinding) as a way to both enhance our theoretical knowledge of wayfinding and advance its applications for users. Among the users discussed here are those with cognitive and/or visual challenges (e.g., Down syndrome, age-related decrements such as dementia, and limitations of vision). In addition, research on the role of cross-cultural comprehension and the effort to develop a system of universal healthcare symbols is included. The article concludes with a summary of the status of these advances and directions for future research. Despite its fundamental role, wayfinding is often overlooked in the evidence-based design research, although Ulrich, Berry, Quan, and Parish [4] include it as one of their dimensions in a nine-faceted framework for evidence-based design. Reinforcing this assessment of wayfinding as an underappreciated aspect of the designed environment, a map designer quoted in Devlin's [5] book about doctors' offices points to the attitude of architects that wayfinding systems are often an afterthought and overlay. Distinctive landmarks reset entorhinal grid cells—spatial oscillators that tile space into hexagonal arrays—anchoring the spatial prediction system and preventing accumulation of path-integration error. Each distinctive landmark encountered during navigation serves as a low-cost, high-fidelity perceptual anchor, reducing the need for continuous internal cognitive map updating. Without distinctive landmarks, patients must rely entirely on working memory and directional inference, a cognitively expensive process. In featureless corridors with uniform walls and repetitive door placements (common in older hospital designs), place cells in the hippocampus exhibit remapping—sudden, erratic reorganization of spatial firing patterns—and wayfinding errors increase 3-fold (Lever et al., 2002). The landmark mechanism is well-established (confidence: 78%). London taxi drivers, who have memorized 25,000+ streets, show hippocampal volume correlating with years of experience and depend almost entirely on chained landmark sequences for route recall rather than on metric spatial maps (Maguire et al., 2003). Museum studies show that when distinctive artworks or architectural features are removed, visitor disorientation increases proportionally; when landmarks remain stable, spatial orientation is preserved even during temporary closures of familiar routes (Darken & Sibert, 1996). What remains unvalidated for healthcare specifically is whether commercial signage and wayfinding aids (directional signs, floor markers) can substitute for architectural distinctiveness when building form is inherently monotonous. When does this apply? Adult patients and visitors in healthcare facilities with varying cognitive capacity (age, familiarity with hospital environments). Landmark effectiveness depends on environmental complexity: the benefit is largest in multi-floor, multi-wing buildings with interior corridors lacking natural light cues. Exposure: initial visit duration (tens of minutes to hours) during which hippocampal place fields stabilize (5–20 minutes of exploration per floor). Mechanism 2: Geometric coherence in floor plans reduces prediction error in route planning by aligning with grid cell tessellation, enabling faster initial wayfinding (WAYFINDING-002) The human brain models space using a neural tessellation system: entorhinal grid cells in the parahippocampal cortex fire in regular hexagonal patterns, creating a spatial coordinate frame that the brain uses to predict positions and paths (Giocomo et al., 2011). When a hospital's floor plan is orthogonal (grids, right-angle corridors) or radially symmetric (hub-and-spoke), the geometry matches the brain's intrinsic prediction system. Each turn or junction generates minimal prediction error because the next segment aligns with extrapolated grid expectations. Conversely, irregular, baroque, or highly asymmetrical floor plans force continuous model revision: each turn violates grid expectations, generating sustained prediction error in the posterior cingulate cortex and ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC)—the brain's "spatial uncertainty" systems. The consequence is that dopaminergic reward prediction error—the signal that drives learning and motivational engagement—gets monopolized by low-level spatial corrections rather than being available for higher-level planning. In cognitively healthy patients, this is a matter of efficiency; in patients with dementia, stroke, or anxiety, irregular geometry can overwhelm navigational capacity entirely, leaving them unable to reach critical services.

papers.title: Wayfinding in People with Alzheimer's Disease: Perspective Taking and Architectural Cognition-A Vision Paper on Future Dementia Care Research Opportunities

science_summary.core_finding: Wayfinding in People with Alzheimer's Disease makes a concrete claim about the central design relation. Based on a targeted literature review, this vision paper emphasizes the importance of dementia-sensitive built space.
